explanation.summary: Adjunctive corticosteroid in bacterial meningitis works by blunting the cytokine surge that follows bacterial lysis, which is why the timing of the first dose relative to the first antibiotic dose matters more than the total duration. The clearest benefit is a reduction in sensorineural hearing loss in Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis, with a smaller effect in pneumococcal disease, and the trials enrolled children beyond the neonatal period. Neonates are excluded because the blood brain barrier, immune response and dominant organisms all differ, and the available data show no benefit. The organisms that dominate this age group are group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli and Listeria monocytogenes, which is why empirical cover pairs a third generation cephalosporin with amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin. In context, the reasoning being tested is recognising an age boundary written into a recommendation rather than applying the paediatric default down to birth.
key_points: Dexamethasone is not recommended for bacterial meningitis under 1 month of age.
When used, it is given just before or with the first antibiotic dose.
The clearest benefit is reduced hearing loss in Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis.
Group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli and Listeria dominate neonatal meningitis.
Neonatal empirical cover pairs cefotaxime with amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin.
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone loses its benefit entirely if given more than about an hour after the first antibiotic dose, because the cytokine cascade it is meant to blunt has already been triggered by bacterial lysis.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

options.rationale: Adjunctive dexamethasone is not recommended in infants under 1 month because the trials that showed reduced hearing loss enrolled older children, and neonatal data show no benefit with a signal toward harm. Antibiotic therapy alone continues at meningitic dosing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

options.rationale: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg six-hourly for four days is the regimen for children over 1 month, started just before or with the first antibiotic dose to modify the inflammatory response. Both the age and the timing are wrong here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This alternative adult schedule has no paediatric evidence base and shares the same age and timing problems. Higher dosing does not rescue a regimen started after antibiotics are established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Hydrocortisone is used for adrenal insufficiency and for catecholamine resistant shock, not as an anti-inflammatory adjunct in meningitis. She is not shocked and has no features of adrenal insufficiency. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis)

Methylprednisolone has no role in bacterial meningitis at any age and is not interchangeable with dexamethasone, which was chosen in trials for its cerebrospinal fluid penetration and long half life. Its paediatric indications are inflammatory and autoimmune. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Treatment duration in bacterial meningitis is organism specific rather than age specific, and the neonatal gram negative group sits at the long end because sterilisation is slow and ventriculitis, infarction and abscess formation are common. A repeat lumbar puncture at 24 to 48 hours is standard in this group because continued growth identifies the infants who need imaging, a longer course and neurosurgical input. Cranial imaging is indicated for persistent positive cultures, seizures, focal deficits, an enlarging head or failure to improve. Even with optimal therapy, neurodevelopmental sequelae including hearing loss, epilepsy and cognitive impairment are common, so structured audiology and developmental follow up is arranged before discharge. In context, the reasoning being tested is that a well looking infant partway through treatment still needs the course that the organism dictates.
key_points: Gram negative neonatal meningitis requires at least 21 days of parenteral therapy.
Group B streptococcal meningitis is treated for 14 to 21 days.
Repeat lumbar puncture at 24 to 48 hours documents sterilisation in gram negative disease.
Intraventricular aminoglycoside increases mortality and is not used.
Audiology and developmental follow up are arranged before discharge.
explanation.pearls: Persistently positive cerebrospinal fluid cultures at 48 hours in neonatal gram negative meningitis predict ventriculitis or abscess and should trigger cranial imaging rather than simply a longer antibiotic course.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

options.rationale: Ten days is the course for uncomplicated pneumococcal meningitis in an older child and is too short for a neonatal gram negative infection, which relapses at unacceptable rates. The shortened duration is the error rather than the drug. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Oral step down is not used in neonatal meningitis because cerebrospinal fluid concentrations cannot be assured and absorption is variable. Parenteral therapy is maintained for the whole course. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Fourteen days is the group B streptococcal duration; gram negative organisms require longer because ventriculitis and sterilisation delay are common. Waiting for fever to return before imaging misses the abscess that presents as failure to improve. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Intraventricular aminoglycoside was studied in neonatal gram negative meningitis and increased mortality, so it is specifically not recommended. The route, not the agent, is what makes this harmful. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Gram negative neonatal meningitis requires at least 21 days of parenteral therapy, and a repeat lumbar puncture at 24 to 48 hours documents sterilisation because persistent positivity predicts complications and extends the course. Clinical improvement alone does not confirm clearance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

explanation.summary: Fever with a non-blanching rash is one of the highest stakes presentations in paediatrics precisely because the great majority of children who have it do not have invasive meningococcal disease, and an undiscriminating approach either overtreats hundreds of children or misses the one who is deteriorating. The distribution is the most useful single feature: mechanical petechiae from raised venous pressure during coughing, vomiting or straining appear only in the superior vena cava territory, above the nipple line, and do not progress. Features that mandate immediate antibiotics include any purpura or lesion larger than 2 mm, spread below the nipple line, progression during observation, abnormal perfusion or conscious state, and abnormal inflammatory markers, platelets or coagulation. Observation over several hours with repeated rash mapping is itself the investigation, because invasive disease evolves visibly within that window. In context, the distribution and trajectory of the rash are the data that decide treatment, not the word petechiae.
key_points: Mechanical petechiae from coughing or vomiting are confined above the nipple line.
Any purpura, lesions over 2 mm, or spread below the nipple line mandates antibiotics.
Progression of the rash during observation is an indication to treat.
Normal platelets, coagulation and inflammatory markers support a mechanical cause.
Structured observation with rash mapping is part of the assessment, not a delay in it.
explanation.pearls: Petechiae limited to the superior vena cava distribution after forceful coughing or vomiting carry a risk of invasive meningococcal disease well under 1 in 100, whereas purpuric lesions larger than 2 mm carry a risk an order of magnitude higher.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Petechiae and purpura
RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child
RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

options.rationale: Reflex parenteral antibiotics for any febrile child with non-blanching spots is overtreatment, and it commits a well child to admission and cannulation without benefit. It would be correct with spreading purpura, any lesion below the nipple line, or abnormal perfusion or markers. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Petechiae and purpura)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Petechiae and purpura

options.rationale: Sending cultures without treating creates the worst of both approaches, since a child judged sick enough to culture is sick enough to treat and one judged well enough to discharge needs neither. Cultures belong with antibiotics, not instead of them. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Petechiae and purpura)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Petechiae and purpura

options.rationale: A single intramuscular dose is a pre-hospital measure for a child with suspected invasive disease who is being transferred, not an outpatient hedge for a well child. It partially treats, blunts cultures and does not provide ongoing cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Petechiae confined to the distribution of the superior vena cava after forceful coughing or vomiting, in a well perfused child with normal inflammatory markers, platelets and coagulation and no new lesions over several hours, are mechanical and do not require antibiotics. Structured observation with explicit return criteria is the safety net. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Petechiae and purpura)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Petechiae and purpura
RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.rationale: There are no features of meningitis and cerebrospinal fluid sampling in a well child with mechanical petechiae adds risk with no diagnostic return. This would be appropriate in a child with altered conscious state or meningism. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric sepsis pathways specify boluses of 10 to 20 mL/kg with reassessment after each one, and the reassessment exists because septic myocardial dysfunction is common in young children and converts fluid from the treatment into the problem. The three signs that mark the transition are new or increasing hepatomegaly, a gallop rhythm and new crackles, and any of them means the next intervention is an inotrope rather than another bolus. Cold shock with poor contractility and high systemic vascular resistance is the commoner phenotype in this age group and responds to adrenaline, which can be run peripherally or intraosseously at low dose while central access and retrieval are organised. Continuing to a fixed volume target regardless of these findings is associated with worse oxygenation, longer ventilation and higher mortality. In context, the reasoning being tested is abandoning a volume target that the child's own physiology has just invalidated.
key_points: Reassess after every 10 to 20 mL/kg bolus rather than running to a fixed total.
New hepatomegaly, gallop rhythm or crackles signal fluid intolerance.
Cold shock with poor contractility responds to adrenaline, not to more volume.
Adrenaline may be started peripherally or intraosseously at low dose while access is obtained.
Diuresis belongs to the deresuscitation phase, not to ongoing hypoperfusion.
explanation.pearls: An increase in liver span of 2 cm or more during bolus therapy is the earliest bedside sign of fluid intolerance in a young child and appears before crackles or a falling saturation.

sources.label: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: Completing 60 mL/kg is the reflex taught for fluid responsive shock, but hepatomegaly, a gallop and new crackles mark the point at which further volume worsens oxygenation without improving output. The pathway explicitly instructs reassessment after each bolus for exactly these signs. (Source: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: Colloid still expands intravascular volume and has not been shown superior to crystalloid in paediatric sepsis, so it shares the problem of a further crystalloid bolus. Switching fluid type does not address a heart that cannot handle the preload it already has. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis)

New hepatomegaly, a gallop rhythm and crackles during bolus therapy indicate that myocardial dysfunction has become the limiting problem, so volume is stopped and an inotrope with vasoconstrictor activity is started for this cold shock phenotype. Retrieval and intensive care involvement are activated at the same time. (Source: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: Diuresis in a child who is still hypoperfused reduces preload and cardiac output further and does not treat the underlying myocardial depression. Furosemide has a role in the later deresuscitation phase once perfusion is restored. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis)

A haemoglobin of 104 g/L does not limit oxygen delivery here and a transfusion is simply another volume load in a child showing signs of overload. Red cells would be reasonable at a much lower haemoglobin once perfusion pressure is supported. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Melioidosis caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei is endemic in the Top End of the Northern Territory and in tropical Queensland and Western Australia, with the overwhelming majority of cases presenting in the wet season after exposure to soil and surface water. Diabetes, hazardous alcohol use, chronic kidney and lung disease and immunosuppression are the dominant risk factors, and pneumonia with cavitation progressing to septic shock is the commonest severe presentation. The organism is intrinsically resistant to third generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone, to aminoglycosides and to most penicillins, so a sepsis pathway that works for every other presentation fails here and treatment appears to stall over the first 24 hours. Intensive phase therapy uses a carbapenem or ceftazidime for a minimum of two weeks, followed by at least three months of oral eradication therapy with trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole to prevent relapse. In context, the reasoning being tested is recognising that a correctly executed sepsis pathway can still deliver the wrong antibiotic when geography and season change the organism.
key_points: Melioidosis is a wet season disease of northern Australia linked to soil and water exposure.
Diabetes is the single commonest predisposing condition.
Burkholderia pseudomallei is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone and to aminoglycosides.
Intensive phase therapy is a carbapenem or ceftazidime for at least 14 days.
Eradication therapy with trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole runs for at least three months.
explanation.pearls: Neurological melioidosis and severe septic shock are treated with meropenem rather than ceftazidime, and the eradication phase must run for a minimum of three months because shorter courses relapse in up to one in four patients.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Series of National Guidelines

options.rationale: Wet season exposure to soil and surface water in the Top End, diabetes, cavitating pneumonia, septic shock and gram negative bacilli that are not responding to ceftriaxone point to an organism intrinsically resistant to third generation cephalosporins, for which a carbapenem is the Australian intensive phase therapy in severe disease. Eradication therapy follows for at least three months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This broadens gram negative and anaerobic cover but is not reliable against the organism this exposure history predicts, and it is not among the recommended intensive phase agents. It is a reasonable choice for hospital acquired gram negative sepsis in a southern Australian centre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Aminoglycosides have poor activity against this organism and poor lung penetration, and adding nephrotoxicity to an already rising creatinine is a real harm. Synergy with a cephalosporin is a strategy for enterococcal endocarditis, not for tropical gram negative sepsis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Macrolide cover addresses Mycoplasma and Legionella, which do not cavitate in this pattern and would not grow as gram negative bacilli in aerobic bottles. Adding it leaves the resistant organism untreated for another day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Fluoroquinolones are associated with unacceptable relapse rates in this infection and are not recommended for either the intensive or the eradication phase. Ciprofloxacin looks attractive for gram negative sepsis generally, but not for this infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: An umbilical granuloma is overgrown granulation tissue at the base of the cord stump, appearing in the first weeks after separation and presenting as persistent moist serous discharge. The differential is short and each alternative has a discriminating feature: omphalitis brings periumbilical erythema and systemic upset, a patent urachus leaks urine, a vitellointestinal duct remnant leaks bowel content, and an umbilical polyp is firm bright red mucosa that does not respond to cautery. Clarifying which of these is present is entirely a bedside task and needs no imaging in a thriving infant. Missed omphalitis in a neonate progresses rapidly to necrotising fasciitis and portal vein thrombosis, which is why erythema changes the plan completely.
key_points: Soft pink pedunculated lesion with serous discharge and no erythema is granulation tissue, not infection
Silver nitrate cautery with barrier protection of surrounding skin is the office treatment of choice
Urine or faeculent discharge points to a urachal or vitellointestinal remnant and mandates imaging and surgical referral
Periumbilical erythema or systemic upset means omphalitis and requires intravenous antibiotics, not cautery
A lesion that fails two or three cautery treatments should be reassessed as a possible umbilical polyp
explanation.pearls: Silver nitrate burns normal skin, so smear petroleum jelly around the umbilicus before applying it and wipe the area with saline afterwards; a granuloma that has not shrunk after three weekly applications is probably an umbilical polyp and needs surgical referral.

options.rationale: Systemic antibiotics treat omphalitis, which requires periumbilical erythema, induration or systemic upset before it can be diagnosed, and none of those are present here. Treating a granuloma with antibiotics delays the definitive treatment while exposing a well infant to unnecessary drug risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

A patent urachus leaks urine from the umbilicus and a vitellointestinal duct remnant leaks bowel content, neither of which was expressed on examination, so imaging for a remnant is not indicated. Imaging is reserved for persistent discharge after cautery or for a lesion that does not respond to two or three treatments. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

A soft pink pedunculated lesion at the umbilical base with a serous discharge and no erythema is granulation tissue, and chemical cautery is the standard office treatment with the surrounding skin protected by a barrier. Most granulomas resolve after one or two applications, which is why review at one week is built into the plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

Surgical excision is reserved for lesions that fail chemical treatment or that prove to be a true umbilical polyp, which is a firm bright red mucosal remnant rather than the soft pale granulation tissue described. Referring first exposes a well 3-week-old to anaesthesia for a condition that usually resolves in the consulting room. (Source: RACGP: Umbilical lesions in infancy)

Swabs of the neonatal umbilicus grow skin and bowel flora in well infants and do not distinguish colonisation from infection, so a positive result here would mislead rather than guide. Topical antibacterials neither shrink granulation tissue nor treat the discharge it produces. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Unsettled crying in early infancy follows a well described curve that begins at around 2 weeks, peaks at 6 to 8 weeks, is concentrated in the late afternoon and evening, and resolves by 3 to 4 months, and it affects roughly one in five infants at a level that prompts a consultation. The clinical task is to separate this from organic causes through a thorough history and a genuinely complete examination, which includes the eyes for a corneal abrasion, the digits for a hair tourniquet, the groin for an incarcerated hernia, the anus for a fissure and the growth chart. Once organic causes are excluded, the evidence does not support formula change, acid suppression, simethicone or anticholinergics, and management centres on explanation, practical settling strategies and support for parental fatigue. That support is not a soft option: inconsolable infant crying is the leading trigger for abusive head trauma, so asking directly how parents are coping and arranging early review is a safety intervention.
key_points: Crying peaks at 6 to 8 weeks and resolves by 3 to 4 months in most infants
Examination must include eyes, digits, groin, anus and the growth chart
Proton pump inhibitors and simethicone do not reduce crying and carry harms
Formula change is reserved for infants with other features of cow milk protein allergy
Inconsolable crying is the commonest trigger for abusive head trauma, so ask how parents are coping
explanation.pearls: Teach parents to put the baby down safely in the cot and walk away for a few minutes when they feel overwhelmed; naming this plan explicitly in the consultation is the single most effective thing said in a crying baby review.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

options.rationale: Crying that peaks in the late afternoon and evening, begins around 2 to 3 weeks and occurs in an infant who is thriving with a normal examination is the normal crying curve, which peaks at 6 to 8 weeks and resolves by 3 to 4 months. Structured explanation with settling strategies and planned review addresses the parental exhaustion that is the actual risk here, since inconsolable crying is the commonest trigger for abusive head trauma. (Source: RCH CPG: Crying baby)

A hydrolysed formula trial is reserved for infants with other features of cow milk protein allergy such as blood or mucus in the stool, eczema, vomiting or faltering growth, none of which are present. Replacing breastfeeding with formula on this history removes its protective benefits without evidence of a food protein cause, particularly as maternal dairy exclusion has already failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Crying baby)

Randomised trials show acid suppression does not reduce crying in unsettled infants, and it is associated with increased rates of gastroenteritis, lower respiratory infection and fracture in infancy. Reflux is only implicated when there is genuine distress with feeds, back arching during feeding or faltering growth. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

options.rationale: Simethicone has been tested against placebo in this setting and does not reduce crying duration, so it offers reassurance rather than effect. Recommending it also reinforces a gastrointestinal explanation the examination does not support. (Source: RCH CPG: Crying baby)

Imaging is indicated when the history or examination suggests an organic cause, such as bilious vomiting, a palpable mass, abdominal distension or episodic pallor with drawing up of the legs between periods of lethargy. A thriving infant with a normal abdomen and a predictable daily pattern does not warrant it. (Source: RCH CPG: Crying baby)

explanation.summary: Umbilical hernia results from incomplete closure of the fascial ring after cord separation and is present in a substantial proportion of infants, with a higher prevalence in those born preterm and in children of African ancestry. It behaves quite differently from an inguinal hernia: the neck is wide, incarceration is rare, and spontaneous closure occurs in the great majority by 4 to 5 years, so the standard approach is observation rather than repair. Families frequently arrive having tried coins, straps or binders, none of which work and all of which can damage the skin, so correcting that advice is part of the visit. The features that change the plan are a tender or irreducible lump, overlying skin change, vomiting or distension, all of which mandate urgent surgical assessment. Persistence beyond 4 to 5 years, a very large or proboscoid defect, or a previous incarceration are the usual indications for elective repair.
key_points: Wide necked defect with low incarceration risk, unlike inguinal hernia
Most close spontaneously by 4 to 5 years of age
Taping, coins and binders are ineffective and cause skin injury
Tenderness, irreducibility, vomiting or distension mandate urgent surgical review
Elective repair is for persistence beyond 4 to 5 years or a very large defect
explanation.pearls: An inguinal hernia in an infant is the opposite situation and should be referred for repair on the day it is diagnosed, because incarceration risk is highest in the first months of life and rises the longer repair is delayed.

sources.label: RACGP: Common surgical problems in childhood

options.rationale: Elective repair is offered for defects that persist beyond about 4 to 5 years of age, for very large or proboscoid defects, or after an episode of incarceration. Operating on an 18-month-old commits her to a general anaesthetic for a defect that will most likely close on its own. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

Strapping, coins and binders have never been shown to accelerate closure and they cause skin maceration and pressure injury under an occlusive dressing. Advising the family to stop the taping they have already started is part of the consultation. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

The defect is measured clinically with a fingertip and imaging adds nothing to a diagnosis made by inspection and palpation. Ultrasound is reserved for an atypical periumbilical mass or when the swelling cannot be reduced. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

Umbilical hernias in children have a wide fascial ring and a low incarceration risk, unlike inguinal hernias, and the great majority close spontaneously by 4 to 5 years of age, with larger defects simply taking longer. The consultation therefore consists of reassurance, stopping ineffective home remedies, giving red flag advice about a tender irreducible lump with vomiting, and setting a review point at which referral becomes appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

Urgent referral is for a hernia that has become irreducible, tender or discoloured, or is accompanied by vomiting and abdominal distension, which signals incarceration or strangulation. This hernia reduces completely with one finger in a thriving, well child. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

explanation.summary: Non-specific vulvovaginitis is the commonest gynaecological problem of childhood and reflects anatomy and physiology rather than infection: the prepubertal vulva is thin, unoestrogenised, unprotected by labial fat or pubic hair, and sits close to the anus. Soaps, bubble baths, chlorinated water, damp swimwear or leotards and imperfect wiping technique all contribute, and the history in this case names several of them. Management is entirely conservative, and the great majority improve with irritant avoidance, salt baths and a barrier ointment, with complete resolution once puberty oestrogenises the epithelium. A swab is not routine but is taken when the vulva is bright red and painful, suggesting group A streptococcus, or when discharge is purulent. The findings that take the child out of this pathway are blood stained or offensive discharge, which suggests a retained foreign body, and any sign of trauma, a sexually transmitted infection or disclosure, which requires child protection assessment.
key_points: The condition is irritant rather than infective and reflects prepubertal vulval anatomy
Soaps, bubble baths, chlorinated water and damp clothing are the usual contributors
Candida is rare before puberty and suggests diabetes or recent antibiotics if present
Blood stained or offensive discharge suggests a retained foreign body needing vaginoscopy
Trauma, a sexually transmitted infection or disclosure require child protection assessment
explanation.pearls: A bright red, sharply demarcated, painful vulvitis, especially following a sore throat, is group A streptococcal vulvitis and needs a swab and oral penicillin rather than the conservative measures that treat the non-specific form.

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are used when a specific bacterial cause is identified, most often group A streptococcus producing a bright red painful vulvitis often after a sore throat, or when a urinary tract infection is confirmed. Non-specific vulvovaginitis is not primarily an infective condition and antibiotics alter the flora without relieving it. (Source: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis)

Prepubertal vulvovaginitis is an irritant condition arising from unoestrogenised thin vulval skin, proximity to the anus and exposure to soaps, bubble baths and damp clothing, so treatment is stopping the irritants, salt baths, loose cotton clothing, front to back wiping and a bland barrier ointment. Most children improve within weeks and the condition resolves entirely once oestrogenisation begins at puberty. (Source: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis)

Candida is rare in prepubertal girls outside nappies because the unoestrogenised vagina lacks the glycogen that supports it, and it should prompt consideration of diabetes or recent antibiotics if genuinely present. Treating empirically for thrush in this age group usually treats the wrong organism. (Source: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis)

Examination under anaesthetic with vaginoscopy is indicated for persistent blood stained or offensive discharge suggesting a retained foreign body, for a suspected tumour, or for an injury that cannot otherwise be assessed. The examination here is normal apart from erythema, with no bleeding and no visible foreign material. (Source: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis)

Vulval symptoms alone are not an indicator of abuse, and non-specific vulvovaginitis is common, but bruising, lacerations, bleeding, a sexually transmitted infection, disclosure or behavioural change would change that assessment entirely. Referring without any such feature medicalises a common problem while diverting a scarce service. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Laryngomalacia accounts for the majority of chronic stridor in infants, typically starting in the first weeks of life, worsening over the first few months and resolving by 12 to 24 months. The history is characteristic: inspiratory stridor that is worse supine, worse with feeding or crying and better prone. Severity is graded by what the obstruction is costing the infant, so feeding difficulty, recession, cyanosis, apnoea or faltering growth move a child from watchful waiting to endoscopic assessment. A synchronous second airway lesion is present in a significant minority, which is another reason the airway is looked at rather than assumed.
key_points: Positional inspiratory stridor from the first weeks of life is laryngomalacia until proven otherwise
Mild disease is stridor alone and needs only review and parental reassurance
Feeding difficulty, recession, apnoea or faltering growth define moderate to severe disease
Flexible laryngoscopy identifies synchronous airway lesions in 15 to 20 per cent
Supraglottoplasty is effective for severe disease and reverses growth failure
explanation.pearls: Stridor that is present from birth rather than appearing at 2 to 6 weeks, or that is biphasic rather than inspiratory, argues against laryngomalacia and points towards vocal cord palsy or subglottic stenosis, which need endoscopy regardless of severity.

options.rationale: Expectant management is right for mild laryngomalacia, defined by stridor without feeding difficulty, recession or growth failure, and this infant has all three. Waiting to 12 months accepts continued faltering growth at the age of fastest brain growth. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

Reflux frequently coexists with laryngomalacia and acid suppression is often used as an adjunct, but it does not relieve the supraglottic collapse that is causing the obstruction and it has not been shown to reverse growth failure in this setting. Committing to a 6 week trial defers the assessment that decides whether surgery is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

Corticosteroid treats the subglottic oedema of croup, which presents acutely with a barking cough and hoarse voice in a child usually over 6 months, not with 3 months of positional stridor. Croup and laryngomalacia both cause inspiratory stridor, but croup is acute and febrile while laryngomalacia is chronic and positional. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

A vascular ring produces biphasic stridor that is not positional and is often accompanied by feeding difficulty with solids, and a plain chest radiograph cannot exclude it in any case. The definitive test would be contrast imaging, and it is not the first step when the history points to a supraglottic cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

Stridor with feeding difficulty and faltering growth defines moderate to severe disease, and awake flexible laryngoscopy confirms the supraglottic collapse and identifies the 15 to 20 per cent of infants with a second synchronous airway lesion. It is also the assessment that determines candidacy for supraglottoplasty, which reliably reverses the growth failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

explanation.summary: Enterobius vermicularis is the most common helminth infection in Australian children and spreads by the faecal oral route when eggs deposited on perianal skin at night are transferred by scratching to hands, bedding, toys and surfaces, where they remain viable for up to 3 weeks. The presentation is characteristic enough to treat on history alone: intense perianal itch confined to the night, often with visible motile white threads, and frequently with affected siblings. Because reinfection within a household is the norm, everyone living in the house is treated at the same time, and the dose is repeated after 2 weeks since the treatment is active against adult worms but not eggs. Hygiene measures reduce recurrence and matter, particularly morning showering to remove eggs laid overnight, trimming nails, and washing bedding and nightclothes in hot water at the time of treatment. Vulvovaginitis and secondary bacterial infection from scratching are the usual complications, and migration causing appendicitis or genitourinary infection is rare.
key_points: Nocturnal perianal itch with visible white threads is enough to treat without testing
Treat all household members simultaneously, symptomatic or not
Repeat the dose after 2 weeks because treatment does not kill eggs
Stool microscopy is insensitive; the adhesive tape test is used if confirmation is needed
Hot washing of bedding and morning showering reduce reinfection
explanation.pearls: Threadworm is a recognised cause of vulvovaginitis in prepubertal girls, so consider it in any girl with vulval itch that is markedly worse at night, and treat the household rather than persisting with topical measures.

options.rationale: A nocturnal perianal itch with visible motile white threads is enterobiasis, and because eggs are shed onto bedding and household surfaces and reinfection is the rule, everyone in the house is treated simultaneously whether or not they have symptoms. The dose is repeated after 2 weeks because the treatment kills adult worms but not eggs, and that interval covers the maturation of any eggs ingested around the first dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Treating one member of a household leaves an untreated reservoir, and reinfection from siblings and shared bedding follows within weeks, which is exactly what is beginning with his sister. It also omits the repeat dose that covers eggs surviving the first treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Stool microscopy is insensitive for this infection because the female worm deposits eggs on perianal skin rather than in faeces, so a negative result is common and misleading. When confirmation is genuinely needed the adhesive tape test applied to the perianal skin on waking is the appropriate investigation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A topical corticosteroid may settle the excoriation but does nothing to eradicate the organism causing the itch, which will continue and spread through the household. It also risks masking a perianal streptococcal infection, which is the main mimic and requires antibiotics instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Hygiene measures such as morning showering, nail trimming and hot washing of bedding reduce reinfection and are part of the advice, but they are an adjunct rather than a substitute for treatment. Withholding treatment leaves an itchy child losing sleep and an expanding household reservoir. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Deformational plagiocephaly became common after supine sleeping was adopted for sudden infant death prevention and is benign, whereas lambdoid craniosynostosis is rare and needs surgery. The two are separated by geometry rather than imaging: deformational flattening pushes the ipsilateral ear and forehead forward, producing a parallelogram viewed from above, while lambdoid fusion pulls the ear posteriorly and inferiorly with contralateral frontal bossing and a mastoid bulge, producing a trapezoid. A palpable ridge over the suture, a closing fontanelle or a head circumference crossing centiles shifts the assessment towards synostosis. Torticollis is the usual driver of the preferential head position and must be treated or the flattening recurs despite repositioning advice.
key_points: Parallelogram with the ear pushed anteriorly is deformational, trapezoid with the ear posterior and inferior is lambdoid synostosis
A palpable sutural ridge or mastoid bulge is the physical sign of synostosis
Treating coexisting torticollis is essential or repositioning fails
Helmet therapy is second line and has not outperformed repositioning for mild to moderate deformity
Three dimensional computed tomography confirms synostosis but is not a screening test
explanation.pearls: Head circumference crossing centiles upwards in an infant with an abnormal head shape suggests multi suture fusion with raised intracranial pressure and warrants craniofacial referral within days rather than a repositioning trial.

sources.label: RACGP: Abnormal head shape in infants

options.rationale: Three dimensional computed tomography is the confirmatory test for craniosynostosis once the head shape and ear position suggest it, and it delivers a meaningful radiation dose to an infant brain. The parallelogram shape with an anteriorly displaced ear and no sutural ridge argues against synostosis, so the test would be ordered to confirm a diagnosis the examination has already made unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Urgent craniofacial referral is for a trapezoid head shape, a palpable sutural ridge, a mastoid bulge or a head circumference crossing centiles, which together signal fused sutures and rising intracranial pressure. None of those are present, and urgent referral here displaces a child who genuinely needs the appointment. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

A parallelogram head with the ipsilateral ear pushed forward, a mobile open fontanelle and no ridge is deformational plagiocephaly, which responds to repositioning, supervised awake prone time and treatment of the residual torticollis that is driving the preferential head position. Most cases improve substantially by 12 months once the infant sits and spends less time supine. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Helmet therapy is a second line option considered for severe deformity that has not responded to several months of active repositioning, and randomised evidence shows no meaningful advantage over natural improvement for mild to moderate cases while causing skin irritation and considerable cost. Offering it before a repositioning trial skips the treatment that works for most infants. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

Plain skull radiographs are insensitive for partial sutural fusion and a normal film would not exclude synostosis, so a test with this performance cannot safely reassure. The distinction between deformational plagiocephaly and lambdoid synostosis is made by head shape and ear position at the bedside. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

explanation.summary: A buckle or torus fracture is a compression injury of the metaphyseal cortex in which the opposite cortex remains intact, which makes it mechanically stable and unable to displace. Australian and international practice has moved decisively from cast immobilisation to a removable splint with no routine follow up, supported by randomised evidence showing equivalent pain and function with faster return to normal activity. The key task for the treating doctor is distinguishing a buckle fracture from a greenstick or complete fracture, where one cortex is actually broken and the injury can angulate. A scaphoid injury also needs excluding: snuffbox tenderness with normal initial films warrants splinting and repeat assessment because the fracture is often occult at presentation.
key_points: Buckle fracture means an intact opposite cortex and therefore inherent stability
Removable splint for 3 to 4 weeks matches casting on pain and function in randomised trials
Routine follow up radiographs are not required because displacement cannot occur
A broken cortex on either side makes it a greenstick or complete fracture needing casting
Snuffbox tenderness changes the pathway regardless of the radiograph appearance
explanation.pearls: Tell families that the splint is worn for comfort and weaned as pain settles rather than for a fixed period, and that pain persisting beyond 4 weeks is the only reason to return; this single instruction removes the routine review visit entirely.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures
Cochrane: Interventions for treating wrist fractures in children

options.rationale: A backslab plus clinic review is the pathway for a complete or angulated fracture that could displace and therefore needs a check radiograph. A buckle fracture has an intact opposite cortex and is inherently stable, so it cannot displace and the review visit finds nothing to act on. (Source: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures

options.rationale: Six weeks of casting is the treatment duration for a complete forearm fracture and overtreats an injury that heals in 3 to 4 weeks, while adding joint stiffness, muscle wasting, cast complications and lost school and sport time. Repeat imaging of a stable buckle fracture does not change management. (Source: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures

options.rationale: Reduction is indicated for angulation beyond the age related acceptable limits, and this fracture has no angulation to correct. Sedating a child to reduce an undisplaced compression injury exposes them to airway and cardiovascular risk for no gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures

options.rationale: A sling gives no wrist support and leaves the child with unnecessary pain during the 3 to 4 weeks of healing, while repeat radiographs of a stable injury add radiation without altering the plan. A scaphoid fracture is different: it does justify a splint and repeat imaging because it is often radiographically occult, and snuffbox tenderness is absent here. (Source: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures

options.rationale: Randomised trials show a removable splint gives equal or better function and pain scores than casting for buckle fractures, with faster return to activity and no risk of late displacement because the opposite cortex is intact. Parents are told to use it for comfort, wean it as pain settles, and return only if pain persists beyond 4 weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures

explanation.summary: Idiopathic toe walking is a diagnosis of exclusion and requires normal motor milestones, normal strength and a normal neurological examination before the label is applied. The conditions that masquerade as it are cerebral palsy, which adds spasticity and brisk reflexes, tethered cord, which may add bladder symptoms or a cutaneous marker, and Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which adds calf pseudohypertrophy, a positive Gowers sign and delayed motor milestones in a boy. The average age at diagnosis of Duchenne remains around 4 to 5 years despite symptoms from age 2, and toe walking labelled as habit is one of the recurring reasons for that delay. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroids started before significant decline prolong ambulation, and because it allows genetic counselling before another affected pregnancy.
key_points: Idiopathic toe walking requires normal milestones and a normal neurological examination
Calf pseudohypertrophy with a positive Gowers sign in a boy means creatine kinase today
Creatine kinase in Duchenne is typically 10 to 100 times the upper limit of normal
Spasticity, brisk reflexes or clonus point to cerebral palsy rather than muscle disease
Casting or tendon lengthening in undiagnosed dystrophy hastens loss of ambulation
explanation.pearls: A boy who is not yet walking at 18 months, or who has a creatine kinase above 1000 units per litre at any age, needs dystrophin gene testing; corticosteroids begun before the plateau of motor function extend independent walking by 2 to 3 years.

options.rationale: Serial casting treats fixed equinus contracture in idiopathic toe walking, and this boy still achieves dorsiflexion beyond neutral, so there is no contracture to stretch. More importantly, casting a child with an undiagnosed myopathy causes disuse weakness and can precipitate loss of ambulation. (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking)

Calf hypertrophy, a positive Gowers sign, late independent walking and frequent falls in a boy of this age point to Duchenne muscular dystrophy, in which creatine kinase is typically elevated 10 to 100 times the upper limit of normal and is the screening test that triggers genetic confirmation. It is cheap, immediate, and the single test that changes the diagnosis from a gait habit to a progressive neuromuscular disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking)

Central imaging looks for a tethered cord or an upper motor neuron cause, both of which produce increased tone, brisk reflexes, sustained clonus or upgoing plantars, and all of those are normal here. A positive Gowers sign with preserved reflexes localises to muscle rather than to cord or brain. (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking)

Surgical lengthening is considered for persistent idiopathic toe walking with fixed contracture after conservative treatment has failed, in a child whose muscle disease has already been excluded. Operating on a boy with an undiagnosed dystrophy accelerates functional decline. (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking)

Nerve conduction studies interrogate peripheral nerve and would be appropriate for a hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy, which characteristically produces pes cavus, distal wasting and absent ankle reflexes. This boy has proximal weakness with bulky calves and preserved reflexes, the opposite pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking)

explanation.summary: Achondroplasia results from a gain of function variant in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 gene and causes rhizomelic short stature, macrocephaly, midface hypoplasia and a narrow foramen magnum. Infants normally show mild hypotonia and delayed gross motor milestones, so the clinical skill is separating that expected pattern from cord compression, which adds hyperreflexia, sustained clonus, upgoing plantars and central apnoea. Sudden unexplained death in the first two years of life has historically affected a small but significant proportion of infants with achondroplasia and is largely attributable to unrecognised craniocervical compression. Structured surveillance with neurological examination, sleep study and imaging in the first year is the response to that risk, and decompression is effective when compression is found.
key_points: Hypotonia and motor delay are expected, but hyperreflexia, clonus and upgoing plantars never are
Foramen magnum stenosis is the leading cause of infant death in achondroplasia
Central apnoea points to brainstem compression, obstructive apnoea to midface and adenotonsillar narrowing
Polysomnography is required because oximetry cannot separate central from obstructive events
Head circumference must be plotted on achondroplasia specific charts, not standard charts
explanation.pearls: In achondroplasia, plot growth on condition specific charts and treat any new central apnoea or long tract sign as foramen magnum compression until magnetic resonance imaging says otherwise; suboccipital decompression reverses the apnoea in most affected infants.

sources.label: RACGP: Genetic conditions in general practice

options.rationale: Mild hypotonia and motor delay are indeed typical in achondroplasia, which is exactly why the abnormal findings must be separated from the expected ones. Sustained clonus and upgoing plantars are never part of the natural history and signal cord compression. (Source: RCH CPG: Achondroplasia)

Home oximetry detects desaturation but cannot distinguish central from obstructive events, which is the whole question when craniocervical compression is suspected. A three month delay in a child with long tract signs risks irreversible cord injury or sudden death. (Source: RCH CPG: Achondroplasia)

Obstructive sleep apnoea is common in achondroplasia from midface hypoplasia and adenotonsillar tissue, but the tonsils are small here and obstruction does not cause pyramidal signs. Operating without characterising the apnoea leaves an untreated cord compression and subjects the child to an anaesthetic with an unstable craniocervical junction. (Source: RCH CPG: Achondroplasia)

Foramen magnum stenosis is the leading cause of death in infants with achondroplasia, and the combination of new central apnoea with hyperreflexia, sustained clonus and upgoing plantars is its presentation. Magnetic resonance imaging defines the compression while polysomnography separates central from obstructive events, and together they determine whether decompression is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Achondroplasia)

Dynamic radiographs assess atlantoaxial instability, which belongs to conditions such as Down syndrome and the mucopolysaccharidoses rather than to achondroplasia, where the problem is bony narrowing at the foramen magnum. Plain films cannot show the cord or the degree of compression. (Source: RCH CPG: Achondroplasia)

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas appear in the first weeks of life, proliferate until around 5 months and then involute slowly over years, so most need no treatment. The exceptions are lesions that threaten function or life, and a segmental haemangioma over the chin, lower lip and anterior neck is the classic marker for airway involvement because the subglottic lesion follows the same developmental segment. Such infants are typically misdiagnosed as having recurrent croup, and the clue is that the stridor is biphasic, progressive over weeks, afebrile and unresponsive to corticosteroid. Propranolol has replaced systemic corticosteroid and tracheostomy as first line treatment and usually produces rapid improvement, but initiation requires baseline assessment for cardiac and glycaemic risk.
key_points: Beard distribution segmental haemangioma predicts subglottic involvement in a majority of infants
Biphasic progressive stridor in an afebrile infant under 6 months is not croup
Flexible laryngoscopy is the assessment that confirms and grades the airway lesion
Propranolol is first line treatment but is initiated with monitoring, not by telephone
Large segmental facial haemangiomas also warrant assessment for associated cerebrovascular and cardiac anomalies
explanation.pearls: Propranolol for infantile haemangioma is started at a low dose and uptitrated towards 2 to 3 mg/kg/day in divided doses, with feeding maintained every 4 to 6 hours because the main serious adverse effect in infants is hypoglycaemia during fasting or intercurrent illness.

options.rationale: Croup causes a barking cough and inspiratory stridor over a few days in a child usually older than 6 months, with a febrile viral prodrome, and it responds to a single dose of corticosteroid. Two weeks of progressive afebrile stridor that did not respond to dexamethasone is not croup, and repeating the dose tests a diagnosis already excluded by the course. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

A segmental haemangioma in the beard distribution carries roughly a 60 per cent risk of a synchronous subglottic haemangioma, which proliferates over the same months and presents as biphasic stridor unresponsive to steroid. Direct visualisation confirms the airway lesion, grades the degree of narrowing and allows propranolol to be started with appropriate monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

Propranolol is the correct drug for a subglottic haemangioma and often shrinks it within days, but starting it at home in an infant with stridor at rest and recession leaves an unsecured airway and unmonitored risks of hypoglycaemia, bradycardia and hypotension. The drug is right and the setting is wrong: initiation belongs in hospital once the airway has been assessed. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

Bacterial tracheitis presents with high fever, a toxic appearance and rapid deterioration over hours, whereas this infant has been afebrile and well perfused for two weeks. A chest radiograph cannot assess the subglottis adequately and would delay definitive visualisation. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

Ultrasound characterises the cutaneous lesion and can confirm a high flow vascular anomaly, but it cannot visualise the subglottis and therefore does not answer the question the stridor is asking. Two weeks of observation spans the period of most rapid haemangioma proliferation. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

explanation.summary: Varicocele affects roughly 15 per cent of adolescent boys and is almost always left sided, a consequence of the left gonadal vein entering the left renal vein at a right angle with a longer column of blood above the valves. The two findings that break that pattern are a right sided varicocele and a varicocele that does not empty when the patient lies down, and either should prompt imaging of the retroperitoneum for a mass obstructing venous return. Routine management of an ordinary left varicocele is observation with annual testicular volume measurement, since most cause no harm and intervention is reserved for pain, a volume differential above 20 per cent or abnormal semen analysis in older adolescents. The clinical examination that matters is therefore done both standing and supine.
key_points: About 90 per cent of varicoceles are left sided for anatomical reasons
An isolated right sided varicocele is an indication for retroperitoneal imaging
Failure to decompress when supine indicates fixed obstruction rather than valvular reflux
Routine left varicoceles are observed with annual testicular volume measurement
Intervention is indicated for pain, a volume differential above 20 per cent or abnormal semen parameters
explanation.pearls: Examine every varicocele both standing and lying flat; a varicocele that persists when supine has a fixed obstructive cause and needs retroperitoneal imaging, whatever side it is on.

sources.label: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents
RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

options.rationale: Annual review with volume measurement is reasonable surveillance for a typical left sided adolescent varicocele that decompresses when supine and is not causing testicular growth arrest. Applying that plan to a right sided varicocele that does not decompress accepts a year of delay for a possible retroperitoneal mass. (Source: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents

options.rationale: Embolisation treats the varicocele itself and is considered for pain, testicular growth arrest or abnormal semen parameters, but treating the dilated veins without establishing why they are obstructed leaves the cause untreated. Intervention should follow, not precede, the search for an obstructing lesion. (Source: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents

options.rationale: Scrotal ultrasound confirms venous dilatation and measures testicular volumes, both of which are already evident clinically, and it does not image the retroperitoneum where the answer lies. Scrotal imaging characterises the varicocele, while abdominal imaging explains it. (Source: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents

options.rationale: Surgical ligation is an option for symptomatic varicocele with growth arrest, and the indication has not been established here since the testes are equal in volume. It also carries the same flaw as embolisation, namely treating the venous consequence while the retroperitoneal cause goes unexamined. (Source: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents

options.rationale: Around 90 per cent of adolescent varicoceles are left sided because the left gonadal vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein, so an isolated right sided varicocele is anatomically unexpected. Failure to decompress on lying flat indicates fixed obstruction to venous drainage rather than reflux, and both features together mandate imaging of the retroperitoneum for a renal or retroperitoneal mass. (Source: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents

explanation.summary: Cyanosis in a newborn that does not improve with high inspired oxygen points to a structural cardiac cause or to persistent pulmonary hypertension, and prostaglandin E1 is the standard holding treatment because most such lesions depend on the duct for either pulmonary or systemic flow. Obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage is the important exception: the pulmonary veins drain into the systemic venous circulation through a channel that is narrowed, so the lungs are congested while the heart is small, and opening the duct increases flow into an already obstructed system. The radiographic signature is a normal or small cardiac silhouette with diffuse pulmonary venous congestion, which is routinely misread as respiratory distress syndrome or congenital pneumonia. It is one of the few congenital cardiac lesions that is a true surgical emergency, because no catheter or drug intervention relieves the obstruction.
key_points: Cyanosis unresponsive to 100 per cent oxygen indicates a cardiac or pulmonary vascular cause
Pulmonary venous congestion with a normal sized heart is the signature of obstructed anomalous pulmonary venous drainage
Prostaglandin worsens obstructed pulmonary venous return rather than helping it
Equal pre and post ductal saturations with present femoral pulses argue against duct dependent systemic obstruction
Definitive treatment is immediate surgical repair, so retrieval is activated at the same time as stabilisation
explanation.pearls: In a cyanosed neonate, read the chest radiograph before committing to prostaglandin: pulmonary oedema on a normal sized heart means obstructed pulmonary venous drainage, where prostaglandin worsens hypoxaemia and only surgery helps.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection

options.rationale: Severe cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, with pulmonary venous congestion on a normal sized heart and equal pre and post ductal saturations, indicates obstructed pulmonary venous return, in which the obstruction lies downstream of the lungs and no amount of ductal patency helps. Intubation with positive pressure recruits the oedematous lung and buys time, while the only definitive treatment is surgical relief of the obstruction at a cardiac centre. (Source: RCH CPG: The cyanosed neonate)

Prostaglandin is the correct reflex for most duct dependent cyanotic lesions, but the picture here is pulmonary venous obstruction, where increasing pulmonary blood flow through a patent duct raises pulmonary venous return against a fixed obstruction and worsens the pulmonary oedema and hypoxaemia. The findings that break the default are a normal cardiac silhouette with pulmonary oedema and equal pre and post ductal saturations with present femoral pulses. (Source: RCH CPG: The cyanosed neonate)

Volume expansion is the reflex for shock with poor perfusion, but this infant has an enlarged liver and interstitial pulmonary oedema, indicating a congested rather than an underfilled circulation. Further volume worsens pulmonary venous pressure and the oedema that is already causing the hypoxaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: The cyanosed neonate)

This is the treatment of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from left ventricular failure, and diuresis cannot relieve a fixed anatomical obstruction to pulmonary venous drainage. Nasal CPAP is also inadequate respiratory support for an infant with a pH of 7.18 who needs transfer by air or road. (Source: RCH CPG: The cyanosed neonate)

Echocardiography is the definitive diagnostic test and will be performed, but it is unavailable on this site overnight and waiting for it leaves a profoundly acidotic infant unsupported. Stabilisation and activation of the retrieval service happen first and in parallel with, not after, diagnostic imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: The cyanosed neonate)

explanation.summary: Pubertal gynaecomastia is a physiological phenomenon affecting up to around two thirds of adolescent boys, peaking at Tanner stages 3 and 4, and arises because testicular oestradiol secretion and peripheral aromatisation rise earlier in puberty than testosterone production does. The tissue is typically tender, symmetrical or nearly so, and lies concentrically beneath the areola, which separates it from the soft diffuse fat of pseudogynaecomastia in an overweight boy and from the hard eccentric fixed mass of the very rare adolescent breast malignancy. Resolution occurs within about two years in the large majority, so explanation and review are usually all that is required, and acknowledging the psychological impact matters because distress and social avoidance are common. Investigation is reserved for atypical features, and the differential then includes human chorionic gonadotrophin secreting germ cell tumours, Klinefelter syndrome, liver and thyroid disease, and drugs, with spironolactone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, antipsychotics, anabolic steroids and cannabis among the commoner causes. Tamoxifen is used for persistent painful tissue and surgery for tissue that has not resolved after two to three years and continues to cause distress.
key_points: It affects up to two thirds of boys and peaks at Tanner stages 3 and 4
Tissue is tender, concentric beneath the areola and largely symmetrical
The great majority resolve spontaneously within about two years
Investigate for prepubertal onset, tissue over 4 cm, rapid growth or a testicular mass
Ask specifically about anabolic steroids, cannabis, spironolactone and antipsychotics
explanation.pearls: Palpate both testes at the same visit rather than examining the chest alone: a unilateral testicular mass with gynaecomastia signals a human chorionic gonadotrophin secreting germ cell tumour, and the breast tissue is frequently the symptom that brings the boy in while the testicular lump has gone unnoticed.

sources.label: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence

options.rationale: A hormonal workup is indicated when the presentation is atypical, meaning onset before puberty, tissue larger than 4 cm, rapid growth, asymmetrical or hard tissue, or any testicular abnormality, since a human chorionic gonadotrophin secreting tumour is the finding that must not be missed. Symmetrical concentric tissue with equal normal testes in a boy at the expected pubertal stage does not meet any of those criteria. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence)
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence

options.rationale: Surgery is offered for persistent tissue causing significant distress after two to three years, by which time spontaneous resolution has clearly failed. Operating during active puberty risks recurrence as the hormonal imbalance continues, and carries scarring and nipple sensory loss. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence)
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence

options.rationale: Breast tissue develops in up to two thirds of boys during mid puberty because testicular oestradiol production rises before testosterone does, and it resolves spontaneously within about two years in the great majority. Symmetrical tender concentric tissue with normally progressing puberty and equal testes is the physiological pattern, so explanation and planned review is the management. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence)
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence

options.rationale: Tamoxifen has been shown to reduce breast volume and tenderness in adolescents and is sometimes used for painful tissue that persists, though it is not registered for this purpose in Australia. It is reserved for persistent or markedly symptomatic cases rather than offered before the natural history has been allowed to run. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Tamoxifen)

Scrotal imaging is indicated when a testis is asymmetrical or a mass is felt, and a karyotype is arranged when the testes are small and firm with tall stature and learning difficulties, which suggests Klinefelter syndrome. His testicular volumes are equal and appropriate for his pubertal stage with no mass, so neither test is indicated. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence)
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence

explanation.summary: Intoeing is assessed by working down the rotational profile rather than by looking at the feet, because the three causes sit at three different levels and have different natural histories. Metatarsus adductus arises in the foot and is recognised by a curved lateral forefoot border, usually resolving in infancy. Internal tibial torsion arises in the tibia, is measured by the thigh foot axis, peaks in the second year and unwinds by school age. Femoral anteversion arises at the hip, is recognised by internal rotation well exceeding external rotation in the prone position, presents later at four to six years and also corrects spontaneously in the great majority. Referral is reserved for asymmetry, pain, progression after age eight, or a functionally disabling rotational profile.
key_points: Work down the rotational profile: hip rotation, thigh foot axis, then forefoot border
Symmetrical hip rotation with an internal thigh foot axis localises the cause to the tibia
Internal tibial torsion peaks in the second year and resolves by around eight years
Braces, twister cables and corrective footwear do not alter torsional correction
Asymmetry, pain or progression after eight years are the triggers for referral
explanation.pearls: Measure the thigh foot axis with the child prone and the knee flexed to 90 degrees: values between 10 degrees internal and 15 degrees external are normal at two years, and only persistence beyond 30 degrees internal after eight years has ever justified surgery.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric lower limb variants
BMJ Best Practice: Intoeing in children

options.rationale: Symmetrical hip rotation excludes femoral anteversion and a straight forefoot border excludes metatarsus adductus, localising the rotation to the tibia, and an internal thigh foot axis at this age is the expected finding. Internal tibial torsion unwinds with normal growth and resolves in nearly all children by about eight years without any intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations

options.rationale: Derotation bracing and twister cables were historically used for this exact presentation but randomised comparison showed no change in the rate of correction over untreated children, and they disturb sleep for years. (Source: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations

options.rationale: Plain films measure angular deformity in the coronal plane but cannot quantify rotation, which is a torsional profile measured clinically at the hip, tibia and foot. Imaging a child whose rotational profile is already normal for age adds radiation without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations

options.rationale: Osteotomy is reserved for a thigh foot axis beyond about 30 degrees that persists past eight to ten years with functional disability, by which age spontaneous correction has clearly failed. Operating on a 2-year-old within the normal range would be surgery for a variant that is going to resolve. (Source: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations

options.rationale: Discouraging W sitting is directed at femoral anteversion, and this child already sits with her legs in front of her, so the advice addresses a mechanism she does not have. Corrective or wedged footwear has never been shown to alter torsional alignment at any level. (Source: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets in Australia clusters in children of mothers with deeply pigmented skin or extensive sun avoidance who are breastfed beyond twelve months without supplementation, because breast milk contains very little vitamin D and the infant's stores reflect the mother's status. The biochemical signature is a low or low normal calcium with a low phosphate, a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase and secondary hyperparathyroidism, with radiographs showing metaphyseal cupping, fraying and splaying at the fastest growing physes. Treatment replaces colecalciferol and ensures adequate calcium, since hungry bone during healing can otherwise drop the calcium further. The mother and any siblings should be tested, because the deficiency is a household exposure rather than an isolated event. Untreated disease produces permanent limb deformity, delayed motor milestones and hypocalcaemic seizures.
key_points: Breast milk alone beyond twelve months without supplementation is the usual Australian setting
Low phosphate with a very high alkaline phosphatase and raised parathyroid hormone is the signature
Symmetrical metaphyseal cupping and fraying distinguishes rickets from inflicted metaphyseal injury
Calcium is supplemented alongside colecalciferol because healing bone consumes it
Test the mother and siblings, since the exposure is shared
explanation.pearls: Recheck the alkaline phosphatase at four weeks rather than the vitamin D level: a falling alkaline phosphatase confirms the bone is remineralising, whereas the 25 hydroxyvitamin D rises within days of the first dose and says nothing about whether the rickets is healing.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Bone and Mineral Society: Vitamin D and health position statement

options.rationale: Calcitriol bypasses renal 1 alpha hydroxylation and is used in renal rickets or in vitamin D dependent rickets type 1, where that hydroxylation step is the problem. This child has normal renal function with a low 25 hydroxyvitamin D, so the deficient substrate is the native vitamin, not the active metabolite. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

The bowing here is the mechanical consequence of unmineralised growth plate rather than a primary structural deformity, and it remodels once mineralisation is restored. Bracing an actively rachitic limb treats the visible endpoint while leaving the metabolic cause running. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

Intravenous calcium is reserved for symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, seizures or a prolonged QT interval, none of which is present with a calcium of 2.12 mmol/L. Correcting calcium alone also leaves the vitamin D deficit that is driving secondary hyperparathyroidism. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

Metaphyseal irregularity does raise the question of inflicted injury, but the classic metaphyseal lesion of abuse is a corner or bucket handle fracture rather than symmetrical cupping and fraying, and it is not accompanied by a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase with a low 25 hydroxyvitamin D. The biochemical picture explains the radiology without a second mechanism. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Nutritional rickets from maternal and infant vitamin D deficiency is corrected by replacing the deficient substrate as colecalciferol, and calcium intake is increased at the same time because remineralising bone consumes calcium rapidly once treatment starts. Alkaline phosphatase and radiographic healing are used to confirm response over the following months. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

explanation.summary: Almost all childhood epistaxis is anterior and arises from Kiesselbach's plexus on the cartilaginous septum, where a superficial vascular network sits immediately under thin mucosa. The cycle is crusting, picking, bleeding and recrusting, which is why treatment aims at mucosal healing rather than at the vessel itself. First aid taught to families is ten minutes of continuous pressure on the soft part of the nose with the child leaning forwards, not pinching the bony bridge or tipping the head back. Investigation is reserved for bleeding that is bilateral, prolonged despite correct pressure, accompanied by bleeding elsewhere, or associated with an abnormal blood count. Persistent unilateral bleeding with nasal obstruction in an adolescent boy is the one presentation that mandates urgent imaging and specialist review.
key_points: Anterior septal vessels on Little's area are the source in the great majority of children
Antiseptic nasal cream is first line and outperforms cautery in children
Correct first aid is ten minutes of pressure on the soft nose while leaning forwards
Bilateral or prolonged bleeding or bleeding at other sites triggers a haematology workup
Unilateral bleeding with obstruction in an adolescent boy needs imaging for angiofibroma
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the child bled for more than twenty minutes despite correct pressure, or bled after tonsillectomy or dental extraction: those two answers, not the frequency of nosebleeds, are what separate a local septal lesion from undiagnosed von Willebrand disease.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Epistaxis in children

options.rationale: Examination under anaesthesia is for bleeding that is posterior, unable to be controlled, or suspicious for a mass such as juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in an adolescent boy with obstruction. An anterior septal source that is directly visible and stops with five minutes of pressure does not need theatre. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

Recurrent anterior bleeding in a child comes from dilated vessels on Little's area kept raw by crusting, digital trauma and dry air, and an antiseptic cream reduces colonisation and keeps the mucosa moist so the vessels re epithelialise. It outperforms cautery for first line use in children and avoids the discomfort and septal risk of a chemical burn. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

Silver nitrate cautery is second line in children once topical treatment has failed, because it is painful without topical anaesthesia and causes further crusting that can restart the cycle. Cautery is also never applied to both sides of the septum at one sitting given the risk of perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

A bleeding disorder workup is triggered by bleeding from both nostrils, bleeding lasting beyond ten to twenty minutes despite pressure, mucosal bleeding at other sites, a positive family history or an abnormal screening count. This child has a normal platelet count, a normal coagulation screen and none of those features. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

Tranexamic acid has a role in heavy or recurrent bleeding in patients with a diagnosed bleeding disorder or in acute uncontrolled epistaxis, not as seasonal prophylaxis in a child with a visible local lesion. Systemic antifibrinolysis does not address the mucosal breakdown that is generating the bleeding. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Tranexamic acid)

explanation.summary: Labial adhesions are an acquired fusion of the labia minora in the low oestrogen years of childhood, typically appearing between three months and six years, and are frequently mistaken by families for an absent or abnormal vaginal opening. The membrane is thin, translucent and midline, with a visible pale raphe, which distinguishes it from the thickened white atrophic skin of lichen sclerosus and from congenital anomalies where no separate structures are identifiable. Management is determined entirely by symptoms, and the asymptomatic child needs explanation, avoidance of soaps and bubble baths, and review. Treatment with topical oestrogen or corticosteroid is offered for post-void dribbling, recurrent urinary infection or voiding obstruction, and recurrence after any treatment is common until puberty. Vulval bruising, bleeding, or an adhesion with genital injury requires assessment for sexual abuse.
key_points: A thin translucent midline membrane with a pale raphe is diagnostic on inspection
Adhesions arise in the low oestrogen years and resolve as puberty approaches
Symptoms, not appearance, determine whether any treatment is offered
