Topical oestrogen or corticosteroid is for dribbling, infection or obstruction only
White atrophic plaques with fissuring indicate lichen sclerosus instead
explanation.pearls: Ask whether urine dribbles out when she stands up after voiding: that single symptom, caused by urine pooling behind the fusion, is the usual indication that turns an observed adhesion into one worth treating with topical oestrogen.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology

options.rationale: Topical oestrogen is reserved for adhesions causing urinary symptoms such as post-void dribbling, recurrent infection or voiding difficulty, since it commonly produces local irritation, breast budding and vaginal bleeding on withdrawal. Treating an asymptomatic child accepts those effects for no clinical gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

Forcible separation tears the epithelium, is painful and frightening for a preschool child, and leaves raw opposed surfaces that refuse at a higher rate than before. Separation under topical anaesthesia belongs only to symptomatic adhesions that have failed medical treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

Surgical division is limited to dense adhesions with urinary retention or recurrent infection that have not responded to topical treatment, and recurrence is common while oestrogen levels remain low. This is an operation for a finding that resolves by itself at puberty. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

Asymptomatic labial adhesions occur in oestrogen deficient vulval skin between about three months and six years, and they separate spontaneously as endogenous oestrogen rises at puberty if not before. Normal voiding with a visible urethral meatus and no infection confirms there is nothing to treat, so the intervention is explanation and simple vulval care. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

Topical corticosteroid is an alternative to oestrogen for symptomatic adhesions and is the treatment of choice for the white atrophic plaques of lichen sclerosus, which this child does not have. Steroid on normal vulval skin in an asymptomatic child risks local atrophy without addressing a problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

explanation.summary: Physiological phimosis is the normal state of the prepuce in childhood, where the inner preputial epithelium remains adherent to the glans and separates over years under the influence of intermittent erections and desquamation. Ballooning during voiding reflects urine entering that unseparated space and is not evidence of obstruction, provided the stream is normal and the child is comfortable. Pathological phimosis is a different entity, recognised by a white fibrotic ring at the preputial tip that does not pout on traction, and is usually caused either by forced retraction or by balanitis xerotica obliterans. It is treated first with a topical corticosteroid, which avoids surgery in most cases, with circumcision reserved for failure or for recurrent balanoposthitis. Preputial adhesions that are torn by retraction bleed, hurt, and heal with the scarring that later justifies the operation the family originally wanted.
key_points: Non retractility at four years is normal and roughly half of boys are retractile by ten
Ballooning with a normal stream indicates unseparated adhesions, not obstruction
A soft pink pouting preputial opening excludes pathological phimosis
Forced retraction causes the cicatricial scarring that creates true phimosis
Topical corticosteroid resolves most pathological phimosis without circumcision
explanation.pearls: Look for whether the preputial opening pouts outwards on gentle traction: a soft pink pout is physiological and needs no treatment, whereas a rigid white ring that stays contracted is balanitis xerotica obliterans and warrants a six week course of topical corticosteroid before any surgical referral.

sources.label: RACP: Circumcision of infant males position statement

options.rationale: The prepuce is normally adherent to the glans in early childhood and separates spontaneously, with only about half of boys retractile at ten years and nearly all by the late teens, and ballooning is the normal consequence of urine passing into a preputial space that has not yet separated. Forced retraction tears the adhesions and creates the scarred ring that genuinely does require treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

Topical corticosteroid is effective treatment for pathological phimosis, where a fibrotic white ring prevents retraction, and it resolves the majority of such cases without surgery. Applying it to a physiologically non retractile foreskin with a soft pink opening treats normal developmental anatomy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

Medical indications for circumcision are pathological phimosis with scarring, recurrent balanoposthitis and recurrent urinary infection with an abnormal urinary tract, none of which is present. Ballooning alone has never been an indication for operation. (Source: RACP: Circumcision of infant males position statement)
source_refs: RACP: Circumcision of infant males position statement

options.rationale: Graded retraction is the very practice that produces microtears, bleeding and secondary cicatricial scarring at the preputial tip, converting a normal foreskin into one that is pathologically phimotic. The father is already doing this and needs to be asked to stop. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

Antibiotics and imaging follow a confirmed urinary tract infection, and this boy has no fever, no dysuria and a negative dipstick, so there is no infection to treat or to image. Ballooning does not indicate obstruction and does not raise the risk of infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and cervical adenitis is the commonest periodic fever syndrome of childhood, typically starting before five years of age and running a clockwork cycle of three to six weeks. The diagnosis is clinical and depends on three things that are all present here: rigid periodicity, complete wellbeing between attacks, and normal growth and development. Inflammatory markers rise steeply during episodes and normalise fully between them, which is why a count taken during fever is so informative. A single dose of corticosteroid aborts an attack within hours, although it may shorten the interval to the next episode, and families are counselled about that trade off. The syndrome resolves spontaneously over several years, and tonsillectomy is reserved for children whose episodes remain disruptive.
key_points: Clockwork periodicity with complete wellness between attacks defines the syndrome
Normal growth and development is required and its absence forces a wider workup
A neutrophilia during fever excludes cyclical neutropenia, where fever coincides with the nadir
A single corticosteroid dose aborts an episode within hours and supports the diagnosis
Steroid may shorten the interval to the next attack, which families should be told
explanation.pearls: Time the blood count to the febrile day rather than the well interval: a neutrophil count above 1.5 x10^9/L taken during fever excludes cyclical neutropenia in one test and saves six weeks of twice weekly venepuncture in a preschool child.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Periodic fever syndromes

options.rationale: Serial counts across a cycle are how cyclical neutropenia is diagnosed, since the nadir is transient and dated to a 21 day rhythm. That diagnosis is already excluded here because the count taken during fever shows a neutrophilia of 11.2 x10^9/L, whereas cyclical neutropenia produces fever precisely when the neutrophils are at their lowest. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

Tonsillectomy does abolish episodes in a substantial proportion of children with this syndrome and is a recognised option, but it is considered only after the diagnosis has been confirmed and when episodes remain disruptive despite medical treatment. Proceeding to surgery before a steroid response has been demonstrated removes the cheapest diagnostic and therapeutic step. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

Antibiotic prophylaxis is directed at recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis, which would be supported by positive swabs during episodes and by a response to treatment. Three negative swabs during separate episodes, and fevers arriving on a fixed calendar rather than after exposures, place this outside a bacterial cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Familial Mediterranean fever is the monogenic syndrome to consider, but its attacks are irregular rather than calendar predictable, last one to three days, and feature serositis with abdominal or chest pain and an erysipelas like rash rather than aphthous ulceration and adenitis. Testing is reserved for that phenotype or for a suggestive family origin and history. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

Periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and adenitis is a clinical diagnosis resting on clockwork periodicity, complete wellness between episodes and normal growth, and a single corticosteroid dose aborts an episode within hours in a way no other cause of recurrent fever does. That response is therefore both the treatment and the strongest confirmation of the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

explanation.summary: A limp in a school-aged child is triaged first by whether it is acute and febrile, where septic arthritis and osteomyelitis dominate, or chronic and afebrile, where structural hip disease dominates. Legg Calve Perthes disease is idiopathic osteonecrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis, peaks between four and eight years, affects boys about four times as often, and presents with weeks of limp and referred thigh or knee pain rather than groin pain. The earliest and most reliable clinical sign is loss of internal rotation and abduction, which is why hip movement is examined in every child presenting with knee pain. Radiographs of both hips with a frog leg lateral are the first line investigation, and magnetic resonance is reserved for normal films with continuing suspicion. The key alternative diagnosis in an older or heavier child is a slipped upper femoral epiphysis, which shares referred knee pain and loss of internal rotation but demands immediate non weight bearing.
key_points: Knee pain in a child requires examination of the hip on the same side
Loss of internal rotation and abduction is the earliest sign of hip pathology
Perthes disease peaks at four to eight years and is four times commoner in boys
The frog leg lateral view shows subchondral collapse missed on the anteroposterior film
Normal inflammatory markers with weeks of symptoms exclude septic arthritis
explanation.pearls: Image both hips rather than the painful side alone: bilateral Perthes disease occurs in around ten per cent of children, and symmetrical involvement should prompt consideration of a skeletal dysplasia or hypothyroidism instead of idiopathic osteonecrosis.

sources.label: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric hip conditions
BMJ Best Practice: Legg Calve Perthes disease

options.rationale: Ultrasound with aspiration is the pathway for suspected septic arthritis, where an effusion is drained and cultured urgently. With a temperature of 36.8 degrees Celsius, a C reactive protein of 3 mg/L and a six week history, none of the Kocher predictors is met and an aspiration would be an invasive test for a diagnosis already excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

Weeks of painless limp with loss of internal rotation and abduction in a child of this age points to a structural problem of the femoral head, and plain films remain the first line test, with the frog leg lateral showing subchondral collapse that the anteroposterior view misses. Both hips are imaged because bilateral disease occurs in about one in ten children and changes the differential. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

Magnetic resonance detects marrow change before radiographic change and is the right test when films are normal but suspicion persists, or when the extent of head involvement must be staged. It is not the first imaging test in a child of this age, since it requires anaesthesia and plain films will usually answer the question. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

Observation is reasonable for transient synovitis, which follows a viral illness, settles within one to two weeks and does not restrict abduction to this degree. A limp persisting for six weeks without a preceding illness has moved outside the window where watchful waiting is safe. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

Cultures and washout are the response to a febrile child with a hot irritable hip and raised inflammatory markers, where delay costs the joint. An afebrile child with normal inflammatory markers over six weeks does not have a surgical emergency. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

explanation.summary: The red reflex test compares the reflection from both eyes simultaneously from about half a metre, and any asymmetry, dullness or white reflex is abnormal regardless of how well the infant appears to see. Retinoblastoma is the commonest intraocular malignancy of childhood, presents most often as leukocoria and second most often as a squint, and is diagnosed at a median age of around eighteen months for unilateral disease. Survival in Australia exceeds ninety five per cent when treatment is timely, so the outcome depends heavily on the interval between the first noticed abnormality and specialist assessment. Families very often report having seen the white pupil in photographs for months before presenting, having been reassured it was the camera. Every infant with an abnormal red reflex needs direct paediatric ophthalmology referral rather than investigation in primary care.
key_points: Compare both red reflexes simultaneously from about half a metre
Leukocoria and squint are the two commonest presentations of retinoblastoma
A reproducible pale pupil across separate photographs is not a camera artefact
A squint in an infant may be secondary to loss of central vision on that side
Refer directly to paediatric ophthalmology without arranging imaging first
explanation.pearls: Treat any squint appearing before three months, or any squint accompanied by an abnormal red reflex, as an urgent referral rather than a developmental variant, because a tumour that destroys central vision causes the eye to deviate and the squint is then the presenting sign of the cancer.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.rationale: A camera artefact appears in both eyes on the same image and varies with the angle of the flash, whereas a consistently pale reflex on one side across separate photographs is the classic way retinoblastoma first comes to attention. The artefact explanation has already failed the test of reproducibility. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.rationale: Routine referral is appropriate for a squint alone persisting beyond three months in an otherwise normal eye. Here the squint is secondary, because a tumour or opacity that destroys central vision causes the eye to drift, so treating it as an isolated strabismus would defer the urgent finding. (Source: RANZCO: Paediatric eye referral guidance)

Ultrasound can demonstrate an intraocular mass with calcification and forms part of the specialist assessment, but arranging it independently inserts a delay of days to weeks before anyone with the means to examine the retina sees the child. Examination under anaesthesia with indirect ophthalmoscopy is what actually establishes the diagnosis and stages the eye. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.rationale: An absent red reflex in an infant carries a differential of retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, retinopathy of prematurity and Coats disease, and all of them are sight threatening or life threatening on a timescale of weeks. Direct specialist referral is therefore made on the clinical finding alone, without waiting for imaging or a second opinion. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.rationale: Optometry and orthoptics manage refractive error and the amblyopia that follows a squint, and they cannot deliver the examination under anaesthesia and oncological staging this child may require. Referral to a service without that capability delays definitive assessment. (Source: RANZCO: Paediatric eye referral guidance)

explanation.summary: Ankyloglossia is common, present in up to one in ten newborns, and the great majority of affected infants feed without difficulty, so the decision to divide rests on demonstrated functional impairment rather than on the appearance of the frenulum. Assessment covers the mother, including nipple trauma, pain pattern and supply, and the infant, including latch, tongue elevation, milk transfer and weight trajectory. Australian practice is that infants regain birth weight by about fourteen days, and failure to do so triggers a structured feeding review rather than immediate intervention. Frenotomy of a thin anterior frenulum is a bedside procedure with low complication rates and reliable improvement in maternal nipple pain, but published trials show smaller and less certain effects on infant weight gain, and substantial improvement occurs in control groups receiving lactation support alone. Rising rates of division in Australia have prompted advice that lactation assessment precede referral in all but the clearest cases.
key_points: Ankyloglossia occurs in up to ten per cent of newborns and most feed normally
Division is decided on demonstrated function, not on the look of the frenulum
A compressed blanched nipple after feeding indicates a shallow latch
Good transfer of expressed milk shows suck and swallow are intact
Frenotomy improves nipple pain more reliably than it improves infant weight gain
explanation.pearls: Look at the shape of the nipple as it leaves the baby's mouth: a wedge shaped or blanched nipple means compression against the hard palate from a shallow latch and predicts a response to attachment correction, whereas a rounded nipple with continuing pain points to a genuinely restrictive frenulum.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Breastfeeding support
RCH CPG: Neonatal weight loss and feeding

options.rationale: Frenotomy relieves nipple pain within days in appropriately selected infants and is a reasonable subsequent step, but around half of infants referred with nipple pain and poor transfer improve with positioning and attachment work alone. Dividing the frenulum before that assessment treats an anatomical finding that may not be the operative cause. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Tongue tie)

Nipple shields can allow feeding to continue through severe trauma and are used under supervision, but they reduce milk transfer if attachment is not corrected and can entrench the shallow latch. Used as a standalone measure in an infant already below birth weight they risk compounding the weight problem. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Breastfeeding support)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Breastfeeding support

options.rationale: A compressed blanched nipple after feeding with a shallow latch is the signature of an attachment problem, and the fact that he transfers expressed milk quickly and settles shows that suck and swallow are intact and that the limiting step is at the breast. Structured feeding assessment is therefore the intervention that addresses both the pain and the weight, and it also defines whether the frenulum is genuinely restricting function. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Tongue tie)

Supplementation is indicated when weight loss is severe or when maternal supply is genuinely inadequate, neither of which applies when she is expressing good volumes. Routine formula top ups here would displace breast stimulation and reduce supply while leaving the attachment problem untouched. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Breastfeeding support)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Breastfeeding support

options.rationale: Formal frenuloplasty under general anaesthesia is reserved for a thick posterior or submucosal frenulum, or for revision after a failed simple division, and carries anaesthetic risk in a neonate. This infant has a thin anterior frenulum, which is divided at the bedside without anaesthesia if division is required at all. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Tongue tie)

explanation.summary: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, also called chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis, is an autoinflammatory bone disease of childhood that mimics infection but has no organism and does not respond to antibiotics. It has a median onset around ten years, affects girls more often, and characteristically involves the metaphyses of long bones, the clavicle, the mandible, the pelvis and the vertebrae. Associations with psoriasis, palmoplantar pustulosis and inflammatory bowel disease in the child or a first degree relative support the diagnosis. It is a diagnosis of exclusion built on a compatible whole body imaging pattern together with sterile histology, and biopsy is directed at excluding infection and malignancy rather than at confirming the condition. First line treatment is a non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug, with bisphosphonates or tumour necrosis factor inhibitors for spinal involvement or refractory disease, because untreated vertebral lesions can collapse.
key_points: Sterile bone inflammation unresponsive to antibiotics over months is the presenting pattern
Clavicle, mandible, metaphyses, pelvis and spine are the characteristic sites
Psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease in the child or a relative supports the diagnosis
Whole body magnetic resonance demonstrates clinically silent additional lesions
Non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are first line, with bisphosphonates for spinal disease
explanation.pearls: Look specifically at the vertebrae on whole body imaging: asymptomatic vertebral lesions occur in around a third of children with this condition and are the single finding that escalates treatment from a non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug to a bisphosphonate, because vertebra plana from untreated disease is irreversible.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis
RCH CPG: Bone and joint infection
BMJ Best Practice: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis

options.rationale: Sterile multifocal bone inflammation that has not responded to appropriate antistaphylococcal therapy is chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, and the diagnosis rests on demonstrating additional lesions, many of them clinically silent, at typical sites such as the metaphyses, clavicle, mandible and vertebrae. Whole body imaging without radiation both establishes that multifocal pattern and identifies vertebral involvement that would change management. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.rationale: Repeating the biopsy is what should be done when a single sterile sample is the only evidence against infection, since tuberculous and fungal osteomyelitis can require extended culture. Here the clinical course over four months, a second involved site and complete failure to respond to six weeks of therapy have already made an untreated indolent infection very unlikely. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.rationale: Bone scintigraphy also detects multifocal disease and was the traditional test, but it exposes a child to ionising radiation and is markedly less sensitive than magnetic resonance for early marrow oedema and for vertebral lesions. Where whole body magnetic resonance is available it has replaced scintigraphy for this indication. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.rationale: Marrow examination is mandatory when bone pain is accompanied by cytopenias, blasts on film, hepatosplenomegaly or systemic symptoms, since leukaemia presents with bone pain in a substantial minority of children. A normal blood count with normal differential and a preserved general condition over four months argues strongly against it. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone and joint infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bone and joint infection

options.rationale: Computed tomography characterises cortical destruction and sequestra better than other modalities and is useful when a surgical question exists. It images only the symptomatic site, so it cannot address the multifocality that defines the diagnosis, and it delivers radiation to the thyroid and breast tissue of a 10-year-old girl. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

explanation.summary: Hypoglycaemia in a child is classified first by the ketone response, because that single result splits the differential in two. A high ketone level indicates the normal fasting response and points to ketotic hypoglycaemia, glycogen storage disease or adrenal insufficiency, whereas a low ketone level in the face of hypoglycaemia is abnormal and points to hyperinsulinism or to a fatty acid oxidation defect, where fat cannot be converted into ketone bodies. Medium chain acyl coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency is the commonest such defect, is detected on the Australian newborn bloodspot screen, and presents in children missed by screening as hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly and transaminitis during a fasting illness, with a real risk of sudden death. The critical sample, comprising glucose, ketones, insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, free fatty acids, acylcarnitines, ammonia, lactate and the first urine for organic acids, is valid only during hypoglycaemia. Long term management is avoidance of fasting with an emergency regimen of frequent carbohydrate during illness, which converts a potentially fatal condition into a manageable one.
key_points: The ketone level at the time of hypoglycaemia divides the differential in two
Ketones below 1.0 mmol/L during hypoglycaemia are inappropriately low
Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly suggests a fatty acid oxidation defect
The critical sample is interpretable only while the child is hypoglycaemic
Children who arrive from overseas may have had no newborn bloodspot screening
explanation.pearls: Collect the first urine passed after the hypoglycaemic episode as well as the blood: urinary organic acids showing dicarboxylic aciduria without ketonuria can secure a diagnosis of medium chain acyl coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency even when the blood samples were taken slightly late, and the family can then be given an emergency regimen that prevents sudden death during the next gastroenteritis.

sources.label: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Newborn bloodspot screening
BMJ Best Practice: Inherited disorders of fatty acid oxidation

options.rationale: Treating the hypoglycaemia first is correct, but the metabolic investigations are interpretable only in the hypoglycaemic state, because acylcarnitines, free fatty acids, insulin, cortisol and urinary organic acids all normalise within hours of glucose. Deferring them converts a diagnosable episode into one that will have to be reproduced by a supervised fast. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

Glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen and works in hyperinsulinism, where stores are preserved, but after 24 hours of fasting illness those stores are exhausted and the response will be poor. It also leaves the child hypoglycaemic for longer than intravenous glucose while the diagnostic window closes. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

Oral carbohydrate is first line for a hypoglycaemic child who is alert and able to protect the airway, and it is what the family should use at home during future illnesses. A drowsy toddler who has been vomiting for a day cannot be relied upon to absorb or protect, so this route is unsafe here. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

Adrenal insufficiency does cause hypoglycaemia and a cortisol forms part of the sample set, but it typically comes with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypotension, and the sodium here is 138 mmol/L. Giving hydrocortisone as the single intervention also treats a differential that the ketone result argues against. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

A blood ketone of 0.2 mmol/L alongside a glucose of 1.8 mmol/L is inappropriately low, since a normal child mounts a ketotic response to fasting hypoglycaemia, and that combination with hepatomegaly and transaminitis points to a fatty acid oxidation defect that newborn screening would have caught. The samples that identify it are valid only while the child is hypoglycaemic, so they are collected at the moment intravenous access is obtained rather than delaying the glucose. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation is the commonest elbow injury of early childhood and peaks between one and four years, when the annular ligament is still lax enough to slip over the radial head under longitudinal traction. The child characteristically refuses to use the limb rather than localising pain, which can be misread as a fracture or even as a brachial plexus problem. The whole diagnosis rests on the mechanism plus a normal palpation of every long bone in the limb, and the treatment is a bedside manoeuvre. Radiographs are for the child whose story or examination does not fit, or whose arm does not recover after two attempts.
key_points: Mechanism is axial traction on a pronated extended arm, not a fall or a blow
The arm is held flexed and pronated with no swelling, deformity or bone tenderness
Supination with flexion, or hyperpronation, reduces it at the bedside
Imaging is indicated only for atypical features or failure of two attempts
Return of spontaneous use within 30 minutes confirms the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: If the child is still not using the arm 30 minutes after a second reduction attempt, abandon the diagnosis and radiograph the elbow, because a supracondylar or radial neck fracture presents identically in a toddler who cannot localise pain.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

options.rationale: Slinging treats a presumed fracture and leaves a reducible subluxation in place for a week, during which the child continues not to use the arm. Slings are also poorly tolerated at this age and are not part of the management of a subluxed radial head. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

Axial traction on an extended pronated arm displaces the annular ligament over the radial head, and the diagnosis is made on the mechanism plus the absence of swelling, deformity and focal bone tenderness. Reduction by supination then flexion, or by hyperpronation, is done at the bedside and most children use the arm again within 30 minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

Radiographs are reserved for an atypical mechanism, swelling, deformity, focal bone tenderness, or failure of two reduction attempts, none of which apply here. Films in this setting are usually normal and delay a manoeuvre that is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

A pseudoparalysed arm in a toddler does raise clavicular and humeral injury, but each of those requires a fall or a direct blow and produces localised tenderness over the injured bone. Both are absent, which is what separates this presentation from an occult fracture. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

Backslabbing is the answer for a suspected undisplaced fracture with normal initial films, such as a toddler fracture of the tibia after a twisting fall. Here the mechanism is longitudinal traction and there is no bone tenderness, so immobilisation treats the wrong problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

explanation.summary: The toddler fracture is an undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibial shaft produced by a twisting force in a child who has recently begun walking, and it is the commonest cause of an acute atraumatic looking limp in this age group. Initial radiographs miss a substantial proportion because the fracture line is hairline and may be visible in only one plane. The decision to treat therefore rests on the mechanism and on point tenderness over the tibia, not on the film. The differential that must be actively excluded is infection, which is why fever, systemic upset and inflammatory markers are checked before committing to a mechanical diagnosis.
key_points: Low energy twisting injury in a newly walking child is the classic mechanism
Initial radiographs are commonly normal, so a negative film does not exclude it
Point tenderness over the tibial shaft with a normal hip examination localises it
Above knee immobilisation for two to three weeks is the usual treatment
Fever or raised inflammatory markers should redirect towards osteomyelitis
explanation.pearls: Periosteal new bone becomes visible on repeat radiographs about ten to fourteen days after a toddler fracture, so a film taken at the two week review confirms the diagnosis retrospectively while an immediate repeat film usually does not.

options.rationale: An undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibia after a low energy twisting injury is frequently invisible on initial films, and focal tibial tenderness with a consistent mechanism is enough to treat it as one. Immobilisation gives comfort and protection, and the diagnosis is confirmed at review by periosteal reaction rather than by repeating films early. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

Hip ultrasound looks for the effusion of transient synovitis or septic arthritis, both of which restrict and pain passive hip rotation. Full painless hip rotation with tenderness localised to the tibial shaft points away from the hip entirely. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

Focal bone tenderness does raise osteomyelitis, which is why the history matters: this child is afebrile, well, and has a clear mechanical trigger the day before with a normal C reactive protein. Osteomyelitis in a toddler usually shows fever, systemic upset or raised inflammatory markers. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute osteomyelitis)

Simple analgesia alone is reasonable for a soft tissue injury with diffuse tenderness, but not when tenderness is point localised over a long bone. Walking on an unprotected undisplaced fracture prolongs pain and risks displacement. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

Bone scanning belongs to the limping child with no localising signs and no mechanism, where the site of pathology is genuinely unknown. Here the mechanism and the tender point already identify the bone, so the scan adds radiation without changing treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

explanation.summary: Inturned feet at birth span a spectrum from a positional deformity caused by intrauterine crowding, which corrects passively and needs only reassurance, to a structural deformity with fixed hindfoot equinus, cavus and forefoot adduction. The examination that separates them is whether the foot can be brought to a neutral ankle with gentle pressure, supported by secondary signs of a true structural problem such as deep creases and a smaller calf. Structural deformity is treated by the Ponseti method, usually with a percutaneous tendo Achilles tenotomy at the end of the casting sequence, followed by a foot abduction brace for several years. Relapse is driven almost entirely by brace non-adherence, so parental counselling at the outset matters as much as the casts.
key_points: Correctability to neutral by gentle pressure defines a positional deformity
Fixed equinus, deep creases and calf wasting indicate a structural deformity
Serial manipulation and above knee casting is first line and starts within weeks
Most children need a tendo Achilles tenotomy before the final cast
Long term bracing is required and non-adherence is the main cause of relapse
explanation.pearls: The foot abduction brace after Ponseti casting is worn 23 hours a day for three months and then at night until about age four, and stopping it early is the single strongest predictor of recurrence.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.rationale: Passive stretching is the treatment for a positional deformity, which is defined by being correctable to neutral by gentle hand pressure, as the left foot is here. A hindfoot that cannot be brought out of equinus will not respond to stretching and will stiffen further if casting is delayed. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

A rigid equinus hindfoot with medial and posterior creases and calf wasting is a structural deformity rather than an intrauterine packing problem, and the Ponseti method of weekly manipulation and above knee casting is the first line treatment in Australia. Starting within the first few weeks exploits ligamentous laxity and reduces the proportion of children who need extensive surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

Hip imaging is appropriate where a risk factor for developmental dysplasia is present, but this baby was not breech, has a normal family history and has stable hips on examination. Waiting six weeks before addressing a rigid foot also wastes the period of greatest correctability. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.rationale: Primary surgical release was the historical approach and is now reserved for deformity that resists or relapses after a full casting program. Operating before casting produces a stiffer, more painful foot in the long term than the same result achieved by manipulation. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

Strapping below the knee cannot hold the corrected position because the deformity includes hindfoot equinus, which requires the knee to be flexed and included in the cast. Below knee immobilisation allows the foot to rotate within the cast and correction is lost. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

explanation.summary: Napkin rash is usually an irritant contact dermatitis from prolonged contact with urine and faeces, and its signature is that it affects the convex surfaces and spares the depths of the creases. Candidal infection is the common secondary problem, and it reverses that distribution by growing preferentially in the warm moist folds while throwing off satellite lesions onto adjacent skin. Recent antibiotics, recent diarrhoea and a rash that has failed barrier treatment all raise the likelihood. Rash that fails a proper antifungal course should prompt reconsideration of seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis, zinc deficiency or, rarely, Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
key_points: Irritant napkin dermatitis spares the creases, candidal infection involves them
Satellite papules and pustules beyond the main plaque are the key sign
Recent antibiotic exposure is a common precipitant in infants
Topical imidazole at each change is first line, continued a week after clearing
Potent steroids are avoided under the occlusion of a nappy
explanation.pearls: A napkin rash that persists despite both barrier and antifungal treatment, especially with petechiae or erosions in the folds, should prompt consideration of Langerhans cell histiocytosis and dermatology referral rather than a further topical trial.

options.rationale: Involvement of the skin creases with satellite papules and pustules beyond the confluent area is the pattern of candidal infection, which is favoured by the recent antibiotic course. A topical imidazole such as clotrimazole or miconazole applied with each change, continued for a week after clearance, is the treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Napkin rash)

Barrier preparations and air exposure are the treatment for irritant dermatitis, which characteristically spares the creases because urine and faeces do not reach them. This rash involves the creases and has already failed a week of exactly this approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Napkin rash)

Moderate and high potency steroids are avoided under a nappy because occlusion greatly increases absorption and risks atrophy and striae in thin infant skin. Steroids also worsen untreated candidal infection by suppressing the local inflammatory response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Oral antibiotics treat bacterial superinfection, which presents with honey coloured crusting, pustules concentrated within the plaque, or systemic upset rather than a creased distribution with outlying lesions. A further antibiotic course would in fact make candidal overgrowth worse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Microscopy and culture are reserved for rash that fails appropriate antifungal treatment or where an unusual organism is suspected. The clinical pattern here is diagnostic enough to treat, and waiting several days for a culture leaves a distressed infant untreated. (Source: RCH CPG: Napkin rash)

explanation.summary: Labial adhesion affects up to around two percent of prepubertal girls and arises because the unoestrogenised vulval epithelium is thin and sticks together after minor irritation. It is usually an incidental finding on bathing or nappy changing and parents commonly fear either an obstruction or abuse, so the consultation is largely about explanation. Treatment is directed only at symptoms, with topical oestrogen for obstruction, pooling or recurrent infection, and surgery reserved for failure of that. The adhesion resolves as endogenous oestrogen rises at puberty, and recurrence after any treatment is common until then.
key_points: It is acquired from the low oestrogen state of childhood, not congenital
Asymptomatic adhesion with a normal stream needs explanation only
Topical oestrogen is reserved for obstruction, pooling or recurrent infection
Forcible separation causes bleeding and firmer readherence
It is not a sign of sexual abuse in the absence of other findings
explanation.pearls: Topical oestrogen applied to the fusion line for more than about six to eight weeks can produce breast budding and vulval pigmentation, both of which reverse on stopping, so courses are time limited and reviewed rather than repeated indefinitely.

options.rationale: Surgical division is reserved for adhesions causing urinary obstruction, recurrent infection or symptoms that persist after topical treatment. It carries a high recurrence rate while the child remains oestrogen deficient, so it is not a first response to an asymptomatic finding. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

Forcible separation is painful, frequently bleeds, and creates raw surfaces that readhere more firmly than before. It also risks a frightening genital examination for a child in whom nothing needs fixing. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

Labial adhesion is an acquired consequence of the low oestrogen state of childhood and resolves spontaneously around puberty in the great majority, with many separating earlier. With a normal stream, no infections and no symptoms there is nothing to treat, so explanation plus avoidance of soaps and bubble baths is the management. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

Topical oestrogen is the treatment when adhesions obstruct the stream, cause pooling with post-void dribbling or drive recurrent urinary infection, none of which apply here. It also causes breast budding and vulval pigmentation with prolonged use, so it is not used for cosmetic indications. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

Labial adhesion is not a finding associated with sexual abuse, and the examination shows no bruising, tears or other injury and no concerning history or behaviour change. Referral on this finding alone subjects the child to an unnecessary examination. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: A capillary malformation is a permanent developmental anomaly of dermal capillaries, present and fully formed at birth, and is distinguished from the common salmon patch by its unilateral distribution, sharp midline border and failure to fade. When it involves the skin supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, particularly the forehead and upper eyelid, it is associated with Sturge Weber syndrome. The two associated problems are ipsilateral glaucoma, which is frequently congenital and silent, and a leptomeningeal vascular malformation that causes seizures, hemiparesis and developmental impairment. Management is therefore multidisciplinary, combining lifelong ophthalmic pressure surveillance, neurological assessment with magnetic resonance imaging, and pulsed dye laser for the skin.
key_points: Capillary malformation is present at birth, persists and darkens over decades
Salmon patch is symmetrical, blanches readily and fades in the first year
Forehead and upper eyelid involvement raises Sturge Weber syndrome
Ipsilateral glaucoma is common, often congenital, and initially asymptomatic
Leptomeningeal involvement causes seizures and warrants neurology review
explanation.pearls: Intraocular pressure in a child with a forehead capillary malformation needs checking at diagnosis and then periodically for life, because glaucoma develops after infancy in a substantial minority whose first examination was entirely normal.

options.rationale: Fading is the natural history of the salmon patch, which sits on the glabella, eyelids or nape, is symmetrical and blanches readily. A unilateral capillary malformation respecting the midline persists, darkens and thickens with age. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular malformations)

Propranolol shrinks proliferating infantile haemangiomas, which are absent or faint at birth and then grow rapidly over weeks. A capillary malformation is fully formed at birth and static, and does not respond to beta blockade. (Source: RCH CPG: Haemangioma of infancy)

Pulsed dye laser is the established treatment for the cutaneous mark and is often started in infancy, so this is part of the plan rather than wrong in itself. It does not address the ocular and intracranial risks, which are the time-critical part of the assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular malformations)

A capillary malformation involving the forehead and upper eyelid carries a substantial risk of ipsilateral glaucoma, which is present at birth in about half of affected children and can otherwise appear at any age, and of leptomeningeal angiomatosis. Glaucoma in infancy is silent until the eye is damaged, so early and repeated intraocular pressure measurement is the priority, alongside neurology input and imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular malformations)

Biopsy is not required because capillary malformation is a clinical diagnosis based on a flat, sharply demarcated, persistent patch present from birth. It also delays the assessments that actually change outcome and leaves a scar on the face. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular malformations)

explanation.summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is diagnosed clinically when two or more established criteria are present, among them six or more flat brown macules, skin fold freckling, two or more neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma, Lisch nodules, a characteristic bone lesion and an affected first degree relative. About half of cases arise from new mutations, so an absent family history does not argue against it. Because features accumulate with age, the pigmented macules often appear in infancy while freckling, neurofibromas and Lisch nodules follow through childhood, and a young child may not yet meet criteria. Management is lifelong annual surveillance for treatable complications rather than treatment of the skin.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical and needs two or more established criteria
Six or more macules over 5 mm plus skin fold freckling meets the threshold
About half of cases are new mutations, so family history is often negative
Annual review covers blood pressure, vision, spine, puberty and development
Routine neuroimaging of an asymptomatic child is not recommended
explanation.pearls: Hypertension in a child with neurofibromatosis type 1 should never be attributed to essential hypertension, because renal artery stenosis and phaeochromocytoma are both over represented and both are correctable once identified.

sources.label: Genetics in Medicine: Revised diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1

options.rationale: Routine neuroimaging of an asymptomatic child is not recommended, because incidental findings are common and the optic pathway tumours it might detect are managed on the basis of visual and clinical progression rather than on images alone. Imaging is triggered by declining acuity, proptosis, precocious puberty or new neurological signs. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

The flat brown macules are asymptomatic markers of the underlying condition and are not treated, unlike the dermal neurofibromas that may be removed later for symptoms or appearance. Directing care at the pigmentation misses the systemic surveillance that determines outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

One or two flat brown macules are indeed a common and benign finding in healthy children and need nothing. Six or more of them combined with skin fold freckling meets established diagnostic criteria, which changes the finding from incidental to diagnostic. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

Molecular testing is useful where the clinical picture is incomplete, in a young child with pigmentation alone, or for reproductive counselling. Where criteria are already met clinically the diagnosis does not wait on a result, and deferring surveillance is what causes harm. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

Six or more flat brown macules over 5 mm with axillary or inguinal freckling satisfies the clinical diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1, so the task is surveillance rather than further confirmation. Annual review targets the complications that are treatable if found early, principally hypertension from renal artery stenosis or phaeochromocytoma, optic pathway glioma, scoliosis and learning difficulty. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy typically begins between four and ten years in a neurologically normal child and produces frequent brief lapses with abrupt onset and offset and no postictal state, which is what separates it from focal impaired awareness seizures. Hyperventilation for two to three minutes provokes an event in most untreated children and is a useful bedside confirmation before the electroencephalogram. The head to head comparative evidence places ethosuximide and valproate ahead of lamotrigine for seizure freedom, with ethosuximide producing less attentional impairment than valproate. Most children remit by adolescence, although a minority develop generalised tonic clonic seizures or evolve to juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, so review of seizure type continues after control is achieved.
key_points: Abrupt onset and offset with no postictal confusion characterises absence
Hyperventilation for two to three minutes provokes an event in most children
The electroencephalogram shows generalised 3 Hz spike and wave
Ethosuximide matches valproate for control with less attentional impairment
Carbamazepine and related sodium channel agents aggravate absence seizures
explanation.pearls: Ethosuximide has no activity against generalised tonic clonic seizures, so the emergence of a convulsion in a child controlled on it is an indication to change agent rather than to increase the dose.

options.rationale: Carbamazepine is effective for focal epilepsy but aggravates generalised absence and myoclonic seizures and can precipitate absence status. This error occurs when brief staring is misread as focal impaired awareness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

For typical childhood absence epilepsy ethosuximide has equivalent seizure freedom to valproate with significantly less attentional impairment, and it is preferred over valproate in girls because of the teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks of valproate across the reproductive years. It does not cover generalised tonic clonic seizures, so the treatment is revisited if those appear. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Valproate controls absence seizures well and also covers generalised tonic clonic seizures, so it remains an option where those coexist. In a girl it is avoided where an equally effective alternative exists, because of teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental effects that persist as a consideration for decades. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Levetiracetam is widely used in generalised epilepsies and is well tolerated in other respects, but its efficacy specifically against absence seizures is lower than ethosuximide or valproate in comparative trials. It is a later choice rather than a first line agent for this syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Clobazam is used as an add on when first line agents fail or during clusters, and tolerance to its effect commonly develops. Starting with it forgoes the agent with the best evidence for attention preserved seizure control in this syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Scalp dermatophyte infection is the one form of tinea that always requires systemic treatment, because the organism invades the hair shaft and follicle where topical agents cannot reach. It presents along a spectrum from subtle scaling with broken hairs, often mistaken for seborrhoeic dermatitis or alopecia areata, to a kerion, which is a boggy inflammatory mass with pustules and regional lymphadenopathy that is frequently mistaken for a bacterial abscess. Painless epilation of hairs within the lesion helps distinguish it from bacterial infection. Scrapings and plucked hairs should be sent before starting treatment because the choice and duration of agent differs between Microsporum and Trichophyton species, but treatment is not delayed waiting for culture.
key_points: Scalp tinea always requires a systemic antifungal, never topical alone
Kerion is a hypersensitivity response, not an abscess, and is not drained
Hairs within the lesion epilate painlessly, unlike in bacterial folliculitis
Zoophilic sources include guinea pigs, kittens and puppies
Topical corticosteroid alone produces tinea incognito
explanation.pearls: Griseofulvin remains preferred for Microsporum canis, the species most often acquired from pets, whereas terbinafine clears Trichophyton species in a shorter course, so the culture result determines both agent and duration even though treatment begins empirically.

options.rationale: Topical agents cannot penetrate the hair follicle where the organism resides, which is why this lesion has progressed over a month of cream. Antifungal shampoo is a useful adjunct that reduces spore shedding to contacts, but it does not clear the infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Incision and drainage treats a true scalp abscess, which is fluctuant, and this lesion is boggy but not fluctuant because the swelling is a hypersensitivity response rather than a collection of pus. Surgery adds scarring and permanent hair loss to an area that can recover with medical treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Antibacterial treatment addresses the pustules and crust but not the dermatophyte driving them, and the lesion recurs once it is stopped. Bacterial folliculitis of the scalp does not usually produce painless hair epilation or a six week boggy plaque. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A boggy plaque with painless hair epilation and occipital nodes is a kerion, the inflammatory form of scalp dermatophyte infection, and it requires a systemic antifungal such as griseofulvin or terbinafine because topicals cannot reach the follicle. Guinea pigs are a common zoophilic source in Australia, so treating the animals and screening household contacts prevents reinfection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Steroid alone suppresses the inflammatory response while allowing the dermatophyte to spread, producing the altered appearance known as tinea incognito. Short adjunctive oral steroid is occasionally used alongside an antifungal in severe kerion, but never as sole treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Brachial plexus birth injury complicates roughly one to three per thousand births and is associated with shoulder dystocia, high birth weight and instrumental delivery, although it also occurs after uncomplicated births and after caesarean section. The commonest pattern involves the upper roots and produces the characteristic adducted internally rotated arm with an extended elbow and pronated forearm, while the hand is spared, so grasp remains intact. Features that indicate a more severe or avulsion injury include a flail insensate limb, an ipsilateral Horner syndrome from first thoracic root involvement, and diaphragmatic paralysis from phrenic nerve injury. The majority recover substantially by three months, and recovery of elbow flexion within that window is the accepted prognostic marker used to decide on referral for nerve reconstruction.
key_points: Upper root injury spares the hand, so grasp is preserved
Physiotherapy from the first days prevents contracture during recovery
Return of biceps function by around three months indicates good prognosis
Horner syndrome or diaphragmatic paralysis indicates a severe injury
Immobilisation worsens outcome by causing joint contracture
explanation.pearls: An ipsilateral ptosis and small pupil in a newborn with a weak arm indicates first thoracic root avulsion, which carries a far worse prognosis than an upper trunk injury and warrants early referral to a specialist brachial plexus service rather than watchful waiting.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Brachial plexus birth injury

options.rationale: Prolonged immobilisation was historical practice and causes contracture at the shoulder and elbow, which worsens the long term functional result. Gentle passive movement is started early precisely to prevent that. (Source: RCH CPG: Brachial plexus injury)

An upper trunk injury affecting the fifth and sixth cervical roots produces this posture with a preserved grasp, and most infants recover spontaneously with physiotherapy to maintain range and prevent contracture. Return of elbow flexion is the accepted marker of a good prognosis, and failure of biceps function to recover by around three months is the trigger for surgical referral. (Source: RCH CPG: Brachial plexus injury)

Early exploration is considered only where the whole plexus is involved with a flail insensate arm, or where Horner syndrome or phrenic involvement indicates avulsion. Operating in the first weeks on an injury with a high spontaneous recovery rate exposes the infant to unnecessary surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Brachial plexus injury)

Electrophysiology performed in the first week cannot distinguish neurapraxia from axonal rupture because Wallerian degeneration has not yet occurred, so the result does not guide management. Serial clinical assessment of biceps function is the practical prognostic tool. (Source: RCH CPG: Brachial plexus injury)

Proximal humeral or clavicular injury does cause pseudoparalysis after a difficult delivery and is a reasonable differential, but it produces pain on handling, local swelling or crepitus rather than a fixed posture with absent reflexes. Absent biceps and brachioradialis reflexes with a normal radiograph point to a nerve rather than a bone problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Brachial plexus injury)

explanation.summary: Most tight foreskins in boys are physiological, reflecting incomplete separation of the prepuce from the glans, and they need only reassurance or a course of topical steroid. Balanitis xerotica obliterans is the important exception and is the only absolute medical indication for circumcision in childhood, becoming more likely after about age five. The history that separates them is loss of a foreskin that previously retracted, and the sign is a firm white sclerotic ring replacing the soft preputial tip. Left untreated it can progress to involve the meatus and navicular fossa, producing meatal stenosis and urethral stricture, so boys need follow up after circumcision rather than simple discharge.
key_points: Physiological non retractility improves with age and responds to topical steroid
Loss of previously present retractility suggests an acquired scarring process
A firm white sclerotic preputial ring is the sign of balanitis xerotica obliterans
Circumcision is the definitive treatment and provides histological confirmation
Meatal and urethral involvement can follow, so follow up is required
explanation.pearls: Balanitis xerotica obliterans is the one absolute medical indication for circumcision in boys, and because up to a fifth develop meatal stenosis the urinary stream should be reviewed at follow up rather than assuming the operation has ended the problem.

options.rationale: Reassurance and gentle hygiene is correct for physiological non retractility, in which the foreskin is soft, pink and simply not yet separated from the glans. A previously retractile foreskin that has become fixed by a firm white ring is an acquired scarring process, not a developmental stage. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

Topical steroid successfully loosens a physiologically tight foreskin in most boys and is the usual first step for that problem. Where the tip is sclerotic and white, steroid alone rarely restores retractility and, more importantly, leaves the underlying scarring process untreated and unconfirmed. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

A previously retractile foreskin that becomes fixed by a firm white sclerotic ring, with spraying, ballooning and recurrent inflammation, is balanitis xerotica obliterans, the genital form of lichen sclerosus. Circumcision is the definitive treatment and the excised tissue confirms the histological diagnosis, which matters because the meatus and glans need ongoing surveillance. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

Oral antibiotics treat an acute bacterial balanitis, which presents with an acutely red, swollen, tender and often discharging prepuce. The current appearance is a chronic sclerotic change with no active infection, and the recurrent sore episodes are a consequence of the underlying process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Upper tract imaging would be relevant if there were recurrent urinary infection or a suspicion of obstruction affecting the kidneys, neither of which is present with a negative dipstick and normal growth. Spraying here is caused by a fixed narrow preputial opening rather than by anything upstream. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets remains the commonest form of rickets in Australia and is concentrated in breastfed infants without supplementation, children with darker skin, those with limited sun exposure for cultural or medical reasons, and those avoiding dairy. Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal calcium absorption, which drives a compensatory rise in parathyroid hormone that maintains calcium at the expense of renal phosphate wasting, producing the characteristic low phosphate with markedly raised alkaline phosphatase. The radiographic hallmarks are metaphyseal cupping, fraying and widening at the fastest growing physes such as the distal radius and knee. The main differential is X linked hypophosphataemic rickets, which shares the low phosphate but has a normal vitamin D and requires entirely different treatment.
key_points: Low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with raised parathyroid hormone indicates nutritional rickets
Low phosphate arises from parathyroid driven renal phosphate wasting
Alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised and is a useful screening test
Calcium is given with vitamin D to prevent hypocalcaemia during remineralisation
Normal vitamin D with low phosphate points to X linked hypophosphataemia instead
explanation.pearls: Starting vitamin D without concurrent calcium in a severely deficient child can precipitate hungry bone hypocalcaemia and seizures within the first days of treatment, which is why replacement is always given as both together.

sources.label: Medical Journal of Australia: Vitamin D and health in adults and children in Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: A low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with secondary elevation of parathyroid hormone, low normal calcium and low phosphate is the biochemical signature of nutritional rickets, and the combination of prolonged unsupplemented breastfeeding, dairy avoidance and low sun exposure explains it. Treatment is vitamin D replacement together with calcium, since giving vitamin D alone to a calcium deplete child can precipitate hypocalcaemia as bone mineralisation resumes. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

Phosphate with calcitriol treats X linked hypophosphataemic rickets, in which renal phosphate wasting produces a low phosphate with a normal calcium, a normal or only mildly raised parathyroid hormone and a normal 25 hydroxyvitamin D. Here the vitamin D is profoundly low and the parathyroid hormone markedly raised, which is the opposite pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

Alkali therapy treats the rickets of renal tubular acidosis, which is identified by a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with a low venous bicarbonate. The bicarbonate is 24 mmol/L, which excludes that mechanism. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

Surgical correction is considered for persistent pathological bowing after the metabolic cause has been treated, or for a growth plate disorder such as tibia vara. Most bowing from nutritional rickets remodels once mineralisation is restored, so operating first would be premature. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

Watchful waiting suits physiological bowing, which is symmetrical, present from the start of walking, resolves by about age two and has normal biochemistry and radiographs. Metaphyseal cupping and fraying with a raised alkaline phosphatase is pathological and progresses if untreated. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

explanation.summary: Scurvy is reappearing in Australian paediatric practice in children with severely restricted diets, most often those with autism spectrum disorder, avoidant restrictive food intake disorder or neurodisability. Vitamin C is a cofactor for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen, so deficiency weakens vessel walls, periosteum and osteoid, producing subperiosteal bleeding that is exquisitely painful and often mistaken for infection, malignancy or non accidental injury. The classic skin findings of perifollicular haemorrhage and corkscrew hairs, along with gingival swelling and bleeding in a child with erupted teeth, are the clue that distinguishes it. Clinical response to replacement is rapid, with pain easing within days and walking usually restored within weeks, and the long term work is on expanding the food range.
key_points: Suspect scurvy in restricted diets lasting more than about three months
Perifollicular haemorrhage and corkscrew hairs are highly suggestive
Subperiosteal bleeding causes bone pain and refusal to weight bear
Normal inflammatory markers and film argue against infection and leukaemia
Symptoms improve within days of vitamin C replacement
explanation.pearls: Gum changes in scurvy only occur around erupted teeth, so an edentulous infant with the same deficiency presents with irritability, pseudoparalysis and leg pain alone and the mouth looks entirely normal.

options.rationale: Perifollicular haemorrhage with corkscrew hairs, gingival bleeding and bone pain severe enough to stop a child walking, in a child whose diet has excluded fruit and vegetables for two years, is scurvy. Vitamin C is required for collagen hydroxylation, so deficiency produces fragile vessels and defective osteoid, and symptoms respond within days of replacement. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutrition)

Osteomyelitis is the usual explanation for bone pain with refusal to weight bear, but it is typically unilateral and accompanied by fever and raised inflammatory markers. Afebrile bilateral metaphyseal pain with a C reactive protein of 6 mg/L does not fit, and the gum and skin findings are unexplained by infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute osteomyelitis)

Leukaemia genuinely presents with bone pain, refusal to walk and bleeding gums, and is the diagnosis that must not be missed. Against it here are a normal white cell count and platelet count, a film without blasts, no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly, and a dietary history that supplies an alternative explanation. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutrition)

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis causes joint pain with swelling, warmth and early morning stiffness that eases through the day, and the pain localises to joints rather than to the shafts and metaphyses. There is no effusion or joint warmth, and bleeding gums are not a feature. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutrition)

Vitamin D deficiency also causes bone pain and osteopenia in a child with a restricted diet, so it is a reasonable competing nutritional diagnosis and often coexists. It does not produce perifollicular haemorrhage, corkscrew hairs or gingival bleeding, which are specific to defective collagen synthesis. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis affects up to one in 250 infants and is associated with instrumental delivery, breech presentation and a crowded intrauterine position. The head tilts towards the shortened muscle and the chin rotates away from it, so a right sided lesion gives a right tilt with the chin to the left. Positional plagiocephaly follows because the infant lies consistently on one side of the occiput, and developmental dysplasia of the hip is found in a small but real proportion, so the hips must be examined at the same visit. Physiotherapy started before six months resolves most cases without surgery, while presentations left beyond one year increasingly need surgical release.
key_points: The head tilts towards the tight muscle and the chin turns away from it
A palpable mass within the sternocleidomastoid supports a muscular cause
Full passive eye movement argues against a compensatory ocular head posture
Examine the hips, since dysplasia coexists in a minority of infants
Plagiocephaly is secondary and resolves as the neck posture corrects
explanation.pearls: Failure of the head tilt to improve after six weeks of physiotherapy, or the appearance of a tilt after four months of age in a previously straight infant, should prompt imaging for a posterior fossa tumour rather than a further course of stretching.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis in children

options.rationale: Ultrasound is reserved for a mass with atypical features such as rapid growth, a location outside the muscle belly, or overlying skin change, none of which are present. Imaging a typical muscular mass delays the stretching program, which is most effective in the first few months. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

A firm mass within the sternocleidomastoid with restricted passive rotation away from the tilt is the classic picture, and graded passive stretching with positioning to encourage active rotation resolves the great majority when started before six months. Referral is made on the clinical findings alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Bony torticollis from a hemivertebra or an atlantoaxial anomaly gives a fixed tilt without a palpable muscle mass, and passive correction is blocked rather than merely restricted. Muscular restriction yields partially to gentle pressure while bony restriction does not. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis in children

options.rationale: Ocular torticollis from a superior oblique palsy produces a compensatory head posture with a normal neck on palpation and full passive movement. Smooth conjugate tracking through a full range and a symmetrical red reflex here argue against an ocular cause. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis in children

options.rationale: The occipital flattening is secondary to the fixed head position, so treating the skull without treating the neck leaves the cause in place. Helmet therapy is considered only for severe residual deformity after the torticollis has been treated and repositioning has failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is the commonest form in Australian children and typically presents in girls under six with one or two large joints swollen for more than six weeks. Pain is often unimpressive and the child compensates with a limp that improves as the day goes on, which is why the diagnosis is frequently delayed. The eye complication is the reason the diagnosis matters urgently, because the inflammation is asymptomatic and the child is far too young to report visual change. Treatment of the joint itself usually begins with intra-articular corticosteroid, with methotrexate added for persistent or extending disease.
key_points: Arthritis is defined by six weeks or more of joint swelling or restriction
Morning stiffness that eases with activity separates it from mechanical pain
Antinuclear antibody positivity raises uveitis risk, not diagnostic certainty
Uveitis is silent, so screening is by slit lamp rather than by symptoms
Intra-articular corticosteroid is the usual first treatment for a single joint
explanation.pearls: A child under seven at onset with a positive antinuclear antibody needs slit lamp screening every three months for the first four years, whereas an older antibody negative child can be screened every six to twelve months.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
RCH CPG: Acute joint pain or swelling
BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.rationale: Septic arthritis presents over days with fever, refusal to weight bear and markedly raised inflammatory markers, not with ten weeks of morning stiffness that eases through the day. The inflammatory markers here are barely above range and she is systemically well. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute joint pain or swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute joint pain or swelling

options.rationale: Imaging is useful when a single joint problem might be mechanical or infective, but the diagnosis here rests on the duration and the pattern rather than on the appearance of the synovium. It also carries an anaesthetic that does nothing to protect her sight. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.rationale: Marrow examination is indicated when leukaemia is in the differential, flagged by night pain waking the child, cytopenias, or markedly raised lactate dehydrogenase with a low or normal white cell count. Her counts are normal and her pain eases with movement, which is the opposite of the malignant pattern. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.rationale: Chronic anterior uveitis in this pattern of arthritis is silent, produces no redness or pain, and is detected only on slit lamp examination, yet untreated it causes synechiae, cataract and visual loss. Young age at onset with a positive antinuclear antibody carries the highest risk, warranting screening three monthly. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.rationale: Post streptococcal and rheumatic joint disease is migratory, painful out of proportion to the swelling and follows a documented throat or skin infection within weeks. A single joint swollen continuously for ten weeks does not fit that timeline. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute joint pain or swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute joint pain or swelling

explanation.summary: Dystrophinopathy affects about one in 5000 boys and the average age at diagnosis remains close to five years despite the signs usually being present by three. Late walking, a waddling gait, difficulty with stairs and calf hypertrophy are the recognisable cluster, and mild global developmental delay including speech delay accompanies it in roughly a third because dystrophin is expressed in brain. The diagnostic sequence is creatine kinase first, then genetic testing of the dystrophin gene, with biopsy reserved for unresolved cases. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroids prolong independent walking, cardiac surveillance begins in childhood, and the mother and her sisters need carrier testing.
key_points: Proximal weakness with preserved reflexes points to muscle, not nerve
A positive Gowers manoeuvre signals hip girdle rather than distal weakness
Creatine kinase is the decisive first test and is grossly elevated
Genetic testing of the dystrophin gene confirms the diagnosis
Speech delay coexists in a substantial minority and is not a separate problem
explanation.pearls: Any boy not walking independently by 18 months, or any child with an unexplained transaminase rise on routine bloods, should have a creatine kinase measured, because a raised alanine aminotransferase of muscle origin is a common accidental route to the diagnosis.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness
BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Australian Institute of Musculoskeletal Science: Neuromuscular disorders in children

options.rationale: Neurophysiology localises a neuropathic process, which typically gives distal weakness, absent reflexes and sensory change. Reflexes are preserved and the weakness is proximal here, and the test is invasive in a preschooler when a blood test answers the question. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.rationale: Spinal imaging is for a cord lesion or tethering, signalled by upper motor neurone signs, a sensory level, bladder change or a midline cutaneous marker. None are present and his plantar responses are flexor. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.rationale: Proximal weakness with calf hypertrophy and a positive Gowers manoeuvre is a muscular pattern, and creatine kinase is elevated ten to a hundred times the upper limit in dystrophinopathy, making it the cheap decisive first test. A normal result effectively excludes the diagnosis and redirects the work up. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.rationale: Physiotherapy is part of long term care but delaying the diagnosis by six months costs the family genetic counselling and delays corticosteroid treatment that preserves ambulation. Weakness with calf hypertrophy is never a normal variant of gait. (Source: Australian Institute of Musculoskeletal Science: Neuromuscular disorders in children)
