source_refs: Australian Institute of Musculoskeletal Science: Neuromuscular disorders in children

options.rationale: Biopsy was the historical confirmatory test but has been displaced by genetic analysis of the dystrophin gene, which is performed after the creatine kinase result rather than instead of it. It is reserved for the child with a high creatine kinase whose genetic testing is uninformative. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea affects between one and four per cent of Australian children and peaks between two and eight years when the tonsils and adenoids are largest relative to the airway. The presentation differs from adults, with daytime hyperactivity, inattention and irritability rather than sleepiness, so it is frequently mistaken for a primary behavioural disorder. Untreated disease causes growth faltering, learning difficulty, enuresis and in severe cases pulmonary hypertension. In the otherwise healthy preschool or school-aged child, the Australian pathway accepts a clinical diagnosis and refers for adenotonsillectomy without waiting for a sleep study.
key_points: Habitual snoring with witnessed apnoeas is the core clinical picture
Daytime inattention rather than sleepiness is the childhood presentation
Polysomnography is for under twos, comorbidity, or a discordant history
Adenotonsillectomy is the definitive treatment for adenotonsillar disease
Untreated disease can cause growth faltering and pulmonary hypertension
explanation.pearls: A child under three years, or one with an oxygen saturation nadir below 80 per cent on any sleep study, should have the surgery performed in a centre with paediatric intensive care access because of the risk of postoperative respiratory compromise in the first night.

sources.label: Australian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep disordered breathing

options.rationale: An otherwise healthy child between two and twelve with habitual snoring, witnessed apnoeas and adenotonsillar hypertrophy can be referred for surgery on clinical grounds, and removal of the obstructing tissue is the definitive treatment with documented gains in behaviour and quality of life. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

Formal sleep study is reserved for children under two, those with obesity, craniofacial or neuromuscular disease or Down syndrome, and cases where the history and the airway findings disagree. Insisting on it for a straightforward presentation adds months of waiting without changing the decision. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

Intranasal corticosteroid helps mild snoring driven by allergic rhinitis, and rhinitis gives a pale boggy mucosa, an allergic crease and seasonal symptoms. Her mucosa is normal and she has witnessed apnoeas, which is beyond the reach of a nasal spray. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Behavioural sleep advice addresses settling difficulty and night waking, not an obstructed upper airway. A child who stops breathing in her sleep is not having a behavioural problem and the delay allows the daytime consequences to continue. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

Inattention here is a consequence of fragmented sleep, and assessing it before the airway risks a stimulant prescription for a reversible problem. Behavioural referral is appropriate if the symptoms persist once the obstruction has been treated. (Source: Australian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep disordered breathing)
source_refs: Australian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep disordered breathing

explanation.summary: Tics affect up to one in five school-aged children at some point and the combination of multiple motor tics with at least one vocal tic for over a year defines the syndrome that carries Gilles de la Tourette's name. The defining features are a premonitory urge, brief voluntary suppressibility followed by a rebound, and a fluctuating course that typically worsens with fatigue, excitement or illness. Severity peaks around puberty and improves substantially in most by the late teens, which is why the first intervention is accurate information for the child, the family and the school. Comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive symptoms cause more impairment than the tics themselves and should be actively sought.
key_points: Suppressibility with rebound distinguishes tics from seizures and chorea
Motor plus vocal tics for over twelve months defines the syndrome
Waxing and waning severity with stress and fatigue is expected
Education and monitoring are first line when function is preserved
Screen for attention and obsessive compulsive symptoms at every review
explanation.pearls: Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, built around habit reversal training, is the recommended first active treatment when impairment does appear, and it outperforms medication for tic severity without the metabolic cost of an antipsychotic.

options.rationale: Antipsychotics are reserved for tics causing pain, injury or significant social or educational impairment, none of which apply, and they carry weight gain, sedation and prolactin elevation in a growing child. Treating a well functioning child exposes him to harm for no measurable gain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Clonidine is a reasonable first pharmacological choice when tics do warrant treatment, particularly with coexisting attention difficulties, so what matters is whether any drug is indicated at all. Here the threshold of impairment has not been crossed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Electroencephalography is for events with impaired awareness, automatisms or a stereotyped unvarying pattern, since seizures are neither suppressible nor responsive to distraction. His movements can be held back voluntarily, which is not a feature of epilepsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

Imaging and copper studies belong to the child with a progressive movement disorder, dystonia, cognitive decline or abnormal neurological signs. A normal examination with a fluctuating fourteen month course is characteristic of a primary tic disorder. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Tic disorders)

A combination of motor and vocal tics for more than a year that waxes and wanes is expected to peak around ten to twelve years and then improve through adolescence, and when there is no functional impairment the evidence supports education and monitoring rather than drug treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

explanation.summary: Benign nocturnal limb pain of childhood affects around a third of children between three and twelve years and is a positive diagnosis rather than a diagnosis of exclusion. The defining pattern is bilateral pain in the muscles of the legs, late in the day or in the evening, with the child entirely well and fully mobile between episodes and a normal examination. The features that move a child out of this category are pain that is unilateral, localised over bone, present in the morning, associated with limp, swelling, fever, weight loss or systemic upset, or that wakes the child repeatedly from deep sleep. Massage, stretching and simple analgesia are effective, and the condition resolves over months to a few years.
key_points: The pain is bilateral and muscular rather than over a specific bone
Symptoms appear in the evening and the child is well the next morning
Examination must be entirely normal to make the diagnosis
Limp, morning symptoms or systemic features demand investigation
Massage and simple analgesia with parental reassurance are sufficient
explanation.pearls: Pain that is reliably worst in the morning, or that has been present for weeks over a single bony point, should prompt a full blood count with film and a plain radiograph of that bone, because leukaemia can present with normal peripheral counts in about one in ten children.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Limb pain in children

options.rationale: Blood testing is indicated when pain wakes the child from established sleep, is unilateral or localised to bone, or comes with pallor, bruising, fever or weight loss. None of those are present and her daytime function is unaffected. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

Bilateral pain confined to the evening with complete freedom of movement and a normal examination the following day is the recognised benign pattern, and positive diagnosis with safety netting avoids a cascade of tests. The parents are told exactly which changes would prompt reassessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

Radiographs are for focal bone tenderness, a palpable mass or a limp, since osteoid osteoma and osteosarcoma are localised rather than symmetrical. Symmetrical pain with no tenderness anywhere does not fit a structural lesion. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Limb pain in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Limb pain in children

options.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain with proximal weakness, a waddling gait and sometimes deformity or fracture, and its pain persists through the day rather than resolving by morning. Testing without those features usually yields an incidental result that is then treated pointlessly. (Source: RACGP: Vitamin D testing)

Inflammatory joint disease shows morning stiffness with swelling or restricted movement of a specific joint, the opposite of the diurnal pattern here where mornings are her best time. The family history raises the possibility but her examination does not support it. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

explanation.summary: Fluid collecting within the tunica vaginalis is common in the first year of life and reflects incomplete obliteration of the processus vaginalis after testicular descent. The clinical task is to separate it from an inguinal hernia, which is the lesion that threatens the bowel and the testis, and the three distinguishing features are a palpable upper border, transillumination, and whether the swelling changes size with crying or through the day. A collection that fluctuates in size indicates a communication with the peritoneum and behaves more like a hernia, warranting earlier surgical opinion. Persistence beyond two years, rapid enlargement, or the appearance of a new collection in an older boy all justify referral, the last because it may signal an underlying testicular tumour or torsion of an appendage.
key_points: A palpable upper border places the swelling below the inguinal canal
Transillumination indicates fluid rather than bowel within the sac
Size that varies with crying indicates a patent communication
Most non communicating collections resolve before two years of age
A new collection in an older boy warrants ultrasound of the testis
explanation.pearls: A scrotal swelling that is larger at the end of the day and smaller after a night in the cot indicates a communicating processus and should be referred for repair rather than observed, because the same defect can admit bowel.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions
BMJ Best Practice: Scrotal swelling in children

options.rationale: Urgent repair is for an inguinal hernia, which extends into the groin, has no palpable upper border, and characteristically enlarges with crying and reduces when the child is relaxed. The distinction matters because a hernia in this age group carries a real risk of incarceration while this lesion does not. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions

options.rationale: Ultrasound is reserved for a swelling that fails to transilluminate, a testis that cannot be felt separately, or a suspicion of a mass or torsion. Imaging adds nothing when the clinical findings already define the lesion and both testes are palpable. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Scrotal swelling in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Scrotal swelling in children

options.rationale: Aspiration is not part of paediatric practice because the fluid reaccumulates while the underlying processus remains patent, and the procedure risks injuring the testis. It also converts a benign observation problem into an invasive one. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions

options.rationale: Antibiotics would treat epididymo-orchitis, which is painful, tender and often accompanied by fever, dysuria or scrotal erythema. A painless swelling in a well afebrile infant with normal overlying skin has no infective features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A swelling with a palpable upper border that does not vary in size is a non communicating collection around the testis, and the processus vaginalis closes spontaneously in most infants, so the great majority resolve by two years without any intervention. Surgery is considered only for persistence beyond that age. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions

explanation.summary: Around a third of ventriculoperitoneal shunts fail within the first year and the cumulative risk of at least one revision through childhood approaches half. Obstruction is the commonest mode and presents with the classic features of raised intracranial pressure, which in children means headache and vomiting worst on waking, irritability, declining school performance, and eventually drowsiness, impaired upgaze and bradycardia with hypertension. Papilloedema is an unreliable sign because it takes time to develop and is often absent in an acute rise. The standard assessment pairs urgent imaging of the ventricles against a baseline study with a shunt series and early neurosurgical involvement, since definitive treatment is surgical revision.
key_points: Headache and vomiting on waking suggest raised intracranial pressure
Absent papilloedema does not exclude an acute pressure rise
Impaired upgaze reflects pressure on the dorsal midbrain
Compare ventricular size with a previous study, not with a normal range
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated when obstruction is suspected
explanation.pearls: A shunt reservoir that refills slowly after compression suggests proximal obstruction and one that is difficult to depress suggests distal obstruction, but neither finding is sensitive enough to exclude failure, so a normal reservoir examination never overrules a convincing history.

options.rationale: Antiemetic treatment suits gastroenteritis, which would give diarrhoea, abdominal pain, fever or a sick contact, none of which are present. Treating the symptom here removes the only visible sign of a rising intracranial pressure while the pathology continues. (Source: RCH CPG: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt complications)

Lumbar puncture in suspected obstructive hydrocephalus risks downward herniation, and shunt infection is sampled by neurosurgical tap of the reservoir rather than by the lumbar route. His supple neck, normal temperature and clean shunt tract also argue against infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Migraine is a diagnosis for a child with a normal conscious state between and during attacks, and it does not progressively reduce the level of consciousness over an afternoon. A first presentation of headache in a shunted child is never assumed to be primary. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

Morning headache and vomiting with declining conscious state in a shunted child is shunt failure until proven otherwise, and the imaging that answers it is a rapid non-contrast head scan compared with previous studies for ventricular size, obtained alongside an immediate neurosurgical discussion. Reduced upgaze and a sluggishly refilling reservoir both support raised pressure. (Source: RCH CPG: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt complications)

An abdominal pseudocyst does cause distal shunt obstruction, but it presents with abdominal distension, pain or a palpable mass, and it is looked for after the head has been imaged. His abdomen is soft and the immediate threat is intracranial. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hydrocephalus)

explanation.summary: The floppy infant is sorted first into central and peripheral causes, and the single most useful bedside sign is the level of alertness and social interaction, because a baby who engages normally while lying motionless has a problem below the brain. Within the peripheral group, absent reflexes with tongue fasciculations and a normal creatine kinase indicate anterior horn cell degeneration, while a raised creatine kinase points to muscle and distal sensory loss points to nerve. Australian newborn bloodspot screening has included the survival motor neurone gene since 2022, so infants born here are usually identified presymptomatically, and a symptomatic presentation now most often means the child was born elsewhere or predates the program. Diagnosis is urgent because disease modifying therapies work best before motor neurones are lost, and respiratory and nutritional support must be organised in parallel.
key_points: Preserved alertness with profound weakness indicates a peripheral cause
Absent reflexes with tongue fasciculations localise to the anterior horn cell
A normal creatine kinase argues against a primary muscle disorder
Paradoxical breathing reflects intercostal weakness with a spared diaphragm
Genetic confirmation is urgent because treatment is time critical
explanation.pearls: Intercostal weakness with diaphragm sparing produces the bell shaped chest and inward chest movement on inspiration, and these infants decompensate abruptly during minor viral illness, so respiratory review and a cough assist plan should be arranged before the first winter.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness
BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy

options.rationale: Central causes of hypotonia produce reduced alertness, a poor social response, dysmorphism or seizures, and often upper motor neurone signs. A socially engaged infant with absent reflexes has a lower motor neurone problem, and the anaesthetic itself is hazardous with her respiratory pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.rationale: Biopsy is directed at a congenital myopathy or muscular dystrophy, but those raise the creatine kinase or at least do not spare it entirely and do not produce tongue fasciculations. Genetic testing now precedes biopsy for this phenotype. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy

options.rationale: Alertness with a normal facial expression places the lesion below the brain, and areflexia with tongue fasciculations and a normal creatine kinase localises it to the anterior horn cell rather than to muscle or nerve. Deletion testing of the survival motor neurone gene confirms the diagnosis in the great majority and is the test that unlocks disease modifying therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.rationale: Metabolic causes of hypotonia usually announce themselves with encephalopathy, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, organomegaly or a raised lactate, and her gas and glucose are normal. The screen is worth completing for public health reasons but it will not explain a pure motor picture. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.rationale: Neuromuscular junction disease gives fatigable weakness with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia and characteristically preserves the deep tendon reflexes. Her reflexes are absent and her eye movements are full, which points away from the junction. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy

explanation.summary: Not every wheezing toddler has asthma, and the pattern of the noise is the key to the alternatives. Polyphonic wheeze scattered through both fields with a bronchodilator response indicates small airway disease, while a single pitched noise heard loudest centrally indicates one large airway that is narrowing. Dynamic collapse of the trachea or a main bronchus classically causes a brassy or barking cough, noise that worsens with crying, feeding and exertion and improves with rest, and complete failure to respond to inhaled therapy. The differential includes extrinsic compression by a vascular ring or a mediastinal mass, which is why the airway is examined directly and the arch anatomy is checked before the symptoms are attributed to a benign floppy trachea that will improve through the second and third years.
key_points: Monophonic central wheeze indicates a single large airway, not small airways
A brassy barking cough with effort dependent noise suggests dynamic collapse
Failure of an adequate preventer trial should prompt review of the diagnosis
Flexible bronchoscopy during spontaneous breathing shows the collapse
Exclude extrinsic vascular compression before accepting a benign cause
explanation.pearls: A toddler whose noisy breathing is worse when lying prone and better when lying on the side, and whose cough is brassy rather than wet, should be referred before a third preventer escalation, because inhaled corticosteroid has no effect on a collapsing airway and delays the structural diagnosis by months.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing

options.rationale: A brassy cough with a central monophonic wheeze that varies with effort and settles in sleep describes dynamic collapse of a large airway, which is diagnosed by looking at the airway during spontaneous breathing. Flexible bronchoscopy both confirms the collapse and excludes an intraluminal lesion or extrinsic compression. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing

options.rationale: Escalating preventer therapy assumes asthma, which gives polyphonic wheeze scattered through both lung fields, atopy, and at least partial bronchodilator response. He has none of these and has already failed an adequate eight week trial. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

An inhaled foreign body causes abrupt symptoms in a previously well child, usually with a witnessed choking episode and unilateral signs or hyperinflation on the film. Symptoms present since three months of age and a normal radiograph do not fit. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing

options.rationale: Extended antibiotics treat protracted bacterial bronchitis, a common cause of chronic cough in this age group, but that cough is wet and productive rather than brassy and it is not positional or effort dependent. A dry barking cough with a monophonic noise is mechanical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Reflux can aggravate airway symptoms and coexists with large airway collapse, but it is not the primary explanation for a noise that changes with respiratory effort and disappears in sleep. Treating it first leaves the structural question unanswered. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Tracheomalacia)

explanation.summary: Head circumference is interpreted as a trajectory rather than as a single point, and the finding that demands action is crossing centile lines upward, particularly with signs of raised pressure such as a full fontanelle, separated sutures, distended scalp veins or impaired upgaze. The commonest benign explanation in this age group is enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces, which typically runs in families, presents with a rapidly enlarging but soft head, and resolves by two years with normal development. Progressive hydrocephalus from aqueduct stenosis, a posterior fossa lesion or a chronic subdural collection all present identically at the start, and a subdural collection additionally raises the question of inflicted injury. Cranial ultrasound through an open fontanelle is the practical first study in Australian primary care, with magnetic resonance imaging reserved for abnormal or equivocal findings.
key_points: Crossing upward through centile lines matters more than the absolute centile
A full fontanelle and separated sutures indicate raised intracranial pressure
Familial macrocephaly grows parallel to a centile line rather than crossing
Ultrasound through an open fontanelle avoids sedation and radiation
Normal development does not exclude an actively expanding process
explanation.pearls: Benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces carries a genuinely increased risk of subdural haemorrhage after trivial trauma, so a subdural collection found in an infant with this finding does not by itself resolve the question of inflicted injury and still warrants a full safeguarding assessment.

options.rationale: Familial large head is a valid explanation for a head that is large but growing parallel to a centile line, and the parental measurements here are ordinary. A head that crosses centiles is describing a rate of growth, which no family history can normalise. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)

Magnetic resonance imaging is the better test for posterior fossa detail and is appropriate once ultrasound is abnormal or the fontanelle has closed, so the issue is sequence rather than suitability. Starting here commits an infant to sedation for information a bedside study can provide. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)

Premature suture fusion produces an abnormally shaped head with a palpable ridge and a head circumference that falls away rather than accelerates, because the skull cannot expand. His sutures are separated, which is the opposite finding. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Macrocephaly)

Normal development is genuinely reassuring about the past but says nothing about a process still expanding, and infants compensate for raised pressure by enlarging the skull until they suddenly do not. Waiting three months risks presenting later with vomiting and impaired upgaze. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)

Crossing two centile lines with a full fontanelle and separating sutures requires imaging rather than observation, and while the fontanelle remains open an ultrasound shows ventricular size and extra-axial fluid without radiation or sedation. It separates enlarged subarachnoid spaces from progressive ventricular dilatation, which need different follow up. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)

explanation.summary: Vitamin K dependent factors two, seven, nine and ten fall over the first weeks of life because placental transfer is poor, the gut is not yet colonised and breast milk contains very little vitamin K, which is why a single intramuscular dose is offered to every Australian newborn. The late form of the deficiency presents between two and twelve weeks, almost exclusively in breastfed infants who missed prophylaxis or who have unrecognised cholestasis, and roughly half of these infants present with intracranial haemorrhage. The laboratory signature is a markedly prolonged international normalised ratio and activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal platelet count and normal fibrinogen, which separates it from disseminated intravascular coagulation and from thrombocytopenic causes. Treatment is intravenous vitamin K with plasma or prothrombin complex for active major bleeding, alongside imaging and neurosurgical involvement.
key_points: Late presentation occurs between two and twelve weeks in breastfed infants
Prolonged clotting times with normal platelets and fibrinogen is the signature
Intracranial haemorrhage is the presentation in about half of late cases
Intravenous vitamin K corrects the defect, plasma only bridges it
Lumbar puncture is unsafe until the coagulopathy has been corrected
explanation.pearls: An infant with this presentation who has also had pale stools or prolonged jaundice needs a conjugated bilirubin measured on the same admission, because biliary atresia causes fat malabsorption and can produce the identical deficiency despite a correctly given birth dose.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding
National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics

options.rationale: Platelet transfusion treats thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction, and his count is squarely normal at 388. Transfusing platelets into a factor deficiency corrects nothing and delays the treatment that does. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics

options.rationale: A prolonged international normalised ratio and activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal platelet count and normal fibrinogen is the signature of deficient vitamin K dependent factors, and in a breastfed infant who received no prophylaxis this is late haemorrhagic disease with intracranial bleeding until imaged. Replacing the vitamin corrects the underlying defect within hours while the scan defines the bleed. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding

options.rationale: Meningitis is the standard reflex for an irritable infant with a bulging fontanelle, but he is afebrile with a normal C reactive protein, and lumbar puncture with an international normalised ratio of 6.4 risks a spinal haematoma. The coagulation profile redirects the whole assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding

options.rationale: Plasma is a useful adjunct for immediate factor replacement in life threatening bleeding and is given alongside the vitamin, but it fills the gap rather than correcting the deficiency. Plasma alone wears off within hours because the liver still cannot carboxylate the factors. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics

options.rationale: Inflicted injury must be considered in any infant with intracranial bleeding, and the assessment proceeds, but it does not precede treatment and it does not explain a grossly deranged coagulation profile with normal platelets. Correct the coagulopathy first and keep the safeguarding question open. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: The red reflex is the single most useful screening test of the paediatric eye in primary care, and it is performed at the newborn check, the six to eight week check and whenever a parent reports an abnormal appearance. An absent, dull or asymmetric reflex means light is not returning from the retina, which places a media opacity, a retinal detachment or an intraocular mass in the differential. The visual cortex is plastic only for the first months of life, so a dense unilateral opacity that is not cleared early leaves permanent amblyopia even if the opacity is later removed. Parental reports of an abnormal appearance in photographs are a genuinely useful history, because the camera flash reproduces the test under conditions the parent sees repeatedly.
key_points: An absent red reflex is a referral finding in its own right, not an observation finding
A normal newborn red reflex does not exclude an opacity developing later in infancy
Absent discharge and watering argue against nasolacrimal duct obstruction as the cause
Objection to occlusion of one eye implies the fellow eye is the seeing eye
Aetiological investigation must not delay the specialist eye assessment
explanation.pearls: Surgery for a dense unilateral congenital cataract gives the best visual outcome when performed between four and six weeks of age, which is why an absent red reflex found at the six week check is a same week referral rather than a routine one.

sources.label: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions
RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice

options.rationale: Deferring re-examination wastes the window in which occlusion amblyopia becomes irreversible, and an absent red reflex is never a finding to observe. The mother's account of a change since the newborn check makes progression rather than resolution the expectation. (Source: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions)
source_refs: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions

options.rationale: Refraction assesses focusing error in an eye with a clear media and does not address an opacity blocking the reflex. Optometric refraction is the right pathway for a squint with an intact red reflex, which is not this child. (Source: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions)
source_refs: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions

options.rationale: An absent red reflex in one eye requires ophthalmological assessment within days, both because a media opacity must be cleared early enough to allow the visual pathway to develop and because an intraocular tumour presents this way. Deprivation from a dense unilateral opacity produces dense amblyopia if the eye is not treated in the first months of life. (Source: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions)
source_refs: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions

options.rationale: Congenital infection is one cause of a media opacity but serology takes days and does not change the immediate need for specialist examination. Investigating aetiology before securing the eye assessment inverts the order of priorities. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Congenital cataract)

Cranial ultrasound images the brain and does not resolve the anterior segment or the retina to the standard needed here. A normal scan would falsely reassure while the visual deprivation continues. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Congenital cataract)

explanation.summary: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is a structural three dimensional deformity that produces rotation as well as lateral curvature, which is why the rib prominence on forward bending is the physical sign rather than the visible curve itself. Risk of progression is driven by the curve magnitude and the growth remaining, so skeletal maturity markers such as time since menarche and the Risser sign are as important as the Cobb angle. Curves under 25 degrees are usually observed, curves between about 25 and 40 degrees in a growing patient are braced, and curves beyond about 45 to 50 degrees are considered for surgery. Features pointing away from idiopathic disease include pain, a left thoracic curve, neurological signs and cutaneous markers, each of which redirects the workup towards imaging of the neural axis.
key_points: The scoliometer measures trunk rotation, and 7 degrees is the usual threshold for radiography
Progression risk is highest in the two years spanning the pubertal growth spurt
Management is decided on the Cobb angle from an erect whole spine film
Normal reflexes, normal foot arches and no skin lesions argue against a neural axis cause
A right thoracic curve is the expected pattern in idiopathic disease
explanation.pearls: A left sided thoracic curve in an adolescent is atypical for idiopathic scoliosis and should prompt magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine to look for a syrinx, a Chiari malformation or a cord tumour, even when the neurological examination is normal.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

options.rationale: A twelve month interval is far too long in a girl less than two years past menarche, when the residual growth spurt drives the majority of curve progression. Observation without a baseline radiograph also leaves the curve magnitude unknown. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

A scoliometer angle of trunk rotation at or above 7 degrees is the accepted threshold for imaging, because it corresponds to a curve likely to be clinically significant, and management decisions depend on the Cobb angle measured on an erect film. Referral alongside imaging allows skeletal maturity and curve magnitude to be combined into a progression risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

Spinal magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for features suggesting an underlying neural axis abnormality, such as a left thoracic curve, a midline skin lesion, a cavus foot, asymmetric reflexes or pain waking the child. None of those features is present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

Scoliosis specific exercises are an adjunct considered once a curve has been measured and staged, not a substitute for establishing the Cobb angle. Starting therapy without imaging risks missing a curve already in the bracing or surgical range. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

options.rationale: Bracing is indicated for a curve between about 25 and 40 degrees in a patient with remaining growth, so it cannot be prescribed before the Cobb angle is known. Bracing an unmeasured curve exposes the patient to a demanding treatment that may be unnecessary. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets remains common in Australian children whose skin is rarely exposed to sunlight, whether because of latitude, clothing practices, or prolonged indoor time, and exclusive or prolonged breastfeeding without supplementation compounds the risk because breast milk contains very little vitamin D. The biochemical signature is a low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with a raised alkaline phosphatase and a raised parathyroid hormone, with phosphate falling as parathyroid hormone drives renal phosphate loss and calcium held near the lower limit until decompensation. Normal renal function distinguishes nutritional disease from the rickets of chronic kidney disease, and a raised parathyroid hormone distinguishes it from X linked hypophosphataemia, where parathyroid hormone is normal or only slightly raised. Radiographs of the wrist show cupping, splaying and fraying of the metaphysis and are useful for confirming healing.
key_points: Alkaline phosphatase is the most sensitive routine marker of active rickets in a child
Secondary hyperparathyroidism explains the low phosphate and the near normal calcium
Normal renal function excludes renal osteodystrophy as the explanation
Treatment dosing of colecalciferol is far higher than prevention dosing
Calcium intake must be adequate during healing or hypocalcaemia can worsen
explanation.pearls: Alkaline phosphatase rises further in the first weeks of vitamin D treatment as the bone heals before it falls, so a rising value at the four week review is evidence of response rather than treatment failure.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents
Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's Dosing Companion

options.rationale: Calcium alone does not correct the substrate deficiency driving the secondary hyperparathyroidism, so the bone disease persists and the parathyroid hormone stays elevated. Calcium deficiency rickets with a normal vitamin D level is the situation in which calcium alone is appropriate. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

options.rationale: Calcitriol bypasses renal hydroxylation and is reserved for renal disease or the rare hydroxylase defects, neither of which fits normal renal function with a profoundly low 25 hydroxyvitamin D. Its narrow therapeutic index makes hypercalcaemia a real hazard in nutritional deficiency. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

options.rationale: Four hundred units is the daily dose used to prevent deficiency in an at risk infant, not to heal established rickets, and at this dose the radiological and biochemical abnormalities correct slowly if at all. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

options.rationale: Untreated rickets continues to deform the growing skeleton and carries a risk of hypocalcaemic seizures and cardiomyopathy in young children. A skeletal survey adds radiation without altering the treatment that the biochemistry already indicates. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

Established nutritional rickets in a child over twelve months is treated with high dose colecalciferol for three months, together with an adequate calcium intake because healing bone consumes calcium rapidly. Treatment dosing is an order of magnitude above prevention dosing, and maintenance supplementation continues once the course is complete. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

explanation.summary: Neonatal conjunctivitis is stratified by the day of onset and by the organism, because the treatment and the consequences differ sharply. Gonococcal disease presents within the first two to five days with hyperacute purulent discharge and threatens the cornea within hours, whereas chlamydial disease presents at the end of the first week to the middle of the second with a more indolent mucopurulent discharge and lid swelling. Chlamydial infection is acquired during passage through the birth canal and colonises the nasopharynx as well as the eye, which is why systemic rather than topical therapy is mandatory and why an afebrile infant with a staccato cough at six weeks may be the same infection presenting again. Any neonatal chlamydial or gonococcal infection is a sexually transmitted infection in the mother, so contact tracing and testing for co-infection are part of the management, not an optional extra.
key_points: Onset at the end of the first week points away from gonococcal disease
A negative Gram stain and culture for Neisseria excludes the hyperacute sight threatening cause
Topical therapy leaves the nasopharyngeal reservoir and the pneumonitis risk untreated
Maternal and partner treatment with contact tracing is part of the infant's management
Clear corneas on fluorescein staining exclude established corneal involvement
explanation.pearls: Chlamydial pneumonitis appears between four and twelve weeks of age as an afebrile infant with a staccato cough, tachypnoea and eosinophilia, and a history of a sticky eye in the second week of life is often the only clue linking the two presentations.

options.rationale: Chloramphenicol has poor activity against this organism and topical therapy alone does not reach the nasopharyngeal reservoir, so up to a fifth of infants go on to develop a pneumonitis at four to twelve weeks. Chloramphenicol is a reasonable choice for ordinary bacterial conjunctivitis beyond the neonatal period. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Systemic therapy is required because the organism colonises the nasopharynx as well as the conjunctiva, and oral azithromycin for the infant is the Australian regimen of choice. The infection is sexually transmitted, so the mother and her sexual partners must be treated and offered testing for other infections at the same time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Ceftriaxone is the treatment for gonococcal ophthalmia, which is excluded here by a negative Gram stain and culture, and it has no useful activity against this organism. Ceftriaxone also displaces bilirubin from albumin, which is an added reason to avoid it in the neonate without indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Erythromycin has the right spectrum but the wrong route, since topical delivery clears the eye while leaving the nasopharynx colonised and the pneumonitis risk untouched. The same drug class given systemically would be an acceptable alternative regimen. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

Eye toilet is useful supportive care but does not eradicate an organism that causes scarring conjunctivitis and later respiratory disease if untreated. Saline alone is appropriate for the sticky eye of nasolacrimal duct obstruction, where there is watering without lid oedema or purulent discharge. (Source: RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis)

explanation.summary: The irritable hip in a young child sits on a spectrum from transient synovitis, which is self-limiting, to septic arthritis, which destroys cartilage and can infarct the femoral head within days. The Kocher predictors of fever above 38.5 degrees, refusal to weight bear, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 and a white cell count above 12 stratify that risk, with the probability of infection rising steeply as the number of predictors increases, and Australian practice adds a C reactive protein above 20 as a further strong predictor. Ultrasound reliably shows an effusion but cannot distinguish an infected effusion from a sterile one, so it guides aspiration rather than replacing it. The hip is held flexed, abducted and externally rotated in both conditions because that position maximises capsular volume and minimises intracapsular pressure.
key_points: The position of comfort is common to both diagnoses and does not discriminate
Plain radiographs are normal early in septic arthritis and cannot exclude it
Ultrasound shows an effusion but cannot tell an infected joint from a sterile one
Synovial fluid must be obtained before antibiotics wherever possible
A preceding viral illness is compatible with either diagnosis
explanation.pearls: A child with an irritable hip who is afebrile, weight bears with a limp and has a C reactive protein below 20 can usually be managed as transient synovitis with review in 48 hours, whereas any one of fever above 38.5 degrees, complete refusal to weight bear, or a C reactive protein above 20 moves the child into the aspiration pathway.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Septic arthritis in children

options.rationale: He meets four of the predictors used to separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis, which places the probability of infection high enough that the joint must be sampled. Aspiration under anaesthesia confirms the diagnosis and decompresses a joint whose cartilage and femoral head blood supply are at risk within hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain)

Anti inflammatory treatment and review is the pathway for transient synovitis, which typically follows a viral illness in a child who is afebrile, still weight bears with a limp and has normal or near normal inflammatory markers. A temperature of 38.7 degrees with a C reactive protein of 62 and complete refusal to weight bear does not fit that pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain)

Antibiotics before aspiration reduce the yield of synovial culture and can leave the child on a prolonged empirical course without an organism or a drained joint. Antibiotics are started immediately after the sample is taken, not instead of taking it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A radiograph has already been taken and is normal, which is expected because plain films stay normal for the first one to two weeks of joint or bone infection. Repeating imaging that cannot exclude the diagnosis simply delays the definitive test. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain)

Scintigraphy is a second line study when the site of infection is genuinely unclear, and it takes hours to arrange while adding radiation. Here the hip is clinically localised, so the sampling procedure is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Septic arthritis in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Septic arthritis in children

explanation.summary: Faecal incontinence in a school-aged child is usually overflow from chronic functional constipation rather than a behavioural problem, and framing it that way to the family is an important part of the consultation because blame is common and unhelpful. The cycle starts with a painful or frightening stool, leads to withholding, and produces a dilated rectum that loses the sensation of fullness so that soft stool leaks past the retained mass without the child noticing. Treatment has two distinct phases, disimpaction and then maintenance, and skipping the first phase is the commonest reason treatment appears to fail. Red flags that redirect the workup include delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours, ribbon stools with an empty rectum, faltering growth, a sacral dimple or hair tuft, and abnormal lower limb neurology.
key_points: Soiling in this setting is overflow incontinence, not deliberate behaviour
Disimpaction must precede maintenance or the soiling continues
Passage of meconium on day one makes an aganglionic segment unlikely
A normal back and normal lower limb neurology argue against a spinal cause
Maintenance is continued for months, and stopping early causes relapse
explanation.pearls: Warn the family before starting disimpaction that soiling usually gets worse for the first several days as the retained mass breaks up, because families who are not warned stop the macrogol at exactly the point it is starting to work.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Constipation in children

options.rationale: Rectal treatment is distressing in a child who is already withholding and reinforces the aversion that drives the cycle, and repeated phosphate enemas carry a risk of electrolyte disturbance. Enemas are reserved for oral disimpaction that has failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Starting maintenance without clearing the impaction leaves soft stool to leak past the retained mass, so the soiling continues and the family concludes the treatment has failed. This is exactly the right regimen once disimpaction is complete. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

The overflow soiling is caused by liquid stool passing around a retained faecal mass, so the mass must be cleared before any maintenance regimen can work, and an escalating oral macrogol course achieves this without rectal intervention. Maintenance then continues for months, because stopping as soon as the stools normalise is the commonest cause of relapse. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Manual evacuation under anaesthesia is a last resort for impaction resistant to oral and rectal treatment, and it exposes the child to an anaesthetic for a problem that usually resolves medically. It is not a first line intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Manometry and rectal biopsy investigate an aganglionic segment, which is made unlikely by passage of meconium on the first day, normal growth and a rectum loaded with stool rather than empty. Investigating before treating delays relief in a child with a clear functional picture. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Constipation in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Constipation in children

explanation.summary: Classical galactosaemia presents in the first two weeks once milk feeding is established, because galactose from lactose accumulates as galactose 1 phosphate and injures the liver, kidney and brain. The triad that should trigger suspicion is a jaundiced unwell neonate with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia, and Gram negative sepsis, since Escherichia coli sepsis is characteristically associated with the condition through impaired neutrophil function. Newborn screening in Australia includes galactosaemia, but the result may not be back before the infant becomes unwell, so the diagnosis is made clinically and the feed is changed immediately rather than waiting. Even with prompt dietary treatment, long term outcomes include learning difficulties and primary ovarian insufficiency in girls, so treatment is not curative and follow up is lifelong.
key_points: Positive reducing substances with a negative glucose strip indicates a non glucose sugar
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a neonate always indicates liver disease
Gram negative sepsis is characteristically associated with this metabolic disorder
Dietary galactose is removed on suspicion rather than after confirmation
Hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy reflect hepatic involvement rather than sepsis alone
explanation.pearls: Galactose free soy formula is started on clinical suspicion, but the diagnostic red cell galactose 1 phosphate uridyltransferase assay must be taken before any red cell transfusion, because transfused donor enzyme masks the deficiency for up to three months.

options.rationale: Phototherapy acts on unconjugated bilirubin and does nothing for a conjugated fraction of 92 micromol/L, and continuing lactose containing milk sustains the toxic metabolite load. A conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia always signals liver disease rather than the exaggerated physiological jaundice that phototherapy treats. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Positive urinary reducing substances with a negative glucose oxidase strip means a non glucose reducing sugar is present, which in a jaundiced neonate with coagulopathy and Gram negative sepsis points to galactose accumulation, and the specific treatment is immediate removal of dietary galactose. Waiting for the newborn screening result risks progressive liver failure, so the feed is changed on suspicion and the diagnostic samples are taken alongside. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic conditions)

Ursodeoxycholic acid is a bile flow agent used in established cholestatic disease and does not address a substrate that is actively injuring the liver while the feed continues. It would leave the galactose load in place. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Galactosaemia)

Extensively hydrolysed formulas break down the protein but most still contain lactose, so the offending sugar is delivered unchanged. Hydrolysed formula is the right choice for cow's milk protein allergy, where the protein rather than the sugar is the problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic conditions)

Dextrose corrects the hypoglycaemia but prolonged starvation of a septic neonate is not a sustainable plan, and a galactose free feed both removes the substrate and provides nutrition. Intravenous glucose is a useful adjunct rather than the definitive feeding decision. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic conditions)

explanation.summary: Fractures in infants who are not yet independently mobile carry a high probability of inflicted injury, and femoral, humeral, rib and metaphyseal corner fractures sit at the more specific end of that spectrum. The assessment turns on whether the described mechanism plausibly generates the force observed, and a roll from a low couch onto carpet does not fracture a healthy femoral shaft. Blue sclerae, easy fracturing in a parent and dentinogenesis imperfecta genuinely raise the possibility of a collagen disorder, but that possibility is investigated in parallel with the protective assessment rather than instead of it, because the two are not mutually exclusive and because a child left unprotected during a weeks long genetic workup is at continuing risk. Mandatory reporting obligations in every Australian jurisdiction are triggered by reasonable suspicion, which is a far lower threshold than diagnostic certainty.
key_points: A long bone fracture in a non ambulant infant is high specificity for inflicted injury
The stated mechanism must plausibly generate the force required for the injury
Bone fragility disorders and inflicted injury can coexist in the same child
Normal calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase do not exclude a collagen disorder
Mandatory reporting is triggered by reasonable suspicion, not by proof
explanation.pearls: A skeletal survey in a child under two should be repeated at 11 to 14 days, because healing periosteal reaction makes rib and metaphyseal fractures visible that were radiographically silent on the initial films.

sources.label: RACGP: Abuse and violence, working with our patients in general practice

options.rationale: Densitometry is difficult to interpret in infancy, has no validated threshold for excluding inflicted injury, and returns too slowly to inform the decision in front of you. It does not answer the safeguarding question. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Collagen and genetic testing takes weeks and, crucially, a positive result would not by itself explain a femoral fracture in an infant who cannot yet roll, since brittle bone disease and inflicted injury can coexist. Accepting a plausible medical explanation to close the assessment is the anti pattern this case tests. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

The fracture does need immobilisation, but treating the bone and discharging the child leaves the mechanism unexplained and the infant potentially unprotected. Orthopaedic management runs alongside the assessment rather than replacing it. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

Bisphosphonates are used in confirmed moderate to severe brittle bone disease under specialist supervision, not empirically on the basis of blue sclerae and a family history. Normal calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase also make a metabolic bone disorder less likely. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Osteogenesis imperfecta)

A femoral shaft fracture in an infant who is not yet independently mobile is a high specificity injury for inflicted trauma, and the stated mechanism of a roll from a low couch does not generate the force required. Admission allows a full skeletal survey, ophthalmology and neuroimaging as indicated, and specialist assessment of the possibility of an underlying bone fragility disorder, none of which removes the statutory obligation to notify. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Unwitnessed ingestion in a toddler is managed by reading the toxidrome rather than waiting for a history that may never come, and the grandparent's medication box is the classic source of a one tablet exposure that is dangerous in a small child. Central alpha two agonists such as clonidine produce a picture that closely mimics opioid poisoning, with sedation, miosis and bradycardia, but ventilation is usually better preserved, and the bradycardia with hypotension is more prominent. The pitfall is to treat the apparent opioid picture with naloxone and then discharge the child early, because the alpha two agonist effect long outlasts the naloxone and the child deteriorates after leaving. Australian practice is to discuss any significant or uncertain paediatric ingestion with the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26, which provides agent specific observation periods.
key_points: Read the toxidrome when the agent is unknown rather than waiting for a history
Bradycardia with hypotension and miosis but preserved ventilation suggests alpha two agonism
A narrow QRS argues against sodium channel blocking agents
There is no specific antidote, so monitored supportive care is the treatment
Observation must be long enough to outlast the agent, not the antidote
explanation.pearls: A single clonidine tablet can produce coma and bradycardia in a toddler, and because the effect commonly persists beyond 12 hours, any child with symptoms needs at least 12 to 24 hours of monitored observation rather than the four to six hours used for many other ingestions.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Paediatric poisoning guidelines
RCH CPG: Poisoning, acute guidelines for initial management

options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine sedation but benzodiazepines do not produce this degree of bradycardia with hypotension and miosis, and flumazenil can precipitate seizures in an unknown mixed ingestion. Giving an antidote for the wrong toxidrome adds risk without diagnostic gain. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Paediatric poisoning guidelines)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Paediatric poisoning guidelines

options.rationale: Charcoal is of little value two hours after ingestion and carries an aspiration risk in a child with a reduced conscious level and an unprotected airway. A four hour observation period is also far too short for agents whose effects characteristically last many hours. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Paediatric poisoning guidelines)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Paediatric poisoning guidelines

options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is the treatment for sodium channel blockade, which is identified by a broad QRS, and the QRS here is 82 ms. Treating a narrow complex bradycardia with bicarbonate addresses a mechanism that is not operating. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Naloxone is a reasonable diagnostic trial in an undifferentiated sedated child, and central alpha two agonist poisoning sometimes responds partially, but it is unreliable and short acting, so it can never be the basis for early discharge. Preserved respiratory rate and oxygenation also argue against a pure opioid effect. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Paediatric poisoning guidelines)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Paediatric poisoning guidelines

options.rationale: The combination of bradycardia, hypotension, miosis and sedation with preserved ventilation fits central alpha two agonist poisoning, for which there is no specific antidote, so management is supportive with continuous monitoring in a setting able to treat haemodynamic compromise. Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia and fluid for hypotension are the interventions that matter, and the child is observed for at least 12 to 24 hours because sedation and bradycardia are prolonged. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Paediatric poisoning guidelines)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Paediatric poisoning guidelines

explanation.summary: Vascular birthmarks divide into tumours, chiefly infantile haemangiomas, and malformations, chiefly capillary malformations, and the distinction is made on natural history rather than appearance at a single visit. A haemangioma is typically absent or faint at birth, proliferates for several months and becomes raised, then involutes slowly, whereas a capillary malformation is present at full extent from birth, stays flat, and grows only in proportion to the child. A capillary malformation involving the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, meaning the forehead and upper eyelid, carries a substantial risk of an associated leptomeningeal vascular malformation with seizures, hemiparesis and developmental delay, and a lifelong risk of ipsilateral glaucoma. Both risks are silent at six weeks, which is exactly why the imaging and the eye review are arranged before symptoms appear.
key_points: A lesion present at full extent from birth and staying flat is a malformation
Forehead and upper eyelid involvement defines the at risk distribution
Glaucoma can present at any age and is asymptomatic until vision is lost
Cranial ultrasound cannot exclude a leptomeningeal vascular malformation
Laser treatment of the skin does not address the associated risks
explanation.pearls: Early magnetic resonance imaging before about six months can be falsely reassuring because incomplete myelination obscures the leptomeningeal enhancement, so a normal early scan in a child with the at risk distribution is repeated if seizures or developmental concerns emerge.

options.rationale: A flat capillary malformation involving the forehead and upper eyelid occupies the territory at risk for an associated leptomeningeal vascular malformation and for glaucoma, so both the brain and the eye must be assessed rather than the skin alone. Ophthalmology review is needed on a recurring basis because raised intraocular pressure can develop at any age and is silent until vision is lost. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

Propranolol treats proliferating infantile haemangiomas, which are absent or minimal at birth, then grow rapidly and become raised over the first months. A lesion present at full extent from birth that has stayed flat is a malformation rather than a tumour and does not respond to propranolol. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

Reassurance is appropriate for a midline nape or glabellar patch that fades over the first years, but not for a unilateral lesion in this distribution. Delaying to twelve months would allow untreated glaucoma or unrecognised seizures to cause avoidable harm. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

Cranial ultrasound through the fontanelle does not reliably demonstrate leptomeningeal vascular malformation or the associated cortical changes, so a normal study gives false reassurance. Magnetic resonance imaging with contrast is the study that answers the question. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sturge-Weber syndrome)

Pulsed dye laser is the right treatment for the cutaneous lesion and is most effective started early, but arranging it alone treats the appearance while leaving the intracranial and ocular associations unexamined. The laser referral is made in addition to, not instead of, the neurological and ophthalmic assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

explanation.summary: Hip displacement occurs in around a third of children with cerebral palsy and the risk rises steeply with gross motor severity, from a few per cent in children who walk independently to the majority of those who cannot sit unsupported. The process is silent for years, so by the time a child has pain, asymmetric abduction or difficulty with perineal care the hip is often already subluxed or dislocated, which is the reason Australian practice uses radiographic surveillance at intervals set by the child's gross motor function level rather than symptom triggered imaging. Migration percentage, the proportion of the femoral head lying lateral to a line dropped from the lateral edge of the acetabulum, is the measurement that drives decisions, with values above 30 per cent or a rise of more than 10 points per year prompting orthopaedic referral. Preventive surgery such as adductor release or a varus derotation osteotomy performed at this stage preserves a located, painless hip, whereas salvage surgery after dislocation is major and less predictable.
key_points: Hip displacement in cerebral palsy is silent until it is advanced
Migration percentage above 30 per cent triggers orthopaedic referral
A rise of more than 10 points in a year is itself an indication to refer
Surveillance interval is set by gross motor function level, not by symptoms
Full painless abduction does not exclude significant displacement
explanation.pearls: Children at the most severe gross motor function levels need a pelvic radiograph every six months from diagnosis until skeletal maturity, whereas a child who walks independently by two years of age needs only a single film at around three years if the examination stays normal.

sources.label: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Waiting a further twelve months allows displacement that is already beyond the action threshold and rising by more than ten points a year to progress towards dislocation. Once the hip is dislocated the surgery required is far more extensive and the outcome less reliable. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Abduction bracing has not been shown to prevent progressive hip displacement in cerebral palsy and is frequently poorly tolerated overnight. Using it as the primary response substitutes an unproven measure for the surgical assessment the radiograph has triggered. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: A migration percentage above 30 per cent is the accepted threshold for orthopaedic referral regardless of symptoms, and the rise from 24 to 35 per cent in twelve months indicates active progression. The entire purpose of a surveillance program is to act on the measurement before pain and dislocation appear, since displacement is silent until late. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Migration percentage is measured on a standardised plain radiograph and that measurement is what the surveillance thresholds are built on, so cross sectional imaging adds cost and often sedation without changing the decision. Advanced imaging is arranged by the surgical team if it is needed for planning. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.rationale: Botulinum toxin reduces adductor tone and may help with positioning and care, but it does not reliably alter the natural history of progressive bony displacement. Tone management is an adjunct alongside, not a substitute for, surgical assessment once the threshold is crossed. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

explanation.summary: The two commonest solid abdominal tumours of early childhood are separated largely at the bedside. A renal tumour is usually a smooth mass that does not cross the midline, is often found incidentally by a parent during bathing in an otherwise well child, and may be accompanied by hypertension and haematuria. A sympathetic chain tumour is typically irregular, crosses the midline, occurs in a child who is systemically unwell with bone pain and anaemia, and metastasises to bone, marrow, liver and skin. Periorbital ecchymoses with proptosis are the classic presentation of orbital bony metastasis and are frequently mistaken for inflicted injury, which is a well recognised source of diagnostic delay. Urinary catecholamine metabolites are elevated in around 90 per cent, and staging in Australia proceeds through cross sectional imaging, meta iodobenzylguanidine scanning and bone marrow examination at the treating centre.
key_points: A mass crossing the midline argues against a renal primary
Bilateral periorbital bruising with proptosis suggests orbital metastasis
A normal coagulation screen does not make inflicted injury more likely here
Urinary homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid are elevated in most cases
Bone pain with anaemia indicates marrow involvement at presentation
explanation.pearls: Around half of children with this tumour present with metastatic disease, and the rare infant pattern with skin nodules, liver enlargement and limited marrow involvement can regress spontaneously, which is why staging rather than the presence of metastases alone determines how aggressively it is treated.

options.rationale: Periorbital bruising does raise inflicted injury as a differential, but the coagulation screen is already normal and bruising confined to both upper eyelids in a child with an abdominal mass, anaemia and bone pain is far better explained by orbital metastatic deposits. Anchoring on the bruise and missing the mass is the anti pattern this case tests. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass)

A fixed abdominal mass that crosses the midline arises from the sympathetic chain or retroperitoneum rather than the kidney, and the combination with bone pain, anaemia and orbital deposits indicates metastatic disease requiring urgent specialist referral. Urinary homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid are elevated in the great majority and are the specific non-invasive test to send while the referral is being made. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass)

A skeletal survey in this child would likely show metastatic deposits that could be misread as healing injuries, sending the assessment further down the wrong pathway. Bone tenderness with anaemia and an abdominal mass points to marrow infiltration rather than trauma. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass)

Alpha fetoprotein is the marker for hepatoblastoma and germ cell tumours, neither of which produces periorbital deposits, and a hepatic mass moves with respiration rather than staying fixed. Both are urgent oncology referrals, but the wrong marker delays the diagnosis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Neuroblastoma)

Lactate dehydrogenase is non-specific and a two week wait is unsafe for a child with a rapidly progressive mass and evidence of disseminated disease. Any delay in referral risks tumour lysis, cord compression or respiratory compromise developing before review. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Neuroblastoma)

explanation.summary: Delayed puberty in boys is defined as no testicular enlargement beyond 4 mL by 14 years, and constitutional delay accounts for the large majority of referrals, particularly where a parent also matured late. The diagnostic task is to separate that benign pattern from chronic disease, from hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and from primary gonadal failure, which is done with a small screening panel, a bone age and a careful history rather than with extensive endocrine testing. A bone age delayed by roughly the same interval as the pubertal delay is the reassuring finding, because it means skeletal maturation and pubertal maturation are running together on a slow clock and final height is preserved. Weight falling disproportionately below height suggests undernutrition or a chronic inflammatory or gastrointestinal disorder, while anosmia, headache or visual field defects point towards a central structural cause.
key_points: Testicular volume of 4 mL marks the onset of puberty in boys
A bone age delayed in proportion to the pubertal delay supports constitutional delay
Basal gonadotrophins cannot separate constitutional delay from gonadotrophin deficiency
Weight falling below height suggests chronic disease rather than constitutional delay
An intact sense of smell argues against the commonest congenital gonadotrophin deficiency
explanation.pearls: If testicular volume has still not reached 4 mL by the time the bone age passes about 12 years, constitutional delay becomes much less tenable and gonadotrophin deficiency should be investigated, because bone age rather than chronological age is the clock that puberty follows.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Puberty and adolescent health
Australian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Delayed puberty

options.rationale: A sex chromosome aneuploidy such as Klinefelter syndrome typically produces small firm testes with tall stature and a normal or advanced bone age, which is the opposite of the pattern here. Karyotyping is directed by the phenotype rather than ordered on delayed puberty alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty and adolescent health)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Puberty and adolescent health

options.rationale: A short course of low dose testosterone is a reasonable option when delay is causing significant psychological distress, but it is offered after the assessment is complete rather than as the first step, and it is not needed in a boy who is untroubled. Treating before the pattern is established also makes interpretation of subsequent growth harder. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty and adolescent health)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Puberty and adolescent health

options.rationale: Pituitary imaging is indicated when there are headaches, visual field loss, anosmia, other pituitary hormone deficiencies or a growth velocity that has fallen away disproportionately. None of these is present, and an intact sense of smell argues specifically against the commonest congenital cause of isolated gonadotrophin deficiency. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty and adolescent health)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Puberty and adolescent health

options.rationale: Basal gonadotrophins cannot separate constitutional delay from gonadotrophin deficiency in early adolescence, because both give low values, so the test cannot change management at this point. The same measurements become informative once the bone age reaches about 12 years, when puberty would be expected to have begun. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Delayed puberty)

A bone age delayed in proportion to the pubertal delay, a preserved height velocity, a family history of late maturation and normal screening investigations describe constitutional delay, in which growth potential is retained and puberty begins spontaneously. Structured review with serial height and testicular volume both confirms the diagnosis when puberty starts and detects the minority whose pattern turns out to be pathological. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty and adolescent health)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Puberty and adolescent health

explanation.summary: Paediatric neck lumps divide usefully by position, with midline lesions dominated by thyroglossal remnants and dermoid cysts and lateral lesions by reactive nodes and branchial remnants. The thyroglossal duct runs from the foramen caecum at the tongue base to the final position of the thyroid gland, which is why traction on a remnant cyst causes it to rise when the tongue is protruded. Definitive treatment is the Sistrunk procedure, in which the central portion of the hyoid bone is removed along with the tract, because simple cyst excision leaves tract epithelium behind and recurrence follows. Imaging before surgery matters because a small proportion of these cysts contain ectopic tissue that represents the child's entire functioning thyroid.
key_points: Elevation on tongue protrusion localises the lesion to the thyroglossal tract
Ultrasound confirms a normally sited thyroid gland before excision
Definitive surgery removes the central hyoid with the tract, not the cyst alone
Acute infection defers surgery until inflammation has settled
Dermoid cysts are also midline but do not move with the tongue
explanation.pearls: Simple cyst excision without removing the central third of the hyoid bone carries a recurrence rate of around 40 to 50 per cent, which falls below 5 per cent with the Sistrunk procedure, so the operation named in the referral matters as much as the decision to operate.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of neck lumps in children

options.rationale: A midline swelling that elevates on tongue protrusion sits along the embryological tract of the thyroglossal duct, and ultrasound both confirms the cystic lesion and documents that a normally sited thyroid gland is present before any excision. Thyroid function is checked because the cyst occasionally contains the only functioning thyroid tissue the child has. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck lumps)

Aspiration of a cystic midline lesion risks introducing infection into a tract that will later need surgical excision, and it does not answer the question the surgeon needs answered, which is whether functioning thyroid tissue lies elsewhere. Cytology would be the right first move for a suspicious solid lateral nodal mass, which this is not. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck lumps)

Cross sectional imaging with ionising radiation is not required for a clinically typical midline cyst and would be reserved for a mass with features suggesting malignancy or airway compromise. Ultrasound answers the anatomical question in a child without a radiation dose. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck lumps)

There is no erythema, tenderness or fever to suggest infection, so antibiotics treat nothing and delay definitive assessment. Antibiotics would be appropriate if the cyst had become acutely infected, in which case excision is deferred until the inflammation settles. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
