Excision is the eventual treatment but proceeding before imaging risks removing a child's only thyroid tissue and leaving them permanently hypothyroid without anticipating it. The operation itself is correct; the sequencing is not. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck lumps)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis is the commonest cause of a fixed head tilt in early infancy and is associated with instrumental or difficult delivery, breech presentation and intrauterine crowding. The diagnosis is clinical and rests on a tilt towards the affected muscle with chin rotation away from it, often with a palpable pseudotumour within the muscle belly in the first weeks. The important differentials are ocular torticollis, vertebral anomaly, posterior fossa or spinal cord lesions, and in older children an acquired cause such as an atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation or a retropharyngeal abscess; each produces a tilt that does not correct passively or is accompanied by neurological or systemic signs. Untreated tilt drives positional skull flattening and facial asymmetry, and hip examination matters because developmental dysplasia of the hip is more common in these infants.
key_points: Tilt towards the affected muscle with chin rotation away from it is the pattern
A palpable mass within the muscle belly supports the diagnosis and settles over months
Passive correctability is the feature that separates muscular from bony causes
Physiotherapy started in the first months resolves the large majority
Screen for developmental dysplasia of the hip in the same consultation
explanation.pearls: Referral before 3 months of age is associated with resolution in over 90 per cent with stretching alone, while referral after 12 months raises the likelihood of needing surgical release substantially, so the age at referral is the single strongest modifiable predictor of outcome.

options.rationale: A helmet treats established skull deformity, and her occiput is symmetrical with no flattening, so there is nothing for an orthosis to remodel. Positional skull flattening is a common secondary consequence of untreated head tilt, which is an argument for starting physiotherapy now rather than for fitting a helmet. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

A fusiform swelling within the sternocleidomastoid in an infant with a traumatic delivery and a passively correctable tilt is the typical picture, and supervised stretching with positioning advice resolves the great majority when started in the first few months. Earlier referral predicts both faster resolution and a lower chance of needing surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Imaging the muscle adds nothing when the mass is palpable within it and the neck corrects passively, and it delays the treatment that actually changes the outcome. Ultrasound of the neck earns its place when a mass lies outside the muscle or the tilt does not correct, raising the possibility of another lesion. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Ocular torticollis from a fourth nerve palsy or nystagmus produces a compensatory head posture without a muscle mass, and here she fixes and follows across the midline in both directions with symmetrical red reflexes. That combination makes an ocular cause very unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

Radiographs look for vertebral anomalies such as hemivertebrae or atlantoaxial abnormality, which present with a fixed tilt that will not correct passively. Full passive correction with a palpable muscle mass points away from a bony cause. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation, usually called pulled elbow, accounts for a large share of upper limb presentations in children between 1 and 4 years and follows longitudinal traction on an extended pronated arm. The annular ligament is relatively lax at this age and slips proximally over the radial head, and it tightens again once the radius is reduced, which is why recurrence becomes uncommon after about age 5. The key clinical finding is the combination of a pronated resting posture with refusal to supinate and the complete absence of swelling, deformity or focal bony tenderness. Where the history is not witnessed or does not fit, a supracondylar or forearm fracture and inflicted injury both need active consideration before any manipulation.
key_points: Typical age is 1 to 4 years with traction on a pronated extended arm
Pronated posture with refused supination and no focal tenderness is the pattern
Radiographs are normal and reserved for atypical cases or failed reduction
Supination with flexion or hyperpronation both reduce it at the bedside
Recurrence is common under age 5 and parents need anticipatory advice
explanation.pearls: After a successful manoeuvre most children use the arm again within 5 to 30 minutes, so a deliberate period of observation with a toy offered at shoulder height is the confirmatory test; persistent non-use beyond 30 minutes after two attempts is the trigger for radiographs.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

options.rationale: Radiographs are normal in this condition and are reserved for an atypical mechanism, focal bony tenderness, swelling or deformity, or failure of a reduction attempt. Imaging every child with this classic history delays a bedside manoeuvre that works within minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

Immobilisation leaves the annular ligament entrapped and the child not using the arm for days when a single manoeuvre restores function immediately. A sling with clinic review is the right answer for an undisplaced fracture, which the absence of focal tenderness makes unlikely here. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

Axial traction on a pronated forearm slips the annular ligament over the radial head, and supinating the forearm then flexing the elbow fully reduces it, usually with a palpable click and return of use within 5 to 30 minutes. A hyperpronation manoeuvre is an equally accepted alternative with comparable success. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

This is a bedside procedure that needs no anaesthesia and no specialist involvement when the history and examination are typical. Orthopaedic referral becomes appropriate only after two or three failed attempts or if imaging shows a fracture. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

Ultrasound is not part of the assessment pathway for this diagnosis and an effusion is neither expected nor relevant to treatment. Looking for a joint effusion with ultrasound belongs to the assessment of an irritable hip or a suspected septic joint. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

explanation.summary: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction affects up to a fifth of infants and reflects failure of the distal duct to canalise at the valve of Hasner. The picture is watering and morning crusting from stagnant tears with a white conjunctiva, which distinguishes it from conjunctivitis, and mucoid reflux from the sac on digital pressure confirms it. The conditions that must not be missed are infantile glaucoma, signalled by photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal clouding or enlargement, and dacryocystitis, signalled by a tender erythematous swelling over the sac needing systemic antibiotics. Spontaneous resolution occurs in the large majority within the first year, so referral for probing is timed to persistence beyond about 12 months rather than to parental frustration.
key_points: A white conjunctiva with watering points to outflow obstruction, not infection
Mucoid reflux on pressure over the lacrimal sac confirms the diagnosis
Around 90 per cent canalise spontaneously within the first year
Photophobia, corneal clouding or enlargement mandate urgent ophthalmology review
A tender red swelling over the sac is dacryocystitis needing systemic antibiotics
explanation.pearls: Massage is most effective when applied as firm downward strokes from the medial canthus along the side of the nose two to three times daily, because the hydrostatic pressure generated in the sac is what ruptures the membrane at the valve of Hasner; sideways wiping of the lashes achieves nothing.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction

options.rationale: Probing is reserved for obstruction that persists beyond about 12 months of age, because the great majority canalise spontaneously in the first year and early probing exposes an infant to anaesthesia for a self resolving condition. Earlier referral is warranted if there is a distended lacrimal sac or recurrent dacryocystitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Sticky eye)

Repeated topical antibiotics do not relieve a mechanical outflow obstruction and the white uninjected conjunctiva shows there is no conjunctivitis to treat, which is why three previous courses made no difference. Antibiotic drops are appropriate for a genuinely red eye with purulent discharge. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Infantile glaucoma causes watering but with photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal clouding and an enlarged corneal diameter, none of which is present here. Those features, or an asymmetric red reflex, would make urgent referral mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG: Sticky eye)

Mucoid reflux on pressure over the sac with a white eye localises the problem to a blocked nasolacrimal duct, and around 90 per cent open spontaneously during the first year, so cleaning with water and downward massage over the sac with review towards the end of the first year is the appropriate plan. Parents are advised to return sooner for a red or swollen sac or a genuinely inflamed eye. (Source: RCH CPG: Sticky eye)

Those organisms cause a florid purulent conjunctivitis with marked lid swelling in the first weeks of life, not four months of intermittent morning crusting on a white eye. A swab is mandatory for purulent neonatal conjunctivitis in the first month. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Preauricular pits and sinuses occur in roughly 1 per cent of newborns and arise from incomplete fusion of the hillocks that form the external ear. Older teaching linked any external ear anomaly to renal tract malformation and generated routine renal ultrasound, but the evidence supporting that in an isolated pit with an otherwise normal examination is weak, and current Australian practice reserves imaging for babies with additional features. The syndromic associations worth knowing are branchio-oto-renal syndrome, in which pits accompany branchial sinuses, sensorineural or mixed hearing loss and renal anomalies, and the broader group of babies with several minor anomalies who merit genetic review. The practical risk to the individual child is infection of an associated sinus tract, which can become a recurrent abscess requiring complete excision.
key_points: Isolated pits occur in about 1 per cent of newborns and need no imaging
Additional dysmorphic, branchial, auditory or renal features change the plan
A passed newborn hearing screen does not need repeating for a pit alone
Surgery is for recurrent infection or discharge, not for the pit itself
A pit plus branchial sinus plus hearing loss suggests a syndromic diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Incision and drainage of an infected preauricular sinus leaves the tract behind and recurrence is the rule, so once infection has settled the definitive step is complete excision of the tract, typically after a course of antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus.

sources.label: NSW Health: Statewide Infant Screening Hearing program
BMJ Best Practice: Preauricular sinus and pits

options.rationale: Routine renal imaging for an isolated preauricular pit is no longer recommended, because the yield in an otherwise normal baby with a normal antenatal renal survey is very low. Imaging is indicated when the pit accompanies other dysmorphic features, a branchial sinus, hearing loss or a family history of renal disease or deafness. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal examination)

An asymptomatic pit requires no surgery, and excision is offered only for recurrent infection or discharge from an associated sinus tract. Operating on an uncomplicated pit exposes the infant to anaesthesia and a scar for no benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal examination)

Genetic testing is directed at infants with a syndromic combination such as pits with branchial sinuses, hearing loss and renal anomalies, which is a recognisable phenotype rather than an isolated finding. Here the hearing screen is normal and there are no branchial or renal features to justify it. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Preauricular sinus and pits)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Preauricular sinus and pits

options.rationale: A passed automated auditory brainstem response screen does not need repeating on the basis of an isolated ear pit, and scheduling an unnecessary repeat generates parental anxiety. Any later parental or clinician concern about hearing warrants formal audiology assessment regardless of the newborn result. (Source: NSW Health: Statewide Infant Screening Hearing program)
source_refs: NSW Health: Statewide Infant Screening Hearing program

options.rationale: An isolated preauricular pit with a passed hearing screen, no dysmorphic or branchial features and no relevant family history needs no investigation, so explanation with advice to present if the pit becomes red, painful or discharging is the whole management. Ongoing surveillance of hearing and development continues through routine child health checks. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal examination)

explanation.summary: Umbilical hernia in infancy results from incomplete closure of the umbilical ring and is common, particularly in preterm infants and in children of African ancestry. Its natural history contrasts sharply with that of an inguinal hernia in a child: the umbilical defect narrows and closes spontaneously in most children over the first few years, whereas an inguinal hernia does not close and carries a meaningful incarceration risk that mandates early repair. Defect diameter is the most useful predictor of spontaneous closure, with small defects closing readily and defects beyond about 1.5 to 2 cm less likely to do so. Persistent hernias are repaired around school age, both to avoid a cosmetically obvious bulge and because spontaneous closure after that point is unlikely.
key_points: Most paediatric umbilical hernias close spontaneously by 4 to 5 years
Defect diameter predicts closure better than the size of the visible bulge
Incarceration is rare at the umbilicus, unlike in the groin
Compression bands and taping do not aid closure
Irreducibility with pain or vomiting is a same day surgical presentation
explanation.pearls: The contrast worth holding is that an inguinal hernia diagnosed in an infant is referred for repair within weeks because incarceration risk is highest in the first year, while an umbilical hernia of the same size in the same infant is simply reviewed until school age.

sources.label: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons: Paediatric surgery referral guidance

options.rationale: Umbilical hernias in children close spontaneously in the great majority of cases as the abdominal wall musculature develops, so observation with review and referral for persistence beyond about 4 to 5 years is standard, and incarceration is rare at this site. Parents are advised to present urgently if the swelling becomes irreducible, painful or discoloured. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

Repairing at this age operates on a large number of defects that would have closed without surgery, and there is no time pressure because complications are uncommon. Elective repair becomes reasonable once the defect has failed to close by school age or if it is large or symptomatic. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

Strapping, coins and compression bands do not accelerate fascial closure and can cause skin breakdown under the dressing. They persist as folk remedies but have no place in current management. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

The defect is palpable and the diagnosis is clinical, so imaging adds nothing to a decision that rests on age and symptoms. Ultrasound of the abdominal wall is useful where the anatomy is unclear, such as distinguishing an epigastric or paraumbilical hernia from a true umbilical one. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

Urgency is driven by incarceration, which presents with an irreducible tender swelling and vomiting, and none of those features is present in a freely reducible painless hernia. That presentation would require same day surgical assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

explanation.summary: An inguinal hernia in a child is an indirect hernia through a patent processus vaginalis and is far commoner in boys, on the right, and in those born preterm, where the reported incidence reaches 10 to 30 per cent in the most preterm infants. Unlike an umbilical hernia it will not close spontaneously, and the reason for timely surgery is incarceration, which peaks in the first months of life and can compromise bowel or the testicular blood supply. The main differential at this site is a hydrocele of the cord or a communicating hydrocele, which transilluminates, does not extend up to the internal ring on palpation and is not reducible in the same way. In a former preterm infant the anaesthetic plan matters as much as the surgical one, because postoperative apnoea risk persists until around 60 weeks corrected age and mandates postoperative monitoring rather than day surgery.
key_points: A paediatric inguinal hernia will not close spontaneously and needs repair
Incarceration risk is highest in the first year and in preterm infants
Umbilical hernias observe to school age; inguinal hernias are referred promptly
A hydrocele transilluminates and is not reducible in the same way
Former preterm infants need postoperative apnoea monitoring, not day surgery
explanation.pearls: Postoperative apnoea risk after general anaesthesia persists until roughly 60 weeks postconceptional age, so a former 34 week infant repaired at 44 weeks corrected is admitted for overnight cardiorespiratory monitoring rather than discharged the same day.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Perioperative care of the former preterm infant
BMJ Best Practice: Inguinal hernia in children

options.rationale: A reducible swelling appearing on straining above and medial to the pubic tubercle is a clinical diagnosis, and imaging delays a referral whose urgency is driven by age. Ultrasound has a role when the examination is equivocal or when distinguishing a hydrocele of the cord from a hernia is genuinely difficult. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

Paediatric inguinal hernias do not resolve spontaneously and the risk of incarceration is highest in the first year of life and higher again in infants born preterm, so prompt referral for herniotomy rather than watchful waiting is correct. Preterm infants also need repair planned with attention to postoperative apnoea monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

A truss does not close a patent processus vaginalis and can cause skin breakdown or make a segment of bowel harder to reduce. Mechanical appliances have no place in the management of a paediatric inguinal hernia. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

Spontaneous closure is the natural history of an umbilical hernia, not an inguinal one, where the patent processus vaginalis persists and the bowel remains at risk. Confusing the two natural histories is the central error this presentation tests. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

Emergency reduction is for an incarcerated hernia, which presents as an irreducible tender swelling with a distressed or vomiting infant. This swelling reduces spontaneously and completely, so the pathway is elective rather than emergency. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is the commonest reason for infant admission in Australia and is managed supportively with attention to feeding and oxygenation, since bronchodilators, corticosteroids, adrenaline and antibiotics have no routine role. Severity assessment is based on work of breathing, feeding, oxygen saturation and apnoea, and the last of these behaves differently from the others because it can occur in an infant whose respiratory examination looks unremarkable. Young age is the dominant risk factor, with apnoea concentrated in infants under 6 to 8 weeks and in those born preterm, and it is one of the few features in bronchiolitis that mandates admission on its own. Where oxygen is needed, Australian practice starts with low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L per minute and reserves high flow for failure of low flow.
key_points: Witnessed apnoea mandates admission irrespective of work of breathing
Apnoea risk concentrates in infants under 6 to 8 weeks and in preterm infants
Management is supportive; bronchodilators and steroids are not recommended
Low flow nasal prong oxygen is first line if oxygen is required
Feeding adequacy and hydration drive the other admission decisions
explanation.pearls: The RCH oxygen threshold in bronchiolitis is a saturation below 90 per cent rather than the 92 to 94 per cent often quoted, so an infant sitting at 91 per cent with mild recession and adequate feeding does not need oxygen, while this infant needs admission for apnoea despite a saturation of 96 per cent.

sources.label: Paediatric Research in Emergency Departments International Collaborative: Australasian bronchiolitis guideline

options.rationale: Witnessed apnoea in an infant of this age is an independent indication for admission regardless of how well the child looks at the time of assessment, because apnoea recurs and is not predicted by the degree of respiratory distress. Discharge with review would be reasonable for a well feeding infant with mild bronchiolitis and no apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

High flow is reserved for infants who fail low flow oxygen, and this infant is not hypoxaemic at all with an SpO2 of 96 per cent in air, so there is no oxygen requirement to escalate. Admission is right but the intervention attached to it is not. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Apnoea is a recognised presentation of bronchiolitis in infants under about 6 to 8 weeks and carries a risk of recurrence, so admission with continuous cardiorespiratory and saturation monitoring plus support of feeding is the appropriate response even when respiratory distress is mild. Treatment otherwise remains supportive, with oxygen only if saturations fall below the accepted threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Bronchodilators do not alter the course of bronchiolitis in infants and are not recommended at any severity, because the obstruction is from mucosal oedema and debris rather than reversible smooth muscle constriction. A trial of salbutamol belongs to the assessment of an older wheezing child in whom asthma is plausible. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

A short observation period is not sufficient to exclude recurrent apnoea, which is characteristically intermittent and often occurs overnight during sleep. Brief departmental observation is appropriate for assessing feeding in a well older infant, not for clearing apnoea in a neonate. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Australian newborn bloodspot screening for cystic fibrosis uses immunoreactive trypsinogen as a first tier, then a gene panel on trypsinogen positive samples, and refers those with one or two variants for definitive testing. Genotype alone is often insufficient because panels include variants of uncertain significance and variants with variable clinical consequence, so sweat chloride remains the arbiter, with values of 60 mmol/L or more diagnostic, 30 to 59 mmol/L intermediate and requiring extended genotyping and follow up, and under 30 mmol/L making the diagnosis unlikely. Infants with an intermediate result and inconclusive genotyping are labelled as having a screen positive inconclusive diagnosis and enter structured surveillance rather than treatment. Prompt resolution matters because early nutritional support and airway surveillance in a specialist centre are what convert a screening program into improved long term lung function.
key_points: Trypsinogen screens, genotype triages, sweat chloride diagnoses
A variant of uncertain significance prevents diagnosis on genotype alone
Sweat chloride 60 mmol/L or more is diagnostic; under 30 mmol/L makes it unlikely
Faecal elastase guides enzyme replacement but does not diagnose the condition
Normal growth at a few weeks of age does not exclude the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Sweat testing requires an adequate sweat weight, so it is scheduled once the infant is at least 2 weeks old and over 2 kg; an inadequate collection is reported as a failed test and must be repeated rather than read as a low chloride.

sources.label: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway

options.rationale: Treatment should not begin before the diagnosis is established, and this baby has normal growth and no features of fat malabsorption to justify enzyme replacement. Enzymes are started once pancreatic insufficiency is demonstrated, guided by faecal elastase and growth. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway

options.rationale: Trypsinogen falls with age irrespective of whether the infant has cystic fibrosis, so a repeat level is uninterpretable and cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis. Its only role is as the first tier of the screening algorithm on the newborn bloodspot. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway

options.rationale: Faecal elastase measures exocrine pancreatic function and guides enzyme replacement, but it neither confirms nor excludes cystic fibrosis because a proportion of affected children are pancreatic sufficient at diagnosis. It is a functional test rather than a diagnostic one. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway

options.rationale: Sweat chloride measurement remains the diagnostic test that resolves a positive screen, and it is essential here because one variant is of uncertain significance so the genotype cannot establish the diagnosis on its own. Testing is performed at an accredited centre once the infant is over 2 kg and at least 2 weeks old, with a chloride of 60 mmol/L or more diagnostic. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway

options.rationale: Normal growth at 3 weeks does not exclude the diagnosis, since the majority of infants identified by screening are asymptomatic at that age and the point of screening is to intervene before deterioration. Reassurance without completing the diagnostic pathway risks a late diagnosis after preventable lung injury. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway

explanation.summary: The first task in assessing a floppy infant is to separate central from peripheral hypotonia, because that distinction redirects the entire investigation pathway. Central causes preserve or exaggerate deep tendon reflexes and are often accompanied by reduced alertness, seizures or dysmorphic features, whereas peripheral causes at the anterior horn cell, nerve, junction or muscle typically depress or abolish reflexes and may raise creatine kinase. Prader-Willi syndrome is a leading genetic cause of profound neonatal central hypotonia and is recognised by the combination of severe feeding difficulty needing tube feeds, reduced antenatal movement, hypogonadism and later hyperphagia with developmental delay. Early diagnosis changes management substantially, since growth hormone therapy, dietetic and feeding support and structured monitoring for obesity, scoliosis and sleep disordered breathing all begin in infancy.
key_points: Preserved or brisk reflexes point to a central rather than peripheral cause
Normal creatine kinase argues against a primary muscle disorder
Tube feeding for a weak suck plus cryptorchidism is a recognisable phenotype
Methylation analysis detects deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects
Microarray alone can miss uniparental disomy and is not sufficient
explanation.pearls: The feeding pattern inverts over early childhood in this condition, with profound infantile feeding failure giving way to hyperphagia from around 2 years, so the infant who needed nasogastric feeds becomes the child who needs supervised food access and early growth hormone referral.

sources.label: Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Genetic testing in paediatric practice

options.rationale: Anterior horn cell disease produces absent rather than brisk deep tendon reflexes, usually with tongue fasciculation and paradoxical breathing, and it does not cause cryptorchidism. Preserved brisk reflexes are the finding that makes this diagnosis unlikely and points away from a lower motor neuron cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant)

A normal creatine kinase and preserved reflexes make a primary muscle disorder much less likely, and biopsy is an invasive test to select after non-invasive genetic testing has been exhausted. Congenital myotonic dystrophy would also be expected to produce facial weakness and a history of maternal symptoms. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant)

Neurophysiology localises weakness to nerve, junction or muscle, and here the clinical pattern of central hypotonia with preserved reflexes already points above the motor unit. These studies are uncomfortable in a neonate and are reserved for suspected peripheral causes. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant)

Transient neonatal myasthenia from transplacental antibody presents with ptosis, poor suck and fatigable weakness in the infant of a mother with myasthenia, and it resolves over weeks. There is no ptosis or ophthalmoplegia here and no maternal history. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant)

Severe central hypotonia with a weak suck requiring tube feeding, reduced fetal movements, cryptorchidism and preserved reflexes with a normal creatine kinase is the neonatal phenotype of a disorder of imprinting at chromosome 15, and methylation analysis detects all molecular subtypes including deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects. Standard karyotype and microarray can miss uniparental disomy, which is why methylation testing is the specific first line test. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant)

explanation.summary: Gynaecomastia is present in up to two thirds of boys at mid puberty and reflects a transient imbalance between oestrogen and androgen action, resolving within 18 to 24 months in the great majority. The clinical task is to identify the minority in whom it signals pathology, and the most useful sign is testicular volume, because physiological gynaecomastia occurs in a boy whose testes are enlarging normally. Small firm testes with advanced pubic hair indicate that adrenal androgens are driving virilisation while the testes are failing, and in a tall boy with long limbs and educational difficulty this is the classic presentation of Klinefelter syndrome, which affects roughly 1 in 600 males and is substantially underdiagnosed. Diagnosis matters because testosterone replacement supports virilisation, bone density and wellbeing, and because fertility preservation options are best discussed in adolescence.
key_points: Testicular volume, not breast size, separates physiological from pathological gynaecomastia
Small firm testes with Tanner 4 pubic hair indicate primary testicular failure
Raised gonadotrophins with low testosterone confirm a primary gonadal problem
Tall stature with long limbs and learning difficulty supports sex chromosome aneuploidy
Drugs, thyrotoxicosis, liver disease and testicular tumours are the other causes to exclude
explanation.pearls: Testicular volume above about 12 mL at Tanner 4 fits physiological pubertal gynaecomastia, whereas volumes under about 6 mL at the same pubic hair stage should trigger gonadotrophin measurement and a karyotype, since Klinefelter syndrome is diagnosed in only about a quarter of affected males across their lifetime.

options.rationale: Small firm testes of 3 mL despite Tanner 4 pubic hair, tall stature disproportionate to parental heights with long limbs, and a history of learning difficulty together point to primary testicular failure from a sex chromosome aneuploidy, and the biochemical pattern of raised gonadotrophins with low or low normal testosterone alongside a karyotype establishes it. Pubertal gynaecomastia is excluded by the testicular findings rather than by the breast tissue itself. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

Reassurance is the correct management of physiological pubertal gynaecomastia, which occurs at mid puberty in a boy whose testes are enlarging normally to 12 mL or more and who is growing along his expected centile. Small firm testes with disproportionate tall stature is the pattern that makes that reassurance unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

A hormone secreting testicular tumour typically produces asymmetric testicular enlargement or a palpable mass, and both testes here are small, symmetrical and free of any mass. Ultrasound earns its place when a testis is asymmetrically enlarged or a nodule is felt. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

Thyrotoxicosis, chronic liver disease and hyperprolactinaemia all cause gynaecomastia, but thyroid and liver function are already documented as normal and prolactin excess would be expected to suppress rather than preserve pubertal virilisation. Repeating normal tests does not address the testicular finding that drives this presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

Surgery addresses the symptom while leaving an unrecognised cause of hypogonadism untreated, and it is considered only for persistent gynaecomastia after the underlying cause has been established and treated. Proceeding to surgery first also forfeits the chance to start testosterone at the right developmental point. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Coeliac disease requires gluten exposure to be diagnosed, because both the serological and histological abnormalities are consequences of an active immune response to dietary gluten and both normalise on exclusion. This makes a family initiated gluten free diet one of the commonest reasons a child ends up with an unresolvable diagnostic question, and the only way out is a formal gluten challenge with repeat serology and, in most children, duodenal biopsy. HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing is frequently misused in this situation: the haplotypes are carried by a large minority of the population so a positive result is not diagnostic, but their absence has a high negative predictive value and can end the investigation. The reason to persist rather than accept an empirical gluten free diet is that a confirmed diagnosis brings coeliac specific follow up, screening of first degree relatives, bone and nutritional surveillance and access to dietetic support, while an unconfirmed label commits a child to lifelong restriction without any of that.
key_points: Serology and histology both normalise on a gluten free diet
A gluten challenge must precede repeat serology or biopsy
HLA DQ2 or DQ8 positivity is common and not diagnostic; absence largely excludes
Falling centiles with iron deficiency makes completing the diagnosis important
An unconfirmed label forfeits coeliac specific follow up and family screening
explanation.pearls: An adequate paediatric gluten challenge is the equivalent of about four slices of wheat bread daily for a minimum of six weeks before retesting, and if a child cannot tolerate that, HLA typing is the test to request first because a negative result removes the need for the challenge altogether.

sources.label: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.rationale: Tissue transglutaminase antibodies fall once gluten is withdrawn, so a negative result taken after six weeks of exclusion cannot be interpreted as evidence against the diagnosis. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.rationale: Valid serology and histology both require adequate gluten intake, so a formal gluten challenge of the equivalent of around four slices of bread daily for six weeks or more must precede repeat antibody testing and any biopsy, and her falling centiles with iron deficiency make completing the diagnosis important rather than optional. The positive HLA result is used only to show the diagnosis remains possible, since it is common in the general population. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.rationale: Villous architecture recovers on a gluten free diet, so a biopsy taken now may be normal in a child who genuinely has the condition and would leave her wrongly labelled for life. Biopsy is the right test but only after an adequate gluten challenge has restored the antigenic stimulus. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.rationale: Around half of the Australian population carries a permissive HLA type, so a positive result has almost no positive predictive value and cannot diagnose the condition. Its value is the reverse: absence of both permissive haplotypes makes the diagnosis very unlikely and can spare a child a gluten challenge. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.rationale: Repeating the antibody on an unchanged gluten free diet will simply reproduce a negative result, because the antibody titre reflects current gluten exposure rather than underlying susceptibility. A repeat level is informative only once gluten has been reintroduced. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

explanation.summary: A capillary malformation, still widely called a port wine stain, is present at birth, grows with the child and does not involute. Its importance lies in its distribution: involvement of the forehead and upper eyelid, which follows the developmental territory supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, is the pattern associated with leptomeningeal angiomatosis and with ipsilateral glaucoma. Children with intracranial involvement present with focal seizures, hemiparesis and developmental regression, most often in the first two years, and early recognition allows seizure treatment and developmental support to be arranged before damage accumulates. Glaucoma occurs in up to a third of children with upper eyelid involvement and can present at any age, so ophthalmology follow up is ongoing rather than a single visit. Pulsed dye laser remains the treatment for the skin itself and is most effective when started early.
key_points: A capillary malformation is flat at birth, persists lifelong and darkens with age, unlike an infantile haemangioma which appears after birth and proliferates.
Forehead and upper eyelid involvement is the distribution linked to leptomeningeal vascular malformation and to ipsilateral glaucoma.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging and formal ophthalmology assessment are both arranged even when the infant is neurologically normal.
Cranial ultrasound cannot exclude leptomeningeal involvement and a normal scan is falsely reassuring.
Pulsed dye laser treats the cutaneous lesion and is complementary to, not a substitute for, the associated screening.
explanation.pearls: Eyelid involvement is the ocular red flag: children with upper eyelid capillary malformation need intraocular pressure measured at diagnosis and then at least annually through childhood, because glaucoma in this group frequently develops after the first year rather than at birth.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Capillary malformation
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Kids Health Info on birthmarks

options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser is the treatment of choice for the skin lesion itself and early treatment does improve colour, but arranging it as the sole action leaves the neurological and ocular associations of a lesion in this distribution unsearched. Laser referral belongs alongside, not instead of, imaging and ophthalmology review. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Capillary malformation)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Capillary malformation

options.rationale: A capillary malformation involving the forehead and upper eyelid carries a substantial risk of leptomeningeal vascular malformation and of ipsilateral glaucoma, so brain imaging and formal ophthalmological assessment are both indicated even when the infant is neurologically well. Glaucoma may be present at birth or develop later, which is why ophthalmology review is arranged now and then repeated. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Capillary malformation)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Capillary malformation

options.rationale: Fading is the natural history of a salmon patch on the glabella or nape, not of a capillary malformation, which persists and darkens with age. Reassurance without imaging or eye review would miss both intracranial involvement and a glaucoma that can threaten vision in the first year. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Kids Health Info on birthmarks)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Kids Health Info on birthmarks

options.rationale: Propranolol is the treatment for a proliferating infantile haemangioma, which is a vascular tumour that appears after birth, grows for several months and feels raised and firm. A lesion that has been flat and unchanged since birth is a malformation and does not respond to propranolol. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Kids Health Info on birthmarks)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Kids Health Info on birthmarks

options.rationale: Cranial ultrasound images the ventricles and midline structures but does not show the cortical and leptomeningeal changes that matter here, and a normal scan would give false reassurance. Magnetic resonance imaging is the study that answers the question being asked. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sturge-Weber syndrome)

explanation.summary: Benign idiopathic limb pain of childhood affects up to a third of primary school-aged children and is defined by a highly consistent pattern rather than by exclusion through investigation. The pain is bilateral, affects the muscles of the calves, shins and thighs rather than the joints, occurs in the late afternoon, evening or night, and resolves completely by morning with no residual limp or functional loss. The examination is normal, growth is unaffected, and the child is not systemically unwell. The differentials that genuinely demand investigation announce themselves through asymmetry, persistence into the day, or systemic features, so the clinical task is pattern recognition plus explicit safety netting rather than a screening panel of tests. Families are helped by being told that the pain is real, that it is not caused by growth of the bones, and that it settles over months to years.
key_points: The benign pattern is bilateral, muscular rather than articular, confined to evening and night, and fully resolved by the next morning.
A normal gait, normal joints and absence of bony tenderness are the findings that support the diagnosis positively.
Unilateral pain, daytime pain, limp, joint swelling, fever, weight loss, pallor or bruising redirect the assessment towards malignancy, infection and inflammatory arthritis.
Investigations are not required when the pattern is classical, and incidental abnormal results cause harm.
Explicit safety netting substitutes for testing and should name the features that would prompt earlier review.
explanation.pearls: Leukaemia presenting as limb pain typically produces pain that persists into the day and is accompanied by a cytopenia in at least one lineage, so a child who runs and plays normally every morning and has a normal blood count taken for other reasons is very unlikely to have it.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vitamin D deficiency

options.rationale: Bilateral limb pain confined to evenings and nights, with a child who is completely well and fully active by day and who has a normal examination, is the recognised benign idiopathic pattern and needs no investigation. Safety netting matters because the diagnosis is defined by its natural history: unilateral pain, daytime pain, limp, joint swelling or systemic features change the assessment. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children

options.rationale: Blood tests are the right move when pain is unilateral, persistent through the day, associated with a limp, or accompanied by pallor, bruising, lymphadenopathy or organomegaly, none of which are present here. Investigating a classical benign pattern generates false positive results and entrenches the family's anxiety. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children

options.rationale: Radiographs are indicated for focal bony tenderness, night pain in one limb, or a limp, because those features raise osteoid osteoma, osteomyelitis and bone tumour. Symmetrical pain with no bony tenderness does not warrant irradiating both lower limbs. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children

options.rationale: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis produces joint swelling with morning stiffness that eases through the day, which is the reverse of this boy's pattern of an entirely normal morning and evening pain. A normal joint examination with no morning stiffness makes the referral unnecessary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain with tenderness over the long bones, proximal weakness and sometimes deformity, and is tested when there are risk factors such as limited sun exposure or a restrictive diet. Neither the history nor the examination here points that way. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vitamin D deficiency)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vitamin D deficiency

explanation.summary: The toddler fracture is an undisplaced spiral or oblique fracture of the distal tibial shaft that follows a low energy twisting injury in a child between about nine months and three years, and around half are not visible on the first radiographs. The diagnosis is therefore clinical, resting on refusal to weight bear with focal tibial tenderness after a mechanism that involves rotation. Management is immobilisation for comfort and protection, with a repeat radiograph after seven to ten days showing periosteal new bone if the fracture was present. The important alternatives are septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, which bring fever and raised inflammatory markers, transient synovitis, which localises to the hip, and inflicted injury, which is suggested by a mechanism that does not match the child's developmental abilities. Healing is rapid and the great majority need nothing beyond a cast or boot for three to four weeks.
key_points: Around half of toddler fractures are radiographically occult at presentation, so a normal first film does not exclude one.
Focal tenderness over the tibial shaft with refusal to weight bear after a twisting mechanism is enough to treat.
Immobilisation plus a repeat radiograph at seven to ten days is the standard pathway and avoids irradiating or sedating the child further.
Fever with raised inflammatory markers or a hip held flexed and externally rotated redirects to infection or synovitis.
Inflicted injury is suggested by a mechanism inconsistent with the child's mobility, changing accounts, or associated bruising, not by the fracture pattern alone.
explanation.pearls: Periosteal new bone becomes visible on plain film from about seven to ten days after a toddler fracture, which is why the review radiograph is booked for that window rather than at three or four days when it will still look normal.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on child abuse
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of limp in children

options.rationale: A bone scan will show increased uptake but exposes a toddler to radiation and to the need for sedation in order to answer a question that immobilisation and a repeat radiograph answer safely. It is reserved for persisting unexplained refusal to weight bear after simpler steps. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child

options.rationale: Discharge without immobilisation leaves an undisplaced spiral fracture unsupported and prolongs pain, and a week of walking on it risks displacement. Analgesia is necessary but is not on its own an adequate plan for a child with focal bony tenderness. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child

options.rationale: An undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibial shaft in a newly walking child is frequently invisible on the initial films and becomes apparent as periosteal reaction on a film repeated a week to ten days later. Treating on clinical grounds with immobilisation gives symptom relief and protects the bone while the diagnosis declares itself. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child

options.rationale: Hip ultrasound is the right test when the pain localises to the hip or groin, when the hip is held flexed and externally rotated, or when there is fever with raised inflammatory markers. Tenderness over the tibial shaft with pain free hip movement and a normal C reactive protein points elsewhere. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child

options.rationale: A skeletal survey is indicated when the injury does not fit the developmental stage or the stated mechanism, when there are multiple or unexplained bruises, or when the account changes, none of which apply to a witnessed twisting injury in an independently mobile toddler with an intact skin examination. A spiral tibial fracture in this age group is a common accidental injury and is not in itself suspicious. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on child abuse)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on child abuse

explanation.summary: Vulvovaginitis is the commonest gynaecological problem of prepubertal girls and in the large majority is non-specific, driven by thin unoestrogenised vulval skin, close proximity of the anus, and contact irritants such as soap, bubble bath, shampoo and prolonged wet bathers. Symptoms are soreness, itch, dysuria at the vulva rather than within the urethra, and a scant discharge that marks the underwear. Management is education and irritant avoidance, with a barrier ointment to protect the skin and simple measures such as showering rather than bathing and drying thoroughly after swimming. Antibiotics, antifungals and swabs are not part of routine care, but specific causes are considered when the discharge is purulent or offensive, when there is bleeding, or when symptoms persist despite good hygiene. Persistent blood stained discharge warrants vaginoscopy for a foreign body, and any behavioural change, genital injury or specific disclosure requires assessment for sexual abuse.
key_points: Non-specific vulvovaginitis is an irritant dermatitis, so the treatment is removal of irritants plus a barrier preparation.
Vulval swabs usually grow mixed flora and are reserved for offensive or purulent discharge.
Candida is rare before puberty because the vaginal pH is neutral without oestrogen.
Nocturnal perianal itch with excoriation points to threadworm rather than to vulvovaginitis.
Persistent bloody or foul discharge raises a retained foreign body and warrants vaginoscopy.
explanation.pearls: Dysuria in a prepubertal girl with a negative dipstick is usually urine stinging inflamed vulval skin rather than a urinary tract infection, and asking whether the pain is felt outside or inside distinguishes the two at the bedside.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis
BMJ Best Practice: Vulvovaginitis in children

options.rationale: Vulval swabs in prepubertal girls grow mixed perineal flora that do not guide treatment, and oral antibiotics do not alter the course of non-specific vulvovaginitis. A swab is worth taking when there is offensive or purulent discharge, suggesting a specific pathogen such as group A streptococcus. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis

options.rationale: Candidal vulvovaginitis is rare before puberty because the unoestrogenised vagina has a neutral pH that does not favour candida, and it would be expected only after antibiotics, in nappy wearing children or with diabetes. Treating empirically with an antifungal delays the advice that actually works. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis

options.rationale: Threadworm causes intense perianal itch that is worst at night and usually produces perianal excoriation, whereas this girl has vulval erythema with intact perianal skin and daytime symptoms. Mebendazole would be reasonable if the itch were nocturnal and perianal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Non-specific vulvovaginitis in prepubertal girls is an irritant dermatitis of thin unoestrogenised skin, and treatment is removal of the irritants together with a bland barrier preparation and attention to drying after swimming. Most improve within a few weeks on these measures alone, which is why review is planned rather than a prescription given. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis

options.rationale: Vaginoscopy is indicated for persistent blood stained or foul discharge, which suggests a retained foreign body such as toilet paper, and for symptoms that do not respond to hygiene measures. A non offensive discharge with no bleeding does not justify an anaesthetic at this stage. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis

explanation.summary: Stuttering typically begins between two and four years of age and affects up to eight per cent of preschool children, with natural recovery in many during the first year after onset. The decision that matters in primary care is whether to watch or to refer, and it turns on duration since onset, the presence of secondary features such as facial tension, blocks and avoidance, the child's own distress, and a family history of persistent stuttering. Early intervention delivered by parents under speech pathology supervision, of which the Lidcombe Program developed in Australia is the best studied example, produces high rates of resolution when started in the preschool years. Untreated persistent stuttering is associated with social anxiety and reduced educational and occupational participation in adolescence and adulthood, which is why the preschool window is defended. Advice that puts the child on the spot, such as telling him to slow down or start the word again, tends to worsen struggle behaviour.
key_points: Natural recovery is common in the first twelve months after onset, so duration since onset is a central triage question.
Physical tension, blocks, avoidance of words or speaking situations, and family history all predict persistence.
Parent delivered behavioural treatment supervised by a speech pathologist is the intervention with the strongest evidence in preschoolers.
Asking a child to slow down or repeat a word increases attention to the stutter and is not recommended.
Normal sentence structure, comprehension and social play separate stuttering from language disorder and from autism.
explanation.pearls: The strongest single trigger for referral rather than watchful waiting is dysfluency persisting beyond twelve months from onset, because natural recovery rates fall sharply after that point and treatment before school entry has substantially better outcomes than treatment in the school years.

sources.label: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on speech and language delay

options.rationale: Natural recovery is common in the first year of dysfluency, but this boy has already stuttered for eight months, has developed physical tension and negative reaction to his own speech, and has a first degree relative who stuttered, which are the features that predict persistence. Waiting another year forfeits the preschool window in which treatment works best. (Source: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering)
source_refs: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering

options.rationale: Instructing a child to slow down or start again draws attention to the moment of stuttering and tends to increase struggle and avoidance rather than reduce dysfluency. Parents are instead coached within a structured program to give specific contingent feedback about smooth speech. (Source: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering)
source_refs: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering

options.rationale: Autism assessment is prompted by differences in social communication, restricted interests or repetitive behaviour, whereas this boy converses, plays imaginatively and uses age-appropriate sentence structure. Referring him down that pathway delays the intervention he needs. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on speech and language delay)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on speech and language delay

options.rationale: Hearing loss produces articulation and language difficulties rather than repetition of initial sounds with physical struggle, and this boy responds to conversational speech across the room with age-appropriate language. Audiology is a reasonable background check but is not the step that changes his outcome. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on speech and language delay)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on speech and language delay

options.rationale: Stuttering that has persisted beyond twelve months, or that carries risk markers such as physical tension, avoidance and a family history, warrants referral rather than further watchful waiting, and preschool treatment delivered by parents under speech pathology supervision has the strongest evidence for eliminating stuttering. Treatment is most effective before school entry, when the child's reaction to his own speech is still forming. (Source: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering)
source_refs: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering

explanation.summary: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection of the skin that spreads by direct contact and autoinoculation, and in healthy children it clears spontaneously, usually within twelve to eighteen months although occasionally longer. Lesions are pearly dome shaped papules with a central dimple, and an individual lesion that becomes red, swollen and crusted is most often undergoing immune mediated resolution, a phenomenon families find alarming unless it is explained in advance. Australian guidance does not support exclusion from school, childcare or swimming, and children should not be kept out of the pool, although lesions are covered for contact sports and towels are not shared. Treatments including cryotherapy, curettage, cantharidin and imiquimod carry pain, pigment change or scarring and have limited evidence of benefit in children. Extensive or atypical disease, particularly with facial or genital involvement outside the usual pattern, prompts consideration of underlying immunodeficiency or of coexisting atopic dermatitis that facilitates spread.
key_points: Molluscum resolves spontaneously in immunocompetent children, usually within twelve to eighteen months.
Exclusion from school, childcare or swimming is not recommended; lesions are covered for close contact activities.
An inflamed crusted lesion that is shrinking usually signals immune clearance rather than bacterial infection.
Cryotherapy, curettage and imiquimod carry pain, pigmentary change or scarring without meaningfully shortening the illness.
Coexisting eczema promotes spread, so treating the dermatitis reduces autoinoculation.
explanation.pearls: The red crusted lesion that worries parents, sometimes called the beginning of the end sign, predicts clearance of the whole eruption within the following weeks to months and is a useful piece of anticipatory explanation at the first consultation.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum
Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews: Interventions for cutaneous molluscum contagiosum

options.rationale: Molluscum contagiosum in an immunocompetent child resolves spontaneously over months to a couple of years, and active treatment is painful, may scar and does not shorten the course meaningfully. Exclusion from school or swimming is not recommended, and covering lesions during close contact activities is the proportionate measure. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum

options.rationale: Cryotherapy is painful, poorly tolerated by young children and risks hypopigmentation and scarring, and thirty lesions would require several sessions for a condition that resolves without treatment. It is occasionally offered to older patients with a few troublesome lesions. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum

options.rationale: A general anaesthetic to remove a self-limiting viral skin infection exposes the child to more risk than the condition carries, and new lesions commonly appear afterwards through autoinoculation. Curettage has a role only for a small number of persistent disfiguring lesions in an older child. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum

options.rationale: A single molluscum lesion that becomes red, tender and crusted before shrinking usually reflects the host immune response that precedes resolution rather than bacterial infection, and this lesion is already involuting. Antibiotics are reserved for spreading cellulitis with expanding erythema, fever or systemic upset. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Randomised evidence in children shows imiquimod is no better than vehicle for molluscum while causing application site reactions, and it is not recommended for this indication. Its established uses are genital warts and some keratinocyte cancers in adults. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Molluscum contagiosum

explanation.summary: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome is a non immunoglobulin E mediated food allergy that presents with profuse repetitive vomiting one to four hours after ingestion of the trigger, often with pallor, lethargy and sometimes shock, and characteristically without any skin or respiratory features. Rice, cow milk, soy, oat and egg are the commonest Australian triggers, and the first recognised episode frequently follows the very first exposure to a new solid. Because the mechanism is cell mediated, skin prick tests and specific immunoglobulin E are usually negative and the diagnosis rests on the history and the reproducible timing. Acute treatment is isotonic fluid resuscitation with ondansetron, and adrenaline has no role unless the picture is genuinely anaphylactic. Ongoing care involves strict avoidance of the trigger, a written acute action plan for emergency departments that names the syndrome, and supervised oral food challenge to assess tolerance, which develops in most children by three to five years of age.
key_points: The hallmark is repetitive vomiting one to four hours after ingestion, with pallor and lethargy and without urticaria or wheeze.
Around fifteen per cent of acute episodes present with hypovolaemic shock, and isotonic crystalloid is the treatment.
Ondansetron shortens acute episodes in children over six months and is used alongside fluids.
Skin prick tests and specific immunoglobulin E are usually negative because the reaction is cell mediated.
Most children outgrow the syndrome by three to five years, confirmed by supervised oral food challenge.
explanation.pearls: The most useful bedside distinction is timing with an absence of skin signs: anaphylaxis begins within minutes and involves skin or mucosa in about eighty per cent of cases, whereas this syndrome begins one to four hours after the meal and leaves the skin entirely clear.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on sepsis
BMJ Best Practice: Non IgE mediated food allergy

options.rationale: Adrenaline is the treatment for anaphylaxis, which requires acute skin or mucosal features with respiratory or cardiovascular compromise, or sudden hypotension after exposure to a known allergen, and it typically begins within minutes rather than two hours. This boy has profound vomiting with shock, no skin involvement and no airway signs, which is the non immunoglobulin E mediated pattern that does not respond to adrenaline. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

options.rationale: Sepsis is the usual initial working diagnosis in this presentation and antibiotics are defensible when the picture is unclear, but this child is afebrile with a clear temporal link to a first food exposure and a normal respiratory and abdominal examination. Fluid resuscitation is still the first priority even when antibiotics are given. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on sepsis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on sepsis

options.rationale: Acute food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome causes massive fluid shift into the gut, and around fifteen per cent of episodes present in shock, so isotonic crystalloid resuscitation is the intervention that reverses the physiology. A single dose of ondansetron shortens the vomiting in children over six months and is now standard in acute episodes. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

options.rationale: An orally administered drug is futile in a child who is vomiting repeatedly and shocked, and corticosteroid has no established role in reversing the acute fluid shift of this syndrome. Deferring intravenous access for four hours in a shocked infant risks deterioration. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

options.rationale: Skin prick and specific immunoglobulin E testing are typically negative in this condition because the mechanism is cell mediated, so a negative result would falsely reassure and a positive one would mislead. Testing is a question for the allergy clinic after resuscitation, not an immediate intervention in a shocked infant. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

explanation.summary: Sandifer syndrome is the association of gastro-oesophageal reflux with paroxysmal dystonic posturing, most often back arching with lateral head rotation, and it is a common reason for infants to be referred with suspected seizures. The features that separate it from epilepsy are its relationship to feeds, complete preservation of awareness and responsiveness during the event, immediate relief with upright positioning, and a normal interictal neurological examination. Infants are typically thriving, so failure to gain weight, haematemesis, bilious vomiting or a bulging fontanelle should redirect the assessment. Management is the standard conservative approach to infant reflux, with positional measures, smaller more frequent feeds and consideration of thickened feeds or a trial of an extensively hydrolysed formula when cow milk protein allergy is suspected. Acid suppression is reserved for infants with clear complications of reflux rather than for posturing alone, because proton pump inhibitors in infants carry risks of gastroenteritis and lower respiratory infection without good evidence of benefit for these episodes.
key_points: Dystonic posturing tightly linked to feeds with preserved awareness is the signature of reflux associated posturing, not of seizures.
Relief on being held upright and absence of events during sleep are strong negative predictors of epilepsy.
A normal interictal examination with age-appropriate development and normal head growth argues against structural pathology.
Conservative feeding measures both treat the problem and serve as a diagnostic trial with planned review.
Poor weight gain, haematemesis, bilious vomiting or neurological signs move the child out of this pathway.
explanation.pearls: Infantile spasms are the seizure type that must not be missed at this age: they occur in clusters of brief symmetrical flexion or extension movements, classically on waking rather than around feeds, and they warrant an electroencephalogram within days because treatment delay worsens developmental outcome.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on torticollis

options.rationale: An electroencephalogram is the right investigation when the events are stereotyped clusters with impaired awareness, developmental regression or occurrence during sleep, none of which fit episodes that arise only around feeds in a fully alert infant. Ordering it first tends to prolong uncertainty and invites over interpretation of normal infant variants. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

options.rationale: Dystonic posturing that is tightly time locked to feeds, preserves awareness and abates on being held upright is the recognised reflux associated movement pattern, and conservative feeding measures both treat it and confirm the diagnosis when the episodes settle. Review is built in so that failure to improve triggers reconsideration rather than open ended reassurance. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

options.rationale: Starting an antiepileptic drug commits an infant to treatment and monitoring for events that are not epileptic, and it will not change episodes driven by oesophageal acid exposure. Antiepileptic treatment follows a diagnosis of epilepsy rather than preceding it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Imaging is indicated for a fixed head tilt that does not correct, for focal neurological signs, for an abnormally growing head, or for developmental regression, whereas this infant has symmetrical tone, normal development and head circumference tracking along her centile. Anaesthetising a thriving 4-month-old for a pattern explained by feeding is not justified. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on torticollis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on torticollis

options.rationale: A contrast study assesses anatomy such as malrotation and strictures but is poor at quantifying reflux, with both false positives and false negatives, and it delivers radiation to answer a question a therapeutic trial answers better. It earns its place when bilious vomiting or a suspected obstruction is in play. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

explanation.summary: Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood is an acquired pure red cell aplasia that typically affects children between six months and four years, often several weeks after a viral illness, and it resolves spontaneously within one to two months. The blood picture is an isolated normocytic anaemia with a strikingly low reticulocyte count and normal white cell and platelet counts, with a normal blood film. Its two important mimics are iron deficiency, which is microcytic with a low ferritin, and Diamond Blackfan anaemia, which presents in the first year with macrocytosis, raised fetal haemoglobin and often thumb or craniofacial anomalies. Leukaemia is excluded clinically and on the film by the absence of blasts, additional cytopenias, organomegaly and bone pain. Management is observation with serial counts, and transfusion is reserved for the child who is symptomatic at rest or haemodynamically compromised because most children compensate remarkably well even at low haemoglobin levels reached slowly.
key_points: Isolated normocytic anaemia with reticulocytopenia and normal other lineages after a viral illness is the defining pattern.
A rising reticulocyte count on a repeat sample confirms recovery and is the key follow up measurement.
Normal ferritin with normocytic indices excludes iron deficiency as the cause.
Diamond Blackfan anaemia presents earlier, with macrocytosis, raised fetal haemoglobin and congenital anomalies.
Transfusion is decided on symptoms and haemodynamics rather than on a haemoglobin threshold alone.
explanation.pearls: Anaemia that develops over weeks is tolerated far better than the same haemoglobin reached acutely, so a toddler with a haemoglobin in the 60s who is playing normally with a normal blood pressure and no tachypnoea can usually be watched with serial counts rather than transfused.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on iron deficiency
BMJ Best Practice: Pure red cell aplasia

options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for children who are haemodynamically compromised, symptomatic at rest or still falling, because in this condition spontaneous recovery is the rule and transfusion exposes the child to sensitisation without changing the course. A boy who is running about with a compensated circulation does not meet that threshold. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children

options.rationale: Iron deficiency produces microcytosis with a low ferritin and a raised red cell distribution width, whereas this boy has normocytic cells with a ferritin in the normal range. Iron will not correct an anaemia caused by temporary failure of red cell production. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on iron deficiency)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on iron deficiency

options.rationale: Marrow examination is indicated when more than one lineage is affected, when blasts or tear drop cells appear on the film, or when there is organomegaly, lymphadenopathy or bone pain, and none of those are present. An isolated normocytic anaemia with a low reticulocyte count and otherwise normal counts is investigated by serial monitoring first. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on anaemia in children

options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is used for parvovirus associated red cell aplasia in immunocompromised children with persistent viraemia, not for the self-limiting post viral aplasia of an immunocompetent toddler. Giving it here adds risk and cost without changing the natural history. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pure red cell aplasia)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Pure red cell aplasia

options.rationale: Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood follows a viral illness in a previously well toddler and recovers spontaneously over four to eight weeks, heralded by a rising reticulocyte count that is the single most informative repeat measurement.
