Refusal to weight bear, a documented fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/h and a significant effusion satisfy enough predictive criteria that septic arthritis must be excluded by aspirating the joint. Synovial fluid for Gram stain, cell count and culture is obtained before antibiotics because prior dosing reduces the culture yield that guides later therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

Antibiotics before aspiration compromise the synovial culture and leave the team without an organism to guide a treatment course lasting weeks. A septic hip also needs joint decompression, which antibiotics alone do not provide. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for suspected osteomyelitis or when the site is unclear, but here ultrasound has already localised a substantial effusion. In a preschooler it needs anaesthesia and would delay the intervention that is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

Corticosteroid would suppress the inflammatory response and the fever while allowing an untreated joint infection to destroy articular cartilage. It has no place until infection has been definitively excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema complicates roughly one per cent of paediatric episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis but accounts for the majority of deaths and lasting neurological disability, and it characteristically appears four to twelve hours into treatment, when the numbers are improving and the team has begun to relax. Risk is concentrated in younger children, in new onset diabetes, and in those presenting with more severe acidosis and a higher urea. The warning features are headache, recurrent vomiting, irritability or drowsiness, incontinence, and specific cranial nerve palsies, with bradycardia and hypertension representing the late Cushing response rather than an early sign. A failure of the sodium to rise as the glucose falls is an important biochemical warning, since corrected sodium should climb during treatment. Because computed tomography is often normal early and transfer wastes time, treatment with hyperosmolar therapy is given on clinical grounds.
key_points: Onset is typically four to twelve hours into treatment, as the biochemistry is improving
Bradycardia with rising blood pressure is a late Cushing response, not a sign of hypovolaemia
Risk concentrates in younger children, new onset diabetes and more severe presenting acidosis
Treat clinically with hypertonic saline or mannitol and reduced fluid rate rather than awaiting imaging
A corrected sodium that fails to rise as glucose falls is an early biochemical warning sign
explanation.pearls: Corrected sodium rises by about 2.4 mmol/L for every 5.5 mmol/L fall in glucose, so plotting it hourly during treatment gives an objective early warning that precedes any change in conscious state.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Diabetes management

options.rationale: The biochemistry is in fact correcting steadily and the ketone fall is appropriate, so the deterioration is not explained by insufficient insulin. Raising the rate would accelerate the osmotic shift that is the likely driver of the neurological change. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Hypovolaemia produces tachycardia with a narrow pulse pressure, not bradycardia with hypertension, so the haemodynamic pattern points the opposite way. A fluid bolus would add to intracranial volume at precisely the wrong moment. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Headache with a falling conscious state, bradycardia and rising blood pressure occurring while the biochemistry improves is cerebral oedema, and the Cushing response means treatment cannot wait for imaging. Hyperosmolar therapy with reduction of the fluid infusion rate and immediate critical care involvement is the intervention that alters outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Imaging is frequently normal in the early hours of this complication and a transfer to the scanner delays treatment during the period when deterioration is fastest. The diagnosis in this setting is clinical and treatment precedes confirmation. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Glucose is added to the fluid once the level approaches 14 to 17 mmol/L so that insulin can continue to clear ketones, and that adjustment is indeed due here. It does not account for bradycardia and hypertension, and treating this as hypoglycaemia at a glucose of 14 mmol/L misreads the picture. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Any infant still jaundiced at fourteen days of age needs a split bilirubin, and a conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total defines cholestasis that is never physiological. Pale acholic stools and dark urine point to obstruction, and a non-visualised gallbladder on a fasted ultrasound supports it although a normal scan would not exclude it. The definitive investigation is intraoperative cholangiography with liver biopsy at a paediatric liver centre, arranged without delay. Outcome after Kasai portoenterostomy falls sharply once the infant passes about sixty days, so referral is measured in days rather than weeks.
key_points: Jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days requires a split bilirubin, not observation
A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of total bilirubin is always pathological
Pale stools with dark urine indicate obstruction until proven otherwise
A normal ultrasound does not exclude biliary atresia; cholangiography is definitive
Portoenterostomy before about sixty days gives markedly better bile drainage
explanation.pearls: Ask the parents to compare the nappy against a printed stool colour chart rather than asking whether the stools look pale, because parental description alone misses about a third of acholic stools. A normal coagulation profile is reassuring only transiently: vitamin K dependent factors fall within weeks in cholestasis, so give intramuscular vitamin K before any biopsy is contemplated.

sources.label: Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice

options.rationale: A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent with pale stools and a non-visualised gallbladder is obstructive cholestasis until disproven, and the definitive test is operative cholangiography with biopsy at a specialist centre. The urgency is driven by the fact that portoenterostomy performed before around sixty days of age gives far better bile drainage than surgery after that point. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Fasting technique does affect gallbladder visualisation and a repeat scan is sometimes useful, but a normal ultrasound never excludes the diagnosis and repeating it costs days inside a narrow surgical window. Ultrasound is best used to find the alternative lesions such as a choledochal cyst. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Radionuclide scanning has largely fallen out of favour because it is highly sensitive but poorly specific, and the phenobarbital priming period adds close to a week of delay. It cannot exclude the diagnosis when it is abnormal, so the patient ends up at cholangiography regardless. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and by definition has a conjugated fraction below 20 per cent with normal stool colour, so this infant fails both criteria. A well feeding thriving baby looks reassuring, and that is how the diagnosis is missed. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Supportive nutritional and choleretic therapy belongs after the cause is established, and fat soluble vitamin replacement is certainly needed in prolonged cholestasis. Beginning it alone treats the consequences of obstruction while the window for surgery closes. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice)
source_refs: Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice

explanation.summary: Knee pain in an adolescent with a normal knee examination should always redirect attention to the hip, because the obturator nerve refers hip pathology to the medial knee. Loss of internal rotation with obligatory external rotation as the hip is flexed is close to specific for slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and the risk factors of adolescence and raised body mass index fit. A frontal pelvic radiograph alone misses early slips because the displacement is posterior, so frog leg lateral views of both hips are required. Weight bearing must stop the moment the diagnosis is suspected, since progression from a stable to an unstable slip sharply increases the risk of avascular necrosis.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee pain
Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is the characteristic bedside sign
Frontal radiographs alone miss early posterior slips; frog leg laterals are essential
Image both hips, since bilateral involvement occurs in a substantial minority
Make the child non-weight-bearing on suspicion, before imaging confirms the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Trace Klein's line along the superior femoral neck on the frontal film: it should intersect part of the epiphysis, and failure to do so indicates a slip even when the report reads as normal. Screen for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency and renal osteodystrophy when a slip occurs outside the usual age band of ten to sixteen years or in a child of normal weight, since an endocrinopathy underlies a meaningful proportion of those cases.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: An inflammatory arthropathy would be expected to produce joint swelling, morning stiffness or involvement elsewhere, none of which are present. Serology has no role in a mechanical presentation and delays the imaging that will make the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

A frontal film misses early posterior slip of the femoral epiphysis in a substantial minority of cases, and the lateral projection is where the displacement is seen. Non-weight-bearing begins immediately on clinical suspicion because continued loading can convert a stable slip into an unstable one with a much higher rate of avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance detects a pre-slip and is useful when plain films are genuinely normal, but it is not the immediate next test and permitting weight bearing while awaiting it is the part that causes harm. The lateral radiograph is faster and answers the question in most cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Ultrasound answers the question of joint effusion, which serves transient synovitis and septic arthritis, and he is afebrile with six weeks of symptoms rather than days. The distinguishing relationship is that synovitis restricts rotation in all directions while a slip produces the characteristic obligatory external rotation on flexion. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

Anterior knee pain in an adolescent is frequently patellofemoral, but a normal knee examination with restricted hip rotation relocates the problem to the hip entirely. Six weeks of loaded rehabilitation is exactly the interval in which a stable slip progresses. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

explanation.summary: Breech presentation beyond 34 weeks and a first degree relative are the two strongest risk factors for hip dysplasia, and this girl has both. After about three months the reducible clunk disappears, so limited abduction and apparent femoral shortening on Galeazzi testing become the signs that matter. The imaging choice is governed purely by ossification of the femoral head, which occurs around four to six months: ultrasound before that point, plain radiography after it. At seven months the correct request is a frontal pelvic radiograph, with orthopaedic referral to follow because harness treatment is generally ineffective beyond six months.
key_points: Breech presentation after 34 weeks and a positive family history are the principal risk factors
Ortolani and Barlow testing loses sensitivity after about three months of age
Limited abduction and a positive Galeazzi sign replace the clunk in older infants
Ultrasound is the test under four months; plain radiography is the test after ossification
Pavlik harness treatment is generally ineffective beyond six months of age
explanation.pearls: Unilateral limitation of abduction to less than 60 degrees in an infant beyond three months should prompt imaging even when every other finding is normal, since it is the single most reliable late sign. Expect an acetabular index above 25 degrees at one year to indicate dysplasia, and remember that a hip which was normal on newborn ultrasound can still present late, so reassess abduction at every routine check until walking.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists: Paediatric Imaging Referral

options.rationale: The Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres lose their sensitivity after about three months because the hip becomes fixed rather than reducible, so a negative clunk in an older infant is expected and reassures nobody. Limited abduction and apparent limb shortening become the reliable signs at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Computed tomography gives a high radiation dose to the gonads of an infant girl for information that a plain film provides adequately before treatment. It has a role in postoperative assessment, not in diagnosis. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists: Paediatric Imaging Referral)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists: Paediatric Imaging Referral

options.rationale: Ultrasound depends on the femoral head being cartilaginous, and once the ossific nucleus appears at roughly four to six months it casts an acoustic shadow that obscures the acetabulum. From this age onward the plain radiograph is the investigation of choice, assessed using the acetabular index and Perkin's and Hilgenreiner's lines. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Avoiding radiation is a sound instinct and ultrasound is genuinely the right test under about four months of age, but after ossification begins the image quality collapses and the study becomes unreliable. The distinguishing factor is the age of the child rather than a preference for one modality. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance does image both tissues but requires sedation at this age and is reserved for assessing reduction after closed or open treatment. It is not a screening or first line diagnostic study. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

explanation.summary: Persistent arthritis of four or fewer joints for more than six weeks in a child under sixteen, with normal inflammatory markers and no systemic features, describes oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis. The complication that determines long term disability is chronic anterior uveitis, which is entirely asymptomatic with a white quiet eye and is detected only by slit lamp examination. Risk is stratified by age at onset, disease subtype and antinuclear antibody status, and a young girl with oligoarticular disease and a positive antibody falls into the highest risk band requiring three monthly screening. Eye disease flares independently of joint activity, so screening continues regardless of how the arthritis behaves.
key_points: Oligoarticular disease with a positive antinuclear antibody in a young child is the highest uveitis risk group
The uveitis is asymptomatic with a white eye and normal acuity until damage is established
Slit lamp examination is the only adequate screening test
Eye and joint activity are independent, so surveillance is not tied to arthritis control
Normal inflammatory markers do not argue against the diagnosis in oligoarticular disease
explanation.pearls: Screen three monthly for a girl under seven with oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody, six monthly when the antibody is negative or onset is later, and twelve monthly for systemic onset disease, continuing for at least four years after arthritis remission. Intra-articular corticosteroid injection is the usual first treatment for a single persistently swollen joint and often achieves prolonged remission without any systemic agent.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis

options.rationale: Acuity remains normal until the inflammation has already caused structural damage, so waiting for it to fall means referring after the harm is done. Acuity testing is a useful adjunct but cannot substitute for the slit lamp. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis

options.rationale: Eye inflammation runs a course independent of joint activity and commonly flares while the joints are quiet, so tying surveillance to arthritis activity is unsafe. Screening continues for years after the arthritis settles. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

options.rationale: Fundoscopy examines the posterior segment, whereas this uveitis is anterior and its cells and flare are visible only through a slit lamp. Loss of the red reflex indicates established cataract, which is a late complication rather than a screening finding. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis

options.rationale: Chronic anterior uveitis in this form of childhood arthritis is asymptomatic, produces no redness or pain, and is detected only on slit lamp examination, so screening intervals are set by risk rather than by symptoms. A girl under seven with oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody sits in the highest risk band and is screened three monthly. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

options.rationale: Twelve monthly screening applies to the lowest risk groups such as older children with systemic onset disease, and using the absence of symptoms to set the interval defeats the purpose of screening. The whole reason this uveitis is dangerous is that it is silent until synechiae or cataract have formed. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

explanation.summary: Prednisolone at 2 mg/kg daily, or more than 20 mg daily in a child over 10 kg, given for fourteen days or longer is considered high dose immunosuppression for vaccination purposes. Live attenuated vaccines are deferred until one month after such a course finishes, whereas the three month deferral belongs to chemotherapy and biologic agents. Measles, mumps and rubella and varicella vaccines may be given on the same day at separate sites, and if they are not, they must be separated by at least four weeks. Nephrotic syndrome itself is never a contraindication, and these children benefit particularly from complete varicella and pneumococcal protection.
key_points: Prednisolone at or above 2 mg/kg daily for fourteen days or more counts as high dose immunosuppression
Defer live vaccines for one month after stopping high dose corticosteroid
Three month deferral applies after chemotherapy or biologic therapy, not after steroids alone
Two live parenteral vaccines are given the same day or separated by at least four weeks
Nephrotic syndrome is an indication for careful catch up, not a contraindication
explanation.pearls: Inactivated vaccines can be given at any point during or after immunosuppression, so never delay the influenza or pneumococcal dose while waiting out a steroid course, even though the response may be blunted. For a documented measles exposure in a susceptible immunosuppressed child, normal human immunoglobulin within six days is the protection strategy rather than vaccine, because the live vaccine is contraindicated during the deferral window.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome

options.rationale: Clinical remission is not the same as restored cell mediated immunity, and vaccinating within days of stopping high dose steroid risks disseminated infection from the attenuated virus. The deferral is tied to the steroid, not to disease activity. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Three months is the interval used after more profound immunosuppression such as chemotherapy or biologic therapy, and applying it here delays protection unnecessarily. The distinguishing factor is the depth and type of immunosuppression rather than its duration alone. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

The timing is right but separating the two live vaccines unnecessarily is wrong, because they may be co-administered at different sites. The four week rule applies only when two live parenteral vaccines are not given on the same day. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Nephrotic syndrome is not a contraindication to any vaccine, and these children in fact need particular attention to pneumococcal and varicella protection because of their infection risk. The only contraindication relates to the timing of immunosuppressive therapy. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome

options.rationale: A course of 2 mg/kg daily of prednisolone for more than fourteen days counts as high dose immunosuppression, and Australian practice is to defer live vaccines for one month after it stops so that immune competence is restored. Measles, mumps and rubella and varicella vaccines may be given on the same day at different sites, which is the efficient choice ahead of his travel. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis and an operative emergency, and imaging exists to support it rather than to overrule it. Abrupt severe pain with vomiting, a high riding transverse testis, an absent cremasteric reflex and no relief on elevation are together highly predictive. Preserved arterial flow on ultrasound occurs with partial torsion, intermittent torsion and early presentations, so a reassuring scan in a patient with these findings must not delay theatre. Delayed presentation from embarrassment is common in this age group and reduced pain often signals ischaemic nerve death rather than resolution, so exploration is still warranted.
key_points: Torsion is diagnosed clinically; ultrasound cannot exclude it when examination is characteristic
Absent cremasteric reflex with a high riding transverse testis is the key sign cluster
Relief on elevation favours epididymo-orchitis, the main differential
Salvage falls sharply beyond six hours, so exploration is not deferred for further imaging
Both testes are fixed at operation because the underlying anomaly is bilateral
explanation.pearls: Torsion of the appendix testis is the commonest mimic in this age group and shows a focal tender blue dot at the upper pole with a normal cremasteric reflex, and it is managed with analgesia alone. Even beyond twenty four hours, explore rather than assume the testis is lost: the contralateral side still requires fixation, and documented necrosis at operation is far better than an unexplored scrotum for the boy's future fertility discussion.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute Scrotum

options.rationale: A high riding transverse testis with an absent cremasteric reflex after abrupt onset pain and vomiting is a clinical diagnosis of torsion, and preserved flow on ultrasound does not exclude it because partial or intermittent torsion and residual capsular flow are both well described. Exploration with fixation of both sides is the only action that can salvage the testis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)

Epididymo-orchitis would be supported by gradual onset, fever, pyuria and relief on elevation, none of which are present here. Treating him as an infection on the basis of an oedematous epididymis on ultrasound is how torsion is missed. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)

Salvage rates fall steeply beyond six hours and he is already fourteen hours in, so an overnight delay for a repeat scan effectively decides against the testis. Reducing pain over time reflects ischaemic nerve death rather than improvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)

Manual detorsion is a reasonable temporising manoeuvre while theatre is prepared, but it is never definitive because the underlying bell clapper anomaly remains and retorsion is common. Discharge without fixation leaves him at immediate risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)

Nuclear imaging adds hours and its result would not override a bedside examination this characteristic. Imaging is for the equivocal presentation, and this one is not equivocal. (Source: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute Scrotum)
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute Scrotum

explanation.summary: Neonatal conjunctivitis is stratified by the day of onset and the organism, because management differs sharply. Chemical irritation appears in the first twenty four hours, gonococcal disease at two to five days with hyperacute purulent discharge and tense lid oedema, and chlamydial disease at five to fourteen days with a more indolent course. Intracellular Gram negative diplococci confirm the gonococcal diagnosis, which threatens the cornea within a day or two and requires systemic third generation cephalosporin rather than topical therapy. Frequent saline irrigation removes the proteolytic enzyme laden discharge, and both parents require testing and treatment.
key_points: Day of onset narrows the cause: chemical under one day, gonococcal two to five, chlamydial five to fourteen
Intracellular Gram negative diplococci mandate systemic, not topical, therapy
Corneal perforation can occur within twenty four to forty eight hours in gonococcal disease
Hourly saline irrigation is part of treatment, not merely comfort care
Chlamydial ophthalmia requires oral erythromycin because topical treatment leaves nasopharyngeal carriage
explanation.pearls: Always treat the parents as well as the baby and notify as required, since the infection is sexually transmitted and reinfection of the newborn from an untreated carer is common. A baby treated topically for chlamydial conjunctivitis still develops pneumonitis at four to twelve weeks, which is why the oral course is mandatory even when the eye looks better.

sources.label: Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases: Neonatal Conjunctivitis

options.rationale: The Gram stain has already given an actionable answer and waiting a further day for confirmation risks the cornea. Nucleic acid testing remains valuable for confirming the organism and for contact tracing, but it does not gate treatment. (Source: Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases: Neonatal Conjunctivitis)
source_refs: Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases: Neonatal Conjunctivitis

options.rationale: Intracellular Gram negative diplococci on day three with hyperacute purulent discharge and lid oedema is gonococcal ophthalmia, which perforates the cornea within twenty four to forty eight hours if treated topically alone. Systemic cephalosporin plus frequent saline irrigation to clear the enzyme rich discharge, with urgent ophthalmology involvement, is the standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Fourteen days of oral erythromycin is the correct regimen for chlamydial ophthalmia, which is the other vertically acquired cause but presents at five to fourteen days with a more mucopurulent and less explosive discharge. The distinguishing relationship is the organism on Gram stain and the timing of onset. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Topical therapy alone does not reach the systemic sites this organism seeds, including joints and the bloodstream, and does not prevent corneal perforation. Chloramphenicol is appropriate for ordinary bacterial conjunctivitis in an older infant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Chemical conjunctivitis appears within the first twenty four hours and settles spontaneously, and it produces a watery rather than thick purulent discharge. Gram negative diplococci on the stain exclude it outright. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Migratory polyarthritis, fever, a new mitral regurgitant murmur, a prolonged PR interval and raised streptococcal serology in a child from a high incidence community meet the Australian criteria for acute rheumatic fever. Initial management includes penicillin to clear residual carriage and anti-inflammatory therapy for the arthritis, but neither changes long term outcome. Secondary prophylaxis with four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin is the intervention that prevents recurrences, and recurrences are what convert mild regurgitation into established rheumatic heart disease. Minimum duration is ten years from the last episode or until age 21, whichever is longer, and it is extended where carditis has occurred.
key_points: Australian criteria apply a high risk definition in populations with high incidence
A prolonged PR interval counts as a minor criterion and supports carditis
Secondary prophylaxis, not the treatment of this episode, determines valve outcome
Four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin is the standard regimen
Minimum duration is ten years or until age 21, whichever is longer, and longer with carditis
explanation.pearls: Register every case with the state or territory rheumatic heart disease control program on the day of diagnosis, because recall for four weekly injections depends on that register far more than on any single clinic's follow up. Salicylates should be withheld until the arthritis pattern has been documented, since rapid symptomatic response can obscure the migratory course that the diagnosis depends upon.

sources.label: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.rationale: Corticosteroid is considered only in severe carditis with heart failure, and mild mitral regurgitation with a normal ventricle does not reach that bar. It also addresses this episode rather than the recurrences that determine long term valve damage. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.rationale: Surveillance detects deterioration but does nothing to prevent it, and treating sore throats as they arise fails because many streptococcal infections are subclinical. In primary prevention, for a child with no prior episode, treating symptomatic pharyngitis is indeed the strategy. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.rationale: Once acute rheumatic fever is diagnosed, long term secondary prophylaxis is the single intervention that changes the trajectory, because each recurrence worsens valve damage. Australian guidance sets the minimum duration at ten years from the last episode or until age 21, whichever is longer, with longer courses when carditis is present. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.rationale: Eradication of residual pharyngeal carriage is part of initial management but treats only this episode, and stopping there leaves him fully exposed to the recurrences that cause chronic valve disease. Primary treatment and secondary prophylaxis are separate interventions with different durations. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.rationale: Anti-inflammatory therapy relieves the arthritis and is appropriate symptomatic treatment, but it has no effect on valve outcome or recurrence risk. Reviewing only when markers normalise misses the point that prophylaxis must continue for years. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian Guideline for Prevention and Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever

explanation.summary: Supracondylar fractures are stratified by displacement, and a completely displaced fracture with an absent pulse goes to theatre urgently whatever the hand looks like. The critical distinction is between the pink pulseless hand, where the artery is usually kinked or in spasm around the displaced fragment and reduction restores flow, and the white pulseless hand, which is true ischaemia requiring vascular involvement from the outset. Angiography and pre-reduction exploration both introduce delay without changing the fact that the fracture must be reduced. Anterior skin puckering signals brachialis entrapment and predicts that closed reduction may fail, which is another reason the child belongs in theatre rather than in the emergency department.
key_points: A completely displaced supracondylar fracture with an absent pulse is an operative emergency
Reduction commonly restores flow because the artery is tethered rather than transected
Reassess perfusion after reduction; explore only the hand that stays white and pulseless
Avoid flexing the elbow beyond about forty degrees when splinting, since it compresses the fossa
Anterior skin puckering suggests brachialis entrapment and predicts failure of closed reduction
explanation.pearls: The anterior interosseous nerve is the most commonly injured and is missed on a standard sensory examination because it is purely motor: ask the child to make an oval by pinching the tip of the thumb against the tip of the index finger. Escalating pain requiring repeated analgesia in the hours after injury is the earliest sign of compartment syndrome in a child, and it precedes pulselessness by hours.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus

options.rationale: Flexion beyond about forty degrees compresses the antecubital fossa and can convert a perfused pulseless limb into an ischaemic one, and delaying reduction overnight risks compartment syndrome. Immobilisation in modest flexion is a transport measure, not a definitive plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus

options.rationale: Angiography rarely changes the plan because the fracture must be reduced whatever it shows, and the delay it introduces is the harm. Imaging the vessel belongs after reduction in the child whose perfusion has not returned. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus

options.rationale: A completely displaced fracture is inherently unstable and requires percutaneous wire fixation to hold the reduction, so a closed manipulation without fixation will redisplace. Discharging a child with this injury also forfeits the observation period that compartment syndrome demands. (Source: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric Trauma)

A completely displaced supracondylar fracture with an absent pulse is a surgical emergency regardless of how well the hand looks, because the brachial artery is tethered or kinked by the displaced fragment and reduction usually restores flow. Perfusion is reassessed after reduction, and vascular exploration is reserved for the hand that remains pulseless and poorly perfused at that point. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus

options.rationale: Exploring the artery before reduction addresses a vessel whose problem is usually mechanical tethering that reduction relieves, and it exposes the child to an operation that most do not need. Exploration is the correct step only for the hand that is pale and pulseless after reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus

explanation.summary: Fixed, localised, monophonic wheeze in a toddler that does not respond to bronchodilator or corticosteroid is an airway obstruction until proven otherwise, and asthma is very unlikely without atopy or prior episodes. A witnessed choking event is absent in a large minority of cases, so a plausible circumstantial history such as eating nuts carries real weight. An inspiratory chest radiograph is normal in up to a third of inhaled foreign bodies because most organic objects are radiolucent and the ball valve effect only shows as air trapping on expiration. Rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic and provides airway control, which flexible bronchoscopy does not.
key_points: A fixed monophonic unilateral wheeze is mechanical obstruction, not bronchospasm
Absence of a witnessed choking episode does not exclude an inhaled foreign body
A normal inspiratory chest radiograph is common because most objects are radiolucent
Rigid bronchoscopy allows simultaneous ventilation and instrumented retrieval
Chest physiotherapy risks converting partial to complete obstruction
explanation.pearls: Expiratory or lateral decubitus films raise sensitivity by demonstrating air trapping on the affected side, where the dependent lung fails to deflate, but a negative study never overturns a clinical suspicion strong enough to warrant bronchoscopy. Peanut is the commonest culprit in Australian children and is particularly damaging because the oil provokes an intense chemical bronchitis within days, so delay converts a simple retrieval into a granulation filled airway.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Paediatric Airway

options.rationale: Additional projections genuinely increase sensitivity by demonstrating air trapping, and are worth obtaining, but a negative result would not change the plan because the clinical picture already mandates airway inspection. Relying on them risks a falsely reassuring report in a poorly cooperative toddler. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled Foreign Body)

Preventer therapy assumes an asthma diagnosis that this child does not fit, given no atopy, no prior wheeze, a fixed unilateral monophonic wheeze and no response to a steroid course already given. Another four weeks of retained organic material produces granulation tissue and bronchiectasis. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

Flexible bronchoscopy is useful for inspection and lavage but has no adequate instrument channel for retrieving a solid object and offers no airway control if the object dislodges. The distinguishing relationship is that the rigid scope simultaneously ventilates and permits forceps retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled Foreign Body)

Physiotherapy risks dislodging an object into the trachea where it can obstruct completely, and antibiotics treat a secondary infection without removing the cause. Neither addresses the mechanical obstruction. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Paediatric Airway)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Paediatric Airway

options.rationale: A localised monophonic wheeze that does not respond to bronchodilator or corticosteroid in a toddler with a plausible aspiration event is an inhaled foreign body until the airway is inspected, and a normal inspiratory film does not exclude it because a ball valve obstruction shows only on expiration. Rigid bronchoscopy is both the diagnostic and the therapeutic procedure. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled Foreign Body)

explanation.summary: A term baby who feeds normally for two days and then deteriorates with vomiting, encephalopathy and tachypnoea is following the classic latent interval of a metabolic disorder, because the protein load only accumulates after feeding is established. The blood gas separates them: ammonia stimulates the respiratory centre and produces a respiratory alkalosis, whereas an organic acidaemia produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with ketosis, and both are absent here. An ammonia above 500 micromol/L is a neurological emergency in which the duration of exposure predicts outcome, so management runs in parallel rather than in sequence. Nitrogen intake stops, a high glucose infusion rate with lipid reverses catabolism, nitrogen scavengers are started on metabolic advice, and transfer for haemodialysis is arranged without waiting for a diagnosis.
key_points: A symptom-free interval of one to three days followed by encephalopathy suggests a metabolic disorder
Respiratory alkalosis with normal lactate and absent ketones points away from organic acidaemia
Ammonia must be collected free flowing, on ice and run immediately or it reads falsely high
Ammonia above 500 micromol/L warrants dialysis planning, not scavengers alone
Treat empirically for sepsis in parallel, but stop all protein intake
explanation.pearls: Run dextrose at an infusion rate of about 8 to 10 mg/kg/min with intravenous lipid to shut down endogenous protein breakdown, because the baby's own muscle is the dominant nitrogen source once feeds have stopped. Neurological outcome correlates with the number of hours the ammonia spends above 300 micromol/L, so activate the retrieval service and the metabolic unit at the first result rather than after a confirmatory repeat.

sources.label: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

options.rationale: A normal anion gap with a respiratory alkalosis, absent ketones, normal lactate and an ammonia above 500 micromol/L on day four points to a urea cycle defect rather than an organic acidaemia, and ammonia at this level is directly neurotoxic. Immediate management removes the nitrogen load, reverses catabolism with a high glucose infusion rate plus lipid, and transfers for haemodialysis, which clears ammonia far faster than scavengers alone. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism)
source_refs: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

options.rationale: Late onset sepsis is the correct parallel consideration and antibiotics should indeed be given while cultures are pending, but continuing enteral protein in the face of an ammonia of 620 micromol/L drives the encephalopathy further. Sepsis also does not produce this degree of hyperammonaemia with a normal lactate and normal white cell count. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Sepsis)

The subtle seizures are a manifestation of ammonia neurotoxicity and will not settle while the level stays above 500 micromol/L, so anticonvulsant alone treats the symptom. Serial monitoring without intervention wastes the hours in which neurological outcome is determined. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism)
source_refs: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

options.rationale: A glucose of 3.6 mmol/L is acceptable on day four and is not the explanation for the encephalopathy, so treating it as the primary problem misreads the picture. Dextrose is central to management, but as a continuous high rate anticatabolic infusion rather than a single bolus. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

There is no acidosis to correct, since the gas shows an alkalotic pH driven by ammonia stimulated hyperventilation, and alkali would worsen it. Newborn screening results take days and several urea cycle defects are not reliably detected on it at all. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism)
source_refs: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Acute Management of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

explanation.summary: Middle ear effusion after an upper respiratory illness is extremely common in preschool children and the large majority clear without any intervention within three months, which is why the first pass of management is structured waiting with documentation rather than treatment. The decision to operate rests on a triad of persistence beyond three months, a measured bilateral hearing level in the impaired range, and a functional consequence for speech, language or schooling. Children with Down syndrome, cleft palate or existing developmental delay are moved to referral earlier because they tolerate a conductive loss less well. The reason documentation matters is that a single abnormal tympanogram taken during a cold cannot distinguish a transient effusion from a persistent one. Missing a persistent bilateral loss in the preschool years costs language acquisition at exactly the point it is most rapid.
key_points: Type B tympanogram means a flat trace with no compliance peak, indicating fluid behind an intact drum rather than infection.
Three separate documented assessments across at least three months are what convert an effusion from transient to persistent.
A pure tone average worse than 25 to 30 dB in the better hearing ear is the hearing limb of the referral trigger.
Antibiotics, antihistamines, decongestants and intranasal steroids all fail to change the course of a non-infected effusion.
Syndromic children and those with pre-existing developmental delay are referred without waiting the full three months.
explanation.pearls: Autoinflation using a purpose made nasal balloon is the one non-surgical measure with trial support in this setting, giving a modest improvement when performed three times daily for up to three months, and it is worth offering to a co-operative child who is waiting for a surgical list.

sources.label: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s

options.rationale: Bilateral effusion documented over at least three months with a hearing level worse than 25 to 30 dB in the better ear, together with a speech and educational impact, is the accepted trigger for surgical referral rather than further observation. He meets all three limbs at four months of documented persistence, 32 dB, and independent teacher concern. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media)
source_refs: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s

options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroid produces no clinically meaningful improvement in effusion clearance or hearing in randomised trials and delays definitive management by another three months in a child who has already waited four. It is a reasonable adjunct only where coexisting allergic rhinitis is being treated in its own right. (Source: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s)
source_refs: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for the first three months because most effusions resolve spontaneously, but that window has already closed and a further wait risks entrenching the speech delay. The distinguishing point against the correct option is that observation is time limited, not open ended. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media)

Adenoidectomy alone gives a smaller and slower hearing benefit than ventilation tubes and is added to tubes rather than substituted for them, and then usually at revision surgery or where nasal obstruction dominates. He has no reported snoring or mouth breathing to justify it as the primary procedure. (Source: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s)
source_refs: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s

options.rationale: Antibiotics do not alter the natural history of a non-infected middle ear effusion and this child has had no pain, fever or discharge at any point, so there is no acute infection to treat. Antibiotics are considered for acute otitis media, which presents with an acutely bulging red drum and fever. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Boys with a dystrophinopathy are frequently picked up first through incidentally raised transaminases, because alanine and aspartate aminotransferase are released from skeletal muscle as well as liver and a clinician reasonably reads them as hepatic. The distinguishing result is a normal gamma glutamyl transferase, which is liver specific and stays normal when the source is muscle. Any boy with late walking, a Gowers manoeuvre or unexplained transaminitis warrants a creatine kinase before any hepatic imaging. Confirmation is molecular in the first instance, with biopsy held back for genetically unresolved cases. Early diagnosis matters because glucocorticoids, cardiac surveillance and spinal monitoring all start on a schedule counted from diagnosis.
key_points: A normal gamma glutamyl transferase alongside raised aminotransferases points the source to muscle rather than liver.
Creatine kinase in Duchenne muscular dystrophy is typically ten to one hundred times the upper limit of normal from birth.
Deletion and duplication analysis of the DMD gene finds about 70 per cent of cases, with sequencing capturing most of the rest.
Calf hypertrophy reflects replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue, not genuine muscle bulk.
Identifying the exact variant determines eligibility for exon skipping agents and enables maternal carrier testing.
explanation.pearls: Glucocorticoids change the trajectory rather than merely the symptoms: prednisolone started around age four to five, before the plateau in motor function, prolongs independent walking by roughly two to three years and delays scoliosis surgery.

sources.label: Genetics in Medicine: DMD Diagnostic Care Considerations

options.rationale: Electrophysiology separates a neuropathic from a myopathic process but this distinction is already settled by the creatine kinase in the thousands together with the clinical pattern. It is a painful test in a preschool child and would not name the responsible gene. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy)

A creatine kinase in the thousands with proximal weakness and calf hypertrophy in a boy of this age points to a dystrophinopathy, and targeted DMD analysis identifies a deletion or duplication in around 70 per cent with sequencing finding most of the remainder. Naming the variant also determines eligibility for exon skipping therapy and allows carrier testing for the mother and her sisters. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy)
source_refs: Genetics in Medicine: DMD Diagnostic Care Considerations

options.rationale: The raised transaminases came from muscle rather than liver, which the normal gamma glutamyl transferase and bilirubin already establish, so a hepatic workup chases a result that is not hepatic in origin. Referral to gastroenterology first commonly delays the diagnosis by months. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy)

Biopsy is now reserved for the minority in whom genetic testing is uninformative, because it requires an anaesthetic and a surgical wound to reach an answer that genomic testing usually reaches first. Dystrophin immunostaining shows how much protein is present but not which variant to report for family testing. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy)

Muscle imaging can show selective fatty replacement and is useful for directing a biopsy in an undiagnosed myopathy, but it never delivers a molecular diagnosis and would simply add a sedated scan. It earns its place in the limb girdle dystrophies where the genetic answer is far less predictable. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy)

explanation.summary: Infants of mothers with any form of diabetes, infants who are large or small for gestational age, preterm infants and unwell infants are all screened for low blood glucose in the first hours of life because transient hyperinsulinism is common and initially silent. The operational threshold used across Australian services is 2.6 mmol/L, with a lower trigger in the first few hours reflecting the physiological nadir that every newborn passes through. Buccal dextrose gel changed practice because it treats the biochemical problem while keeping mother and baby together, which in turn protects breastfeeding. Escalation to intravenous glucose is driven by symptoms or by failure to respond, not by the number alone. Persistent low readings beyond 48 to 72 hours are a different problem and require a hypoglycaemia screen taken at the time of the low glucose.
key_points: Screen at risk newborns before feeds rather than after, since a post feed value can mask the true trough.
The working threshold in Australian neonatal units is 2.6 mmol/L for an at risk but asymptomatic baby.
Buccal 40 per cent dextrose gel with a feed is first line and can be repeated once before escalating.
Jitteriness, apnoea, hypotonia or seizures move the baby straight to intravenous glucose regardless of the number.
Low glucose persisting past 72 hours should prompt a formal hypoglycaemia screen drawn during the episode.
explanation.pearls: Draw the critical hypoglycaemia screen, including insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones and free fatty acids, while the glucose is still below 2.6 mmol/L: once it is corrected the sample no longer distinguishes hyperinsulinism from a fatty acid oxidation defect.

sources.label: Cochrane: Oral Dextrose Gel for Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.rationale: Feeding alone is the right response at the higher end of the low range, but at 1.9 mmol/L a feed by itself is unlikely to correct the glucose quickly and leaves the baby exposed for a further three hours. Colostrum volumes on day one are measured in millilitres and deliver very little substrate. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

Routine formula supplementation is not the first response to a single low reading and undercuts a breastfeed that is already attaching well, and a 3 hour interval is too long to detect a falling glucose. Supplementation has a place only once gel and breastfeeding have failed and the mother has agreed to it. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

Buccal dextrose gel with a feed is the first line treatment for an asymptomatic at risk newborn with a low glucose, and it reduces admission to the nursery and separation from the mother without increasing later harm. The recheck at 30 minutes after the gel confirms the response and drives the decision about a second dose. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)
source_refs: Cochrane: Oral Dextrose Gel for Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.rationale: Intravenous glucose is reserved for a baby who is symptomatic, who cannot feed, or whose glucose stays low after adequate gel and feeding, none of which applies to a well baby who is rooting at 3 hours. Starting it here separates mother and baby and undermines the establishment of breastfeeding for no measurable gain. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

A glucose bolus is the treatment for a symptomatic infant with seizures or obtundation, and giving one to an asymptomatic baby provokes rebound insulin release and a second lower trough. Route matters: buccal absorption raises the glucose without the insulin surge that a rapid intravenous load produces. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Retinopathy of prematurity develops because an incompletely vascularised retina is exposed to a relatively hyperoxic extrauterine environment, which first arrests vessel growth and then drives disordered neovascularisation as the retina grows and becomes ischaemic. Australian entry criteria are a gestational age below 31 weeks or a birth weight at or below 1250 g, with clinician discretion to include larger or more mature infants who had an unstable course. The first examination is timed to 4 weeks postnatal or 31 weeks corrected, whichever is later, and subsequent intervals are set by what the ophthalmologist sees, typically every one to two weeks. Treatment with laser or intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor is indicated for type 1 disease and should occur within 72 hours of the decision. The program only works if the infant is tracked through transfers between hospitals, which is where most failures occur.
key_points: Entry criteria in Australia are gestation under 31 weeks or birth weight at or below 1250 g.
First examination is at 4 weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks corrected age, whichever falls later.
Examination is by indirect ophthalmoscopy with mydriatics, with sucrose and swaddling for comfort.
Type 1 disease requires treatment within 72 hours, most often laser or intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor.
Screening continues until the retina is fully vascularised or the ophthalmologist documents low risk of progression.
explanation.pearls: Aggressive posterior retinopathy can progress from mild to treatment requiring disease in under a week, so an infant with plus disease is reviewed within days rather than at the routine one to two week interval.

sources.label: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.rationale: Waiting until 36 weeks corrected risks missing aggressive posterior disease, which can reach a treatable stage between 32 and 35 weeks corrected and progress within days. Being in air is a marker of respiratory recovery and has no bearing on when retinal vascularisation becomes visible. (Source: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.rationale: A discharge examination is the endpoint of a screening series rather than its start, and by term corrected age treatable disease may already have scarred or detached. Screening exists precisely to find disease during the window in which laser or intravitreal therapy still works. (Source: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.rationale: Oxygen exposure and sepsis worsen the risk but are not the entry criteria, which are gestation below 31 weeks or birth weight at or below 1250 g, and he meets both independently of his oxygen history. Restricting screening to oxygen exposed infants would miss disease in infants who were never ventilated. (Source: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.rationale: Screening starts at 4 weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks corrected gestational age, whichever falls later, which for a 29 week infant means his first examination is due now at 32 weeks and 6 days corrected. Timing it this way catches disease before it becomes treatable rather than after, because vision threatening changes almost never appear before 31 weeks corrected. (Source: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.rationale: A fixed postnatal interval ignores the maturity of the retina, so it screens the most immature infants too late while examining more mature ones before there is anything to find. The schedule deliberately uses two clocks, postnatal and postmenstrual age, and takes the later of them. (Source: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

explanation.summary: Around one in ten children carry a penicillin allergy label, yet fewer than one in ten of those labels survives formal assessment, and most originate in a viral exanthem that coincided with an antibiotic course. Risk stratification is by history alone in the first instance: timing from the dose, morphology of the rash, and the presence or absence of mucosal involvement, blistering, organ involvement or cardiovascular compromise. Low risk histories such as a delayed benign maculopapular rash in a well child proceed to direct oral challenge, which is safe to perform in a suitably equipped outpatient setting. Histories suggesting immediate reactions go to specialist skin testing first, and histories of severe cutaneous adverse reactions are never challenged at all. Removing an incorrect label restores access to narrow spectrum first line therapy for the rest of the child's life.
key_points: Timing separates mechanisms: within one hour suggests immunoglobulin E mediated, after several days suggests a T cell mediated rash.
Direct oral challenge without skin testing is the pathway for low risk delayed benign rashes.
Mucosal involvement, blistering, skin pain or organ dysfunction are absolute contraindications to challenge.
Skin testing and specific immunoglobulin E only address immediate reactions and cannot clear a delayed rash.
De-labelling reduces use of broader agents such as macrolides, cephalosporins and glycopeptides.
explanation.pearls: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions, meaning Stevens Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, are a permanent bar to re-challenge, and the clues that separate them from a benign rash are mucosal ulceration, skin pain, facial oedema and fever beyond day 7.

options.rationale: Skin testing is validated for immediate immunoglobulin E mediated reactions such as urticaria, angioedema or anaphylaxis within an hour of a dose, and it neither predicts nor excludes a delayed rash. Reaction timing matters: hers began on day 6, which places it outside the mechanism that skin testing interrogates. (Source: ASCIA: Penicillin Allergy De-labelling)

Specific immunoglobulin E to penicillin has poor sensitivity even in genuine immediate allergy, so a negative result cannot remove a label and a positive one in this context would be a false alarm. Ordering it here tests a mechanism the history has already argued against. (Source: ASCIA: Penicillin Allergy De-labelling)

An unexamined label is not a neutral act: it drives use of broader agents with more resistance selection, more adverse effects and higher cost, and around nine in ten labelled children are not truly allergic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Desensitisation is for a patient with proven allergy who has no alternative agent, and it induces temporary tolerance that is lost once the drug is stopped rather than removing the label. Using it here would treat a diagnosis that has not been established. (Source: ASCIA: Penicillin Allergy De-labelling)

A benign delayed non urticarial rash appearing after several days of a penicillin, with no mucosal, systemic or blistering features, is a low risk history and is assessed by direct oral challenge rather than by skin testing. Australian de-labelling pathways use this route because skin testing has no predictive value for delayed T cell mediated rashes and adds cost and delay. (Source: ASCIA: Penicillin Allergy De-labelling)

explanation.summary: Congenital hypothyroidism affects roughly one in 2000 to 3000 births and is the most successful condition on the newborn screening panel precisely because treatment is cheap, effective, and time critical. Affected newborns look entirely normal at birth, since maternal thyroxine crosses the placenta and masks the deficit, which is why screening rather than clinical detection drives diagnosis. The screening card measures thyroid stimulating hormone, so the primary gland disorders that make up the great majority are detected while rare central hypothyroidism is missed. Treatment is thyroxine started within the first two weeks, with the dose titrated to keep free thyroxine in the upper half of the reference range and thyroid stimulating hormone suppressed. Aetiological imaging, whether ultrasound or radionuclide scan, is useful but always subordinate to starting treatment.
key_points: Newborn screening measures thyroid stimulating hormone, so central hypothyroidism is not detected by the card.
Affected infants appear clinically normal at birth because maternal thyroxine crosses the placenta.
Thyroxine should begin within the first two weeks of life, at a starting dose of 10 to 15 micrograms per kilogram daily.
Titrate to a free thyroxine in the upper half of the reference range rather than to the thyroid stimulating hormone alone.
A trial off treatment at around age three distinguishes permanent from transient disease when imaging was not diagnostic.
explanation.pearls: Thyroxine tablets are crushed and given in a small volume of water rather than mixed into a bottle of formula, because soy protein, calcium and iron all bind thyroxine in the gut and can halve the absorbed dose.

options.rationale: Treatment is started as soon as the venous result confirms the diagnosis, ideally within the first two weeks of life, because the developing brain depends on thyroxine and every week of delay costs cognitive outcome. Imaging defines the underlying aetiology and guides later counselling but never justifies withholding the hormone. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism)

Deferring treatment for six days to obtain an aetiological scan inverts the priority, since knowing whether the gland is absent, ectopic or dyshormonogenetic changes nothing about the initial dose. A scan can still be done after treatment starts if performed within the first few days, and if the window is missed the question can be revisited by a trial off treatment at age three. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism)

A confirmatory venous sample with this degree of abnormality is diagnostic and does not need a second confirmation, and a further two weeks of untreated hypothyroidism falls outside the window in which outcomes are preserved. Repeat testing is appropriate only for borderline elevations near the action threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism)

Maternal blocking antibodies cause a transient form that is worth identifying, but the antibody result takes days and the infant needs thyroxine whether the cause is transient or permanent. Antibody testing informs the later decision about a trial off treatment, not the decision today. (Source: ESPE: Congenital Hypothyroidism Consensus)

Iodine deficiency is a population level cause of hypothyroidism in iodine deplete regions and is not the mechanism in an Australian newborn with a low free thyroxine and a high thyroid stimulating hormone. Supplementing iodine would leave her hypothyroid for another week. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism)

explanation.summary: The diarrhoea associated thrombotic microangiopathy of childhood follows infection with Shiga toxin producing bacteria acquired from undercooked meat, unpasteurised dairy, contaminated water or direct animal contact, and characteristically declares itself five to ten days after the diarrhoea begins, often as the bowel symptoms are improving. The diagnostic triad is microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with fragmented red cells, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury, and the negative direct antiglobulin test is what separates this mechanical haemolysis from an immune one. Around half of affected children need dialysis during the acute phase, yet the large majority recover renal function. Treatment is entirely supportive, and the two interventions that feel most natural, antibiotics and antimotility agents, both worsen outcomes. Long term follow up is required because a minority develop hypertension, proteinuria or chronic kidney disease years later.
key_points: Onset is typically five to ten days after the onset of bloody diarrhoea, often as stools are settling.
A negative direct antiglobulin test distinguishes this mechanical haemolysis from autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.
Antibiotics and antimotility agents both increase the risk of progression and are avoided.
Platelets are transfused only for active bleeding or before a procedure, since they feed ongoing microthrombosis.
Annual review of blood pressure and urinalysis is needed for years after apparent recovery.
explanation.pearls: Eculizumab is reserved for complement mediated disease rather than the Shiga toxin form, and because it blocks terminal complement the child needs meningococcal vaccination plus antibiotic cover before the first dose.

options.rationale: Antimotility agents prolong contact between toxin and gut mucosa and raise the risk of progression, and her oliguria reflects renal injury rather than ongoing losses so pushing oral fluid risks overload. Her diarrhoea has in any case already settled, which removes the stated indication. (Source: RCH CPG: Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome)

Management is supportive, centring on meticulous fluid balance, correction of electrolyte disturbance, transfusion when indicated and early nephrology input for possible dialysis, because no specific therapy shortens the illness. Most children recover renal function with this approach, and the work of the admission is anticipating hyperkalaemia, hypertension and fluid overload rather than treating the organism. (Source: RCH CPG: Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome)

Antibiotics given in this setting increase toxin release from dying organisms and are associated with a higher rate of progression to the full syndrome, so they are actively avoided unless another infection demands them. The positive culture invites treatment that makes the outcome worse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Corticosteroids have no role because the process is toxin mediated endothelial injury rather than immune mediated inflammation, and immunosuppression adds infection risk during an acute illness. In immune mediated thrombotic microangiopathy, by contrast, plasma exchange and immunosuppression do have a place. (Source: RCH CPG: Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome)

Platelets are consumed within microthrombi rather than failing to be produced, so transfused platelets fuel further thrombosis and are withheld unless there is active bleeding or a procedure is planned. She has no purpura and no bleeding, which is the finding that removes the indication. (Source: RCH CPG: Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Slippage of the proximal femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and peaks around the growth spurt, with obesity the dominant risk factor because it increases shear across a physis that is already widening under hormonal influence. Roughly a quarter of affected adolescents present with pain felt only in the thigh or knee, and every one of those is at risk of a delayed diagnosis if the hip is not examined. The most reproducible bedside sign is obligatory external rotation of the hip as it is passively flexed, which reflects the posterior and inferior displacement of the epiphysis. Radiographs must include a frog lateral view of both hips, since up to a fifth are bilateral and early slips can look normal on the anteroposterior projection alone. Treatment is surgical fixation in situ, and the single most important determinant of outcome is whether the slip was stable at the time of presentation.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee or thigh pain, whatever the knee examination shows.
Obligatory external rotation on passive hip flexion is the most useful bedside sign.
Request anteroposterior and frog lateral views of both hips, as up to 20 per cent are bilateral.
Make the patient non weight bearing at the moment of suspicion, before imaging confirms it.
An unstable slip, meaning one the child cannot weight bear on, carries a far higher risk of avascular necrosis.
explanation.pearls: A slip presenting before age 10 or in a child of normal weight should prompt screening for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, panhypopituitarism or renal osteodystrophy, since an endocrine cause underlies a substantial proportion of these atypical cases.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Scintigraphy is non-specific, delivers a radiation dose, and would take days to arrange for a diagnosis that two plain films can make immediately. A stress injury is also improbable in a boy who does no organised sport. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Escalating knee imaging pursues a joint that examines normally and ignores the hip findings, and it is the single most common reason this diagnosis is missed for weeks. Referred pain travels along the obturator nerve from hip to distal thigh and knee, so the site of the pain is a poor guide to the site of the problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent with knee pain points to the proximal femoral physis, and the frog lateral view is required because early displacement is often invisible on the anteroposterior film alone. Making him non weight bearing immediately matters because continued walking can convert a stable slip into an unstable one, which carries a far higher risk of avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Anterior knee pain in an adolescent is commonly patellofemoral and does respond to a loading program, but that diagnosis requires a normal hip examination which he does not have. Six weeks of continued weight bearing is exactly the interval over which a stable slip progresses. (Source: RACGP: The Limping Child)

Aspiration answers the question of septic arthritis, but he is afebrile with normal inflammatory markers and a six week history, which is the wrong tempo for infection. Duration and fever separate them: septic arthritis presents over days with systemic upset, not over six weeks in a well child. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

explanation.summary: Myocarditis in childhood most often follows a viral illness and presents with non-specific symptoms, so it is regularly mistaken for gastroenteritis, asthma or sepsis in the first hours of care. The features that should raise it are vomiting without diarrhoea, breathlessness out of proportion to the chest examination, right upper quadrant pain from hepatic congestion, and a heart rate that stays high after fever and distress are addressed. Hepatomegaly with crackles in a shocked child is the bedside pairing that separates cardiogenic from distributive or hypovolaemic shock. Fluid in cardiogenic shock is given, if at all, in small aliquots of 5 to 10 mL/kg with reassessment after each, and the mainstay is early inotropic support and paediatric intensive care involvement. Presentation can progress to arrhythmia or cardiac arrest within hours, which is why the electrocardiogram cannot wait.
key_points: Vomiting without diarrhoea is a red flag against a gastroenteritis label in a shocked child.
Hepatomegaly plus crackles points to cardiogenic rather than septic or hypovolaemic shock.
Persistent tachycardia that does not settle with antipyretics and analgesia warrants an electrocardiogram.
Give fluid in 5 to 10 mL/kg aliquots with reassessment after each when the heart is the problem.
Troponin, brain natriuretic peptide and echocardiography confirm the diagnosis and guide intensive care referral.
explanation.pearls: Low voltage QRS complexes across all limb leads, with T wave inversion and any ventricular ectopy, is the electrocardiographic signature that should stop a fluid bolus in a child labelled as gastroenteritis.

options.rationale: Nasogastric rehydration is first line for mild to moderate dehydration from gastroenteritis that has failed oral intake, and it assumes the circulating problem is a fluid deficit. He has no diarrhoea, a normal urine output and an enlarged liver, all of which argue against a deficit. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

An antiemetic treats the symptom that got him triaged and would let a child in cardiogenic shock sit unmonitored for two hours. Vomiting in this context is a manifestation of hepatic congestion and low cardiac output, not of gastric irritation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Escalating fluid to 60 mL/kg with antibiotics is the correct pathway for septic shock, and the fever and lactate make sepsis a genuine competing diagnosis worth covering. The finding that separates them is the combination of hepatomegaly and crackles, which belongs to a congested circulation rather than a vasodilated one. (Source: RCH CPG: Paediatric Sepsis)

Hepatomegaly with bibasal crackles and shock in a child who has vomited without diarrhoea points to a failing myocardium rather than volume depletion, and a large bolus into a poorly contractile ventricle precipitates pulmonary oedema. The electrocardiogram, troponin and chest film are the three tests that establish the mechanism within minutes and redirect management towards inotropic support. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

A rapid 20 mL/kg bolus is correct in septic or hypovolaemic shock but is dangerous when the liver is already enlarged and the lung bases are already wet, because those two findings mark a ventricle that cannot accept the preload. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

explanation.summary: Jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in a term infant, or beyond 21 days in a preterm infant, requires a split bilirubin in every case, because the common benign cause and the one time-critical surgical cause are clinically indistinguishable at the cot side. Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated, occurs in a thriving baby, and resolves over weeks to months without intervention. Biliary atresia produces a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with pale acholic stools and dark urine, and the infants characteristically look well and gain weight early on, which is precisely what disarms the clinician. Outcomes after the Kasai portoenterostomy depend heavily on age at surgery, with the best results before 45 to 60 days and a steep decline thereafter. Every infant with a conjugated fraction needs same week specialist assessment rather than a watchful review.
key_points: Any jaundice persisting past 14 days in a term infant requires a split, not a total, bilirubin.
A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total or above about 25 micromol/L is always pathological.
Pale stools with dark urine indicate obstructed bile flow and are the key history question to ask.
Thriving and contentedness do not exclude biliary atresia in the first two months of life.
Kasai portoenterostomy performed before 45 to 60 days gives substantially better long term outcomes.
