explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to compare the nappy against a printed stool colour card rather than describing the colour in words, since pale acholic stool is commonly reported as yellow and the visual comparison is what converts a vague history into a referral.

options.rationale: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin into water soluble isomers and does nothing for a conjugated fraction that is already water soluble, and in cholestasis it can produce the bronze baby discolouration. Which fraction is raised decides treatment, which is why the split bilirubin must be requested rather than the total alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Interrupting breastfeeding to demonstrate a fall in bilirubin is an outdated test for breast milk jaundice, undermines lactation, and again addresses the unconjugated fraction only. It would waste two more days in an infant whose surgical window is measured in weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice)

A haemolytic workup investigates an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, and the identical maternal and infant blood groups with a negative direct antiglobulin test on day 2 have already argued against it. Haemolysis also does not produce pale stools, because the bile pigment that colours stool is still being made. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

Reassurance fits an unconjugated prolonged jaundice in a thriving breastfed infant, and the good weight gain and contented baby make that label tempting, but the conjugated fraction and the pale stools take this out of that category entirely. Two weeks of waiting at 3 weeks of age consumes a large part of the window in which surgery still works. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total, or above roughly 25 micromol/L, is never physiological and combined with pale stools and dark urine it demands urgent specialist investigation for biliary obstruction. Referral is urgent rather than routine because the outcome of surgery for biliary atresia falls sharply once the infant passes about 60 days of age. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is the commonest form in Australian children, typically affecting a young girl with one or a few large joints and normal inflammatory markers, which is why a normal C reactive protein never excludes it. The associated chronic anterior uveitis is the complication that determines long term disability, and it is entirely silent in its early stages. Risk is highest in children under seven at onset, with few joints involved, and with a positive antinuclear antibody, and screening intervals are set accordingly, most often three monthly in this highest risk group and extending as the child ages and the disease settles. Treatment of the joint itself usually begins with intra-articular corticosteroid, with methotrexate added for persistent or polyarticular disease. Screening continues for years after the arthritis is quiescent, because uveitis can appear or recur long after the joint has settled.
key_points: Normal inflammatory markers are common in oligoarticular disease and do not argue against the diagnosis.
Chronic anterior uveitis in this group is painless and the eye remains white until damage is established.
Highest risk is young age at onset, few joints, and a positive antinuclear antibody.
Slit lamp examination is the only adequate screening test, since the disease is in the anterior chamber.
A persistent fixed flexion deformity and limb length discrepancy are the joint level consequences of undertreatment.
explanation.pearls: Untreated anterior uveitis produces posterior synechiae that tether the iris to the lens, so an irregular or sluggishly reacting pupil found on routine examination in a child with arthritis means the disease has been active for months and needs same day ophthalmology assessment.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.rationale: A young child with few involved joints and a positive antinuclear antibody sits in the highest risk group for chronic anterior uveitis, which is asymptomatic and produces a white quiet eye until irreversible damage has occurred. Only slit lamp examination detects the anterior chamber cells at a stage where topical treatment prevents cataract, band keratopathy and glaucoma. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.rationale: Acuity stays normal until the uveitis has already caused structural damage, and a 3-year-old cannot reliably perform the test in any case. Acuity measures the consequence, whereas the slit lamp detects the process. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.rationale: Symptom triggered review is the default reasoning for most eye disease and is precisely what fails here, because the chronic anterior uveitis of childhood is painless and the eye stays white. Waiting for symptoms means the first presentation is often a cataract or a distorted pupil. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

Fundoscopy examines the posterior segment while this disease lives in the anterior chamber, and an annual interval is far too long for a condition that can cause damage within months. The correct instrument and the correct interval are both wrong in this option. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.rationale: The antibody is used once, to stratify risk and set the screening interval, and serial titres do not track uveitis activity or predict its onset. Following the titre instead of the eye substitutes a blood test for the examination that actually detects disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

explanation.summary: Most abnormal head shapes seen in infancy are deformational and follow sustained supine positioning, which is a tolerable trade against the large reduction in sudden infant death that back sleeping achieved. Deformational plagiocephaly produces an asymmetrical parallelogram when viewed from above, with the ipsilateral ear and forehead displaced forward, and it improves with repositioning, tummy time, and treatment of any coexisting torticollis. True suture fusion produces a characteristic symmetrical distortion determined by which suture is involved, with sagittal fusion giving a long narrow skull, and it worsens rather than improves as the brain grows. A palpable ridge, a shape that deteriorates despite conservative measures, or a head circumference crossing centiles all warrant craniofacial referral. The functional risks of untreated multi-suture disease include raised intracranial pressure and visual loss, while single suture disease is more often an issue of head shape and skull growth.
key_points: Viewed from above, positional plagiocephaly is a parallelogram whereas sagittal fusion is long and narrow.
A positional head shape improves with repositioning; a fused suture worsens as the brain grows.
A palpable ridge along a suture line with a small anterior fontanelle points to fusion.
Check neck rotation in every infant with an abnormal head shape, since torticollis drives positional flattening.
Endoscopic strip craniectomy with post-operative helmeting is generally limited to infants under about six months.
explanation.pearls: Sagittal synostosis is the commonest single suture fusion and the head circumference stays on its centile, because the skull compensates by growing front to back, so a normal head circumference offers no reassurance against it.

options.rationale: Repositioning is the correct treatment for a deformational head shape, and four months of it with worsening rather than improvement is the history that argues against that diagnosis. Persisting with it here delays surgery past the age at which the simplest operations are possible. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

A ridged suture with a head that is long and narrow, symmetrical ears and a shape that has worsened despite repositioning indicates a fused sagittal suture rather than a positional moulding, and this requires surgical assessment. Referral is time sensitive because endoscopic strip craniectomy with helmeting is generally restricted to infants under about six months, after which open vault remodelling becomes necessary. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

Physiotherapy is central where torticollis drives a positional flattening, but his neck rotation is full and symmetrical in both directions, which removes the mechanism. Positional flattening produces an asymmetrical parallelogram shape with one ear pushed forward, whereas his skull is symmetrically narrowed. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

Helmet therapy redirects growth through open sutures and cannot reshape a skull whose suture has already fused, so it would waste the remaining months of rapid brain growth. Helmets have a defined role after endoscopic surgery but not as an alternative to it. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

Metabolic bone disease can distort the growing skull, but rickets softens bone and produces frontal bossing and craniotabes rather than a ridged fused suture. His growth and development are normal, which further argues against a systemic metabolic cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

explanation.summary: Salt wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia typically presents in the second week of life, once the protective effect of maternal and placental steroid has worn off, and boys are at particular risk because they have no ambiguous genitalia at birth to trigger earlier investigation. The presentation overlaps almost completely with the far commoner pyloric stenosis in its history, since both produce forceful non bilious vomiting in a hungry infant of the same age, and the separation is biochemical. Loss of aldosterone drives urinary sodium loss with potassium and hydrogen retention, producing hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and a metabolic acidosis, while cortisol deficiency adds hypoglycaemia and impaired vascular tone. Treatment is simultaneous volume expansion, glucose, and stress dose hydrocortisone, with the diagnostic samples for cortisol and 17 hydroxyprogesterone drawn before the first dose but never allowed to delay it. Newborn screening for this condition is not performed uniformly across all Australian jurisdictions, so a normal or pending card cannot be relied on to exclude it.
key_points: Pyloric stenosis gives a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis; adrenal crisis gives hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemic acidosis.
Male infants with salt wasting disease have normal genitalia and so are not detected at birth on examination.
Draw cortisol and 17 hydroxyprogesterone before the first hydrocortisone dose, but never delay the dose for the result.
Hydrocortisone at stress doses provides enough mineralocorticoid activity for the acute phase.
Hyperkalaemia in this setting warrants an electrocardiogram and treatment in its own right alongside volume expansion.
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone for an infant in adrenal crisis is given as 25 mg intravenously as the initial bolus, followed by 25 mg over the next 24 hours as a divided or continuous dose, with the same 25 mg figure used for children under three years.

options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for hyponatraemic seizures or obtundation attributable to cerebral oedema, and here the low sodium is a marker of aldosterone deficiency with salt wasting rather than a free water excess. Correcting the number without replacing the missing hormone leaves the underlying loss running. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis)

Fludrocortisone is the long term mineralocorticoid and has no parenteral form, and it is the wrong drug for an acute crisis in any case. Hydrocortisone is chosen precisely because at stress doses it delivers both glucocorticoid and sufficient mineralocorticoid effect. (Source: APEG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and a metabolic acidosis in a collapsed second week infant is the biochemical signature of mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency, and hydrocortisone must be given at the same time as volume resuscitation rather than after it. Delaying steroid until a cortisol result returns is the error that turns a treatable crisis into an arrest, so the sample is drawn and the drug given without waiting. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis)

Pyloric stenosis produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from losing gastric acid, which is the exact inverse of his acidotic, hyperkalaemic, low chloride picture, and no mass was palpable after a test feed. The projectile vomiting and hungry rebound are genuine shared features, which is why the electrolytes rather than the history decide this. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

Late onset sepsis is a legitimate competing diagnosis in a collapsed neonate and antibiotics are commonly given alongside, but sepsis does not by itself explain the combination of a sodium of 119 mmol/L with a potassium of 7.4 mmol/L. Treating only the infection would leave the steroid deficiency uncorrected and the infant would not improve. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in children under 12 months with viral upper respiratory prodrome progressing to wheeze, crackles and increased work of breathing. RCH guidance targets oxygen saturation 90 percent or greater. Low-flow nasal prong oxygen (up to 2 L/min) is first line when supplemental oxygen is needed. High-flow humidified nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min is escalation after failure of low-flow for at least one to two hours. Bronchodilators, adrenaline, steroids, hypertonic saline and chest physiotherapy are not routinely indicated in bronchiolitis. Feeding via nasogastric tube or intravenous fluid at two-thirds maintenance is used when oral intake falls below 50 percent.
key_points: Oxygen target in bronchiolitis is SpO2 at or above 90 percent (RCH).
Low-flow nasal prong oxygen up to 2 L/min is first-line escalation before HFNC.
Salbutamol, adrenaline, steroids, hypertonic saline are not recommended routinely.
explanation.pearls: Titrate low-flow nasal prong oxygen up to 2 L/min in bronchiolitis before escalating to high-flow; SpO2 target is 90 percent or greater at RCH.

options.rationale: Low-flow nasal prong oxygen up to 2 L/min is the first-line escalation for bronchiolitis; reassessment before moving to high-flow is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

High-flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low-flow therapy (persistent desaturation or worsening work of breathing at 2 L/min); premature escalation is not supported. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
CPAP is reserved for severe bronchiolitis with impending failure (grunting, apnoea, exhaustion, HFNC failure); not indicated at this severity. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months; salbutamol has no benefit and may worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Hypertonic saline is not routinely recommended in Australian bronchiolitis pathways; escalation of oxygen is the priority when saturations remain below 92 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Croup is a viral laryngotracheobronchitis with barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor, typically age 6 months to 6 years. RCH severity grades on the Westley score: mild (score 0-2), moderate (3-5), severe (6-11). Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is first line for mild and moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup. Nebulised adrenaline (5 mL of 1:1000 as a flat dose, not per kilogram) is used for severe croup or failure to improve; minimum three-hour observation is required after the last adrenaline dose. Nebulised budesonide 2 mg is an alternative when oral steroid cannot be tolerated.
key_points: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is first line for mild and moderate croup at RCH.
0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone is reserved for severe croup or with nebulised adrenaline.
Nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1:1000, three-hour minimum observation after.
explanation.pearls: Moderate croup at RCH gets oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once; reserve 0.6 mg/kg and nebulised adrenaline for severe croup with stridor and marked distress at rest.

options.rationale: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg is inferior to dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg in croup due to shorter half-life and higher relapse rate; RCH prefers dexamethasone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
0.6 mg/kg is the higher dose reserved for severe croup or those receiving nebulised adrenaline; not required for moderate croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup (stridor at rest with marked respiratory distress) or failure of steroid; not indicated when stridor settles at rest. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Nebulised budesonide is a second-line option when oral dexamethasone cannot be tolerated; oral dexamethasone is preferred first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
RCH recommends dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild or moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is only for severe croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation is diagnosed by Rome IV criteria (two or more of: two or fewer defecations per week, one or more episodes of incontinence per week after toilet training, history of retentive posturing, history of painful or hard bowel movements, presence of a large faecal mass in the rectum, history of large-diameter stools that may obstruct the toilet). Red flags mandating investigation include failure to pass meconium in first 48 hours (Hirschsprung), failure to thrive, abnormal lower limb neurology or spine, palpable abdominal mass extending past umbilicus, and failure of standard laxative therapy. Management is oral osmotic disimpaction (Movicol Junior four sachets escalating over four days) then maintenance titrated to soft daily stools, with behavioural and dietary advice.
key_points: Rome IV criteria and absence of red flags define functional constipation.
Osmotic macrogol (Movicol Junior) oral disimpaction is first line; enemas rarely needed.
Meconium within 48 hours effectively excludes Hirschsprung as a cause.
explanation.pearls: Toddler with hard pellet stools, normal exam and meconium in first 24 hours is functional constipation - start Movicol Junior disimpaction then maintenance, no imaging or biopsy needed.

options.rationale: Meconium in first 24 hours, normal growth, normal exam and no failure of oral laxatives make Hirschsprung very unlikely; biopsy is not first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
This is functional constipation (Rome IV) without red flags; RCH recommends osmotic laxative disimpaction and maintenance with behavioural advice. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Plain radiograph is not recommended for diagnosis or severity of constipation; thyroid screening not indicated without other features of hypothyroidism. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Cow milk protein trial is considered when standard laxative treatment has failed for 4 weeks; not first line without a trial of osmotic laxative. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Rectal disimpaction is reserved for oral disimpaction failure; oral macrogol (Movicol Junior) is first line and better tolerated than enemas. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a self-limited medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood; the major complication is coronary artery aneurysm. Classical criteria require fever for four or more days plus four of five: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy above 1.5 cm (usually unilateral), oral mucosal changes (strawberry tongue or cracked lips), and peripheral extremity changes. Incomplete Kawasaki is diagnosed when fever plus fewer criteria is combined with supportive laboratory or echocardiographic findings: raised CRP or ESR, platelets above 450 after seven days, anaemia, raised ALT, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria, or a coronary z-score above 2.5. Treatment is intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg single infusion plus aspirin (30-50 mg/kg/day) until afebrile 48-72 hours then low-dose 3-5 mg/kg/day for 6-8 weeks.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever plus 2-3 criteria plus supportive labs or echo (coronary z-score >2.5).
Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg single dose plus aspirin (high then low dose).
Steroids adjunctive for high-risk; infliximab for IVIG resistance.
explanation.pearls: A febrile infant with two Kawasaki features plus raised CRP plus coronary z-score above 2.5 meets AHA criteria for incomplete Kawasaki: give IVIG 2 g/kg without waiting for classical criteria.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement: Diagnosis Treatment and Long-term Management of Kawasaki Disease 2017

options.rationale: Bacterial infection alone does not explain sterile pyuria plus coronary dilatation plus classical features; delaying IVIG risks coronary aneurysm. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Incomplete Kawasaki (4 days fever + coronary z-score >2.5 + supportive labs) meets AHA treatment criteria; IVIG plus aspirin is standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Adjunctive corticosteroids may be added for high-risk Kawasaki or IVIG failure; corticosteroid alone without IVIG is not first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Infliximab is reserved for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki (persistent fever after second IVIG); it is not first-line therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Antibiotic monotherapy delays definitive treatment; the coronary z-score of 3.2 with supportive features requires immediate IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Methaemoglobinaemia occurs when haem iron is oxidised from ferrous to ferric form, unable to bind oxygen and shifting the oxygen dissociation curve. In neonates, sources include high-nitrate well water used in home-prepared vegetable puree, topical anaesthetics (benzocaine, prilocaine) and dapsone. The pathognomonic finding is cyanosis with normal arterial PaO2 and chocolate-brown blood; pulse oximetry reads falsely between 82 and 88 percent. Co-oximetry measures true methaemoglobin. Treatment above 20 percent methaemoglobin or with symptoms is methylene blue 1 to 2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes. Methylene blue is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk); ascorbic acid or exchange transfusion is the alternative.
key_points: Chocolate-brown blood with high PaO2 and refractory cyanosis is methaemoglobinaemia.
Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV is first-line antidote (5-minute infusion).
Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk); use ascorbic acid instead.
explanation.pearls: A neonate with cyanosis on oxygen, PaO2 above 200 mmHg and chocolate-brown blood has methaemoglobinaemia; give methylene blue 1 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes and screen for G6PD deficiency.

options.rationale: The picture is refractory cyanosis with normal PaO2 not septic shock; antibiotics do not address the methaemoglobin. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Cyanosis)
Cyanotic congenital heart disease is excluded by structurally normal echocardiogram with normal outflow tracts; prostaglandin is not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Cyanosis)
Chocolate-brown blood with PaO2 240 mmHg and refractory cyanosis is methaemoglobinaemia; methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV is the antidote. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe methaemoglobinaemia unresponsive to methylene blue or when methylene blue is contraindicated (G6PD deficiency). (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Ascorbic acid is a slow reducing agent used only when methylene blue is contraindicated; methylene blue is first line. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Paediatric Crohn disease often presents with abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss and growth failure. Ileocolonoscopy with biopsy plus MR enterography is standard workup. For induction of remission in luminal ileocolonic Crohn without perianal, fistulising or severe systemic disease, exclusive enteral nutrition (polymeric formula as sole nutrition for 6-8 weeks) is first line and equivalent to corticosteroids for symptom relief with superior mucosal healing and no growth suppression. Corticosteroids are reserved for EEN failure or intolerance. Anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab) first-line induction is reserved for aggressive phenotype (penetrating or stricturing disease, extensive small bowel disease, perianal disease, severe growth failure). Maintenance is typically azathioprine 2-2.5 mg/kg/day or methotrexate 15 mg/m2 weekly.
key_points: Exclusive enteral nutrition is first-line induction in paediatric luminal Crohn.
Steroids suppress linear growth and are second line.
First-line biologic induction is reserved for penetrating, fistulising, perianal or severe growth failure phenotypes.
explanation.pearls: Newly diagnosed paediatric Crohn with luminal ileocolonic disease and growth failure but no fistula or perianal disease gets exclusive enteral nutrition for 6-8 weeks as first-line induction, not oral steroids.

options.rationale: Biologic first-line induction is reserved for aggressive disease with penetrating or stricturing phenotype, perianal disease, or growth failure with prior treatment failure. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)
Corticosteroids suppress linear growth in paediatric Crohn; enteral nutrition avoids this and is preferred first line for luminal disease. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

Exclusive enteral nutrition is first-line induction in paediatric luminal Crohn without perianal or fistulising disease, equivalent to steroids for mucosal healing without growth suppression. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

IV steroids are reserved for severe acute colitis with systemic upset; not indicated for stable luminal ileocolonic Crohn without severe systemic features. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)
5-ASA has minimal role in Crohn induction; benefit is limited to mild colonic disease and it does not induce mucosal healing here. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

explanation.summary:
Tachypnoea with crackles in a small infant is usually bronchiolitis, but several features here do not fit: the illness has run for 10 days rather than peaking at day 3 to 5, there is no fever, weight gain has almost stopped, feeding provokes sweating, the liver is enlarged and there is a pansystolic murmur. That combination at 6 to 8 weeks is the classic timing for a left to right shunt to declare itself as pulmonary blood flow rises with falling pulmonary vascular resistance. A chest radiograph and echocardiogram answer the question directly.

In context: bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis, which makes it important to know which findings should stop you making it. Poor weight gain, sweating or breathlessness with feeds, hepatomegaly, a murmur, an illness that does not follow the expected trajectory, or symptoms from birth all warrant a different line of thought. The cost of anchoring is high, because untreated heart failure in infancy deteriorates while the team waits for a viral illness to turn the corner.
key_points: Left to right shunts declare at 6 to 8 weeks as pulmonary resistance falls
Sweating with feeds, poor weight gain and hepatomegaly suggest heart failure
Bronchiolitis peaks around day 3 to 5 and does not enlarge the liver
Echocardiography with a chest radiograph is the discriminating investigation
explanation.pearls: An infant who is breathless doing the one thing that matters most, feeding, and who is not gaining weight, has a cardiac problem until the echocardiogram says otherwise.

options.rationale: Hepatomegaly, a pansystolic murmur, sweating with feeds and poor weight gain at the age a left to right shunt unmasks point away from a viral illness, and imaging of the heart is the discriminating test. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs; RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Viral testing is used for cohorting infants admitted with typical bronchiolitis, which runs over days rather than a fortnight and does not cause hepatomegaly or a murmur. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

A septic screen is indicated for a febrile infant under 3 months or one who looks unwell with unexplained tachypnoea; this boy is afebrile with localising cardiac findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

These tests pursue cystic fibrosis, which would be suggested by faltering growth with greasy stools and recurrent chest infection, and newborn screening makes it an unlikely first line here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Reflux studies are reserved for infants with suspected complicated reflux after conservative measures fail, and reflux does not produce hepatomegaly or a pansystolic murmur. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management deliberately uses smaller boluses (10 mL/kg over 30 minutes) and longer rehydration (48 hours) than adult protocols because cerebral oedema is the leading cause of death. Insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/h starts an hour after fluid begins, never before. Bicarbonate is reserved for cardiac-arrest-level acidosis. Hypotonic fluids are avoided during resuscitation because they worsen the drop in serum osmolality that drives cerebral oedema.
key_points: 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus over 30 minutes for non-shocked moderate to severe DKA
Deficit plus maintenance replaced evenly over 48 hours
Insulin infusion starts 1 hour after fluid; bicarbonate almost never indicated
explanation.pearls: In children with DKA, keep the fluid slow: rapid rehydration and hypotonic fluids are the two biggest reversible cerebral oedema risks.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA and HHS

options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg rapid bolus and 24 hour rehydration is deprecated in paediatric DKA because faster fluid delivery is associated with cerebral oedema; RCH and ISPAD both cap the initial bolus at 10 mL/kg in the absence of shock (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

Insulin is deferred by 1 hour after fluid resuscitation begins because starting insulin before restoring intravascular volume drives potassium intracellularly and worsens hypovolaemia and cerebral oedema risk (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

APEG and RCH paediatric DKA guidance sets an initial isotonic bolus of 10 mL/kg over 30 minutes for haemodynamically stable moderate to severe DKA, followed by rehydration of the assumed 7 to 10 percent deficit plus maintenance evenly across 48 hours to reduce cerebral oedema risk (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

Oral rehydration and subcutaneous insulin are not appropriate for moderate to severe DKA with drowsiness and vomiting; delaying intravenous rehydration risks progression to shock and cerebral oedema (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

Hypotonic fluid is avoided in the resuscitation phase and bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia because it worsens cerebral oedema and paradoxical CNS acidosis (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

explanation.summary: Meningococcal B vaccine is markedly more pyrogenic than the rest of the infant schedule, producing fever above 38 degrees in over half of infants when given with the other routine vaccines, usually within six hours and settling within two days. The Australian Immunisation Handbook therefore makes an explicit exception to the general rule against prophylactic antipyretics: children under two years receiving this vaccine are given paracetamol 15 mg/kg with or shortly before the dose, then two further doses six hours apart. This reduces both the rate and the height of the fever without meaningfully reducing the antibody response. Routine prophylaxis is not recommended for any other vaccine because it may slightly blunt immunogenicity for no clinical gain. In context, fever after immunisation in an infant under three months still needs clinical judgement, because a recent vaccine does not exclude a concurrent serious bacterial infection in an unwell or poorly perfused baby.
key_points: Meningococcal B vaccine causes fever in over half of infants under two years.
Prophylactic paracetamol 15 mg/kg with the vaccine then two six-hourly doses.
Routine antipyretic prophylaxis is not recommended for other vaccines.
Post-immunisation fever does not exclude serious bacterial infection in an unwell infant.
explanation.pearls: Write the three paracetamol times on the vaccination record: families who are told to give it only if fever appears usually start too late to prevent the peak.

options.rationale: Meningococcal B vaccine causes fever in more than half of infants, and the Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends prophylactic paracetamol 15 mg/kg given with or just before the vaccine and repeated six-hourly for two further doses in children under two years. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
Ibuprofen is not recommended under three months of age and has not been studied for this indication; paracetamol is the agent with the supporting evidence. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)
Reactive dosing is the standard advice for every other vaccine on the schedule, where routine prophylaxis is not recommended. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
Corticosteroids have no role in vaccine reaction prophylaxis and may blunt the immune response to the vaccine. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
A single dose the night before has worn off by the time fever appears, which is typically within six hours of the injection. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: A simple febrile seizure in a child aged 6 months to 5 years is generalised, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, and followed by return to baseline. RCH policy is no bloods, no imaging, no LP, and no EEG for children meeting these criteria who look well. Discharge with antipyretic advice and a written safety net is the standard. Rescue medication is reserved for children with prolonged or recurrent complex febrile seizures. Long-term prophylaxis is not warranted.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure: generalised, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, baseline return
No LP, EEG, imaging, or prophylactic antiepileptic required
Discharge with education about recurrence and antipyretic use
explanation.pearls: Recurrence of febrile seizures is common (about 1 in 3) but does not increase epilepsy risk enough to warrant prophylaxis.

options.rationale: LP is not indicated for a simple febrile seizure in a well child aged 18 months without meningism; the RCH criteria specifically identify this presentation as low risk and mandate no lumbar puncture (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).
EEG has no role after a first simple febrile seizure; it does not change management and has a false-positive rate that generates unnecessary anxiety (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

Prophylactic anticonvulsants are not recommended after simple febrile seizures; the modest reduction in recurrence does not justify long-term drug exposure in a benign self-limiting condition (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

Prophylactic benzodiazepines at fever onset are not routine after a first simple febrile seizure and expose the child to sedation without changing meaningful outcomes; rescue midazolam is reserved for prolonged or recurrent complex seizures (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

This meets RCH criteria for a simple febrile seizure (generalised, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, age 6 months to 5 years, back to baseline); no bloods, no imaging, no LP, no EEG is indicated and safe discharge with parental education is the standard (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease requires fever for at least 5 days plus 2 to 3 clinical criteria and supportive laboratory findings. The AHA algorithm activates when CRP is at least 30 mg/L or ESR at least 40 mm/h plus three of anaemia, thrombocytosis above 450, albumin below 30, ALT above the reference range, leucocytes above 15, or sterile pyuria. This 2-year-old satisfies both the clinical and laboratory arms. Coronary aneurysm risk is minimised when IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin is given before day 10, so delay for further culture or observation is unsafe.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever plus 2 to 3 criteria plus supportive labs triggers immediate treatment
IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day reduces coronary aneurysm risk when given before day 10
Steroids are adjunct in high-risk children (Kobayashi score), never a replacement for IVIG
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria, thrombocytosis, and hypoalbuminaemia are the three most useful Kawasaki labs that support an incomplete presentation; a normal ESR does not exclude Kawasaki when CRP is high.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy is not first-line; steroids are added to IVIG only in high-risk children (Kobayashi score suggestive of IVIG resistance) and never replace IVIG in initial treatment (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.rationale: The child meets incomplete Kawasaki criteria today; withholding IVIG for 24 hours of culture surveillance costs a treatment window that reduces coronary aneurysm risk and does not add diagnostic information the current data does not already give (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.rationale: The clinical picture with sterile pyuria and mucocutaneous features fits Kawasaki not bacterial sepsis; antibiotics without IVIG leave the coronary risk untreated and can be given alongside IVIG when infection is a genuine competing possibility (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.rationale: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when fever for at least 5 days is accompanied by 2 to 3 clinical criteria plus supportive laboratory findings (CRP 30 mg/L or above, ESR 40 mm/h or above, and 3 or more of anaemia, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, elevated ALT, sterile pyuria, leucocytosis); this child meets both and IVIG should not wait for confirmation to minimise coronary aneurysm risk (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.rationale: Delaying IVIG past day 10 substantially increases coronary aneurysm risk; a child meeting incomplete Kawasaki criteria on day 6 needs treatment now, not further observation (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

explanation.summary: The AU pathway for asymptomatic at-risk neonatal hypoglycaemia (late preterm, infant of diabetic mother, macrosomia, or small-for-gestational-age) starts with 40 percent dextrose gel 200 mg/kg buccally with a supported breastfeed, then repeats the glucose in 30 minutes. This protocol reduces NICU admission and preserves breastfeeding and skin-to-skin. Intravenous glucose is reserved for symptomatic infants, a BSL under 1.5 mmol/L, or a failed gel-plus-feed trial. Glucagon is a niche rescue for refractory hypoglycaemia awaiting intravenous access.
key_points: Asymptomatic at-risk baby with BSL under 2.6 mmol/L: dextrose gel 200 mg/kg plus feed first
Repeat glucose 30 minutes after gel to guide escalation
Intravenous 10 percent dextrose only for symptomatic, BSL under 1.5, or gel-and-feed failure
explanation.pearls: Dextrose gel has been shown to reduce NICU admission when used first-line in asymptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia; it does not replace a feed but keeps mother and baby together.

sources.label: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia
Australian and New Zealand Neonatal Network Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Formula alone without dextrose gel takes longer to correct the glucose and dextrose gel with breastfeeding is proven to reduce NICU admission; deferring repeat testing to the next 3 hour check misses a rebound below 2.6 (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.rationale: The ANZ Neonatal Network hypoglycaemia pathway makes 40 percent dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) plus a feed the first-line response to asymptomatic hypoglycaemia (BSL under 2.6) in an at-risk late-preterm baby, with repeat glucose in 30 minutes to guide escalation (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.rationale: Intravenous glucose is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia, glucose under 1.5 mmol/L, or failure of dextrose gel plus feed to correct the BSL; separating this baby from the mother now is disproportionate to a single asymptomatic pre-feed reading of 2.2 mmol/L (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.rationale: A late-preterm infant of a diabetic mother with a documented BSL of 2.2 mmol/L requires active correction, not observation for 3 hours which risks progression to symptomatic hypoglycaemia and neurodevelopmental harm (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.rationale: Intramuscular glucagon is reserved for refractory or symptomatic hypoglycaemia where intravenous access is delayed; it is not the initial response to an asymptomatic BSL of 2.2 mmol/L when dextrose gel and a feed will correct most episodes (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

explanation.summary: A well-appearing term newborn presenting on day 2 to 3 with poor feeding, pre-post ductal saturation split, reduced femoral pulses, and metabolic acidosis has a duct-dependent systemic circulation until proven otherwise. The single stabilising drug is prostaglandin E1 at 10 to 20 nanograms/kg/min, which maintains patency of the ductus arteriosus and restores systemic flow. Antibiotics may run in parallel if sepsis is a competing possibility but should not delay prostaglandin. Volume loading and high-flow oxygen are actively harmful in this setting.
key_points: Pre-post ductal saturation split plus reduced femoral pulses suggests duct-dependent systemic circulation
Prostaglandin E1 10 to 20 ng/kg/min stabilises before echocardiography and transfer
Avoid high-flow oxygen and large volume loading before ductal patency is secured
explanation.pearls: Duct closes physiologically around day 2 to 5, which is when duct-dependent lesions unmask; a pre-post ductal saturation difference of at least 3 percent flags urgent cardiology assessment.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.rationale: The saturation and blood pressure splits with metabolic acidosis point to a duct-dependent systemic circulation such as coarctation or interrupted arch; prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency and buys time for cardiac assessment and surgical planning (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.rationale: Inotropic support without opening the duct addresses the wrong physiology; adrenaline may increase myocardial oxygen demand and worsen ischaemia in a duct-dependent lesion before prostaglandin restores systemic flow (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.rationale: Furosemide and afterload reduction do not maintain ductal patency and worsen perfusion in a duct-dependent circulation before echocardiography and surgery; prostaglandin is the immediate stabilising drug (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.rationale: Volume loading a duct-dependent systemic circulation can precipitate pulmonary oedema and cardiovascular collapse and antibiotics without prostaglandin do not address the anatomical driver of the shock (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.rationale: High-flow oxygen can accelerate ductus arteriosus closure, worsening a duct-dependent lesion; the pre-post ductal split needs prostaglandin, not more oxygen, and this baby requires transfer not ward observation (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

explanation.summary: A 2-week-old boy with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and shock has a salt-losing crisis of 21-hydroxylase deficiency until proven otherwise, because male infants have no ambiguous genitalia to flag the diagnosis earlier. The immediate treatment is fluid and glucose correction with parenteral hydrocortisone (25 mg stat in neonates), then continued hydrocortisone at stress dose. Blood for 17-hydroxyprogesterone must be drawn before the second hydrocortisone dose so newborn-screen confirmation is possible. Hyperkalaemia rarely needs additional treatment once hydrocortisone and volume are given.
key_points: Hyponatraemia plus hyperkalaemia plus hypoglycaemia plus shock in a 2-week-old male = CAH salt-losing crisis
Hydrocortisone 25 mg stat and saline resuscitation are the immediate steps
Draw serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone before continuing hydrocortisone
explanation.pearls: Male CAH typically presents around day 7 to 14 as a salt-losing crisis because there is no genital ambiguity to prompt earlier diagnosis; newborn screening turnaround in Australia is usually about 1 week.

sources.label: APEG Position Statement on Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia

options.rationale: Missing steroid replacement in a salt-losing crisis is a fatal omission even with fluid and antibiotics; sepsis may coexist but hydrocortisone must not wait, and 20 mL/kg initial bolus is larger than the RCH neonatal pathway recommends in the absence of overt shock signs (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

Oral fludrocortisone alone acts too slowly to reverse a salt-losing crisis and this shocked vomiting neonate cannot rely on oral rehydration; intravenous fluid and parenteral hydrocortisone are needed first (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

This picture of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and shock in a term male neonate on day 12 fits a salt-losing crisis in classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia; RCH pathway is fluid and glucose resuscitation with parenteral hydrocortisone as a stat 25 mg dose in neonates, and blood for 17-hydroxyprogesterone before ongoing hydrocortisone is essential to lock in the diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

Hyperkalaemia treatment without addressing the underlying adrenal insufficiency does not correct the driving pathology; hydrocortisone plus saline and dextrose start the definitive treatment and typically bring potassium down without calcium or nebulised beta-agonist (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

Rapid correction of hyponatraemia in a hypovolaemic child risks central pontine myelinolysis; the driver is aldosterone deficiency and sodium corrects gradually once fluid and hydrocortisone are given (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

explanation.summary: Mild croup is defined by a barking cough with no stridor at rest and no significant chest recession at rest, with the child alert. The Royal Children's guideline first line is a single oral dose of dexamethasone at 0.15 mg/kg with disposition home once the child is settled and tolerating oral fluids. The higher 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup, and nebulised adrenaline is added only for severe presentations. Any child who has received nebulised adrenaline requires a minimum of 3 hours of post administration observation before discharge to detect rebound obstruction.
key_points: Mild croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally once.
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000.
Observe 3 hours after any nebulised adrenaline before discharge.
explanation.pearls: In Australian paediatric practice a single 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone dose provides 72 hours of anti-inflammatory effect and covers the natural history of most croup without needing repeat dosing.

options.rationale: This child has mild croup: stridor only when upset, no stridor at rest, no significant recession at rest. Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once is first line for mild and moderate croup and discharge is safe once the child is settled and taking fluids (Source: RCH CPG: Croup; TG Respiratory).

The dose is correct for mild croup, however observation for 30 minutes only applies when nebulised adrenaline has been given; for children receiving oral steroid alone the practice is to observe until settled and confirm oral tolerance (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

Prednisolone is an alternative when dexamethasone is unavailable, however a single dexamethasone dose has a longer duration of action and is preferred; a 3 day course of prednisolone is not required and adds risk without benefit (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

The higher 0.6 mg/kg dose and nebulised adrenaline are reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession; using them for mild croup exposes the child to unnecessary tachycardia and mandates 3 hours of observation for rebound (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

Nebulised budesonide is used only when the child cannot tolerate oral dexamethasone; it is second line to oral steroid, and admission for mild croup without stridor at rest is not indicated (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

explanation.summary: For a child with mild to moderate dehydration from gastroenteritis who fails a supervised oral trial, nasogastric rapid rehydration with oral rehydration solution is preferred before intravenous fluids. Nasogastric administration achieves comparable rehydration to intravenous fluids with fewer complications and shorter emergency stays. A single dose of ondansetron may reduce vomiting during the first hour. Intravenous fluids are reserved for severe dehydration, shock, ileus, or nasogastric failure.
key_points: Failed oral trial with mild to moderate dehydration: escalate to nasogastric before intravenous.
Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg once reduces vomiting in the first hour.
Reserve intravenous fluids for severe dehydration, shock, or nasogastric failure.
explanation.pearls: Nasogastric rapid rehydration delivers oral rehydration solution at 20 mL/kg in the first hour and completes replacement over 4 hours, matching intravenous outcomes at lower cost for children with ongoing vomiting.

options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg bolus is indicated for shock or severe dehydration with poor perfusion; this child has capillary refill 2 seconds, warm peripheries and no hypotension, so full bolus resuscitation is not required and risks unnecessary sodium load (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

The child has mild to moderate dehydration with failure of a supervised oral trial; the RCH pathway is nasogastric rapid rehydration with oral rehydration solution as first line before moving to intravenous fluids, with equivalent efficacy and lower cost (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

Ondansetron 4 mg is the correct wafer dose for a 12 kg child and it does help vomiting, however after two vomits during a supervised oral trial the delivery route should be escalated rather than continued (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

Intravenous fluids are second line to nasogastric rapid rehydration for mild to moderate dehydration; a maintenance only rate at 46 mL per hour also fails to address the fluid deficit and delays correction (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

Ad libitum offering already failed at the point of care and admission without an active rehydration strategy is not appropriate; a structured nasogastric or intravenous regimen is required in the setting of ongoing vomiting (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

explanation.summary: An infant under 4 weeks old with a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius receives a full septic workup including blood culture, urine by suprapubic aspirate or catheter, and lumbar puncture, then empirical intravenous antibiotics without waiting for deterioration. Cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin covers neonatal pathogens including group B streptococcus, Listeria monocytogenes and Escherichia coli. Ceftriaxone is avoided during the first month because it displaces bilirubin from albumin. A viral illness in an older sibling does not remove the need for the neonatal septic workup because concurrent bacterial infection remains possible.
key_points: Under 4 weeks and fever above 38 C: full septic workup plus empirical antibiotics.
Cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin covers group B streptococcus, Listeria and Escherichia coli.
Avoid ceftriaxone under 1 month due to bilirubin displacement risk.
explanation.pearls: In an infant under 28 days old use cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin rather than defaulting to ceftriaxone; the 28 day threshold is driven by the risk of kernicterus with ceftriaxone during the neonatal jaundice window.

options.rationale: Any infant under 4 weeks old with a fever above 38 degrees receives a full septic workup and empirical intravenous antibiotics without waiting for clinical deterioration because bacterial meningitis at this age presents with subtle signs (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

Identification of a viral cause does not exclude concurrent invasive bacterial infection in an infant under 4 weeks old; the septic workup and empirical antibiotics remain required (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

Any infant under 4 weeks old with a fever above 38 degrees requires a full septic workup including lumbar puncture followed by empirical broad spectrum antibiotics; cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin covers the neonatal group of organisms including group B streptococcus, Listeria and Escherichia coli (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child; TG Antibiotic).

Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin and is avoided in neonates under 1 month; more importantly no infant under 4 weeks with a fever is discharged without a full workup and inpatient antibiotic completion (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child; AMH Neonatal).

A negative dipstick does not exclude urinary tract infection in young infants and observation only delays treatment; the required approach is lumbar puncture plus urine plus blood cultures followed by empirical antibiotics (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

explanation.summary: In bronchiolitis with hypoxia the Royal Children's approach is to start with low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L per minute and escalate to high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg per minute if low flow fails after around 2 hours or the child has red flag features. The SpO2 target on the guideline is 90 percent to avoid hyperoxia and unnecessary escalation. Salbutamol, hypertonic sodium chloride and nebulised adrenaline are not routinely recommended in infants under 12 months old. A history of apnoea, prematurity or feeding failure lowers the threshold for admission and closer monitoring.
key_points: Low flow oxygen first, high flow at 2 L/kg per minute if failing.
SpO2 target 90 percent for bronchiolitis at RCH.
Salbutamol, hypertonic saline and nebulised adrenaline not recommended in under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: A reported apnoea in a young infant with bronchiolitis mandates a monitored bed and lowered SpO2 target of 90 percent, even when the child appears clinically stable at triage.

options.rationale: Low flow nasal prong is the correct first line oxygen delivery, however this infant is still tachypnoeic with recession and has already had an apnoea at home; a further 2 hour delay before escalation is inappropriate given the risk profile (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).
Salbutamol is not recommended in infants under 12 months with bronchiolitis; there is no evidence of benefit and it may cause tachycardia and tachyphylaxis (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).
Nebulised hypertonic sodium chloride has been removed from the RCH pathway; systematic reviews do not show meaningful benefit in bronchiolitis (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

High flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg per minute is appropriate for a bronchiolitic infant who has failed low flow oxygen with ongoing work of breathing, with an SpO2 target of 90 percent to avoid oxygen toxicity; admission to a monitored bed is required given the reported apnoea (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; PREDICT bronchiolitis guideline 2022).

Intubation is not first line here; the infant is oxygenating adequately on low flow oxygen and non-invasive support with high flow has not been trialled, so early intubation is not indicated (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: A spiral long bone fracture in a non ambulant infant, together with bruises on multiple non bony sites and faltering growth, is a classic non accidental injury pattern that requires admission for a full child protection workup and mandatory notification to child protection services. The workup includes skeletal survey, retinal examination for haemorrhages, coagulation screen and social assessment. Mandatory notification obligations for doctors apply once there is a reasonable suspicion of harm, not once harm is proven. Delaying disposition until the fracture is orthopaedically fixed is not appropriate because safeguarding runs in parallel with medical care.
key_points: Spiral fracture in a non ambulant child: mandatory child protection referral.
Full workup: skeletal survey, retinal examination, coagulation screen, social assessment.
Reasonable suspicion, not proof, triggers the mandatory notification duty.
explanation.pearls: Bruising in a pre cruising infant (less than about 9 months old) is uncommon from normal activity, so any bruise in a non ambulant infant warrants a low threshold for a safeguarding assessment before discharge.

sources.label: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.rationale: This is a red flag presentation for physical abuse with a spiral fracture in a non ambulant child, unexplained bruising in different sites, and faltering growth; a community follow up alone would leave the child at ongoing risk (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.rationale: Discharge before a child protection workup risks further harm; a suspected non accidental injury requires admission and formal safeguarding assessment before disposition (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.rationale: Ordering the tests without safeguarding action is inadequate; mandatory notification to child protection services and involvement of paediatric team are required whenever non accidental injury is suspected in a child under 2 years (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.rationale: Fracture management does not take priority over safeguarding; the safeguarding pathway runs in parallel and is a mandatory reporting obligation for the doctor at the point of suspicion (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.rationale: A spiral humeral fracture in a non ambulant infant with additional unexplained bruises and faltering growth is highly suggestive of physical abuse; an admission for a skeletal survey, retinal examination, coagulation screen and social assessment, mandatory notification to child protection services, and paediatric team involvement is the correct standard of care (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury; RCH CPG: Child abuse).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

explanation.summary: A conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in an infant beyond 2 weeks old with pale stools and dark urine must be treated as a surgical emergency until biliary atresia is excluded. Urgent same day admission for hepatology review, imaging including hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scan and possibly cholangiography allows the Kasai portoenterostomy to be performed before 60 days of age when outcomes are markedly better. Phototherapy is only useful for unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and does not treat the biliary obstruction. A formula trial is appropriate only for stable unconjugated jaundice and should not delay workup in a cholestatic infant.
key_points: Direct bilirubin above 17 micromol/L or above 20 percent of total is always abnormal.
Pale stools plus dark urine in an infant is biliary atresia until proven otherwise.
Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days gives the best outcomes.
explanation.pearls: In any infant beyond 2 weeks of age with persistent jaundice, always split the bilirubin; a conjugated fraction over 17 micromol/L makes biliary atresia the working diagnosis until same day imaging and hepatology review say otherwise.

options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and resolves without pale stools; a direct bilirubin fraction above 17 micromol/L or above 20 percent of total in a 4-week-old requires urgent workup for cholestasis and cannot be reassured (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice; NASPGHAN cholestasis guideline).

A conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a 4-week-old with pale stools and dark urine is a surgical emergency until biliary atresia is excluded; the Kasai portoenterostomy outcome is much better if performed before 60 days of age, so same day paediatric admission for urgent workup and hepatology review is required (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice; NASPGHAN cholestasis guideline).
Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; it is ineffective and inappropriate for conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and delays definitive workup (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

While correcting vitamin K status is part of cholestatic workup, a single injection alone without paediatric referral misses the time-critical requirement to exclude biliary atresia within the first 60 days (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

A formula trial is used only in stable unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; it has no place when the direct fraction is elevated and there are pale stools, and it delays the diagnosis of biliary atresia (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

explanation.summary: The RCH imaging cascade after urinary tract infection reserves renal tract ultrasound for atypical UTI, recurrent UTI, infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring, or when there is a family history of significant renal tract disease. A single typical UTI in a well thriving child between 6 months and 3 years with a normal antenatal morphology scan needs no imaging. Dimercaptosuccinic acid scanning and micturating cystourethrogram are NICE constructs and are not part of the RCH cascade. Parents are safety netted for prompt review and culture of any future febrile illness.
key_points: Single typical UTI plus normal antenatal scan plus well child equals no imaging.
Ultrasound only for atypical, recurrent, under 6 months, or absent antenatal monitoring.
DMSA and MCUG are not part of the RCH cascade.
explanation.pearls: Confirm the antenatal morphology scan was actually done and normal before deciding not to image; a missed antenatal scan converts a first typical UTI in an infant under 6 months into an indication for renal tract ultrasound.

options.rationale: RCH advises no imaging after a single typical febrile UTI in a well thriving child aged 6 months to less than 3 years with normal antenatal monitoring; parents are counselled to seek review with any future febrile illness (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).
Dimercaptosuccinic acid scanning is a NICE construct and is not part of the RCH imaging cascade; it should not be requested after a single typical UTI (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

Micturating cystourethrogram is invasive, involves radiation and catheterisation, and is not in the RCH cascade after a single typical UTI in a child with normal antenatal imaging (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

Ultrasound is only indicated for atypical UTI features, recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring; a single typical UTI in a well thriving girl with a normal antenatal scan does not need ultrasound (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended after a single typical UTI in this age group; the PRIVENT trial and RCH guidance restrict prophylaxis to selected recurrent UTI or dilating reflux (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis guidance is deliberately conservative on oxygen delivery: start with low flow nasal prongs at 1 to 2 L/min and titrate to an SpO2 target of at least 90 percent. High flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low flow after at least 2 hours. Bronchodilators and adrenaline are not routinely recommended. Feeding support, hydration and time are the other pillars of care.
key_points: First line oxygen is nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min.
SpO2 target is 90 percent, not 92 to 94.
High flow reserved for failure of low flow after 2 hours.
explanation.pearls: Reassess at 2 hours after starting low flow; a persistent SpO2 under 90 on 2 L/min, sustained tachypnoea over 60 with recessions, or feeding failure defines low flow failure and is the trigger for high flow escalation rather than the initial choice.

options.rationale: High flow is reserved for failure of low flow after a trial of 2 hours; using it up front increases admissions to higher care beds without reducing intubation (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis; PARIS trial).

RCH bronchiolitis guidance recommends low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min as first line, with an SpO2 target of at least 90 percent; higher targets and high flow are not first line (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).
A Hudson mask at this flow is not first line and blunts assessment of respiratory effort and feeding; low flow nasal prongs are preferred (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).
Salbutamol is not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months; RCH advises against routine bronchodilators regardless of wheeze (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).
Nebulised adrenaline is not routinely used in bronchiolitis and does not alter admission or length of stay; oxygen and feeding support are the mainstays (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: RCH advises oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup with 2 hours of observation before discharge. Reserve 0.6 mg/kg for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked respiratory distress. Prednisolone is not first line because of higher representation rates. Nebulised or intramuscular routes are alternatives only when the oral route is not tolerated. Nebulised adrenaline is added for severe cases and mandates 3 hours of post dose observation.
key_points: Mild or moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally.
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000.
Observe 3 hours after last nebulised adrenaline; 2 hours after steroid alone.
explanation.pearls: Croup severity is scored on stridor at rest, retraction and air entry; if a child has only intermittent stridor when upset with mild recession at rest, that is moderate and 0.15 mg/kg is enough.

options.rationale: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 3 days has been shown to have higher representation rates than dexamethasone in croup and is not first line at RCH (Source: RCH CPG Croup; Cochrane).
0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked respiratory distress; using it in mild to moderate cases overtreats without added benefit (Source: RCH CPG Croup).
RCH advises oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup, with 3 hours of observation after any nebulised adrenaline; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup (Source: RCH CPG Croup).
Nebulised budesonide is an alternative when oral intake is not tolerated; this child is tolerating oral fluid so dexamethasone orally is preferred and cheaper (Source: RCH CPG Croup).
Intramuscular dexamethasone is reserved for children who cannot tolerate oral intake; oral dose at 0.15 mg/kg is equivalent and less distressing (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

explanation.summary: ASCIA uses banded intramuscular adrenaline dosing to remove drug arithmetic errors under time pressure: 150 microg for 7.5 to 20 kg (EpiPen Jr band), 300 microg for over 20 kg (EpiPen band), and 500 microg for adults. The intramuscular anterolateral thigh is the first route in every case. Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory shock in a monitored setting.
key_points: 7.5 to 20 kg equals 150 microg IM.
Over 20 kg equals 300 microg IM.
Repeat every 5 minutes while symptoms persist.
explanation.pearls: Do not use 10 microg/kg calculations for community or emergency anaphylaxis dosing; the banded table gives an equivalent effective dose without arithmetic and mirrors the EpiPen strengths.

options.rationale: Intravenous adrenaline bolus in anaphylaxis is reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory shock and only in a monitored setting; the initial route is always intramuscular (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

Weight based arithmetic is discouraged for anaphylaxis in AU; ASCIA banded dosing avoids error under time pressure and matches the EpiPen strengths available in community use (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).
The 300 microg dose is reserved for children 20 kg and over; using this dose in a 16 kg child over doses her by a factor of about 2 (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

ASCIA uses banded intramuscular adrenaline dosing: 150 microg for children 7.5 to 20 kg; a 16 kg child sits in this band and the IM thigh is preferred over any weight based arithmetic (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema but is not a substitute for intramuscular adrenaline in anaphylaxis; delaying IM adrenaline increases the risk of biphasic and fatal reactions (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

explanation.summary: RCH sepsis pathway in a shocked infant is a fixed order: IV or IO access, blood cultures, first IV antibiotic within the hour, then 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline over 5 to 10 minutes, repeat to a total of 60 mL/kg before considering inotropes. Under 2 months the empirical antibiotic is IV cefotaxime to cover Neisseria and Listeria. Normal inflammatory markers do not exclude sepsis in early presentation and must not delay antibiotics in an unwell infant.
key_points: Order: access, cultures, antibiotics, fluid, then inotropes.
Under 2 months: IV cefotaxime empirically to cover Listeria.
Normal WCC and CRP do not exclude bacterial sepsis in early presentation.
explanation.pearls: A hypothermic infant with lactate over 4 and delayed capillary refill is in cold septic shock; treat with warm fluid boluses and expect adrenaline infusion to be needed once 60 mL/kg has been given, not before.

options.rationale: An unwell shocked infant under 3 months needs immediate resuscitation and empirical antibiotics; awaiting cultures overnight without intervention delays sepsis treatment (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis; RCH CPG The febrile child).
Inotropes are added AFTER adequate fluid resuscitation (up to 60 mL/kg) fails to restore perfusion; using adrenaline before fluids and antibiotics inverts the sepsis pathway (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis).

Sequence at RCH is IV access, blood cultures, first antibiotic dose, then fluid bolus; cefotaxime is preferred under 2 months because gentamicin monotherapy misses Listeria and dosing is more forgiving than penicillin plus gentamicin (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis).

Inflammatory markers are insensitive in early sepsis in this age group and are not used to justify withholding empirical antibiotics in an unwell infant under 3 months; delay is a preventable cause of death (Source: RCH CPG The febrile child).

RCH sepsis pathway: IV or IO access, then blood cultures, then IV empirical antibiotic within the hour (cefotaxime for under 2 months to cover Listeria and Neisseria), then 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline over 5 to 10 minutes and repeat to 60 mL/kg total (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis; RCH CPG The febrile child).

explanation.summary: RCH gastroenteritis guidance recommends rapid nasogastric rehydration as first line for mild to moderate dehydration once oral rehydration solution has failed. The standard schedule is 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours of oral rehydration solution via nasogastric tube. Intravenous fluids are reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure. A single dose of ondansetron helps reduce vomiting and IV need in the moderately dehydrated child but is an adjunct rather than a substitute for enteral rehydration.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first line when oral has failed.
25 mL/kg per hour of ORS for 4 hours.
IV reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure.
explanation.pearls: Weigh the child on presentation and again during rehydration; using acute weight change is the most reliable bedside measure of dehydration and of successful rehydration in a child with recent well child weights recorded.

options.rationale: RCH advises rapid nasogastric rehydration as first line for mild to moderate dehydration when oral has failed; 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours is the standard rapid rehydration schedule and works well in gastroenteritis (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

IV fluids are reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure; using them first in a moderately dehydrated child unnecessarily cannulates her and increases hyponatraemia risk (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

Oral rehydration by syringe has already failed at 1 hour with ongoing vomiting; continuing the same failed strategy risks worsening dehydration and delayed reassessment (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

A single dose of ondansetron 2 mg for 8 to 15 kg body weight is a reasonable adjunct but the primary rehydration route is still NGT if oral has failed; this option undertreats a 6 percent dehydration episode (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).
A 20 mL/kg bolus is a resuscitation dose for shock; this child has no signs of shock and is not tachycardic beyond age norms, so a bolus is not indicated (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

explanation.summary: RCH severe croup pathway combines nebulised adrenaline (a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000 per dose regardless of weight) with oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, with a minimum of 3 hours observation after the last adrenaline dose to detect rebound obstruction. Steroid alone is inadequate for severe croup; intubation is reserved for medical failure or impending respiratory failure. Do not use per kg adrenaline arithmetic for the nebulised dose.
key_points: Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PLUS nebulised adrenaline.
Nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000, not per kg.
Observe at least 3 hours after last adrenaline for rebound.
explanation.pearls: Rebound obstruction typically occurs 2 to 3 hours after nebulised adrenaline wears off; discharge before 3 hours risks readmission with worse airway compromise, so treat the 3 hour observation as a hard rule.

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000 per RCH; a per kg calculation is not the RCH protocol and dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg undertreats severe croup (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

Severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession requires both nebulised adrenaline (flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000 by RCH; not per kg) and dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, with 3 hour observation after the last adrenaline (Source: RCH CPG Croup).
Steroid alone at 0.15 mg/kg without nebulised adrenaline is not adequate for severe croup with stridor at rest; risk of airway obstruction is not addressed (Source: RCH CPG Croup).
Intubation is reserved for severe croup that fails medical therapy or shows impending respiratory failure; a trial of nebulised adrenaline and steroids is first (Source: RCH CPG Croup).
Heliox is not a substitute for nebulised adrenaline in severe croup at RCH; oral dexamethasone is equivalent to IV and less distressing than cannulation (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

explanation.summary: Hereditary spherocytosis is the leading cause of chronic congenital haemolytic anaemia in people of northern European heritage; presentation in the newborn period with early unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is common. The diagnostic triad is spherocytes on film with reticulocytosis, a negative direct antiglobulin test, and a family history of unexplained neonatal jaundice, splenectomy or gallstones. The negative direct antiglobulin test kills the immune haemolysis differentials of Rh and ABO incompatibility. Confirmatory testing is by eosin 5 maleimide binding by flow cytometry or by osmotic fragility.
key_points: DAT negative haemolysis with spherocytes points to intracorpuscular defect.
Family history of splenectomy or neonatal jaundice supports HS.
Confirm by eosin 5 maleimide binding by flow cytometry.
explanation.pearls: When bilirubin is over the exchange threshold with haemolytic features in the first 24 to 48 hours of life, start intensive phototherapy first and send for HS confirmatory testing; folate supplementation for the first year of life is standard and up to a third of infants with HS require transfusion in the newborn period.

sources.label: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: ABO incompatibility would be expected to give a positive direct antiglobulin test in most clinically important cases and the film is more likely to show microspherocytes without polychromasia (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is X linked and rare in northern European girls; the film would typically show bite cells and hemighost cells rather than spherocytes with polychromasia (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Spherocytes on film with reticulocytosis, a negative direct antiglobulin test, and a family history of unexplained splenectomy is classic for hereditary spherocytosis presenting in the newborn period; DAT negativity argues against immune haemolysis (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy; HSANZ Australasian hereditary spherocytosis guideline).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy
