explanation.pearls: Ask the child to jump on the spot or to cough, because a positive response has a similar diagnostic accuracy to formally elicited rebound tenderness and spares them the pain of deep palpation and release.

options.rationale: Serial observation is a legitimate strategy for equivocal abdominal pain, but involuntary guarding with percussion tenderness indicates peritonism that will not be clarified by another four hours (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Abdominal Pain).

Ultrasound helps when the diagnosis is uncertain, and a non visualised appendix is common in a distressed child, so imaging must not delay referral once peritonism is established (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Abdominal Pain).

Peritonism with tachycardia and delayed capillary refill after three days of symptoms indicates probable perforation, and resuscitation with a 20 mL per kg bolus alongside immediate surgical referral and antibiotics is the priority (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Abdominal Pain; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Loose stools occur in perforated appendicitis from pelvic irritation of the rectum, and treating this as infective gastroenteritis is the classic error that delays diagnosis in preschool children (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Abdominal Pain).

Computed tomography is avoided as a first line test in children because of radiation exposure, and ultrasound is the preferred modality when imaging is genuinely needed (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Abdominal Pain).

explanation.summary: Facial nerve palsy in a child is only idiopathic once a middle ear cause has been excluded, because the nerve runs through the middle ear in a bony canal that is dehiscent in a proportion of children. Suppuration under pressure produces a lower motor neurone weakness that resolves when the middle ear is drained and the organism treated. The other intratemporal complications to look for at the same time are acute mastoiditis, labyrinthitis and sigmoid sinus thrombosis. Missing the ear and treating as idiopathic palsy with steroid alone risks permanent weakness and intracranial spread.
key_points: Examine both tympanic membranes in every child with facial weakness before labelling it idiopathic
Complicated acute otitis media means admission, intravenous antibiotics and ear nose and throat involvement
Myringotomy both decompresses the middle ear and yields fluid for culture
Vesicles in the canal or on the pinna point instead to herpes zoster oticus
Eye protection is still needed while the eye will not close, whatever the cause
explanation.pearls: A lower motor neurone facial palsy that spares no forehead movement plus a bulging drum is complicated otitis media until proven otherwise, and the drainage should happen on the day of presentation rather than after a trial of oral antibiotics.

options.rationale: Corticosteroid is the treatment for idiopathic facial palsy, but a bulging infected drum on the same side identifies an intratemporal cause, and steroid without drainage and antibiotics leaves the infection untreated (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media).

Oral amoxicillin is right for uncomplicated acute otitis media, but any intratemporal complication moves the child to intravenous therapy and inpatient care rather than community review (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Facial weakness with an acutely infected middle ear is a complicated otitis media, and treatment is intravenous antibiotic cover plus drainage of the middle ear to decompress the nerve in its canal (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Antiviral plus steroid targets herpes zoster oticus, whose distinguishing feature is vesicles in the canal or on the pinna with severe otalgia rather than a bulging purulent drum (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media).

Imaging is reserved for slowly progressive weakness, other cranial nerve signs or suspected intracranial extension, and delaying antibiotics for a scan in a febrile child with an obvious middle ear source risks further spread (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media).

explanation.summary: Otitis media with effusion is fluid in the middle ear without the features of acute infection, and it is extremely common in preschool children after upper respiratory illness. The great majority resolve spontaneously within three months, which is why the first response is documented watchful waiting with an audiogram rather than treatment. Referral is driven by the combination of persistence beyond three months, the size of the hearing loss and a demonstrable effect on speech, language or schooling, not by the appearance of the drum alone. Left untreated in that group the child accumulates months of degraded auditory input during the years when speech sounds are being laid down.
key_points: Three months of documented persistence is the usual trigger to move from watching to referring
A type B flat tympanogram supports effusion but the audiogram quantifies the disability
Antibiotics, antihistamines, decongestants and intranasal steroid do not change outcomes
Speech, language and behaviour concerns lower the threshold for referral
Autoinflation devices are a reasonable adjunct in older cooperative children
explanation.pearls: A bilateral conductive loss of 25 to 30 dB is roughly the volume difference between normal speech and a whisper, which is why a child with persistent effusion at that level appears inattentive rather than deaf.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

options.rationale: Effusion documented beyond three months with a bilateral loss of this size and a clear effect on speech and learning meets the referral threshold, and tubes are the intervention that restores hearing while the eustachian tube matures (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

options.rationale: Antibiotics clear effusion only transiently and confer no benefit on hearing at three months, and there is no acute infection here to treat (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

options.rationale: Intranasal steroid has no demonstrated effect on effusion clearance or hearing, and a further three months of waiting adds to an already documented four month history (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for the first three months because most effusions resolve, but that window has already passed and the loss is affecting speech (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

options.rationale: Temporal bone imaging is for suspected cholesteatoma or a bony complication, neither of which is suggested by intact retracted drums with fluid behind them (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

explanation.summary: Children with atopic eczema have a defective skin barrier and reduced cutaneous antimicrobial defence, so herpes simplex acquired from a cold sore in a carer can spread across affected skin rather than staying localised. The give away is that the lesions are all the same age and shape, are painful rather than itchy, and appear on eczematous rather than intact skin. Bacterial superinfection often coexists, which is why antistaphylococcal cover is usually added, but the antiviral is the treatment that alters the trajectory. Involvement near the eye is a separate emergency because corneal disease can scar, and dissemination to the liver and brain is the feared systemic outcome in an unwell infant.
key_points: Uniform punched out erosions on eczematous skin that hurt rather than itch suggest herpetic superinfection
Fever and poor oral intake move treatment from oral to intravenous antiviral therapy
Do not escalate topical corticosteroid onto suspected herpetic eczema
Periocular lesions require same day ophthalmology assessment
Send a deroofed lesion swab for viral polymerase chain reaction but treat before the result
explanation.pearls: Aciclovir gives the greatest benefit when started within the first 48 hours of the eruption, so treat on the clinical pattern of monomorphic painful erosions and do not wait for the polymerase chain reaction result.

options.rationale: Escalating topical steroid onto an untreated cutaneous herpes infection allows it to spread, and can turn a treatable superinfection into a disseminated one (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema).

Oral cefalexin covers staphylococcal impetiginisation, whose distinguishing feature is golden crusting and pustules rather than uniform punched out erosions that are exquisitely painful (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Wet dressings and dilute bleach baths reduce bacterial load in chronic eczema but do nothing for viral replication, and outpatient review defers treatment in a child who is febrile and not drinking (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema).
Immunoglobulin has no role in cutaneous viral superinfection of eczema and would delay the specific antiviral that changes the course (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema).

Painful monomorphic punched out erosions spreading rapidly across eczematous skin in a febrile child who is not drinking warrants intravenous antiviral therapy, and periocular involvement needs slit lamp assessment on the same day (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Bedwetting is called monosymptomatic when there are no daytime storage or voiding symptoms, and primary when the child has never had a six month dry spell. Before any treatment the two reversible contributors to exclude are constipation and urinary tract infection, because treating either can resolve the wetting on its own. Alarm therapy conditions the child to wake or inhibit voiding and has the best relapse free outcome, but it demands household commitment for six to eight weeks and does not suit every family. Desmopressin has a role as rapid short term cover and as a fallback when an alarm fails or is impractical.
key_points: Exclude constipation and urinary infection before labelling enuresis primary and monosymptomatic
Daytime urgency, wetting or straining shifts the diagnosis away from simple nocturnal enuresis
Alarm therapy has the highest sustained dry rate after treatment ceases
Desmopressin is the practical option for camps and sleepovers
Fluid restriction and lifting are not effective as sole measures
explanation.pearls: Continue an enuresis alarm for at least two weeks beyond fourteen consecutive dry nights before stopping, since ceasing at the first run of dry nights is the commonest cause of early relapse.

options.rationale: Anticholinergic therapy targets overactive bladder, whose distinguishing feature is daytime urgency and wetting, and this boy has no daytime symptoms at all (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

An alarm is the first line treatment for primary monosymptomatic enuresis in a motivated child of this age because it produces the highest sustained dry rate after treatment stops (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

Desmopressin works quickly and is valuable for short term cover such as a camp or a sleepover, but relapse on stopping is the rule so it is not the first choice for durable dryness (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis; Australian Medicines Handbook).
Treating occult constipation is the correct first move when there is loading or infrequent hard stools, but he passes a soft stool daily and has no palpable loading (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

Imaging and urology referral are for daytime symptoms, abnormal stream, recurrent infection or neurological signs, and a normal examination with clear urinalysis does not warrant them (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

explanation.summary: Positional head shape deformity became far more common after infants began sleeping on their backs, and it is benign and self correcting in the large majority. The single most useful bedside sign is the position of the ear on the flattened side, because gravity pushes the whole hemicranium forwards in a positional deformity while a fused suture tethers it backwards. Premature fusion also restricts growth across the affected suture, so head circumference often deviates from its centile and a bony ridge becomes palpable. Because congenital muscular torticollis both causes and is maintained by the positional preference, neck rotation must be assessed at the same visit.
key_points: Positional deformity gives a parallelogram vertex with the ear and forehead displaced forwards
Premature suture fusion gives a trapezoid vertex with the ear displaced backwards and a palpable ridge
Serial head circumference that stays on its centile argues against fusion
Always test neck rotation because torticollis maintains the positional preference
Helmets are reserved for severe deformity after repositioning has failed
explanation.pearls: Look at the vertex from directly above the infant rather than from the front, since the forward displacement of the ear that separates positional deformity from lambdoid fusion is visible only on that view.

options.rationale: Skull computed tomography carries a radiation dose and is reserved for cases where fusion is suspected clinically, which requires a palpable ridge or a head shape that does not fit a positional pattern (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly).

Craniofacial referral is for premature suture fusion, in which the ear on the flattened side is displaced backwards and the head shape is trapezoid rather than a parallelogram (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly).

Helmet therapy is an option only for severe deformity that has not responded to repositioning, and trial evidence shows no advantage over conservative measures for mild to moderate cases (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly).

A parallelogram head with the ear pushed forward on the flattened side, mobile sutures and a normal head circumference is positional, and it remodels with repositioning as the child begins to sit and roll independently (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly).
Physiotherapy is indicated when a shortened sternocleidomastoid restricts rotation and drives the positional preference, but rotation is full and symmetrical here (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly).

explanation.summary: A lithium disc battery lodged in the oesophagus generates hydroxide ions at its negative pole and produces liquefactive necrosis within two hours, long before the child becomes symptomatic. The radiographic signs that separate it from a coin are a double rim or halo on the frontal projection and a step off in profile on the lateral, so both views are mandatory whenever the history mentions a remote control, hearing aid, toy or greeting card. Because the mechanism is chemical rather than obstructive, a well child who is drinking normally provides no reassurance at all. The late complications, which can present days to weeks after removal, include tracheo oesophageal fistula, oesophageal stricture and fatal aorto oesophageal fistula.
key_points: Always obtain frontal and lateral films because the halo and step off signs need both
Injury begins within two hours, so a well child is not a reason to wait
Honey is given while awaiting removal in a child over 12 months who can swallow safely
Do not induce vomiting and do not give charcoal
Follow up matters because stricture and fistula present after removal
explanation.pearls: Give 10 mL of honey every 10 minutes up to six doses while transferring a child over 12 months to theatre, but withhold it entirely if there is drooling or suspected perforation.

options.rationale: The peripheral rim on the frontal film and the step off on the lateral identify a disc battery rather than a coin, which causes hydroxide mediated mucosal injury within two hours, so removal is immediate and honey buffers the alkali in the interval (Source: RCH CPG: Button Battery Ingestion).

Serial films to document passage is the approach for a coin lodged in the oesophagus of an asymptomatic child, but delay of even a few hours with a battery allows full thickness burn (Source: RCH CPG: Button Battery Ingestion).

Expectant management applies once a small blunt object has cleared the oesophagus into the stomach, and this object is still at the thoracic inlet where injury occurs fastest (Source: RCH CPG: Button Battery Ingestion).

Charcoal does not bind an intact battery and adds aspiration risk before an anaesthetic, and observation substitutes monitoring for the removal that the injury mechanism demands (Source: RCH CPG: Button Battery Ingestion).

Induced emesis is contraindicated for any ingested foreign body because it risks aspiration and drags the corrosive surface back across already injured mucosa (Source: RCH CPG: Button Battery Ingestion).

explanation.summary: Drowning injury is driven by the volume and duration of aspiration, and a child who never needed rescue breathing and who has normal respiratory effort and saturations has almost certainly aspirated a trivial volume. The terms secondary and dry drowning have been formally retired because the phenomenon they described, a well child collapsing many hours later, does not appear in prospective series. What does happen is that a child with persistent cough, crackles, hypoxia or altered conscious state at presentation progresses over the following hours, which is why the decision point is the clinical state at four to six hours rather than the story of the immersion. In Australia the majority of toddler drownings occur in domestic swimming pools with a fencing defect, so the safety conversation is a core part of the presentation.
key_points: Four to six hours of observation is sufficient for an asymptomatic child after immersion
Cough, crackles, hypoxia or drowsiness at any point during observation mandates admission
Chest radiography and blood tests are not indicated in the asymptomatic child
Prophylactic antibiotics and corticosteroids have no role
Toddler pool drowning in Australia is overwhelmingly associated with a fencing or gate failure
explanation.pearls: Any child who required rescue breaths at the poolside is admitted regardless of how well they look on arrival, since assisted ventilation at the scene is the single strongest predictor of subsequent respiratory deterioration.

options.rationale: A radiograph in an asymptomatic child yields findings that do not predict deterioration and generates admissions on radiological rather than clinical grounds (Source: RCH CPG: Drowning).

The idea of a symptom-free child deteriorating many hours afterwards is not supported by outcome data, and every child who worsened did so within the first hours after immersion (Source: RCH CPG: Drowning).

A child who is asymptomatic with normal saturations after four to six hours of observation may go home, and the encounter is the moment to act on the four sided isolation fencing that prevents the next event (Source: RCH CPG: Drowning; Royal Life Saving Australia).

Prophylactic antibiotics after immersion in clean water do not prevent pneumonia and select resistant organisms, and they are considered only for grossly contaminated water with established infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
Corticosteroid has no role in aspiration related lung injury and exposes the child to hyperglycaemia and immunosuppression without benefit (Source: RCH CPG: Drowning).

explanation.summary: Australian first aid for bites and stings splits sharply on whether the venom is rapidly life threatening. Snake, funnel web spider, blue ringed octopus and cone snail envenomation all receive pressure immobilisation bandaging to slow lymphatic spread, while red back spider, other spiders, jellyfish, bee and scorpion stings do not, because trapping the venom locally intensifies the pain without any survival benefit. Red back envenomation causes local sweating and piloerection at the site with pain that radiates centrally and can persist for days, but it is not associated with coagulopathy, myotoxicity or death in the modern era. Antivenom remains available and is considered for pain uncontrolled by opioid analgesia or for systemic features, though a randomised Australian trial found its benefit over placebo hard to demonstrate.
key_points: Pressure immobilisation is for snake, funnel web, blue ringed octopus and cone snail only
Local sweating and piloerection at the bite with radiating pain is the red back pattern
Ice and oral analgesia first, escalating to opioid before considering antivenom
No coagulation or muscle enzyme testing is required for this envenomation
Funnel web bites instead cause fasciculation, salivation and autonomic storm and are a true emergency
explanation.pearls: Localised sweating confined to the skin around the bite is close to specific for red back envenomation and is the finding that distinguishes it from the generalised sweating and fasciculation of a funnel web bite.

options.rationale: Pressure immobilisation is used for snake and funnel web bites where the venom is life threatening and systemic, but here it concentrates venom locally and markedly worsens the pain (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline 9.4.7).

Antivenom for this genus is considered only after simple measures fail because its benefit over placebo is contested, and it is given intravenously without high dependency care in an otherwise stable child (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

Cold and simple analgesia are the first measures for this bite, and reassessment determines whether opioid or antivenom is needed, since pressure immobilisation would make the pain worse (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline 9.4.7; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

Coagulopathy and rhabdomyolysis screening belongs to snakebite assessment, and this venom produces neither, so testing delays the analgesia that is the actual treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

Local infiltration does not relieve pain that is already radiating proximally through a systemic mechanism, and discharge before a period of reassessment misses progressive envenomation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the usual cause of obstructive sleep apnoea in otherwise healthy preschool children, and in that setting a convincing history with large tonsils justifies surgery without a sleep study. Trisomy 21 breaks that shortcut, because obstruction arises from midface and mandibular hypoplasia, relative macroglossia, pharyngeal hypotonia and central obesity as well as from lymphoid tissue. Around half of these children have significant residual disease after adenotonsillectomy, so the operation is planned against measured severity and a known site of obstruction rather than offered blind. Australian practice is to screen this group with polysomnography around four years of age regardless of parental report, because habitual snoring is under recognised and untreated disease causes pulmonary hypertension, neurocognitive impairment and behavioural difficulty.
key_points: Tonsil size that does not match symptom severity signals multilevel obstruction
Trisomy 21 carries a high rate of residual apnoea after adenotonsillectomy
Polysomnography quantifies severity and separates obstructive from central events
Overnight oximetry can confirm severe disease but a normal result does not exclude it
Untreated paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea causes pulmonary hypertension and neurocognitive harm
explanation.pearls: Australian sleep guidance recommends a polysomnogram for every child with trisomy 21 by about four years of age even when the parents report no snoring, because parental report has poor sensitivity in this group.

options.rationale: Intranasal steroid can help mild obstruction driven by adenoidal tissue, but witnessed apnoeas with daytime somnolence in a high risk child require characterisation rather than an empirical trial (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).

Small tonsils, midface hypoplasia, macroglossia and hypotonia mean the obstruction is multilevel rather than tonsillar, so severity and the site of obstruction must be measured before an operation that may not resolve it (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea; Australasian Sleep Association).

Proceeding on history alone is reasonable when large tonsils explain the obstruction, but residual disease after surgery is common in this syndrome and the tonsils here are grade 1 (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).

Positive airway pressure is a legitimate treatment in this group, but pressure titration and mask fitting depend on the sleep study that has not yet been done (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

Pulmonary hypertension is the feared consequence of untreated obstruction and warrants an echocardiogram in due course, but it grades the complication rather than establishing the diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).

explanation.summary: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and is repeatedly missed because roughly a quarter of children present with knee or distal thigh pain alone, referred along the obturator nerve. The diagnosis is protected by two habits: examining the hip in every child with knee pain, and ordering a frog lateral as well as an anteroposterior view, since early posterior displacement of the epiphysis may be invisible on the frontal film. Risk is concentrated in overweight peripubertal children, and endocrine causes such as hypothyroidism and growth hormone deficiency should be considered in a child who is young, thin or has bilateral slips. The clinical distinction that determines prognosis is stable versus unstable, defined by whether the child can weight bear, because avascular necrosis follows an unstable slip in a substantial minority.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee pain
Obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion is the most reliable bedside sign
Order anteroposterior and frog lateral pelvic views, not a knee series
Make the child non weight bearing as soon as the diagnosis is suspected
Consider endocrine screening in an atypically young, thin or bilateral case
explanation.pearls: Progression from a stable to an unstable slip raises the risk of avascular necrosis from under 5 per cent to nearly 50 per cent, which is why the child goes onto a trolley the moment the diagnosis is suspected rather than walking to radiology.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
BMJ Best Practice: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Knee imaging pursues the site of the pain rather than its source, and a full painless knee range with no effusion places the lesion at the hip (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Aspiration is for suspected joint sepsis, which presents over days with fever and raised inflammatory markers rather than six weeks of activity related ache with normal bloods (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Loading a hip in this state risks converting a stable slip into an unstable one, and the resulting avascular necrosis rate rises many fold (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion with restricted internal rotation is the classic sign, the displacement is often visible only on the lateral projection, and unloading the hip before surgery prevents progression to an unstable slip (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Bone scanning is used when plain films are normal and the site is genuinely unclear, whereas here the examination localises the hip and a two view radiograph will answer the question far faster (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

explanation.summary: Head lice treatment fails far more often from technique than from true resistance, and the commonest error is a single application, because no topical product reliably kills eggs and the survivors hatch six to seven days later. Australian guidance is therefore for two applications seven days apart with whichever agent is used, combined with regular wet conditioner combing to confirm cure. Physically acting agents such as dimeticone smother the louse rather than poisoning it, so resistance to pyrethrins and other neurotoxic insecticides does not apply. Distinguishing live eggs near the scalp from empty cases further out avoids retreating a child who has already been cured.
key_points: Any topical agent needs two applications seven days apart to catch newly hatched lice
Empty egg cases more than 1 cm from the scalp are old and do not indicate active infestation
Dimeticone acts physically so insecticide resistance does not apply to it
Treat other household members only if live lice are found on them
Australian school policy does not exclude children with head lice once treatment has begun
explanation.pearls: Hair grows about 1 cm a month, so an egg found more than 1 cm from the scalp was laid over a month ago and is almost always an empty case rather than evidence of treatment failure.

options.rationale: Oral ivermectin is held in reserve for infestation that has failed correctly applied topical treatment, and treatment here has never included the repeat application (Source: RCH CPG: Head Lice; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Environmental decontamination adds nothing because lice die within a day off the scalp, and repeating an agent that has already failed three times ignores the likely resistance (Source: RCH CPG: Head Lice).

Empty cases along the shaft are indeed the residue of past infestation, but full brown eggs within a centimetre of the scalp plus live adults confirm ongoing active infestation (Source: RCH CPG: Head Lice).

Systemic antibacterial therapy treats secondary bacterial infection of an excoriated scalp, and the skin here is intact with no pustules or lymphadenopathy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Repeated failure of a neurotoxic insecticide points to resistance, and a physically acting dimeticone applied twice a week apart covers the eggs that hatch after the first application (Source: RCH CPG: Head Lice; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: A squint matters because the developing brain suppresses the image from the deviating eye, and that suppression becomes irreversible as the visual cortex matures through early childhood. Intermittent deviation in the first three to four months of life is common and often resolves, but any squint that is constant, that appears after six months of age, or that is progressing needs specialist assessment rather than observation. The two findings that turn a routine referral into an urgent one are an abnormal or absent red reflex, which raises retinoblastoma or cataract, and a restricted eye movement with other neurological signs. Much paediatric convergent squint is driven by uncorrected long sightedness, so cycloplegic refraction comes before any decision about patching or surgery.
key_points: Any constant squint, or any squint after six months of age, warrants specialist referral
The cover test demonstrates the deviation by showing refixation of the uncovered eye
An abnormal red reflex makes the referral immediate rather than routine
Cycloplegic refraction precedes patching because glasses alone correct some deviations
Amblyopia treatment is far more effective the earlier in childhood it starts
explanation.pearls: The corneal light reflex sits lateral to the pupil centre in a convergent squint and medial to it in a divergent one, which lets you identify the direction of deviation in a child too young to cooperate with cover testing.

options.rationale: Neuroimaging is driven by a restricted eye movement, papilloedema, an abnormal red reflex or other neurological signs, none of which is present here (Source: RCH CPG: Squint).

A constant squint at any age needs assessment because the deviating eye is being suppressed, and treatment of the resulting amblyopia works far better before visual maturity is complete (Source: RCH CPG: Squint).

Intermittent deviation in the first few months of life may resolve, but a constant squint that has progressed over six months in a 3-year-old will not and waiting costs treatable vision (Source: RCH CPG: Squint).
Occlusion therapy is part of amblyopia treatment but it follows cycloplegic refraction, since correcting a hypermetropic error alone resolves a proportion of these squints (Source: RCH CPG: Squint).
Refraction is essential but a child with a constant squint needs the orthoptic and ophthalmological assessment that also grades and treats amblyopia (Source: RCH CPG: Squint).

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis presents in the first weeks as a fixed preference to look one way, with the head tilted towards the affected muscle and the chin rotated away from it, and often with a firm fibrous swelling within the sternocleidomastoid belly. The reason it cannot simply be referred to physiotherapy in isolation is that it shares its risk factors with developmental dysplasia of the hip, namely breech position, first pregnancy and intrauterine crowding, and hip dysplasia is present in a clinically important minority of these infants. Australian practice is therefore to arrange a hip ultrasound at the same time as the physiotherapy referral, using ultrasound rather than radiography because the femoral head is still cartilaginous before about four to six months. Stretching started in the first months resolves the great majority, while delay leads to fixed contracture, facial asymmetry and occasionally surgical release.
key_points: The head tilts towards the tight muscle and the chin rotates away from it
Breech presentation and first pregnancy are shared risk factors with hip dysplasia
Arrange hip ultrasound rather than radiography before about four to six months of age
Early stretching resolves most cases and avoids later facial asymmetry
Painful, late onset or neurologically abnormal torticollis needs imaging instead
explanation.pearls: Any infant diagnosed with congenital muscular torticollis should have a hip ultrasound, because dysplasia is found in roughly one in five and the hip examination alone misses a dysplastic but reduced hip.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Aspiration is for a mass that is growing, cystic, inflamed or associated with systemic features, whereas a static firm swelling within the muscle belly with a matching postural deformity does not need sampling (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis).

Physiotherapy is the correct treatment but a three month interval is too long at this age, and referring without the hip assessment leaves the associated condition unlooked for (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis).
Spinal imaging is indicated when the tilt is painful, of later onset, associated with neurological signs, or has no palpable muscle abnormality (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis).

The muscle swelling with restricted contralateral rotation is congenital muscular torticollis, and the same intrauterine crowding raises hip dysplasia risk enough that ultrasound screening is indicated alongside stretching (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis; RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Untreated restriction produces facial asymmetry and persistent head tilt, and outcomes from stretching are best when it begins in the first three months (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis).

explanation.summary: Chronic cough in children is defined as a daily cough lasting more than four weeks, and the first branch point is whether it is wet or dry, because that single feature reorganises the differential. A wet cough in a child who is otherwise well and growing normally is most often protracted bacterial bronchitis, caused by a biofilm of Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae or Moraxella catarrhalis in the large airways. It is treated with two weeks of amoxicillin clavulanate, extended to four weeks if the response is partial, and it is important to recognise because untreated recurrent episodes progress to bronchiectasis. Persistent failure after two courses, or the presence of clubbing, faltering growth or radiographic change, moves the child towards bronchoscopy and investigation for cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia or immunodeficiency.
key_points: Chronic cough in children means daily cough for more than four weeks
A wet cough without wheeze is not asthma and does not respond to preventer escalation
Protracted bacterial bronchitis is treated with two weeks of amoxicillin clavulanate
Failure of two antibiotic courses is the trigger for bronchoscopy and further workup
Untreated recurrent protracted bacterial bronchitis can progress to bronchiectasis
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent whether the cough sounds wet or dry rather than whether the child brings up sputum, since preschool children swallow secretions and the parental description of a rattly cough is the practical substitute for observed sputum.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.rationale: A daily wet cough for more than four weeks with no pointers to another diagnosis is treated as protracted bacterial bronchitis, and a two week course of a beta lactam with beta lactamase cover resolves the majority (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.rationale: Further preventer escalation in a child who has never wheezed and has not responded to two dose steps repeats a failed trial and exposes her to growth and behavioural effects (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is reserved for cough that fails two antibiotic courses or that suggests an inhaled foreign body or airway malacia, and no antibiotic trial has yet been given (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.rationale: Acid suppression for cough without other reflux features does not outperform placebo in children and delays a treatment that would work (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.rationale: Suppurative lung disease is pursued when there is faltering growth, clubbing, abnormal stools or a persistent radiographic abnormality, none of which is present in this well grown child (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

explanation.summary: Breath holding spells affect up to 5 per cent of young children and are reflex events, not epilepsy, in which a provoking cry or fright is followed by apnoea in expiration, colour change, loss of tone and then loss of consciousness. Brief stiffening or a few clonic jerks follow in a substantial minority because of cerebral hypoperfusion, and these anoxic jerks are the reason the events are so often misdiagnosed as seizures. Iron deficiency is over represented in affected children and correcting it reduces spell frequency, which makes a full blood count and ferritin worthwhile even in a child who looks well. The one mimic that must not be missed is a channelopathy such as long QT syndrome, so a resting electrocardiogram is recommended, and any episode occurring without a provoking cry or during exertion should push the assessment towards a cardiac cause.
key_points: A provoking cry followed by apnoea, colour change and collapse is the defining sequence
Anoxic jerks after loss of consciousness do not make the event epileptic
Check full blood count and ferritin because iron deficiency increases spell frequency
Record an electrocardiogram to exclude a prolonged QT interval
Unprovoked or exertional events shift the differential towards a cardiac arrhythmia
explanation.pearls: Correcting iron deficiency with three to six months of oral iron reduces breath holding spell frequency substantially, so treat to a normal ferritin rather than stopping once the haemoglobin has recovered.

options.rationale: Both actions are correct but this pairing omits the explanation and safety advice to the parents, which is the intervention that most reduces presentations and distress (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells).

Anoxic jerks following a provoked cyanotic episode are secondary to cerebral hypoperfusion rather than epileptic, so antiepileptic therapy treats the wrong mechanism (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells).

Structural cardiac assessment is warranted when episodes occur without a preceding cry or during exercise, and here every episode has followed hard crying with a normal cardiovascular examination (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells).

The episodes are stereotyped breath holding spells, iron treatment reduces their frequency, and a single electrocardiogram excludes a long QT interval that can mimic them (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells).

Reassurance is central but the microcytic anaemia is a treatable driver of the spells and a prolonged QT interval is the one dangerous mimic that must be excluded (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells).

explanation.summary: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction affects up to one in five infants and reflects a persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner. The clinical task is not to make that diagnosis but to exclude the two conditions that share the symptom and threaten sight or systemic health: infantile glaucoma and true conjunctivitis. Glaucoma is signalled by photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal haze and an enlarged cornea, and it needs same week ophthalmology assessment. Once those are excluded, massage and observation are enough, with referral reserved for persistence past the first birthday or an episode of dacryocystitis.
key_points: Measure and compare corneal diameters in any infant with a persistently watering eye
Photophobia and blepharospasm push towards glaucoma, not duct obstruction
Mucoid reflux from the lacrimal sac on digital pressure supports duct obstruction
About 90 per cent of duct obstructions resolve without intervention by twelve months
Probing is the intervention after twelve months, not in early infancy
explanation.pearls: An infant corneal diameter above 12 mm, or one more than 0.5 mm larger than the fellow eye, converts a watering eye into a same week ophthalmology referral for suspected infantile glaucoma.

options.rationale: Urgent examination under anaesthesia is for suspected infantile glaucoma, which presents with photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal clouding and a corneal diameter larger than the other side, none of which are present here (Source: RCH CPG: The Watering Eye).

A white eye with clear cornea, symmetrical red reflexes and mucoid reflux from the sac is uncomplicated congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, and around nine in ten resolve spontaneously in the first year, so massage plus lid hygiene and review at twelve months is the plan (Source: RCH CPG: The Watering Eye).

Topical antibiotic is reserved for a genuinely infected eye with a red conjunctiva and purulent discharge, and crusting alone with a white eye is stagnant tear film rather than conjunctivitis (Source: RCH CPG: The Watering Eye; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis presents at five to fourteen days of life with a red swollen eye and copious discharge, and it is distinguished from duct obstruction by conjunctival injection and age at onset (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Probing is offered when obstruction persists beyond twelve months or when there is recurrent dacryocystitis, and doing it at four months exposes an infant to anaesthesia for a problem that usually settles itself (Source: RCH CPG: The Watering Eye).

explanation.summary: A moist lump appearing in the umbilical pit after cord separation is usually granulation tissue that failed to epithelialise. The two things worth excluding at the bedside cost nothing: periumbilical erythema pointing to omphalitis, and discharge of urine or bowel content pointing to a persistent embryological duct. Australian units now favour topical common salt over silver nitrate because it is as effective, is free, and does not burn the periumbilical skin. Persistence after a course of salt, or a lesion that is deep red and firm rather than soft and pink, is what earns a surgical opinion.
key_points: Ask specifically whether urine or bowel content ever leaks from the umbilicus
Periumbilical erythema or induration converts this into omphalitis needing intravenous antibiotics
Topical salt for two to three days is the Australian first line treatment
Silver nitrate risks chemical burns and is no longer preferred in infants
Refer for surgical review only after failed salt treatment or if a duct remnant is suspected
explanation.pearls: A pinch of table salt held on the lesion for 10 to 30 minutes twice daily for three days flattens most umbilical granulomas, and failure after two such courses is the trigger for surgical referral rather than a repeat course.

options.rationale: Silver nitrate does shrink the lesion, but it causes chemical burns to the surrounding skin in infants and Australian paediatric practice has moved away from it as first line (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical Granuloma).
Imaging is driven by discharge of urine or bowel content from the umbilicus, and its absence here makes a patent duct very unlikely (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical Granuloma).
Intravenous cover is for omphalitis, whose defining feature is periumbilical erythema, induration or systemic upset, and none of those are present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Topical common salt applied for two to three days is the recommended first line treatment in Australian paediatric practice, is done by the parents at home, and avoids the burn risk of chemical cautery (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical Granuloma).

Surgical referral belongs to the bright red firm lesion that persists after salt treatment or discharges enteric or urinary content, which is a vitellointestinal or urachal remnant rather than granulation tissue (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical Granuloma).

explanation.summary: Labial adhesion is an acquired midline fusion driven by the physiologically low oestrogen state of childhood, and it peaks between one and five years. The decision to treat is symptom driven rather than appearance driven, so the history that matters is the urinary stream, post-void dribbling, recurrent infection and local soreness. Most cases separate spontaneously as endogenous oestrogen rises, and parents are much more reassured by being shown the small anterior opening than by a prescription. When treatment is genuinely indicated, topical oestrogen for a short defined course is the first step, with surgical separation kept for failure.
key_points: Confirm a normal urinary stream and absence of post-void dribbling before deciding on treatment
Asymptomatic adhesions need reassurance and follow up rather than any active treatment
Topical oestrogen is for obstruction, recurrent infection or persistent soreness
Manual or surgical separation is followed by recurrence with denser scarring
Adhesions alone are not evidence of sexual abuse
explanation.pearls: Adhesions almost always resolve once endogenous oestrogen rises at puberty, so an asymptomatic 3-year-old needs a review appointment rather than oestrogen cream, which itself causes local irritation and breast budding in about one child in five.

options.rationale: Adhesions that allow a normal urinary stream and cause no symptoms need no treatment, because they are driven by low oestrogen and separate spontaneously as puberty approaches (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions).

Topical oestrogen is reserved for symptomatic adhesions such as urinary obstruction, post-void dribbling or recurrent infection, and it commonly causes local irritation and breast budding when used without an indication (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions).
Forcible separation is painful, distressing and followed by a high rate of recurrence with denser scar tissue than the original adhesion (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions).

Labial adhesion is a common finding in this age group and is not in itself a sign of abuse, and referral here is triggered by bruising, tears, disclosure or behavioural change, none of which are present (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

Surgical separation is the last step for dense adhesions causing urinary retention or recurrent infection that have failed topical oestrogen, not a first move in an asymptomatic child (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions).

explanation.summary: A toddler who will not weight bear needs the septic joint and osteomyelitis pathway considered first, and here the afebrile state, full painless hip range and normal inflammatory markers close that branch. What remains is an occult undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibial shaft, which frequently does not appear on the first radiograph and only becomes visible when periosteal new bone forms at one to two weeks. Treating the clinical picture rather than the film prevents a fortnight of pain and repeated presentations. These fractures are low energy, heal reliably, and do not require operative fixation.
key_points: Normal C-reactive protein with full painless hip movement makes septic arthritis very unlikely
A normal initial radiograph does not exclude an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture
Focal tenderness over the tibial shaft plus a twisting mechanism is enough to treat
Immobilisation with clinic review beats repeat imaging in the first week
Periosteal reaction confirming the fracture appears at about 10 to 14 days
explanation.pearls: Up to half of toddler fractures are radiographically occult on presentation, so a child who localises pain to the tibia after a twisting fall is immobilised on the clinical picture and the confirmatory periosteal reaction is looked for at 10 to 14 days.

options.rationale: Aspiration follows a septic joint picture of fever, raised inflammatory markers and a hip held still in flexion and external rotation, and full painless hip range with a normal C-reactive protein argues against it (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp).

Analgesia alone leaves an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture unprotected, and the child keeps loading a painful limb for the two weeks it takes periosteal reaction to appear (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler Fracture).

Empirical antibiotics treat osteomyelitis, which would show fever, night pain and a raised C-reactive protein rather than an afebrile child with normal markers and a clear mechanism of injury (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Magnetic resonance imaging usually needs sedation at this age and adds nothing when the history, focal tibial tenderness and normal markers already define the management (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler Fracture).

An undisplaced spiral tibial fracture in this age group is invisible on the initial film in a large proportion of cases, so a child with a twisting mechanism and focal tibial tenderness is immobilised and reviewed rather than cleared by the radiograph (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler Fracture).

explanation.summary: Most non retractile foreskins in boys are physiological, reflecting incomplete separation of preputial adhesions that completes during the first decade or into adolescence. The distinction that matters is the appearance of the ring: soft, pink and pouting is physiological, while firm, pale and fibrotic is scar. Scarring with obstructed voiding, recurrent soreness or recurrent infection is the pathological form, and it is the setting in which circumcision is genuinely indicated rather than elective. Steroid and stretching should not be used to delay definitive treatment once the ring is fibrotic, because the outcome is repeated splitting and denser scar.
key_points: Physiological non retraction needs no treatment and no examination under anaesthesia
Ballooning alone in a soft unscarred foreskin is not an indication for surgery
A firm pale non stretching ring signals scarring rather than adhesion
Topical corticosteroid is for the soft ring, not the fibrotic one
Scarring with obstructed voiding is an accepted indication for circumcision
explanation.pearls: Topical betamethasone 0.05 per cent twice daily for four to six weeks resolves the majority of soft physiological phimoses, but a pale fibrotic ring predicts steroid failure and should be sent for surgical opinion at the first visit.

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is right for physiological non retraction, in which the preputial skin is soft and pink and there are no urinary symptoms, and it does not apply once there is scarring with an obstructed stream (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care).

Topical corticosteroid with gentle stretching works well for a soft physiological ring, but a fibrotic pale scar does not soften with steroid and the delay prolongs obstructed voiding (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care).

A firm pale scarred preputial ring with ballooning, spraying and recurrent soreness is pathological rather than physiological phimosis, and it is one of the few absolute indications for circumcision in childhood (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care; RACP Circumcision Statement).

Oral antibiotic treats balanoposthitis, whose distinguishing feature is a red swollen tender foreskin with purulent discharge rather than a pale avascular fibrotic ring (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
Retraction exercises are appropriate for the soft unscarred foreskin, and forcing a scarred ring risks splitting it and creating further cicatricial scarring (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care).

explanation.summary: Ingested foreign bodies are triaged by what the object is, where it sits and whether the child has symptoms, and the number of objects is decisive when they are magnetic. A single blunt object in the stomach can be managed expectantly, whereas two or more magnets, or one magnet with another metallic object, can trap bowel wall between them and cause necrosis within hours. Button batteries lodged in the oesophagus form the other emergency, needing removal within two hours because of alkaline mucosal injury. The apposed pair with a lucent gap between them on the film is the radiographic signature that should trigger the call to the endoscopist.
key_points: One blunt object in the stomach of a well child can be managed expectantly
Two or more magnets are an emergency regardless of symptoms
Objects in the stomach are removed endoscopically, beyond the duodenum surgically
A lucent gap between apposed radio-opaque objects suggests interposed tissue
An oesophageal button battery needs removal within two hours
explanation.pearls: Two magnets anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract mandate removal on the day of presentation, and if they have already passed the ligament of Treitz the decision moves from endoscopy to surgical review rather than to observation.

options.rationale: Watchful waiting with stool checking is the pathway for a single blunt object such as a coin in the stomach of a well child, and it is unsafe once more than one magnetic object is present (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

Accelerating transit does not separate objects that are already held together across tissue, and the delay allows pressure necrosis of the bowel wall to progress (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

Two or more magnets attract across loops of bowel and cause pressure necrosis, fistula and perforation, so while they remain within endoscopic reach in the stomach they are removed urgently even though the child is well (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

Observation wastes the window in which the objects are still retrievable from above, and clinical signs of bowel injury appear only after necrosis is established (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

Open surgery is the answer once the objects have passed the duodenum and cannot be reached endoscopically, or when there are peritoneal signs, and neither applies while they sit in the stomach (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

explanation.summary: Australian community and youth sport guidance deliberately separates the child and adolescent pathway from the professional pathway, because young athletes recover more slowly and repeat injury during the vulnerable window carries disproportionate risk. Return to learn comes before return to sport, and the graded exercise progression only starts once symptoms have settled. Even a straightforward recovery cannot compress the minimum calendar interval to competitive contact play. Any return of symptoms at a stage means dropping back to the previous stage rather than pushing through.
key_points: Return to learn precedes return to sport in school-aged athletes
Symptom resolution alone does not authorise a return to contact
The Australian youth floor is 21 days from injury before competitive contact sport
At least 14 symptom-free days are required before contact training
Neuroimaging has no role in return to play decisions
explanation.pearls: A community athlete under 19 cannot return to competitive contact sport sooner than 21 days after concussion in Australia, even with complete symptom resolution by day five, and non contact aerobic conditioning is what fills the interval.

sources.label: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.rationale: Clearing him at day eight applies the adult community pathway, and the paediatric pathway is deliberately slower because of the longer physiological recovery in the developing brain (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.rationale: Imaging answers the question of structural injury in the acute phase and has no role in return to play decisions in a boy who is now asymptomatic with a normal examination (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.rationale: Tolerating the graded exercise stages is necessary but not sufficient in this age group, because a minimum calendar interval also applies before contact is resumed (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.rationale: The Australian youth pathway sets a floor of 21 days from injury before competitive contact or collision sport, with at least 14 symptom-free days first, and non contact conditioning continues in the meantime (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.rationale: Formal neuropsychological assessment is reserved for persisting symptoms beyond four weeks or repeated concussions, and it does not shorten the minimum interval in an uncomplicated first concussion (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

explanation.summary: A normal newborn hip examination does not exclude dysplasia, because the acetabulum can become progressively dysplastic over the first months and breech presentation remains the strongest single risk factor. The physical signs shift with age: instability signs such as Ortolani and Barlow fade after about three months, and asymmetric abduction with a positive Galeazzi sign takes over. Imaging must follow the same clock, with ultrasound early and plain radiography once the ossific nucleus appears. Late diagnosis matters because harness treatment fails beyond six months and the child then faces closed or open reduction with a spica cast.
key_points: Breech presentation at term is the strongest risk factor even with a normal newborn examination
Ortolani and Barlow signs become unreliable after about three months
Limited abduction and a positive Galeazzi sign are the older infant signs
Ultrasound is the test under four months, plain radiography from about four to six months
Pavlik harness success falls away after six months of age
explanation.pearls: Hip ultrasound loses accuracy once the femoral ossific nucleus appears at around four to six months, so a 6-month-old with asymmetric abduction is imaged with an anteroposterior pelvis radiograph rather than repeat ultrasound.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: DDH

options.rationale: Ultrasound is the modality of choice under about four months, but from four to six months the ossifying femoral head casts an acoustic shadow over the acetabulum and makes measurements unreliable (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Once the femoral head ossifies at around four to six months the plain anteroposterior pelvis film becomes the reliable test, and limited abduction with a positive Galeazzi sign warrants orthopaedic assessment alongside it (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Harness treatment is applied after imaging confirms the diagnosis and its success falls sharply beyond six months of age, so it is not started blind at this visit (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Limited abduction is the most reliable sign of dysplasia after the newborn period, and deferring to twelve months risks presentation with an established dislocation and a limp (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is used to assess reduction after closed or open reduction, not to make the initial diagnosis, and it requires sedation for no additional information here (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

explanation.summary: The nocturnal event history is discriminating if the right five questions are asked: how many per night, when in the night, how long, how similar to each other, and how the child behaves immediately afterwards. Parasomnias are infrequent, arise from slow wave sleep in the first third of the night, last minutes, vary between episodes and end in confusion with amnesia. Sleep related hypermotor seizures are brief, numerous, identical, distributed across the whole night and followed by preserved awareness. Daytime irritability from fragmented sleep is common to both and does not discriminate. Home phone video has become one of the most valuable pieces of evidence in this assessment.
key_points: Count the events per night and note their distribution across the night
Stereotypy between events is the single most useful feature for seizure
Immediate return of awareness after an event argues against a parasomnia
Parasomnias arise from slow wave sleep in the first third of the night
Home video should be actively requested and reviewed
explanation.pearls: More than two identical events in a single night, each under a minute and spread across the whole night, moves a child from the parasomnia pathway to a sleep deprived electroencephalogram rather than to reassurance.

options.rationale: Reassurance suits a parasomnia, which occurs once or twice a night in the first third of sleep, varies between episodes and leaves the child confused rather than immediately alert (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep Problems).
Melatonin addresses delayed sleep onset rather than events arising out of established sleep, and it would delay recognition of an epilepsy syndrome (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep Problems).

Obstructive sleep apnoea causes snoring, witnessed pauses and restless sleep with daytime tiredness, but not brief identical motor events with preserved awareness afterwards (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).
Polysomnography maps sleep architecture and respiratory events, and while video is useful it is not the test that identifies interictal epileptiform discharges (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).

High frequency, brief, stereotyped hypermotor events occurring throughout the night with rapid recovery of awareness point to a sleep related epilepsy, and the sleep deprived recording is the investigation that captures the discharges (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets remains common in Australian children with darker skin, limited sun exposure, prolonged unsupplemented breastfeeding and a monotonous diet. The biochemistry separates the causes efficiently: a low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with secondary hyperparathyroidism is nutritional, whereas a low phosphate with normal vitamin D and normal parathyroid hormone suggests renal phosphate wasting. Alkaline phosphatase is the most sensitive marker of active disease and is what falls first with successful treatment. The maternal vitamin D status should be checked at the same time, because the mother of an affected breastfed child is usually deficient herself.
key_points: Raised alkaline phosphatase with a raised parathyroid hormone signals active nutritional rickets
Give calcium with vitamin D when dietary calcium intake is poor
Cow milk in Australia is not fortified with vitamin D
Milk volumes above about 500 mL daily displace iron rich solids
Screen and treat the mother of an affected breastfed infant
explanation.pearls: Alkaline phosphatase falls before the radiographic changes resolve, so a repeat level at four weeks is the earliest objective sign that colecalciferol and calcium replacement is working.

options.rationale: A low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with a raised parathyroid hormone identifies nutritional deficiency, and a child on high milk intake with poor solid variety still needs calcium alongside replacement to avoid the hypocalcaemia that follows bone healing (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).

Replacing vitamin D without calcium in a child with a poor dietary calcium intake risks symptomatic hypocalcaemia as remineralising bone takes up circulating calcium (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).

Inherited phosphate wasting gives a low phosphate with a normal 25 hydroxyvitamin D and a normal or only mildly raised parathyroid hormone, so the markedly raised parathyroid hormone and deficient vitamin D here point elsewhere (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).

The bowing is a consequence of soft undermineralised bone and straightens with medical treatment, so bracing addresses the deformity while leaving the cause untreated (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).
Cow milk is not fortified with vitamin D in Australia, and volumes at this level displace iron rich solids and cause iron deficiency anaemia (Source: NHMRC Infant Feeding Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Hip pathology in children and adolescents refers pain to the distal thigh and knee through the obturator nerve, and a substantial proportion of slipped capital femoral epiphysis presents with knee pain alone. The examination that redirects the diagnosis costs seconds: compare internal rotation of both hips with the patient supine and watch for obligatory external rotation as the hip is flexed. Delay converts a stable slip, in which the child can still weight bear, into an unstable slip with a markedly higher risk of avascular necrosis. Treatment is in situ screw fixation, and the contralateral hip is assessed at the same time because bilateral disease is common.
key_points: Examine the hips in every child or adolescent presenting with knee pain
Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is the most specific bedside sign
Frog leg lateral views are required because early slips hide on the anteroposterior film
Keep the child non weight bearing once the diagnosis is suspected
Endocrine screening is considered in slips outside the usual age or weight range
explanation.pearls: Around one in five adolescents with a slipped capital femoral epiphysis presents with isolated knee or thigh pain, so a knee examination that is entirely normal should send the film request to the pelvis rather than the knee.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Knee imaging follows a knee examination that is actually abnormal, and a full painless knee with restricted hip rotation makes the knee the referral site rather than the source (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Conservative management fits patellofemoral pain, which reproduces symptoms on patellar compression and squatting rather than restricting hip internal rotation (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Films of the wrong joint are the usual reason for delayed diagnosis in this presentation, and the delay allows a stable slip to become unstable (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion with loss of internal rotation in a heavy adolescent is the classical hip sign, and both anteroposterior and frog leg lateral views are needed because early slips are visible only on the lateral (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.rationale: Inflammatory markers and ultrasound target septic arthritis or an effusion, and three weeks of activity related pain in an afebrile boy with a dry knee does not fit that pattern (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp).

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas appear in the first weeks of life, proliferate rapidly until about five months, then involute slowly over years, and the great majority need no treatment at all. Treatment is reserved for lesions that threaten function, ulcerate, or will leave significant disfigurement, and the periocular site is the classic functional threat because occlusion of the visual axis for even a few weeks in infancy produces deprivation amblyopia. Astigmatism from pressure on the globe is a second mechanism of visual loss that persists even after the lesion shrinks, so ophthalmology follow up continues after treatment. Oral propranolol has replaced systemic corticosteroids and typically produces visible softening and colour change within days, with a pretreatment assessment for heart rate, blood pressure and any history suggesting airway or cardiac disease.
key_points: Proliferation peaks by about five months, before spontaneous involution begins
Periocular lesions cause deprivation amblyopia and astigmatism
Oral propranolol is first line for function threatening lesions
Topical timolol is limited to small superficial lesions
Five or more cutaneous haemangiomas prompts liver ultrasound
explanation.pearls: Five or more cutaneous infantile haemangiomas warrants abdominal ultrasound for hepatic haemangiomas, which can cause high output cardiac failure and consumptive hypothyroidism even when the skin lesions themselves are trivial.

options.rationale: A lesion obstructing the visual axis is a high risk infantile haemangioma that causes deprivation amblyopia within weeks, so it needs urgent specialist assessment and systemic propranolol after a cardiovascular check (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

Watchful waiting is correct for most infantile haemangiomas because they involute, but involution begins around 12 months and by then irreversible amblyopia will have developed (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).
Topical beta blocker is effective for small superficial lesions of a few millimetres, and it penetrates too poorly to control a 25 mm periocular lesion (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

Pulsed dye laser is used for residual telangiectasia after involution or for ulcerated lesions, and it does not control the deep proliferative component causing the obstruction (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

Imaging is reserved for segmental facial lesions raising the possibility of an associated syndrome or for suspected deep orbital extension, and arranging it first would delay sight saving treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

explanation.summary: Precocious puberty means secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years of age in girls and 9 years in boys, and the first branch point is whether the cause is central, meaning early activation of the hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis, or peripheral, meaning autonomous sex steroid production. A stimulated luteinising hormone response separates them, since central causes give a pubertal rise while peripheral causes suppress gonadotrophins through negative feedback. Central precocious puberty is idiopathic in the majority of girls but the proportion with an intracranial lesion rises sharply as the age at onset falls, which is why imaging is mandatory under 6 years and considered between 6 and 8 years. In boys the calculus is reversed, with a much higher rate of underlying pathology at any age, so imaging is arranged for all of them. Treatment with a gonadotrophin releasing hormone analogue aims to preserve adult height and to allow psychosocial development to match chronological age.
key_points: A pubertal luteinising hormone response to stimulation indicates a central cause
Peripheral causes suppress gonadotrophins through negative feedback
Brain imaging is mandatory for central precocious puberty in girls under 6 years
All boys with central precocious puberty need brain imaging
Bone age advance and an oestrogenised uterus separate this from premature thelarche
explanation.pearls: A hypothalamic hamartoma is the commonest intracranial cause of central precocious puberty and may be signalled by gelastic seizures, which parents describe as unexplained bursts of laughing rather than as seizures, so ask about them directly.

options.rationale: The pelvic ultrasound has already been done and repeating a bone age adds nothing when the diagnosis is biochemically established and the priority is to find the cause (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

A pubertal luteinising hormone response to stimulation confirms a central cause, and every girl under 6 years with central precocious puberty needs brain imaging because the likelihood of an intracranial lesion is highest in this age group (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

Adrenal investigation is for virilisation with a suppressed luteinising hormone response, and a peripheral cause suppresses gonadotrophins while a central cause raises them (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

Treatment to halt puberty and preserve adult height is appropriate but is not an investigation, and starting it without imaging risks missing a hypothalamic lesion (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

Isolated premature thelarche without growth acceleration or bone age advance can be observed, and this girl has both a markedly advanced bone age and an oestrogenised uterus (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

explanation.summary: Measles mumps rubella vaccine is grown in chick embryo fibroblast culture rather than in egg and contains no measurable ovalbumin, so egg allergy has never been a contraindication to it. Influenza vaccines are egg grown but modern manufacturing leaves ovalbumin content below 1 microgram per dose, a quantity well below any threshold for reaction, and large studies of children with egg anaphylaxis have shown no excess of reactions. Australian guidance is therefore that children with egg allergy of any severity, including anaphylaxis, receive both vaccines in the usual community setting with the standard 15 minute observation. The vaccine components that genuinely do warrant specialist assessment are gelatin and neomycin, and a previous anaphylactic reaction to a vaccine itself. Unnecessary referral is not neutral, because it delays immunisation and reinforces a family belief that vaccines are dangerous for their child.
key_points: Measles mumps rubella vaccine is not grown in egg and contains no ovalbumin
Influenza vaccines contain less than 1 microgram of ovalbumin per dose
Egg allergy of any severity is not a contraindication to either vaccine
Gelatin and neomycin allergy are the components that warrant specialist input
Unnecessary referral delays immunisation and reinforces vaccine anxiety
explanation.pearls: The one egg containing vaccine that still requires specialist assessment in Australia is yellow fever vaccine, which contains substantially more residual egg protein than influenza vaccine and is given under supervision in a designated travel clinic.

options.rationale: Hospital vaccination is reserved for a previous anaphylaxis to a vaccine or to a vaccine component such as gelatin, not for food allergy to egg (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook; ASCIA).

Modern influenza vaccines contain ovalbumin below 1 microgram per dose and are given routinely to children with egg anaphylaxis, so omitting it withholds protection without reason (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

Egg allergy of any severity is not a contraindication to measles mumps rubella or influenza vaccine, both of which are given in general practice with the routine 15 minute observation period (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook; ASCIA).
Skin testing with vaccines has poor predictive value and is not recommended before routine immunisation of a child with food allergy (Source: ASCIA).
Graded dosing is a specialist protocol used after a genuine vaccine reaction and has no role when the allergy is to a food rather than to a vaccine component (Source: ASCIA).

explanation.summary: The term brief resolved unexplained event replaced apparent life threatening event because the older label implied a danger that the evidence does not support, and it applies only when an infant under one year has a sudden brief episode of altered colour, tone, breathing or responsiveness that has fully resolved and has no explanation after history and examination. The value of the definition is that it creates an explicitly low risk group in whom extensive investigation and admission cause more harm than benefit. The criteria are age over 60 days, gestational age of 32 weeks or more with a corrected age of at least 45 weeks, a first event lasting less than one minute, no cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider, and a reassuring history and physical examination.
