Any infant failing a criterion is higher risk and needs individualised assessment, and the history should always include a careful and non accusatory consideration of inflicted injury, which is why a full skin inspection for bruising is part of the examination.
key_points: The event must have fully resolved and remain unexplained after history and examination
Low risk requires age over 60 days and a single event under one minute
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider excludes the low risk group
Extensive investigation in low risk infants causes net harm
Always inspect the skin for bruising and consider inflicted injury
explanation.pearls: An electrocardiogram is the one investigation reasonable to consider even in a low risk infant, because a long QT syndrome is otherwise undetectable on examination and is a treatable cause of sudden death.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event
American Academy of Pediatrics Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Prolonged monitoring does not improve outcomes in an infant meeting every low risk criterion and generates false alarms that lead to further unnecessary testing (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.rationale: Neurological investigation is indicated when the history describes focal features or when the examination is abnormal, and it has a very low yield after a single brief event with a normal examination (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.rationale: A septic screen is driven by fever or an unwell appearance, and this afebrile well appearing infant with a normal examination does not meet the threshold (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.rationale: He meets every low risk criterion of age over 60 days, born at 32 weeks or later, a single event lasting under one minute, no cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider and a reassuring history and examination, so the recommended course is education, an offer of resuscitation training and discharge with follow up (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.rationale: Reflux is frequently assumed to be the cause of these events but pH studies do not establish causation, and acid suppression in infants carries risks of gastroenteritis and pneumonia without demonstrated benefit here (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

explanation.summary: Congenital hypothyroidism affects about one in 2000 to 3000 births in Australia and is the commonest preventable cause of intellectual disability, which is why it has been part of newborn screening since the 1970s. Most affected infants have no clinical signs at birth because maternal thyroxine crosses the placenta, and the classic features of prolonged jaundice, a large posterior fontanelle, hypotonia, poor feeding, constipation and an umbilical hernia appear only as that supply is exhausted. Outcome depends almost entirely on how quickly treatment starts, with normal cognitive development expected when thyroxine begins within the first two weeks of life and a measurable loss of intelligence quotient for each week of delay thereafter. Imaging with ultrasound or a radionuclide scan distinguishes agenesis, an ectopic gland and dyshormonogenesis, which matters for genetic counselling and for deciding later whether a trial off treatment at three years is worthwhile, but it must never delay the first dose.
key_points: Most affected newborns appear normal because of transplacental maternal thyroxine
Treatment within the first two weeks of life preserves normal cognitive outcome
Imaging determines the cause but must not delay starting thyroxine
Dyshormonogenesis causes hypothyroidism as severe as glandular agenesis
Prolonged jaundice and a large posterior fontanelle are late clinical clues
explanation.pearls: The Australian starting dose is thyroxine 10 to 15 micrograms per kilogram daily, aiming to normalise the free thyroxine within two weeks, and the tablet is crushed in a small volume of water or breast milk rather than mixed into a full feed that the infant may not finish.

options.rationale: Every day of untreated hypothyroidism in the newborn period costs cognitive outcome, and imaging is not required to make the biochemical diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

A repeat is appropriate for a borderline screening result with normal free thyroxine, and this infant already has unequivocal biochemical and clinical hypothyroidism (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

Treatment is determined by the biochemistry rather than the anatomy, since dyshormonogenesis with a normally sited gland causes hypothyroidism just as severe as agenesis (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

Endocrine involvement is appropriate but a four week wait squanders the window in which treatment preserves cognitive outcome, which closes at around two weeks of age (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

A markedly raised thyroid stimulating hormone with a low free thyroxine confirms congenital hypothyroidism, and thyroxine is started the same day while imaging to determine the underlying cause proceeds without delaying treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism; Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).

explanation.summary: Newborns at risk of hypoglycaemia include infants of diabetic mothers, those who are large or small for gestational age, preterm infants and those who are unwell, and these babies are screened with pre feed glucose measurements in the first 24 hours. The Australian operational threshold is 2.6 mmol/L, chosen because it is the level below which neurophysiological changes have been demonstrated rather than because symptoms appear there. Dextrose gel changed practice because it treats effectively without separating mother and baby, and it is given at 0.5 mL per kilogram rubbed into the buccal mucosa, followed immediately by a feed and a repeat glucose 30 minutes later. Failure to respond after two doses, symptoms, or a very low reading move the infant onto the intravenous pathway, and hypoglycaemia persisting beyond 48 to 72 hours prompts investigation for hyperinsulinism or an endocrine cause.
key_points: The Australian operational threshold for newborn hypoglycaemia is 2.6 mmol/L
Dextrose gel 0.5 mL per kilogram buccally plus a feed is first line
Recheck the glucose 30 minutes after the gel is given
Intravenous glucose is for symptomatic infants or failure of gel and feeds
Hypoglycaemia persisting past 48 to 72 hours needs endocrine investigation
explanation.pearls: When hypoglycaemia persists beyond 72 hours, take a critical sample at the time of a low glucose for insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones and free fatty acids, because the diagnosis of hyperinsulinism depends on measuring insulin while the glucose is actually low.

options.rationale: Buccal dextrose gel with a feed is first line for asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in an at risk newborn, reduces admission to special care and does not interfere with establishing breastfeeding (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

An intravenous bolus is reserved for a symptomatic infant or one with a blood glucose below about 1.5 mmol/L, and it separates a well baby from his mother unnecessarily (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

Feeding alone raises the glucose more slowly than gel plus a feed, and introducing a bottle at two hours of age undermines breastfeeding when an equally effective option exists (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

A confirmed value below 2.6 mmol/L in an at risk infant requires treatment rather than observation, because neuroglycopenic injury can occur before clinical signs appear (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

Nursery admission with an infusion is for persistent or symptomatic hypoglycaemia that has not responded to gel and feeds, and it is not the first step in a well feeding baby (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy typically begins between four and ten years of age in a developmentally normal child and is defined by frequent brief staring episodes without postictal confusion, accompanied by generalised 3 Hz spike and wave activity. Hyperventilation for two to three minutes provokes an event in the great majority of untreated children, which makes it the single most useful bedside test and is often achieved by asking the child to blow a windmill or a tissue. The differential is inattention or daydreaming, which is not interruptible in the same way and does not stop mid activity, and focal impaired awareness seizures, which have an aura, automatisms and postictal drowsiness. Prognosis is good with around two thirds achieving remission by adolescence, though attentional difficulties can persist and warrant follow up even after seizures stop.
key_points: Hyperventilation provokes an absence in most untreated children
There is no aura and no postictal confusion in typical absence seizures
Carbamazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin and vigabatrin aggravate absence seizures
Neuroimaging is not needed when syndrome and electroencephalogram are typical
Attentional difficulties can persist after seizure remission
explanation.pearls: In the randomised comparison of the three first line agents, ethosuximide and valproate both achieved around 45 per cent freedom from failure at 12 months against 21 per cent for lamotrigine, and ethosuximide caused less attentional impairment than valproate.

options.rationale: Carbamazepine aggravates absence seizures and can precipitate absence status, making it a specifically contraindicated choice in generalised epilepsies (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

Ethosuximide is first line for childhood absence epilepsy, with a comparative trial showing equal seizure freedom to valproate but less attentional impairment and fewer adverse effects (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).
Levetiracetam is markedly less effective for typical absence seizures than ethosuximide or valproate and is not a first line choice in this syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

Lamotrigine is effective in generalised epilepsy but requires slow titration over weeks and achieved lower seizure freedom rates than ethosuximide in the comparative trial (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

Neuroimaging is not required when the clinical syndrome and electroencephalogram are typical, and is reserved for focal features, developmental regression or an abnormal examination (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).

explanation.summary: Around 3 per cent of term boys have an undescended testis at birth and most descend spontaneously by three months of corrected age, after which further descent is very unlikely. The main clinical task is distinguishing a true undescended testis from a retractile one, which can be brought into the scrotum and stays there until the cremasteric reflex fires again, and which needs annual review rather than surgery. Orchidopexy is recommended between six and twelve months of age because the germ cell population deteriorates from the second year, and earlier surgery is associated with better fertility outcomes and a lower risk of malignancy. Surgery does not abolish the increased risk of testicular cancer but does make the testis examinable, which is why these boys are taught testicular self examination from adolescence.
key_points: Spontaneous descent is very unlikely after six months of corrected age
A retractile testis stays in the scrotum once brought there and needs review only
Orchidopexy is recommended between six and twelve months of age
Ultrasound does not help for either a palpable or an impalpable testis
Bilateral impalpable testes or associated hypospadias warrant endocrine assessment
explanation.pearls: Examine for an undescended testis with warm hands and the child relaxed, sweeping from the anterior superior iliac spine along the inguinal canal towards the scrotum, because a cold room or a cold hand triggers the cremasteric reflex and turns a normal testis into an apparently undescended one.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Spontaneous descent essentially never occurs after six months of corrected age, so further waiting only delays surgery past the recommended window (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

Imaging adds nothing when the testis is already palpable, and ultrasound has poor sensitivity for a truly impalpable testis so it does not change management either way (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

A testis that has never been in the scrotum and cannot be brought there requires orchidopexy, ideally completed between six and twelve months of age, so at 14 months referral should be immediate (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).
Hormonal treatment has low success rates, a high relapse rate and is not used in Australian practice for an isolated unilateral undescended testis (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

Endocrine and genetic assessment is indicated for bilateral impalpable testes or for hypospadias with an undescended testis, because those combinations raise the possibility of a difference of sex development, and neither applies here (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

explanation.summary: Nocturnal enuresis affects around 15 per cent of 5-year-olds and resolves spontaneously in about 15 per cent of affected children each year, so treatment is offered when the child is bothered rather than at a fixed age. The first step is separating monosymptomatic enuresis from enuresis with daytime symptoms, since the latter points to bladder dysfunction and needs a different approach, and the second is excluding and treating constipation, which is the commonest reversible contributor. Urinalysis is done once to exclude diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus and urinary infection, and further imaging is not required in a child with a normal examination. Alarm therapy works by conditioning and takes several weeks to have effect, so families need to be told at the outset to persist for at least six weeks and to continue until 14 consecutive dry nights are achieved.
key_points: Separate monosymptomatic enuresis from enuresis with daytime symptoms
Exclude and treat constipation before starting specific treatment
Urinalysis is the only routine investigation needed
Alarm therapy is first line and has the lowest relapse rate
Desmopressin is useful for short term cover such as camps and sleepovers
explanation.pearls: Continue alarm therapy until the child has achieved 14 consecutive dry nights, usually around eight to twelve weeks in total, because stopping at the first run of dry nights is the commonest cause of relapse.

options.rationale: Desmopressin works quickly but relapse on stopping is common, so it is chosen for short term cover such as a camp or when alarm therapy is not feasible rather than as first line (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).
Evening fluid restriction alone has not been shown to cure enuresis and can lead to daytime under drinking with reduced functional bladder capacity (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).
Anticholinergics are for overactive bladder with daytime urgency and frequency, and this boy has no daytime symptoms at all (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

Alarm therapy is first line for primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a motivated child over six years with engaged parents, achieving lasting dryness in around two thirds with a much lower relapse rate than drug treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).
Tricyclic antidepressants are a last resort for refractory enuresis because of cardiotoxicity in overdose and a high relapse rate on cessation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulin A vasculitis is the commonest vasculitis of childhood and is diagnosed clinically on palpable purpura in a gravity dependent distribution with at least one of arthritis or arthralgia, abdominal pain, renal involvement or a compatible biopsy. A normal platelet count and normal coagulation are what separate it from thrombocytopenic and coagulopathic causes of purpura, and they should be checked in every child. The rash and joint symptoms settle over weeks, but renal involvement is the determinant of long term outcome and is the reason these children need structured follow up rather than simple discharge. Intussusception is the other complication to warn parents about, since it is typically ileoileal in this condition and may not be visible on the ultrasound views used for the usual ileocolic form.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical, with palpable purpura in a gravity dependent distribution
Normal platelets and coagulation separate it from other causes of purpura
Nephritis develops in about a third and almost always within six months
Corticosteroids treat severe abdominal pain but do not prevent nephritis
Warn parents about intussusception, which is usually ileoileal in this condition
explanation.pearls: Continue urinalysis and blood pressure surveillance for at least six months after the rash resolves, because late nephritis presenting after the first month accounts for a substantial minority of cases and is entirely asymptomatic until proteinuria is heavy.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are used for severe abdominal pain or orchitis and do not prevent or treat the renal involvement, so they are not given for isolated haematuria (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

Biopsy is indicated for nephrotic range proteinuria, impaired renal function or a rapidly progressive course, none of which is present with isolated microscopic haematuria (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

Angiotensin blockade is used for established persistent proteinuria rather than for haematuria alone, and starting it now would treat a complication that has not developed (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

Renal involvement can appear weeks after the rash has faded and is silent until it is advanced, so discharge without surveillance is the error that allows nephritis to be missed (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

Australian practice is weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first month, then at decreasing frequency for six to twelve months, because nephritis develops in around a third of children and almost always within the first six months (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

explanation.summary: Cow milk protein allergy in infancy divides into immunoglobulin E mediated disease, which produces urticaria, vomiting or anaphylaxis within minutes to two hours, and non immunoglobulin E mediated disease, which produces delayed gastrointestinal symptoms over hours to days and is not detectable by skin prick or specific immunoglobulin E testing. Allergic proctocolitis is the mildest form of the delayed group and characteristically occurs in a well grown, contented breastfed infant, which is why the visible blood alarms parents far more than it alarms the clinician. Diagnosis rests on resolution during exclusion and recurrence on reintroduction, and formal reintroduction after a period of exclusion is a necessary part of the process rather than an optional extra. Most infants tolerate cow milk by 12 months and almost all by three years.
key_points: A thriving, systemically well infant with blood and mucus in the stool most often has allergic proctocolitis.
Maternal dietary exclusion for two to four weeks allows breastfeeding to continue.
Skin prick and specific immunoglobulin E testing are unhelpful in the delayed non immunoglobulin E mediated forms.
Planned reintroduction confirms the diagnosis and prevents unnecessary long term exclusion.
Faltering growth, systemic illness or failure to respond changes the pathway to specialist investigation.
explanation.pearls: Mothers on strict dairy exclusion need 1000 mg of elemental calcium daily plus vitamin D, because the exclusion typically runs for months and bone mineral loss during lactation is already accelerated.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines
Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.rationale: Endoscopy is reserved for infants with faltering growth, systemic illness or failure to respond to exclusion, and it would subject a thriving infant to anaesthesia for a diagnosis better made by dietary challenge (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Blood and mucus in the stool of a thriving, systemically well breastfed infant is most often a non immunoglobulin E mediated proctocolitis from maternally ingested cow milk protein, and a strict maternal exclusion trial of two to four weeks with calcium supplementation is the treatment while breastfeeding continues (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: A hydrolysed formula is the correct step for a formula fed infant with the same presentation, but stopping breastfeeding is not required and removes its protective benefit unnecessarily (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.rationale: Amino acid formula is reserved for infants who fail an extensively hydrolysed formula or who have faltering growth or severe disease, and this infant has neither (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.rationale: Acid suppression treats a different problem, does not affect colonic mucosal inflammation, and in infants is associated with increased rates of gastroenteritis and lower respiratory infection (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Dystrophinopathy is the commonest inherited muscular dystrophy of childhood and follows X linked inheritance, so a maternal uncle with unexplained wheelchair use in adolescence is a significant clue that is often not volunteered. Boys typically present between three and five years with falls, difficulty with stairs, toe walking and delayed speech, and calf pseudohypertrophy from fatty and fibrous replacement is a characteristic sign. Creatine kinase is the screening test and is usually more than ten times the upper limit of normal, after which multiplex ligation dependent probe amplification detects the deletions and duplications that account for most cases, with sequencing for the remainder. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroid therapy started before loss of ambulation prolongs walking, and because cardiac and respiratory surveillance and family genetic counselling all begin at diagnosis.
key_points: Creatine kinase is the first test and is typically more than ten times the upper limit of normal.
Genetic confirmation follows the enzyme result rather than preceding it.
Calf pseudohypertrophy with proximal weakness and preserved sensation is the classic combination.
Delayed speech accompanies the motor delay in around a third of boys.
Corticosteroid therapy, cardiac surveillance and genetic counselling all start at diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Any boy not walking independently by 18 months, or with an unexplained alanine or aspartate aminotransferase elevation on routine bloods, warrants a creatine kinase, because those transaminases come from muscle and are a common accidental route to the diagnosis.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Attributing the falls to clumsiness is the commonest reason for the average diagnostic delay of two to three years, and progressive proximal weakness with calf hypertrophy is not a normal variant (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: A tethered cord or spinal lesion can also disturb gait, but it produces sensory loss, bladder symptoms, back deformity or a midline skin marker, none of which is present (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Nutritional rickets does cause a waddling gait and proximal weakness, but it also produces bone pain, wrist widening and bowing rather than calf hypertrophy, and the family history here points elsewhere (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).

Proximal weakness with calf hypertrophy and the pattern of climbing up the legs to stand calls for creatine kinase first, because a concentration many times the upper limit is both highly sensitive and available the same day, and it directs which genetic test is sent (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Genetic analysis is the confirmatory test and follows a raised creatine kinase, since sending it first delays a same day answer and commits to one gene before the enzyme has confirmed a dystrophic process (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for the overwhelming majority of childhood constipation and commonly presents as soiling that families interpret as diarrhoea. The mechanism is retention of a large hard stool that distends the rectum, blunts the urge to defecate and allows liquid stool to leak past it, so the child is genuinely unaware of the accidents. Treatment has three phases that must run in order: disimpaction, maintenance for at least several months, and behavioural work with regular post meal toilet sitting and a reward system. Relapse is common and is nearly always due to stopping maintenance too early, so families are told at the outset that treatment continues for months after the symptoms settle.
key_points: Soiling in a constipated child is overflow around impaction, not diarrhoea.
Disimpaction with escalating oral macrogol precedes maintenance dosing.
Maintenance continues for months after symptoms settle to prevent relapse.
Regular toilet sitting after meals uses the gastrocolic reflex and is part of treatment.
Red flags for organic disease include delayed meconium, faltering growth, abnormal spine or anal position.
explanation.pearls: Delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours, a tight empty rectum on examination and ribbon stools point to Hirschsprung disease and require rectal suction biopsy, whereas a rectum loaded with soft stool and normal growth effectively excludes it.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: The loose material is liquid stool passing around a hard impacted mass rather than true diarrhoea, so an antimotility agent worsens the impaction it is being given to treat (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Plain films correlate poorly with clinical impaction and add radiation without changing management when the mass is already palpable and the history is characteristic (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Overflow soiling around a palpable faecal mass requires disimpaction with an escalating oral macrogol dose over several days before a maintenance dose is set, because starting maintenance alone leaves the impaction in place and the soiling continues (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Maintenance dosing is exactly what follows, but applied to an impacted rectum it softens stool around the mass and can transiently worsen the leakage, which is why families abandon treatment (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Oral disimpaction is as effective as rectal treatment and avoids a distressing procedure in a child who is already withholding, and phosphate enemas carry a risk of hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia in children (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis presents between about 10 and 16 years, more often in boys and strongly associated with obesity, and around a quarter are bilateral. Roughly half of affected adolescents complain only of knee or distal thigh pain, which is why every child with knee pain needs a hip examination and why the diagnosis is so often delayed. The clinical sign that is hardest to fake is obligatory external rotation as the hip is flexed, produced by the posterior and inferior displacement of the femoral head on the neck. Classification into stable and unstable turns on whether the child can weight bear with or without crutches, and this distinction drives both urgency and prognosis because avascular necrosis complicates a substantial proportion of unstable slips.
key_points: Knee pain in an adolescent requires examination of the hip in every case.
Obligatory external rotation on passive hip flexion is the characteristic sign.
Frog lateral views are needed because early displacement is posterior.
Inability to weight bear defines an unstable slip and carries a high risk of avascular necrosis.
The child is kept non weight bearing from the moment the diagnosis is suspected.
explanation.pearls: A slip occurring before the age of 10 or in a child of normal weight should prompt assessment for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, panhypopituitarism or renal osteodystrophy, because idiopathic disease outside the typical body habitus and age band is uncommon.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent with knee pain and new inability to weight bear points to the hip, and anteroposterior with frog lateral views are needed because the displacement is posterior and can be invisible on the frontal film alone (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Imaging the symptomatic joint misleads here, since hip pathology refers along the obturator nerve to the medial knee and the knee examination here is entirely normal (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Ultrasound of a joint with no effusion and full painless movement will be normal, and analgesia that allows him to keep weight bearing risks converting a stable slip into an unstable one (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Hip ultrasound detects an effusion and is useful in transient synovitis and septic arthritis, but it does not show the physeal displacement and a week of continued walking risks avascular necrosis (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Septic arthritis also causes unwillingness to weight bear, but it produces fever and raised inflammatory markers, and both are normal here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened for clinically at every infant check in Australia, with selective imaging for those who have risk factors or abnormal examination. The major risk factors are breech presentation in the third trimester, a first degree family history and female sex, and breech position carries the strongest weight. The examination findings change with age: Ortolani and Barlow tests are informative in the first eight to twelve weeks while the hip is still reducible, whereas after that a dislocated hip becomes fixed and limited abduction, leg length discrepancy and asymmetric creases take over. Late diagnosis matters because treatment escalates from a harness worn for several weeks to closed or open reduction with casting and sometimes osteotomy, and untreated dysplasia is a leading cause of hip arthritis in young adults.
key_points: Ultrasound is the imaging test under about four months; radiograph is used from four to six months onward.
Ortolani and Barlow tests become negative once the hip is fixed rather than reducible.
Limited abduction, leg length discrepancy and asymmetric creases are the older infant signs.
Breech presentation, female sex and a first degree family history are the major risk factors.
Harness treatment success falls sharply after six months of age.
explanation.pearls: A normal newborn hip examination does not exclude the condition, because up to a fifth of cases develop after the neonatal period, which is why abduction is checked at every infant health check rather than only at birth.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Ultrasound is the correct modality under about four months of age, but at five months the ossified femoral head shadows the acetabulum and the study becomes unreliable (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Harness treatment is applied by the orthopaedic team after imaging confirms the diagnosis, and its success rate falls sharply beyond six months of age, so it is not started blind in primary care (Source: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons).

Delay to 12 months forfeits the window in which non operative treatment works and makes open reduction with femoral or pelvic osteotomy far more likely (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is used after reduction to confirm concentric position within a spica cast, not as the first line diagnostic study, and it requires sedation for no additional diagnostic yield here (Source: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons).

Beyond about four to six months the femoral head ossific nucleus appears and blocks the acoustic window, so ultrasound loses reliability and the plain radiograph becomes the investigation of choice, with limited abduction now the most useful clinical sign since the provocative tests become negative once the hip is fixed (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Abnormal head shape in infancy is overwhelmingly positional and has become much more common since supine sleeping was recommended, but a small proportion reflects premature fusion of a cranial suture and that group needs surgery. The two are separated at the bedside rather than radiologically: positional flattening produces a parallelogram with the ear and forehead pushed forward on the flattened side, while lambdoid fusion produces a trapezoid with the ear pulled back and down and bossing of the opposite forehead. A palpable ridge over the suture and a bulge behind the ear are additional pointers to fusion. Sagittal fusion is the commonest single suture form and produces a long narrow head, while fusion of multiple sutures raises intracranial pressure and threatens vision and development.
key_points: Positional flattening gives a parallelogram with the ipsilateral ear and forehead pushed forwards.
Lambdoid fusion gives a trapezoid with the ipsilateral ear pulled backwards and downwards.
Contralateral frontal bossing and a mastoid bulge point to fusion rather than moulding.
A palpable ridge along a suture line is an important physical sign.
Referral is time critical because early surgery gives the best result.
explanation.pearls: Head circumference crossing centiles downwards, a bulging fontanelle or new developmental regression suggest multiple suture involvement with raised intracranial pressure, and that combination warrants same day rather than routine specialist referral.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Helmet therapy remodels a skull whose sutures are open and cannot correct a fused suture, so it would waste the months in which surgical correction gives the best cosmetic and functional result (Source: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons).

Congenital muscular torticollis commonly underlies positional flattening and responds to stretching, but his neck rotates fully in both directions so there is no restriction to treat (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Plain films are insensitive for partial fusion and normal images would falsely reassure, so imaging decisions belong to the craniofacial team who use low dose computed tomography with three dimensional reconstruction (Source: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons).

A palpable sutural ridge with the ear displaced posteriorly, bossing on the opposite forehead and a mastoid bulge gives the trapezoid head shape of a fused suture rather than the parallelogram of positional moulding, and this requires craniofacial assessment because surgical correction is time critical (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Repositioning is the correct treatment for positional plagiocephaly, but that condition pushes the ear forwards on the flattened side and produces bossing of the forehead on the same side rather than the opposite one (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines
